papers.title: Toward a Robust Crowd-labeling Framework using Expert Evaluation and Pairwise Comparison
papers.abstract: Crowd-labeling emerged from the need to label large-scale and complex data, a tedious, expensive, and time-consuming task. One of the main challenges in the crowd-labeling task is to control for or determine in advance the proportion of low-quality/malicious labelers. If that proportion grows too high, there is often a phase transition leading to a steep, non-linear drop in labeling accuracy as noted by Karger et al. [2014]. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework called Expert Label Injected Crowd Estimation (ELICE) and extend it to different versions and variants that delay phase transition leading to a better labeling accuracy. ELICE automatically combines and boosts bulk crowd labels supported by labels from experts for limited number of instances from the dataset. The expert-labels help to estimate the individual ability of crowd labelers and difficulty of each instance, both of which are used to aggregate the labels. Empirical evaluation shows the superiority of ELICE as compared to other state-of-the-art methods. We also derive a lower bound on the number of expert-labeled instances needed to estimate the crowd ability and dataset difficulty as well as to get better quality labels.
papers.summary: Crowd-labeling works only while the share of low-quality or malicious labelers stays small. Past a certain proportion, labeling accuracy can drop sharply in a phase transition. The authors propose `ELICE` (Expert Label Injected Crowd Estimation), which uses expert labels on a small number of instances to estimate each crowd labeler's ability and each instance's difficulty, then uses both estimates to aggregate the bulk crowd labels. Several variants of the framework **delay the phase transition and give better labeling accuracy** than state-of-the-art aggregation methods, and the authors derive a lower bound on how many expert-labeled instances are needed.

papers.title: LLM-Enhanced Self-Evolving Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Step E-Commerce Payment Fraud Risk Detection
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to e-commerce payment fraud detection by integrating reinforcement learning (RL) with Large Language Models (LLMs). By framing transaction risk as a multi-step Markov Decision Process (MDP), RL optimizes risk detection across multiple payment stages. Crafting effective reward functions, essential for RL model success, typically requires significant human expertise due to the complexity and variability in design. LLMs, with their advanced reasoning and coding capabilities, are well-suited to refine these functions, offering improvements over traditional methods. Our approach leverages LLMs to iteratively enhance reward functions, achieving better fraud detection accuracy and demonstrating zero-shot capability. Experiments with real-world data confirm the effectiveness, robustness, and resilience of our LLM-enhanced RL framework through long-term evaluations, underscoring the potential of LLMs in advancing industrial RL applications.
papers.summary: E-commerce payment fraud detection is framed as a multi-step Markov Decision Process (MDP), in which a reinforcement learning (RL) agent assesses transaction risk across several payment stages. Designing good reward functions for such agents usually takes significant human expertise, so the authors use large language models (LLMs) to iteratively write and refine the reward functions. Experiments on real-world transaction data report **better fraud detection accuracy than traditional reward design**, along with zero-shot capability and robustness over long-term evaluations.

papers.title: On Seeding Watermarks to Detect Verbatim LLM Copy-Paste Responses
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made fluent essay writing, code drafting, and quiz answering instantly available to students at every level, from secondary school through graduate study. Many educators do not object to LLM use \emph{per~se}; what they need to detect is the case in which a student pastes the assignment prompt into a chatbot and submits the model's reply verbatim, without engaging with the work. Existing post-hoc AI-text detectors remain unreliable and have been shown to penalise non-native English writers, while output-side watermarks require cooperation from the model provider. We propose an alternative that the educator controls directly: an input-side watermark in which an invisible instruction is embedded inside the visible assignment prompt itself. An LLM that ingests the prompt verbatim quietly reads the hidden instruction and writes a tell-tale signature into its reply, exposing the copy-and-paste pathway specifically. We describe SteganoPrompt, a single-page, zero-dependency web tool that encodes an arbitrary printable-ASCII payload into the deprecated Unicode Tags block (\texttt{U+E0000}--\texttt{U+E007F}). The encoded string is visually identical to the original, survives common copy-paste channels (Word, Google Docs, PDF, Markdown, Slack, e-mail, the major learning-management systems), and is tokenized as ordinary text by most frontier models. We evaluate compliance across eight LLM families and a representative set of educational content channels. To keep deployment transparent, disclosure is built into the tool itself: every encoded brief also carries a brief, always-on academic-integrity reminder for the student, and we set out concrete guidance recommending for its disclosed, ethical use in the classroom. The tool is released under the MIT licence at https://ezharjan.github.io/SteganoPrompt/.
papers.summary: Educators often want to catch one specific behavior: a student pasting an assignment prompt into a chatbot and submitting the reply verbatim. Post-hoc AI-text detectors are unreliable for this and penalize non-native writers. The proposed fix is an input-side watermark: `SteganoPrompt` hides an instruction inside the visible assignment text using the deprecated Unicode Tags block, so an LLM that reads the pasted prompt writes a tell-tale signature into its answer. The hidden text **survives common copy-paste channels** such as Word, Google Docs, PDF, Slack, and the major learning-management systems. The authors test compliance across eight LLM families, and the tool always includes a disclosed academic-integrity reminder.

papers.title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
papers.abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code.
papers.summary: The authors audit whether six widely deployed LLMs give the same smoking-cessation advice to different users. They pose four questions to twelve personas, for 2,880 responses in total. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications to teen personas **32 to 67 percentage points less often** than to adult personas, and in five of six models a persona claiming healthcare expertise received fewer facts. A short system prompt that sets a 'factual floor' of core facts narrowed persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varied in size and direction, so a prompt validated on one model cannot be assumed to work on another.

papers.title: FasterRW: An Efficient Prior-Assisted Random Walk Solver for Thermal Analysis
papers.abstract: Thermal simulation is becoming increasingly critical in modern IC design and manufacturing. Feynman--Kac random walk methods can estimate localized temperatures without solving the global field, but in practical settings without Dirichlet boundaries they require very long paths to control the truncation residual. This paper presents FasterRW, a continuation-value framework for accelerating Feynman--Kac thermal random walks. We prove a stopping-time residual identity showing that the expected tail after truncation equals the current attenuation weight multiplied by the temperature at the stopping location. This identity enables a prior-corrected single-point estimator: a cheap, noisy prior replaces the unknown continuation value, making the truncation bias scale with prior error rather than absolute temperature and yielding an error-controlled threshold-selection rule. For multi-point queries, FasterRW further converts cross-query pass-through tails into pseudo-samples and refines the resulting observations in prior-error coordinates through kriging. Compared with prior state-of-the-art methods, FasterRW achieves up to $28\times$ acceleration while maintaining accuracy. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/ShiningSord/FastRW.
papers.summary: Feynman–Kac random walk methods can estimate local temperatures in integrated-circuit thermal simulation without solving the whole temperature field, but without Dirichlet boundaries they need very long paths. `FasterRW` proves an identity showing that the expected tail after truncating a walk equals its current attenuation weight times the temperature at the stopping point. This lets a cheap, noisy prior estimate stand in for the unknown remainder, so truncation bias scales with the prior's error rather than with the absolute temperature. For multi-point queries, it reuses walks that pass through other query points and refines the results with kriging, reaching **up to 28× speedup** at the same accuracy.

papers.title: Embedding Consistent Recurrent Neural Networks in Finite Element Simulations for Path-Dependent Damage Prediction
papers.abstract: Capturing sheet-metal localisation physics with a trained surrogate inside a finite element (FEM) solver requires the surrogate to deliver consistent predictions irrespective of the solver's strain-increment count, which is difficult to control in non-linear explicit codes. We address this by re-implementing a trained recurrent neural network (RNN) damage criterion in Fortran and embed it as a live, increment-by-increment fracture criterion inside an Abaqus/Explicit user material subroutine (VUMAT), advancing the network state alongside the solver. Two architectures are compared: a SimpleRNN and the proposed Consistent RNN (ConsRNN), whose transition function is designed so that predictions converge as the strain path is refined rather than drifting with the increment count. Both are trained on bilinear strain paths and evaluated under varying temporal discretisations and nonlinear histories. SimpleRNN predictions drift as the increment count increases, which disqualifies it for embedding; ConsRNN converges under refinement, at a substantial fixed-resolution accuracy cost relative to SimpleRNN on multilinear paths. Deployed at structural scale, the embedded ConsRNN surrogate governs element deletion in a clamped steel plate and reaches the same peak force and peak displacement as an established two-parameter fracture criterion. This pre-peak agreement is expected by construction, since no element is deleted before the peak and the two runs therefore share an identical constitutive path; the responses diverge only on the post-peak softening branch. The results establish discretisation consistency as the decisive property for embedding recurrent surrogates in explicit FEM solvers, and report the first embedding of a customised, non-standard-transition recurrent cell at structural scale.
papers.summary: A trained surrogate model embedded in an explicit finite element (FEM) solver has to give consistent predictions no matter how many strain increments the solver takes. The authors port a recurrent neural network (RNN) damage criterion to Fortran and run it increment by increment inside an Abaqus/Explicit user material subroutine (`VUMAT`). They compare a standard `SimpleRNN` with a proposed `ConsRNN`, whose transition function is designed to converge as the strain path is refined. `SimpleRNN` predictions drift as the increment count grows, while **`ConsRNN` converges under refinement**, at some cost in fixed-resolution accuracy. At structural scale, `ConsRNN` matches an established fracture criterion's peak force on a clamped steel plate.

papers.title: Rethinking Data Selection as Distribution Matching on Semantic Manifolds
papers.abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.
papers.summary: Data selection for instruction tuning usually optimizes for diversity or sample importance, without requiring the chosen subset to match the full dataset's distribution in embedding space. `QMAC` treats selection as a joint problem of matching the subset's empirical characteristic functions to the full data's across multiple frequency scales, while filtering noisy samples with task-related quality scores. Across 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks, it beats existing selection baselines on image-text instruction data and **in several model-and-budget combinations exceeds training on the full dataset**.

papers.title: Improving Contextual Retrieval for Long Documents using Semantic Chunking and Hybrid Retrieval Strategies
papers.abstract: The vast amount of information available in lengthy, distributed documents makes finding relevant answers difficult, especially when the answer requires connecting evidence from multiple sources. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often struggle with this type of "multi-hop" reasoning and frequently face issues with context fragmentation. In this paper, we propose a hybrid RAG framework that integrates the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs with the broad semantic coverage of dense vector retrieval. Our approach employs a multi-stage pipeline using transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to improve context retention. We construct a dynamic knowledge graph to capture explicit relationships between entities while simultaneously maintaining a dense vector index. During inference, the system uses a hierarchical mechanism that prioritizes graph traversal for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when necessary. We evaluated our framework on the MultiHop-RAG dataset. The results show that this hybrid approach outperforms standalone vector and graph-based baselines, achieving higher Exact Match scores and improved retrieval accuracy for complex queries. This confirms that merging structured reasoning with standard vector retrieval creates a more robust system for handling complex knowledge-intensive questions.
papers.summary: Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) struggles with multi-hop questions whose evidence is spread across long documents. The proposed hybrid pipeline uses transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking, then builds both a dynamic knowledge graph of entity relationships and a dense vector index. At query time it traverses the graph first for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when needed. On the `MultiHop-RAG` dataset, it **achieves higher Exact Match scores** and better retrieval accuracy than vector-only and graph-only baselines.

papers.title: Generative Reconstruction of Full-Field Sensor States for Safety-Critical Digital Twins
papers.abstract: Accurate reconstruction of incomplete sensor fields is critical for state awareness in safety-critical digital twins (DTs). Thermocouples in high-temperature and radiation environments may drift, fail, or become intermittently unavailable, causing partial observability. This study develops a sparse-sensor reconstruction framework for Oregon State University's High Temperature Test Facility (HTTF) and evaluates six methods under intra- and inter-experiment protocols: three conditional generative models (i.e., a diffusion model [DM], variational autoencoder [VAE], and generative adversarial network [GAN]), two deterministic recurrent neural-network models, and ridge regression. For intra-experiment reconstruction within the PG{-}29 depressurized conduction cooldown (DCC) test, the models combine graph-based spatial encoding with gated recurrent units. The graph neural network (GNN)--gated recurrent unit (GRU) VAE achieves the lowest error, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of $11.73,^\circ$C, a root mean square error (RMSE) of $20.54,^\circ$C, and an $R^2$ of 0.98. The deterministic GNN--GRU and plain GRU obtain RMSE values of $25.26,^\circ$C and $35.22,^\circ$C, respectively, demonstrating the benefit of spatial modeling. All three generative models reduce RMSE by more than half compared with ridge regression. The DM maintains an $R^2$ of 0.94 when known sensors decrease from 91 to 45. For inter-experiment reconstruction, models trained on PG{-}27 pressurized conduction cooldown (PCC) are evaluated on PG{-}29 using section-context conditioning. The section-context DM achieves the best transfer performance, with an RMSE of $42.84,^\circ$C and an $R^2$ of 0.91. These results demonstrate the value of spatiotemporal generative modeling for missing-sensor reconstruction in safety-critical DT applications.
papers.summary: Digital twins of nuclear test facilities lose visibility when thermocouples drift or fail, so missing sensor readings have to be reconstructed. Using data from Oregon State University's High Temperature Test Facility (`HTTF`), the authors compare a diffusion model, a variational autoencoder (VAE), a generative adversarial network (GAN), two recurrent models, and ridge regression. Within a single experiment, a graph neural network–gated recurrent unit (GNN–GRU) VAE does best, with **an R² of 0.98**, and the diffusion model keeps an R² of 0.94 even when only half the sensors are available. Across experiments, a diffusion model conditioned on section context transfers best, with an R² of 0.91.

papers.title: Adaptive Depth Aggregation in Graph Transformers for Long-Range Graph Reasoning
papers.abstract: Graph Transformers improve long-range node-to-node communication through global or structure-aware interactions. However, improving cross-node communication does not determine how computations produced at different depths should be combined. Standard residual streams accumulate successive computations with fixed unit coefficients shared across nodes. This fixed aggregation is a residual-interface constraint: once intermediate contributions have been produced, the interface cannot explicitly reweight them by node. We hypothesize that this constraint can create a depth-wise aggregation mismatch when the relative utility of these intermediate contributions varies across nodes and structural contexts. To study this hypothesis, we formalize Graph Transformer residual computation as a causal node-wise history of graph-propagation and feed-forward network (FFN) contributions, making depth aggregation an explicit interface choice. We realize node-adaptive aggregation over this history with Attention Residuals (AttnRes) while preserving the backbone's graph-propagation and auxiliary-state machinery. Block AttnRes reduces the routing cost of long histories relative to Full AttnRes by pooling consecutive contributions. We instantiate the interface in GPS and GRIT and evaluate it on all five ECHO tasks. Both variants achieve lower mean absolute error (MAE) than their independently tuned backbones on every task, and at least one obtains the lowest mean among all compared methods in each task. Routing-only donor-swap interventions support the mismatch hypothesis, while additional ablations examine the key design choices. Together, these results support node-adaptive depth aggregation as a useful complement to cross-node communication in long-range graph reasoning.
papers.summary: In Graph Transformers, residual streams add each layer's output with fixed, equal weights for every node, so the model cannot weight the output of different depths differently for different nodes. The authors recast residual computation as a per-node history of graph-propagation and feed-forward contributions, and apply Attention Residuals (`AttnRes`) to aggregate that history adaptively for each node. A pooled `Block AttnRes` variant reduces cost for long histories. Added to `GPS` and `GRIT`, both variants **achieve lower mean absolute error than their tuned backbones on all five `ECHO` long-range tasks**, and intervention experiments support the hypothesis that fixed aggregation is a real bottleneck.

papers.title: Electoral Intelligence: A Neural Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Model for Forecasting Swedish Municipal Elections
papers.abstract: Forecasting local elections is difficult because electoral competition is geographically heterogeneous, highly overdispersed, and characterized by many party-municipality combinations with little or no electoral activity. This article develops a bounded neural zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model for forecasting party-level vote counts in Swedish municipal elections. The model combines a count component for expected votes, a zero-inflation component for structural electoral absence, municipality-specific dispersion, and learned embeddings capturing latent party, municipality, and party-municipality structure. Model training relies on data from the 2014, 2018, and 2022 Swedish municipal elections and performance is evaluated on a held-out set of municipalities. Testing results show strong predictive accuracy in both vote counts and vote shares. Explanatory diagnostics indicate that latent party structure, local party-municipality relationships, electoral persistence, organizational capacity, and candidate-electorate representational similarity are among the most important determinants of predictive performance. Following model evaluation and diagnostics, the selected specification is refit on all historical data and applied to generate forecasts for the 2026 municipal elections. The proposed framework provides a flexible approach for studying local electoral competition in multiparty systems characterized by heterogeneous party presence and substantial geographic variation.
papers.summary: Party-level vote counts in local elections are highly overdispersed and include many party–municipality pairs with no activity at all. The authors build a bounded neural zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model that combines a vote-count component, a component for structural absence of a party, municipality-specific dispersion, and learned party and municipality embeddings. Trained on Swedish municipal elections from 2014–2022, it shows **strong predictive accuracy on held-out municipalities**, and it is then used to forecast the 2026 elections.

papers.title: Emergent Low-Dimensional Topological Dynamics Dictate Generalization and Escape Mechanics in Billion-Parameter Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The remarkable generalization of modern over-parameterized neural networks defies classical statistical learning bounds. Here we establish that optimization trajectories in billion-parameter models do not sample the ambient dimension $\mathbb{R}^N$ homogeneously; instead, they are dynamically constrained to a low-dimensional execution submanifold $\mathcal{M}_{\text{exec}}$ (with empirically observed effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}} \le 12$). By equipping the parameter space with a regularized Hessian metric $g_{ij} = \nabla_i \nabla_j L + \epsilon \delta_{ij}$ and analyzing stochastic Langevin diffusion on loss sublevel sets, we derive a rigorous Topological Generalization Bound grounded in projected subspace persistent homology. Furthermore, by linking Morse index transitions to Betti number annihilation ($\beta_1 \to 0$), we formulate an exact mathematical mechanism for exponential escape from strict saddles under anisotropic noise. We validate our framework across 80+ architectures (ResNets, Vision Transformers, and 7B LLMs). To bridge theoretical topology with computational feasibility, we resolve the curse of dimensionality by computing projected persistent homology proxies via randomized Lanczos iterations restricted strictly within active Hessian subspaces. Building upon this mathematical foundation, we introduce Topological-Adaptive Optimization (Top-SGD and Top-AdamW)---a family of wrapper algorithms that dynamically modulate learning rates using active curvature signatures. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate a 14.1\% reduction in total wall-clock training time on ImageNet with all computational and memory overheads fully accounted for. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/imslab-research/Topological-SGD.
papers.summary: The authors argue that training trajectories in very large neural networks stay on a low-dimensional submanifold, with an observed effective dimension of at most 12. They use this to derive a topological generalization bound based on persistent homology, along with a mechanism for escaping saddle points under anisotropic noise. They validate the framework across more than 80 architectures, including ResNets, Vision Transformers, and 7B-parameter LLMs, using randomized Lanczos approximations to keep the computation tractable. The resulting curvature-aware optimizer wrappers, `Top-SGD` and `Top-AdamW`, report a **14.1% reduction in total wall-clock training time on `ImageNet`**.

papers.title: Relic and Gumi: Governing Memory, Safety, and Continuity in Diegetic Relational Agents
papers.abstract:
Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say.
  We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system.
  We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.
papers.summary: Long-running companion agents need memory to stay continuous, but remembering can become intrusive, manipulative, or opaque. `Relic` is a governance architecture that separates what the system observes, what researchers review, what the agent remembers, and what it says. It is used to initialize and govern `Gumi`, a companion agent for one specific person. Key mechanisms are safety signals stored as researcher-facing objects rather than as agent memories, a **Shared Continuity Memory built around wording the user has confirmed and explicit recall permissions**, and a runtime layer that mediates delivery. A two-person exploratory pilot offers only descriptive observations and makes no claims about efficacy or safety.

papers.title: Drift-admissibility via Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: We introduce structure-aware optimal transport diagnostics for assessing whether empirical time-series dynamics are compatible with a prescribed predictable-drift class. Our approach translates a pathwise property of stochastic processes into a finite-dimensional projection problem over empirical transition laws, encoding admissibility as row-wise moment constraints on local couplings and quantifying deviations via a Kullback--Leibler projection gap $G_{\lambda,k}$. This yields both a principled diagnostic and a scalable Bregman--Dykstra algorithm that retains the efficiency of Sinkhorn-type methods while incorporating structural constraints. Calibrated against a Brownian reference null, $G_{\lambda,k}$ separates process classes that are indistinguishable by second-order statistics alone---including fractional Brownian motion and BSS processes sharing identical Hurst indices---without asymptotic resampling or continuous-time recovery. This positions the method as a general tool for structure-aware model validation of sequential data.
papers.summary: The authors develop optimal transport diagnostics to test whether observed time-series dynamics are consistent with a given class of predictable drift. Admissibility becomes row-wise moment constraints on local couplings between empirical transition laws, and deviation is measured by a Kullback–Leibler projection gap computed with a Sinkhorn-style `Bregman–Dykstra` algorithm. Calibrated against Brownian motion, the gap **separates process classes that second-order statistics cannot tell apart**, such as fractional Brownian motion and BSS processes with identical Hurst indices.

papers.title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
papers.abstract:
How much of a neural population's measured dimensionality is the code, and how much is the act of measuring it? The slope of the participation ratio against subsample size is reported for cortical populations and for the layers of language models as a number that belongs to the system. It does not. One patch of eleven thousand mouse V1 neurons returns three slopes, 0.25 along random stimulus subsets, 0.31 along drift direction, 0.35 along neuron count, and only the middle one carries structure; the other two are the sampling floor.
  We split every exponent into that floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and read the shift against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance. On V1 the direction-aligned shift clears the label null in eight of eight grating recordings, is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory, and reads both sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry. The even sector sets how the ladder starts: it decides which order of adding classes climbs faster, predicts the opposite order in an equivariant network, and flows under coarse-graining by a closed-form factor that says what orientation columns do to mesoscale signals. The odd sector, carried by the direction-selective neurons, keeps the ladder climbing past half the classes. On language models the same split separates content inherited from the tokens from construction built with depth, on five architectures, and the second null shows that a grammaticality signal of twenty standard deviations is entirely carrier composition. With a floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling is an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it resolves the sector content of the code. The instrument, rung, trains no probe and reads any array or any Hugging Face model layer by layer (https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom).
papers.summary: How fast a neural population's measured dimensionality (its participation ratio) grows with sample size is usually reported as a property of the system. The authors show it depends heavily on how you subsample: **one patch of mouse V1 neurons yields three different slopes depending on the subsampling axis**, and only one reflects real structure. They split each exponent into a sampling floor plus a shift along a declared axis, test the shift against two permutation nulls, and use it to read out the symmetry structure of the visual code. Applied to five language model architectures, the same method shows that a 20-standard-deviation grammaticality signal comes entirely from token composition. The accompanying tool, `rung`, trains no probe.

papers.title: Does Country Matter? Evaluating Geographic Sensitivity of Large Language Models in Zero-Shot Chronic Kidney Disease Screening
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show strong zero-shot reasoning capabilities, yet their sensitivity to prompt context raises questions about reliability in deployment. This study investigates whether geographic context embedded in prompts influences LLM-based chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening, independent of any change in patient features. Using a community-based CKD dataset from Bangladesh (284 participants with 112 CKD and 172 non-CKD), we systematically varied the country attribute across 25 global contexts while holding all clinical inputs constant, and evaluated two open-weight LLMs (Qwen3 8B and Mistral 7B). Experiments were conducted on a common-correct subset of 156 participants for whom both models produced correct baseline predictions. Results show that non-CKD predictions were highly stable across geographic contexts, with both models maintaining consistent non-CKD predictions in nearly all settings. In contrast, CKD-positive predictions were considerably more sensitive. For Qwen3, CKD prediction dropped from a baseline of 65 to as low as 50 across country contexts, while Mistral showed smaller but non-negligible variation. Country contexts did not group according to known epidemiological or healthcare similarities; instead, groupings appear to reflect how country tokens are internally represented within each model. These findings demonstrate that geographic tokens can systematically shift clinical screening outcomes despite identical patient inputs, with implications for the deployment of LLM-based decision support in diverse healthcare settings.
papers.summary: The authors test whether naming a country in the prompt changes zero-shot chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening by LLMs when every clinical input stays the same. They use a Bangladeshi community dataset, vary the country across 25 contexts, and evaluate `Qwen3 8B` and `Mistral 7B`. Non-CKD predictions stayed stable, but CKD-positive predictions were sensitive: **`Qwen3`'s correct CKD detections fell from 65 to as low as 50** depending on the country. The country groupings did not follow epidemiological similarity and instead appear to reflect how each model represents country tokens internally.

papers.title: MeshRT: Compile-Time Governed Wafer-Scale Runtime for Low-Latency High-Throughput Inference
papers.abstract:
Wafer-scale accelerators promise ultra-low-latency AI inference, but current system stacks still carry an unsustainably high cost premium. The reason is that many current and emerging inference techniques, such as batching and MoE, introduce runtime dynamism that existing wafer-scale systems cannot support efficiently. As a result, they must choose between two unsatisfactory options: accept suboptimal latency, or preserve low latency by restricting dynamic techniques, thereby limiting the models they can support and reducing aggregate throughput. This tradeoff significantly increases the cost of low-latency serving.
  We present MeshRT, the first wafer-scale system to achieve both ultra-low latency and high throughput for LLM inference. MeshRT achieves this via a novel system architecture, which we call compile-time governance of runtime dynamism. This architecture features new system abstractions and mechanisms that enable MeshRT to compile dynamic events arising from LLM inference directly into per-core schedules, enabling asynchronous and decentralized execution with low runtime overhead. Implemented on a commodity wafer-scale accelerator, MeshRT preserves ultra-low latency while improving throughput by up to 56$\times$ over the state-of-the-art system for wafer-scale accelerators. Against measured single-instance SGLang results on H200, MeshRT achieves 4.5-7.0$\times$ lower latency. Under ideal linear scaling of those GPU measurements to an approximately power-matched H200 cluster, MeshRT achieves 1.7-13.0$\times$ higher decode system throughput in the low-latency regime.
papers.summary: Wafer-scale accelerators can serve AI models with very low latency, but current software stacks handle runtime dynamism such as batching and mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing poorly. They either give up some latency or restrict dynamic techniques, which limits throughput. `MeshRT` compiles the dynamic events of LLM inference directly into per-core schedules, allowing asynchronous, decentralized execution with little runtime overhead. On a commodity wafer-scale accelerator it **improves throughput by up to 56× over the prior state-of-the-art wafer-scale system** and has 4.5–7.0× lower latency than `SGLang` on a single H200.

papers.title: MorphSched: Workload-Aware Adaptive Scheduler Generation for Linux
papers.abstract: Modern Linux scheduling increasingly requires workload-specific policies to meet the dynamic performance needs of heterogeneous applications. The recent sched_ext framework enables custom BPF schedulers, but building practical policies still requires coordinating Rust user-space control logic, BPF scheduling callbacks, generated user-kernel interfaces, and strict eBPF verifier constraints. This paper presents MorphSched, an LLM-driven system for synthesizing complete Rust+BPF sched_ext schedulers. MorphSched profiles target workloads under Linux EEVDF to construct dynamic, workload-specific optimization objectives, and uses a scaffold-constrained generation pipeline to translate scheduling intent into deployable scheduler implementations. To improve synthesis reliability, MorphSched separates implementation repair from strategy search: verifier, build, and runtime failures are handled through a DAG-structured repair process, while performance feedback is accumulated in an evolutionary memory pool to refine high-level scheduling strategies across iterations. We evaluate MorphSched across 120 machine/workload/interferer configurations on a real Linux kernel. The generated schedulers compile, pass eBPF verification, load successfully, and remain stable throughout our benchmark runs without manual edits to generated scheduler source code. Across these configurations, MorphSched improves the primary foreground metric over EEVDF by 26.5% on average and up to 87.3%. In selected comparisons, the generated schedulers are also competitive with representative hand-written sched_ext schedulers. These results show that scaffold-constrained, system-grounded LLM generation can be a practical tool for exploring workload-specific Linux scheduling policies.
papers.summary: Linux's `sched_ext` framework allows custom BPF schedulers, but writing them means coordinating Rust user-space code, BPF callbacks, and strict eBPF verifier rules. `MorphSched` uses LLMs to synthesize complete Rust+BPF schedulers. It profiles workloads under the default `EEVDF` scheduler, generates code within a fixed scaffold, fixes verifier, build, and runtime failures through a DAG-structured repair process, and refines scheduling strategies with an evolutionary memory pool. Across 120 machine, workload, and interference configurations, the generated schedulers loaded and ran stably without manual edits, and they **improved the primary metric over `EEVDF` by 26.5% on average and up to 87.3%**.

papers.title: Online and Survey Representations of Well-Being: Coherence and Cross-Source Correspondence
papers.abstract: Digital traces may complement population surveys in the measurement of well-being, but the two sources do not necessarily capture identical constructs. We compare the Human Flourishing Geographic Index (HFGI) with World Values Survey and European Social Survey measures across three domains using structural equation models. The results show strong within-source coherence and construct-specific cross-source correspondence. Cross-source convergence varies across domains; the observed pattern is consistent with stronger correspondence where the underlying indicators are more closely aligned conceptually. Near-perfect agreement would be unexpected, since surveys elicit standardized self-reports, whereas HFGI captures naturally occurring public expressions. HFGI should therefore be viewed as a distinct but empirically connected measurement system that complements survey-based evidence on well-being.
papers.summary: The authors compare the Human Flourishing Geographic Index (`HFGI`), built from public online expressions, with `World Values Survey` and `European Social Survey` measures across three well-being domains using structural equation models. Each source is strongly coherent internally, and the two sources show **construct-specific cross-source correspondence**, which is stronger in domains where the underlying indicators are conceptually closer. They conclude that `HFGI` is a distinct but empirically connected measure that complements surveys.

papers.title: Interpretable Multifidelity Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Spatiotemporal Nuclear Reactor Flow Modeling
papers.abstract: High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of nuclear reactor systems are computationally expensive, motivating machine learning methods that reduce cost while preserving accuracy. Multifidelity surrogate modeling addresses this by combining inexpensive low-fidelity data with limited high-fidelity data. This work investigates whether the high-fidelity data required to predict the spatiotemporal mass flow rate across all 193 fuel assemblies of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) core can be reduced, comparing black-box multifidelity feedforward neural networks (MFNNs) with interpretable multifidelity Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (MFKANs). Cross-fidelity correlation across the core is weak, making this a challenging multifidelity problem, and neither architecture predicts the transient particularly well in absolute terms. MFKAN nonetheless performs comparably to MFNN for one-time-step-forward prediction while also providing closed-form symbolic equations unavailable with MFNN. To address the scarcity of CFD transients, with only one available per fidelity level, TabDDPM-generated synthetic data was used to augment cross-fidelity forecasting. KAN and FNN achieve comparable self-evaluation accuracy (Pearson correlation of roughly 0.73--0.81), but both perform poorly at true cross-fidelity forecasting (correlations of 0.03--0.06). Assembly-level analysis shows that each assembly's forecast correlation tracks its real cross-fidelity correlation for both architectures ($r=0.840$--$0.896$ for KAN, $r=0.804$--$0.903$ for FNN), confirming that forecasting accuracy is fundamentally limited by how correlated the fidelity levels already are. Overall, KAN-based multifidelity modeling achieves accuracy consistently comparable to MFNN across all settings, while additionally providing symbolic equations that match or exceed the spline representation's accuracy.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether combining cheap low-fidelity simulations with limited high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) data can predict time-varying mass flow across all 193 fuel assemblies of a pressurized water reactor core. They compare black-box multifidelity feedforward networks (`MFNN`) with interpretable multifidelity Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (`MFKAN`), and augment the scarce transients with `TabDDPM`-generated synthetic data. Both architectures perform comparably, and `MFKAN` additionally yields closed-form symbolic equations. Both do poorly at true cross-fidelity forecasting, and **forecast accuracy closely tracks how correlated the fidelity levels already are** (r of roughly 0.8–0.9).

papers.title: What Are LLM Agents Actually Learning on Low-Budget Molecular Optimization Benchmarks?
papers.abstract: Recent work reports large gains for LLM agents on low-budget molecular optimization. We measure the contributions of online optimization, retrievable task information, and permissive oracle landscapes. On PMO at 50 oracle calls, a GPT-4o mini agent's sum AUC falls from 14.44 to 4.85 after task names and curated reference compounds are hidden. An identity-blinded condition that states only the oracle form (e.g., similarity to a hidden reference) scores 5.39, while a deterministic retrieval-only baseline with no LLM reaches 12.16 (84% of the full agent). A full 23-task 2x2 ablation and a three-seed replication on eight tasks support this interpretation. On a protein-targeted benchmark with an AutoDock Vina composite oracle, a single-edit random walk is a strong lower bound; across three seeds it obtains composite 0.636 +/- 0.008 and docking improvement -1.11 +/- 0.04 kcal/mol. As a positive control, a retrieval-free population agent exceeds REINVENT at a matched 50-call AUC budget, with its strongest result at 100 calls. These results motivate two inexpensive sanity checks: retrieval-safe PMO prompts and a random-walk floor for docking-based optimization.
papers.summary: Recent reports show large gains for LLM agents on molecular optimization with few oracle calls, and the authors test how much of that comes from real online optimization versus information the model can simply retrieve. On the `PMO` benchmark at 50 oracle calls, a `GPT-4o mini` agent's summed AUC drops from 14.44 to 4.85 once task names and curated reference compounds are hidden, while **a deterministic retrieval-only baseline with no LLM reaches 12.16, or 84% of the full agent**. On a protein-targeted benchmark scored with `AutoDock Vina` docking, a single-edit random walk turns out to be a strong lower bound, although a retrieval-free population agent does beat `REINVENT` at a matched budget. The authors recommend two cheap sanity checks: retrieval-safe prompts for `PMO` and a random-walk floor for docking-based optimization.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.
papers.summary: Subliminal learning, where a teacher model passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference, was first shown in LLMs and is tested here in vision-language models (VLMs). A teacher VLM is finetuned to prefer a particular animal or facial attribute, then generates numbers for an unrelated geometric-shapes task, and a student from the same base model is finetuned on those outputs and compared against a student trained on a control teacher's outputs. Across VLMs from 2B to 7B parameters, both kinds of preference transfer, with **biased students picking the target up to about 10 percentage points more often** in the animal task. Transfer tends to grow with more training data, and biased students also borrow the biased teacher's wording when explaining their choices.

papers.title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination
papers.abstract: Aging cohorts increasingly combine imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, but most subjects provide only a partially observed cross-sectional snapshot, leaving latent stage, progression subtype, and stage-varying multimodal coordination to be inferred jointly. Existing methods estimate the cohort-level aging process, model covariance under observed covariates, or fuse modalities for prediction. However, they rarely target the joint problem of endpoint-anchored staging and progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities, even though subject staging, subtype assignment, and multimodal interplay are mutually dependent. We introduce ELPAC, a Bayesian framework with two interlocking constructions. The first integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components encoding modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential ordering priors. The second factorizes residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis into sparse coordination axes whose loadings and activations expose which multimodal patterns are operative in each subtype and when they emerge, with stage-resolved variation supplying the auxiliary structure for conditional identifiability. We use a scalable amortized variational inference scheme that enables joint posterior inference at cohort scale with single-pass deployment on new subjects. On synthetic data and a harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer's cohort, ELPAC demonstrates accurate latent-structure recovery, well-calibrated prediction intervals, and biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.
papers.summary: Aging cohorts often provide only a partial cross-sectional snapshot per subject across imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, so disease stage, progression subtype, and how the modalities interact must be inferred together. `ELPAC` is a Bayesian framework that integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically constrained velocity components. It also factorizes the remaining multimodal variation into sparse coordination axes that show which cross-modal patterns are active in each subtype and when they emerge. With amortized variational inference, it runs at cohort scale and on harmonized `ADNI`+`NACC`/`SCAN` Alzheimer's data **recovers latent structure accurately with well-calibrated prediction intervals** and interpretable, subtype-specific coordination patterns.

papers.title: SAFTAC: Simulation-Augmented Fine-Tuning of Open-Source LLMs for Analog Circuit Design
papers.abstract: Circuit design for analog integrated circuits (ICs) is challenging because circuit topology, device sizing, and circuit performance are tightly coupled. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without directly using simulation outcomes as training signals. A key bottleneck is that existing datasets do not provide sufficient task information for training LLMs on end-to-end specification-conditioned design. To fill this gap, we first construct a large-scale simulation-grounded dataset with 8,626 design tasks across 10 different types of analog circuits, where each task includes a textual description, labeled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Using this dataset, we present SAFTAC, a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit design. SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning, which progressively builds the capabilities required for analog circuit design and feedback-guided correction, with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning, which further optimizes models using simulation-grounded rewards. We evaluate SAFTAC under single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback, showing improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% and 7.8%, respectively.
papers.summary: Analog integrated-circuit design is hard for LLMs because topology, device sizing, and performance are tightly coupled, and existing datasets lack the information needed to train end-to-end, specification-driven design. The authors build a simulation-grounded dataset of 8,626 design tasks across 10 analog circuit types, each with specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. `SAFTAC` fine-tunes open-source LLMs in three supervised stages and then applies reinforcement fine-tuning with rewards computed from circuit simulation. It **beats the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% in single-pass generation** and by 7.8% when a second pass uses simulation feedback.

papers.title: GenStrain: Multi-Conditional Generative Diffusion Model To Synthesize High-quality Motion and Strain Maps From Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Images
papers.abstract: This paper presents GenStrain, a novel method for synthesizing high-quality cardiac motion-based strain maps from routinely collected cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. Existing approaches typically rely on image registration to estimate motion (a sequence of displacements) from cine CMR images, but cine CMR presents very sparse trackable intramyocardial features, presenting challenges to estimate intramyocardial motion. An advanced imaging technique, Displacement Encoding with Stimulated Echoes (DENSE) CMR, is considered as the gold standard for strain assessment, but it requires additional acquisitions, which are not ideal for efficient clinical workflows. To address this gap, we introduce GenStrain, a novel framework designed to learn the data distribution of highly accurate cardiac motion captured by DENSE. In particular, we develop a diffusion process in motion space, where spatiotemporal continuity is carefully considered. To fully leverage both cine CMR images and their associated motion patterns, we introduce a multi-conditional conditioning strategy that integrates anatomical features and motion representations learned by a spatiotemporal registration model to guide the generation process. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model, GenStrain, outperforms existing strain analysis methods based on displacement estimates from both traditional registration approaches and state-of-the-art (SOTA) deep learning models. Our model represents a promising step toward more accurate cardiac function assessment and holds great potential for clinical translation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Rishov-MIA/GenStrain.
papers.summary: Strain maps that measure heart-muscle deformation are usually estimated by registering routine cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images, which have few trackable features inside the heart wall. The gold-standard technique, Displacement Encoding with Stimulated Echoes (`DENSE`) CMR, requires extra scans. `GenStrain` trains a diffusion model in motion space to learn the distribution of `DENSE`-quality motion, conditioning generation on anatomical features and on motion representations from a spatiotemporal registration model. It **outperforms both traditional registration and state-of-the-art deep learning strain-analysis methods**.

papers.title: Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning: A Multi-Objective Framework for Learning Local Distance Functions in Nearest Neighbor Classification
papers.abstract: Nearest neighbour classifiers inherit the geometry of their distance function. Fixed distances and globally learned metrics apply the same geometry throughout the input space, although relevant feature directions may vary across regions. We propose EAML (Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning), a framework that learns instance-dependent positive-definite metrics through a low-dimensional parameterization. Each local metric combines an input-dependent diagonal scaling, generated by softmax interpolation between anchor points, with a global low-rank correlation component. A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes the parameters using a scalar objective combining leave-one-out prediction error, robustness, metric smoothness, and regularization. We establish positive definiteness, metric equivalence, existence of an optimal solution, and Lipschitz continuity of the metric field. We further investigate prediction stability, generalization bounds, and evolutionary convergence under explicit assumptions. Experiments on synthetic data with region-dependent feature relevance show that EAML can recover local metric variations and outperform global metrics. Evaluation on thirteen public datasets using nested 5-fold cross-validation reveals a more nuanced picture: EAML improves performance on selected datasets but does not significantly outperform global metric baselines overall. Additional experiments show that global diagonal metrics can be preferable under nuisance features and test-time noise. These findings identify the conditions under which evolutionary local metric learning is beneficial and highlight its practical limitations.
papers.summary: Nearest-neighbour classifiers usually apply one distance metric across the whole input space, even when the relevant features vary by region. `EAML` (Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning) learns an instance-dependent metric that combines an input-dependent diagonal scaling, interpolated between anchor points, with a global low-rank component, and optimizes it with an elitist genetic algorithm. The authors prove properties such as positive definiteness and Lipschitz continuity, and on synthetic data the method recovers region-dependent metrics. However, **on thirteen public datasets it does not significantly outperform global metric baselines overall**, and global diagonal metrics can do better when there are nuisance features or noise at test time.

papers.title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
papers.abstract: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, na\"ive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.
papers.summary: Training a sparse autoencoder (SAE) requires a huge cache of model activations, which raises the question of how far that cache can be compressed. When an SAE is retrained on a compressed cache, feature retention is noisy even without compression: on `GPT-2`, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, a tiny one-in-a-million perturbation keeps 70.5%, and simply changing the random seed keeps only 23.0%. The authors therefore calibrate each activation site, using retraining on identical bytes as the ceiling and a reseed as the floor. With `TopK` SAEs on `GPT-2 small` and `Pythia-1.4B`, **naive per-token int4 quantization loses more features than a reseed everywhere tested**, but standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor at the same file size.

papers.title: pESTO: Iterative p-greedy kernel regression with risk-driven Early STOpping
papers.abstract: Kernel-based greedy algorithms select suitable approximation nodes by minimizing point-wise error indicators, such as the power function; in this context, they are usually referred to as p-greedy approaches. In the presence of noisy data, deterministic criteria may fail, as the discrepancy between the true solution and its estimate is influenced by both approximation error and noise amplification, and the balance between the two is unknown. This study explicitly separates these two contributions, which are governed by the power function and a Lebesgue-type term, respectively. These bounds motivate the use of the Stein's unbiased risk estimator (SURE) as a proxy of the mean squared error, which in turn provides a principled and computable stopping criterion for the number of nodes to select in the p-greedy procedure. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively balances deterministic accuracy and statistical noise contributions.
papers.summary: Kernel p-greedy algorithms choose approximation nodes by minimizing pointwise error indicators such as the power function, but with noisy data the right number of nodes is unclear. The authors derive bounds that separate the approximation error, governed by the power function, from noise amplification, governed by a Lebesgue-type term. Based on this, they use Stein's unbiased risk estimator (`SURE`) as a proxy for mean squared error to **give a computable early-stopping criterion** for node selection, and numerical experiments show it balances the two error sources.

papers.title: Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation for Wind Energy Predictive Analysis
papers.abstract: Resource-constrained cyber-physical decision systems often apply fixed sensing, knowledge, and computational pipelines despite state-dependent information needs. We introduce Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation (MSKC), a resource-aware computing principle: select the least-costly route meeting decision-risk and deployment constraints, escalating only when cheaper routes are insufficient. As proof of concept, we isolate adaptive knowledge routing, the decision underlying Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning (KGML), which conventionally injects external knowledge unconditionally rather than only where needed. We instantiate this for wind ramp-event predictive analysis, an edge-oriented decision-support task, evaluating local, relational, and physics-informed routes with a state-aware gate on publicly available real data from two wind farms. We establish conditions for feasibility preservation, cost dominance, and strict expected savings over always-on routing. At a 35.9% relational-knowledge injection rate, adaptive routing is statistically indistinguishable from always-on injection on the reported metrics while reducing knowledge calls by 64%, supporting sustainable, Green-IT-aligned deployment. These results support MSKC's premise that uniformly maximal intelligence is unnecessary. This offers intelligent data analysis for big data streams: the analysis itself decides, per state, how much knowledge and computation the data warrant.
papers.summary: Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation (`MSKC`) is a principle for resource-constrained decision systems: use the cheapest sensing, knowledge, and computation route that meets risk constraints, and escalate only when needed. As a proof of concept, a state-aware gate decides when to inject external knowledge in knowledge-guided machine learning for predicting wind-ramp events, tested on public data from two wind farms. **Adaptive routing matches always-on knowledge injection on the reported metrics while cutting knowledge calls by 64%**, and the authors also state formal conditions under which this kind of routing is guaranteed to save cost.

papers.title: PINNeval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Standard for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) literature has produced a rapidly expanding catalogue of methods. We divide a PINN training pipeline systematically into four components and observe that many existing benchmarks study these components in isolation. These components are domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, neural network architecture, and optimization scheme. Moreover, the studies set the surrounding and not considered components of the pipeline to a minimal default that is no longer representative of current best practice approaches. Conclusions drawn under such conditions may not transfer to competitive pipelines. In this work, we propose a new evaluation protocol that (1) treats the four components as an integrated system; (2) crucially requires competitive implementations of the components not under investigation; (3) specifies the metrics and reporting format; and (4) is accompanied by structured documentation that ensures the traceability of evaluations across studies. Based on this comprehensive protocol, we release PINNpipe, an innovative JAX package containing 18 different methods from the current literature as well as nine efficiently implemented benchmark problems. Using PINNpipe, we illustrate our evaluation protocol in relation to established benchmark studies and report results that challenge common assumptions.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) usually study one pipeline component at a time, such as loss balancing, architecture, sampling of domain points, or the optimizer, while leaving the others at minimal defaults that no longer reflect best practice. The proposed evaluation protocol treats all four components as one system and requires competitive implementations of the components not under study. It also fixes the metrics and reporting format and adds structured documentation so evaluations can be traced across studies. The authors release `PINNpipe`, a `JAX` package with 18 methods and nine benchmark problems, and use it to report **results that challenge common assumptions from earlier benchmark studies**.

papers.title: Towards Label-Efficient Geospatial Foundation Model Adaptation via Positive-Unlabeled Learning for Building Damage Mapping
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.
papers.summary: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) pretrained on Earth observation data could speed up mapping of building damage after disasters, but parameter-efficient fine-tuning does not solve the shortage of labels. `PUMA` (Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation) needs annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings and treats everything else as unlabeled. It combines non-contrastive representation refinement that is robust to noisy supervision with latent-state-based label disambiguation that does not require estimating class priors. Experiments on disaster datasets from around the world, plus a real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, show **accurate damage mapping under very limited supervision**.

papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
papers.summary: `CascadeRec` is a two-tier LLM reranking cascade for content recommendation, deployed in production at a financial-planning SaaS provider. A lightweight model reranks every request, and a router escalates only promising requests to a more expensive tier that uses self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model. In a month-long production A/B test it **cut inference cost by about 10% with no observed quality regression**. Experiments on public benchmarks (`MovieLens-1M`, `Amazon-Electronics`) show that uniform LLM reranking can lower `NDCG@10` for users with sparse histories by up to 30%, and that escalating these cold users can make the loss worse.

papers.title: Personalized health coaching via coachable health age and counterfactual wearable trajectories
papers.abstract: Personalized health coaching requires moving beyond retrospective wearable summaries toward quantitative, actionable behavioral prescriptions. We introduce Coachable Health Age (CHA), an interpretable health-age metric built from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals passively captured by consumer wearables. Across the WEAR-ME (N=2,780), All of Us (N=22,748), and longitudinal Fitbit (N=1,464) cohorts, CHA aligns with established cardiometabolic health constructs and improves prognostic discrimination for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and body mass index. To enable prospective behavioral optimization, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned wearable world model pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of longitudinal sensor data from approximately 100,000 participants. SensorWM accurately forecasts multi-week physiological responses to candidate lifestyle changes ($R^2=0.664$), outperforming generic time-series foundation models while preserving downstream clinical signal for diabetes, hypertension, and other health outcomes. Finally, we integrate CHA and SensorWM into an agentic counterfactual coaching system to synthesize personalized 12-week coaching plans. In blinded paired reviews, certified lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over plans grounded in wearable history alone for overall quality (71.4%, P < 0.001) and anticipated adherence (71.0%, P < 0.001), and board-certified clinicians judged 99.2% of counterfactual-grounded plans to meet clinical safety criteria (vs. 97.6% of comparison plans). Automated evaluations across the full cohort (N=2,780) also favored counterfactual-grounded plans. By closing the loop between longitudinal tracking, trajectory prediction, and counterfactual coaching, our framework provides a scalable path to systematically improve cardiometabolic health.
papers.summary: Coachable Health Age (`CHA`) is an interpretable health-age metric built from modifiable signals captured by consumer wearables, and it improves prediction of cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and body mass index across cohorts including `All of Us`. `SensorWM`, an action-conditioned world model pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of sensor data, forecasts multi-week physiological responses to lifestyle changes with R² of 0.664. The two are combined in an agentic system that writes personalized 12-week coaching plans grounded in counterfactual forecasts. In blinded reviews, **certified coaches preferred these plans 71.4% of the time** over plans based only on wearable history, and clinicians judged 99.2% of them clinically safe.

papers.title: Not All Misalignment Is Alike: A Decomposed Benchmark for Emergent Misalignment
papers.abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM), in which fine-tuning on a narrow task induces misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts, has been demonstrated across a wide range of datasets, model families, and training setups. Yet, most studies continue to rely on the evaluation approach introduced in the original EM paper, producing rates that are sensitive to the small set of evaluation questions used, the choice of judge, and the thresholds applied. These evaluations can also conflate misalignment with capability loss and offer little insight into the specific ways misalignment manifests. Differences in datasets, models, and fine-tuning configurations further make findings difficult to compare across studies. We introduce EMERGE, a decomposed benchmark that tracks changes in eight distinct misaligned behaviours from base to fine-tuned models. It evaluates these behaviours on out-of-domain prompts against matched benign controls and tracks capability, coherence, and refusal to account for potential confounders. Applying EMERGE to 8 open-weight models and 13 fine-tuning datasets, we find that models with similar broad misalignment rates can exhibit very different behavioural profiles that a single score cannot capture.
