We hope EMERGE can help establish a shared and robust standard for measuring EM, making findings more comparable and helping move research from detecting the phenomenon towards understanding it.
papers.summary: Emergent misalignment (EM), where fine-tuning on a narrow task causes misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts, is usually measured with the original small question set, and the resulting rates depend on the judge and thresholds and can be confused with capability loss. `EMERGE` is a benchmark that tracks eight distinct misaligned behaviours from base model to fine-tuned model on out-of-domain prompts, compares them against matched benign controls, and monitors capability, coherence, and refusal as confounders. Across 8 open-weight models and 13 fine-tuning datasets, **models with similar overall misalignment rates show very different behavioural profiles** that a single score cannot capture.
papers.highlight_summary:
Fine-tuning on a narrow task can cause emergent misalignment (EM), where a model behaves badly on unrelated prompts, but most studies still measure it as one judge-scored rate from a handful of probe questions. `EMERGE` replaces that single rate with a profile of eight separately scored behaviours, each measured as a change from the base model on prompts outside the fine-tuning domain, with matched benign controls and capability tracking alongside.

- The benchmark draws **3,202 items** from established datasets, about 400 per behaviour, covering hallucination, sycophancy, deception, discrimination, dangerous content, abusive content, anti-human sentiment and CBRN risk; a dual-judge panel (`Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct` and `gpt-4.1-mini`) scores each behaviour with its own rubric, and every shift is normalised by how much room the base model had left to get worse.
- Across 8 open-weight models and 13 fine-tuning datasets, susceptibility spans almost the whole scale, from **0.565** for `Ministral-3-14B` down to **0.001** for `Qwen3.8-27B`, with no clear link to model size; the matched benign controls show near-zero susceptibility, which suggests the behaviour-targeted prompts are not simply acting as jailbreaks.
- Deception rises for every model and is the largest shift in 9 of the 13 datasets, but its base rates are already high (**0.46–0.70**), and coherence drops for every model, by as much as **−0.265** for `Qwen3-8B`.
- The standard `Betley-8` rate tracks overall magnitude well (**ρ = 0.84** with aggregate susceptibility) but leaves **40.5%** of the variance in behaviour profiles unexplained; among fine-tunes with identical Betley rates, **68%** of pairs differ by more than 0.20 on at least one behaviour, and fine-tunes like `insecure_code` score 0.00 on Betley-8 while still shifting discrimination by 0.18.
- Limitations: each model–dataset pair uses a single training seed and LoRA configuration, so confidence intervals cover only evaluation-item variance; scoring relies on LLM judges validated by a single human annotator; and part of `Ministral-3-14B`'s top score may reflect its **6.67-point** capability loss rather than misalignment.

papers.title: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
papers.abstract:
This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology.
  Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.
papers.summary: This thesis applies case-based reasoning (CBR), which solves new problems by retrieving and adapting similar past cases, to academic advising in higher education. It covers the design, development, and validation of a prototype CBR recommender system meant to supplement the conventional advising process. The authors argue that advising is a well-suited domain for CBR expert systems that **has not been successfully addressed before**, and that the system could eventually take over more of human advisors' work.

papers.title: Q-OIL: Optimistic Exploration in Learning from Human Interventions
papers.abstract: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through analyzing intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Building on these insights, we propose Q-OIL, a method that adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions in reinforcement learning and softly guides exploration toward human corrections. We find that decoupled critics are critical for stability because they prevent the bonuses from backing up to pre-intervention states. As a result, Q-OIL learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real robots, and improving pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks. As we ground both evaluation and algorithms in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.
papers.summary: Robot learning from human interventions is mostly developed against simulated human models, but data from real participants shows that people tend to intervene when the robot's progress stalls and that their corrections are often suboptimal. The authors propose a progress-based intervention model whose rankings of algorithms correlate better with rankings from real users. They also introduce `Q-OIL`, which adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions during reinforcement learning, using decoupled critics so the bonuses do not propagate back to states before the intervention. `Q-OIL` **achieves 10-50% higher success than baselines in simulation and on real robots** and improves pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) on two bimanual manipulation tasks.

papers.title: HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields
papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.
papers.summary: Generative priors for human pose rarely account for the object a hand is holding, even though hand poses depend heavily on that object. `HaNDF` represents plausible hand articulations as the zero-level set of an object-conditioned neural distance field and uses Riemannian geometry to project any given pose onto that set. The same field can be optimized in reverse to infer which object is being held. Evaluations show it works as **a flexible prior for pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis**.

papers.title: Just CaloCHILL: fast hadronic shower generation in a learned latent space
papers.abstract: Calorimeter showers are the most expensive part of detector simulation, and highly granular calorimeters, in which a single hadronic shower leaves thousands of energy deposits, make them more expensive still. We present CaloCHILL (Calorimeter Hits In Learned Latents), a generative model that does not produce these deposits one by one: instead it generates a compact summary of the shower in a learned latent space and expands it to full resolution only at the end. The complete shower, including the arrival time of every hit, is built in three stages: a flow-matching model first sets the number of hits and the earliest hit time in each calorimeter layer, a mean-flow model then generates the latent summary, and the decompressor of a variational autoencoder turns it into the full point cloud, giving every hit its position, energy and time. Sparse attention along the shower axis keeps this compression affordable for showers with thousands of hits. On positive-pion showers in the calorimeter of the International Large Detector, a proposed detector for the FCC-ee, CaloCHILL reproduces the main shower observables, including their time structure. This new model is 600 times faster than its predecessor, while improving on all accuracy metrics considered.
papers.summary: Simulating hadronic showers in highly granular particle-detector calorimeters is expensive because each shower leaves thousands of energy deposits. `CaloCHILL` avoids generating deposits one by one: a flow-matching model first sets the number of hits and the earliest hit time in each layer, a mean-flow model then generates a compact latent summary of the shower, and a variational autoencoder decoder expands it into a full point cloud with position, energy, and time for every hit. On positive-pion showers in the calorimeter of the proposed International Large Detector, it reproduces the main shower observables, including their time structure, and is **600 times faster than its predecessor** while improving every accuracy metric considered.

papers.title: AutoPYara: Next-Gen YARA Rule Generator for Malware Family Clustering
papers.abstract: Millions of malware variants threaten users daily, such that clustering these samples is key for fast incident response. AutoYara is the current state-of-the-art for automatic YARA rule generation, but the task remains challenging on realistic datasets, where intra-family diversity and noisy clustering can degrade rule quality. We present AutoPYara, a solution armored with: (1) precise cluster centroid selection based on similarity hashing, and (2) an improved heuristic for estimating subclusters within a malware family using historical VirusTotal data. We implement AutoPYara as an open-source Python package (pip install autopyara) to support reproducibility and practical use. We show that AutoPYara, (1) increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points; (2) reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, comparing the average variance AutoPYara exhibits to that of AutoYara; and (3) improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%. AutoPYara produces robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical settings.
papers.summary: Automatically generating YARA rules, the signatures used to detect malware families, is difficult on realistic datasets where variants within a family are diverse and clustering is noisy. `AutoPYara` improves on the previous state of the art, `AutoYara`, by choosing cluster centroids with similarity hashing and by estimating subclusters within a family from historical `VirusTotal` data. Released as an open-source Python package, it **increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points**, lowers variance by 7.1 points, and improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%.

papers.title: NormGym: Evaluating Normative Competence through Social Interaction
papers.abstract: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction. We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community. Success requires distinguishing what is possible from what is permitted, inferring the norm from observed behavior and sanctions, and applying it in new situations. NormGym contains diverse norms and distinct environments, allowing systematic evaluation of current agents, including large language model (LLM) agents. We find that normative competence remains challenging: the strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%. Our analysis reveals that models can sometimes revise their behavior following sanctions for their own actions, but struggle to use other agents' behavior and the sanctions they receive to infer the underlying norm. We further find that fine-tuning models may be insufficient to improve normative competence. These results suggest that current models lack a robust, transferable capability for acquiring normative knowledge through social interaction.
papers.summary: Normative competence is the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behaviour to match. Existing evaluations mostly check whether agents can apply norms they may already know rather than learn unfamiliar ones. In `NormGym`, a newcomer agent pursues its own task inside a multi-agent community while inferring a hidden, arbitrary norm from other agents' behaviour and the sanctions they receive. **The strongest LLM tested reaches only 55.3% joint task-and-compliance success**: models sometimes correct themselves after being sanctioned but struggle to learn from sanctions applied to others, and fine-tuning appears insufficient to fix this.

papers.title: s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL
papers.abstract: Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems usually rely on fixed, hand-designed setups that decide in advance who does what and what gets shared. `s^3` is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone, when to share findings and when to read teammates' messages, with no predefined roles. The agents learn complementary strategies, develop emergent roles and generalize to larger teams. With matched training and inference budgets, swarms run with twice as many agents as in training solve **over 25× more coordination problems than the strongest baseline**, and in exploration tasks communication cuts repeated work by nearly 50% and beats best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points.

papers.title: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
papers.abstract: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.
papers.summary: Standard inventory classification such as ABC analysis, and its multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) extensions, uses only structured quantitative data and ignores text like customer reviews. The authors turn unstructured sources into quantitative features by combining vector embeddings with evaluation criteria generated by an LLM, then feed these features into an MCIC framework based on the `Hadi-Vencheh` model. Experiments show that **adding customer-sentiment signals measurably changes how items are classified**, which the authors argue improves inventory prioritization in e-commerce supply chains.

papers.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning for Chaotic Three-Body Dynamics in Astrophysics
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) and generative AI have recently made impressive progress in understanding physics. We explore a hierarchy of prediction problems stemming from chaotic three-body systems and benchmark existing ML approaches, including general-purpose prediction algorithms and those that build on top of foundational physics models. We first simulate the trajectories of triple systems near the critical boundary of stable/unstable initial conditions. We then design a hierarchy of learning tasks, focusing mainly on two broad problems: stability prediction and trajectory prediction. The former classifies whether a given triple system has diverged or not up to a specific horizon, while the latter predicts the exact trajectory, both given suitable input features. We benchmark a range of ML approaches, from simple regression methods to state-of-the-art foundational physics models, across these tasks, and compare them against astrophysical methods such as the Mardling-Aarseth stability criterion. Our experiments reveal a clear order of task difficulties in chaotic three-body dynamics: early dynamics enable strong stability prediction, while precise long-horizon trajectory forecasting remains difficult. Code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/Simonwan03/ThreeBodyMLBench.
papers.summary: The authors simulate triple-star systems near the boundary between stable and unstable initial conditions and build a hierarchy of learning tasks around two problems: predicting whether a system diverges within a given horizon, and forecasting its exact trajectory. They benchmark methods ranging from simple regression to foundation models for physics, and compare them with the astrophysical `Mardling-Aarseth` stability criterion. The results show a clear ordering of difficulty: **early dynamics support strong stability prediction, but precise long-horizon trajectory forecasting remains hard**. Code and data are released.

papers.title: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
papers.abstract: Safety benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) commonly use multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. However, prior studies documented that MCQ format reduces refusal rates, which may significantly affect the safety behavior of the model. We provide a first mechanistic explanation of this effect on the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset across two models - Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. First, we use the tuned lens technique to show that when processing MCQ the model commits to an answer-letter token very quickly, which is in contrast to the gradual refusal build-up in open-ended formats. Additionally, we observe that activations on the MCQ format lie roughly 3x further from the refusal direction, compared with their open-ended counterparts. Moreover, ablating the attention heads that carry the MCQ format answer increases the refusal, which is a direct evidence that the MCQ answer-selection competes with refusal. These findings indicate that MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge capabilities and do not assess the safety-mechanisms.
papers.summary: LLM safety benchmarks often use multiple-choice questions (MCQ), a format already known to lower refusal rates. Using the `WMDP` (Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy) dataset with `Llama-3.1-8B` and `Qwen3-8B`, the authors give a mechanistic account of the effect. With the `tuned lens` technique they show that models commit to an answer letter early on MCQ inputs, whereas refusal builds up gradually on open-ended prompts. MCQ activations also sit about 3× further from the refusal direction, and ablating the attention heads that carry the answer letter increases refusal. They conclude that **MCQ safety scores mainly measure knowledge rather than safety mechanisms**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multiple-choice safety benchmarks such as `WMDP` rarely trigger refusals, even on questions a model refuses when asked open-ended. Using `Llama-3.1-8B` and `Qwen3-8B`, the authors trace this to a fast answer-letter commitment, driven by the instruction to reply with a single letter, which takes over before the slower refusal computation can form.

- Behaviorally, models almost never refuse in MCQ format even on items they refuse most of the time open-ended, and MCQ accuracy stays flat across refusal groups (correlation not significant, p > 0.05), so **MCQ scores measure hazardous-knowledge retrieval, not whether refusal activates**.
- `Tuned lens` shows the correct-letter probability jumping sharply in a mid-layer window (**layers 15–18** in Llama, **22–25** in Qwen) while the refusal-proxy token stays near zero, whereas in open-ended prompts the refusal token builds up gradually from around layer 11.
- Under `refusal-direction` analysis (difference-in-means on `BeaverTails`), Llama's open-ended majority-refused items reach cosine **≈0.11–0.12** at layer 11 versus **≈0.035** for the same items in MCQ format, roughly **3× lower** and close to the benign control (≈0.03, against a harmful reference of ≈0.34).
- Ablating the top-10 answer-letter attention heads in Llama lowers correct-letter probability from **≈0.77 to ≈0.65** and raises the refusal proxy from **≈0.007 to ≈0.05**, while layer-matched random-head controls stay near baseline; separately, prompt decomposition shows the letter-forcing format instruction alone cuts the refusal proxy from **≈0.5 to ≈0.05**, whether it sits in the system or user turn.
- Limitations: both models are 8B-scale, the causal ablation result holds only for Llama (in Qwen the answer letter resists ablation and the geometric effect is weak, with small samples), the refusal direction comes from a mismatched dataset, and everything is tested on a single benchmark.

papers.title: Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for Test-Time Selection
papers.abstract: Scaling test-time compute has proven highly effective at improving LLM reasoning. A popular method is best-of-n sampling, where a model generates many candidate solutions and one is selected. This motivates the question: how can we select the best candidate? When humans make choices, we find it more natural to compare two options than judge each in isolation. Additionally, when the options become complex, we like to judge the options one aspect at a time, such as comparing two job candidates on experience, communication, etc. In the test-time setting, candidate solutions should be judged in the same way. Here we introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), which verifies by comparison and compares by aspect. Each matchup of a single elimination tournament is decided by a vote over multiple off-the-shelf aspect verifiers, each expressing a pairwise preference along its own aspect. Across five domains and three generator LLMs, APT improves over binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency and reward model verification, with the largest gains on open-ended tasks. We find that both components matter; neither binary approval over the same aspects nor a generic pairwise judge at a matched budget matches APT. Because aspects are specified in natural language, APT also lets users steer selection toward properties they care about, better aligning with user preferences without needing to regenerate solutions. No component is trained, so APT transfers to new domains by simply rewriting prompts.
papers.summary: In best-of-n sampling, an LLM generates many candidate answers and one has to be chosen. Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (`APT`) picks the winner through a single-elimination tournament in which each matchup is decided by a vote among off-the-shelf verifiers, each comparing the two candidates on one aspect described in natural language. Across five domains and three generator LLMs, `APT` beats binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency and reward-model verification, with **the largest gains on open-ended tasks**. Ablations show that both pairwise comparison and per-aspect judging are needed. No component is trained, so users can steer selection, or move to a new domain, just by rewriting the aspect prompts.

papers.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
papers.abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.
papers.summary: `FinEvolveKG` builds financial knowledge graphs from SEC 10-K filings for several analyst personas. It splits the extraction prompt into a shared general block and a persona-policy block, and confines the reflective prompt optimizer `GEPA` to the persona block, so the approved shared rules stay byte-identical and every edit can be traced. On 10-K splits with no overlapping tickers, the full block-constrained workflow improves on the frozen-prompt baseline by **19.4–30.9%** and on unconstrained full-prompt evolution by 2.2–6.4%. It wins all nine paired-seed comparisons, and the advantage holds under out-of-distribution shifts. Blinded review by subject-matter experts preferred its output in 70.1% of judgments.

papers.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
papers.abstract:
LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge.
  We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query.
  Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
papers.summary: LLM agents do not carry corrections from one session to the next, and existing memory systems store facts rather than procedural knowledge. `Forge Decision Context` (`forge_dc`) collects behavioral signals from human corrections and from the agent's own assessment of failed tool calls, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects each rule at the decision point where it applies. On the new `DC-Bench` benchmark, 71 scenarios built from real agent traces, `forge_dc` reaches **95% compliance versus 55% for naive retrieval** while injecting about 10× fewer tokens per query. The authors identify how rules are represented, when they are activated and where they are placed as the key design choices.

papers.title: From Geometry to Function: A Multi-Task LiDAR Benchmark Dataset for Semantic and Functional Parsing of Urban Facades
papers.abstract: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark
papers.summary: Existing LiDAR facade benchmarks cover geometry and semantic segmentation but not what each architectural element does. `HFX3D` contains about 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across seasons, times of day and weather. It is annotated at three levels: semantic, instance and per-instance functional attributes, which makes it **the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels**. Benchmarks of point-based, graph-based, convolutional and transformer models show that semantic segmentation is already hard under severe class imbalance, and that separating repetitive instances and inferring function from geometry are harder still.

papers.title: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
papers.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.
papers.summary: Intra-weight injection means one model changing another model's behavior by editing its weights directly, without gradients. `IWIBench` measures how well a large editor model, given four tools for reading and writing weights and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting outputs, can edit a smaller target (typically `Gemma 3 4B IT`) to meet one of ten text-editing objectives while preserving its other abilities. Frontier models differ sharply: **a few, notably `Astra` and `GPT-6.1 Sol`, are far ahead**, and the ability is largely absent in slightly older models such as `GPT-5.6 Sol`. Tasks also vary widely: structured-response edits never succeeded, while alias acquisition and recoding were most achievable, and success on one task family predicted little about others.

papers.title: VoluCompose: Constructing Compact Volumetric Visual Representations for Medical Image Understanding
papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models become expensive on volumetric scans because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant sequences of visual tokens. `VoluCompose` is a training-free, model-agnostic compression framework that decides separately which content to keep and how many tokens to spend. It groups neighboring slices and uses the Lorentz distance from hyperbolic geometry to select tokens, and it sets the token budget from how dispersed the visual encoder's attention is. Across three datasets and four backbones, it **retains 22.78% of visual tokens on average while reaching 121.68% mean relative quality** against uncompressed inputs, and it stays robust at a 10% token budget.

papers.title: Turkish Multimodal Video Fact-Checking: A New Dataset and a Comparison of Zero-Shot Agentic and Fine-Tuned Systems
papers.abstract: Video-based misinformation spreads rapidly on social media, but almost all existing fact-checking systems focus exclusively on English text. Tools for low-resource languages such as Turkish are severely limited. In this work, we present TeViD (Turkish Video Fact-checking Dataset), to the best of our knowledge the first multimodal video fact-checking dataset for Turkish. We compiled the dataset from articles published by Teyit.org, an IFCN-certified organisation, and enriched it with translated Snopes articles and synthetic examples to reduce class imbalance. Building on TeViD, we develop two verification pipelines that share the same open-source base model. First, in 3MFact-TR (Pipeline 1), we adapt the multi-role 3MFact framework to Turkish with the Qwen2.5-7B large language model and the Qwen2-VL-7B vision-language model, and add three modules of our own: a semantic inconsistency checker, a 5W1H question manager, and a bilingual evidence retriever that excludes fact-checking sites to prevent leakage. Second, as our Fine-Tuned Model (Pipeline 2), we fine-tune a single Qwen2.5-7B with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to produce closed-book verdicts from the claim and the video's textual description. We report accuracy, macro F1, True class F1, and True class recall for both systems, together with ablation studies.
papers.summary: `TeViD` (Turkish Video Fact-checking Dataset) is presented as **the first multimodal video fact-checking dataset for Turkish**. It is built from Teyit.org articles and supplemented with translated Snopes articles and synthetic examples to balance the classes. The authors compare two pipelines on the same open-source base model. The first, `3MFact-TR`, adapts the multi-role, zero-shot agentic `3MFact` framework to Turkish using `Qwen2.5-7B` and `Qwen2-VL-7B`, adding a semantic-inconsistency checker, a manager for who-what-when-where-why-how questions, and a bilingual evidence retriever that excludes fact-checking sites to avoid leakage. The second is a single `Qwen2.5-7B` fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (`LoRA`) that gives verdicts from the claim and the video's textual description alone.

papers.title: Scoring, Not Learning: Decomposing Catalog-Consolidation Gains in Web-Scraped Retail Product Recognition
papers.abstract: Retail product catalogs assembled from web image search are cheap to build and pervasively noisy: queries return packaging shots instead of products, and entries proliferate under names that cannot be distinguished visually. Consolidating such a catalog can look like an alternative to scaling the model. We show this is not a comparison between two ways of improving a recognizer, but between improving a recognizer and changing what counts as correct. We study a public archive of 165,769 cheese images across 1,824 query-named entries. A packaging filter and near-duplicate removal reduce it to a 998-class recognition set on one fixed, group-aware split. Canonicalizing entries to their base type (844 classes) raises top-1 accuracy by 4.0 points. Scoring the unchanged model against the merged label space, by summing its predicted probability within each canonical group, recovers +4.27 points with no retraining (+4.25 over six seeds). Retraining on the consolidated catalog then adds -0.10$\pm$0.53, +0.08$\pm$0.65 and -0.10$\pm$0.65 points at 28, 50 and 88 M parameters, indistinguishable from zero at every capacity ($\pm$ is the across-seed standard deviation). That component is specific, not mechanical: random merges with the identical size profile yield only +0.68 points, and the three backbones agree to within 0.1 points. But it is overwhelmingly category coarsening, not alias correction: across the 37 merged groups, type coarsenings supply 94% of the gain and alias collapses only 7%. We also detect no interaction between consolidation and backbone size: tripling backbone parameters is worth +1.50$\pm$0.57 points on the raw catalog and +1.42$\pm$00.44 on the canonical one, a within-seed interaction of -0.08 [-0.79,+0.63]. On this archive, the reported consolidation gain primarily reflects the evaluation label space, and separating that out costs one evaluation
papers.summary: Using a public archive of 165,769 web-scraped cheese images, the authors ask where the accuracy gains from cleaning up a noisy product catalog actually come from. Merging entries into their base types raises top-1 accuracy by 4.0 points. **Scoring the unchanged model against the merged labels, by summing its predicted probability within each group, recovers +4.27 points with no retraining**, while retraining on the cleaned catalog adds essentially nothing at any of three model sizes. Almost all of the gain comes from coarsening categories rather than fixing aliases, which suggests that reported consolidation gains largely reflect a change in what counts as a correct answer.

papers.title: Higher Order Component Attribution via Learned Surrogates in High Energy Physics
papers.abstract: Experimental High Energy Physics (HEP) has adopted the transformer architecture for identification of jets, particularly the state-of-the-art Particle Transformer (ParT) which injects explicit information about particle correlations into the attention mechanism. While able to achieve state-of-the-art results in accuracy, interpretability to its effectiveness has been limited. In this paper we propose component attribution methods using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) that directly tie back to the physical descriptors of jets, to probe whether mechanisms such as Multi-Head Attention (MHA), or the ParT architecture, are able to learn these as discriminating features.
papers.summary: The Particle Transformer (`ParT`), a transformer that feeds explicit particle-correlation information into its attention, reaches state-of-the-art accuracy at identifying jets in high-energy physics experiments, but how it does so is poorly understood. The authors propose component-attribution methods based on surrogate Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (`KANs`) that map directly onto physical jet descriptors. The goal is to test **whether mechanisms such as multi-head attention, or the `ParT` architecture as a whole, learn these physical descriptors as discriminating features**.

papers.title: JEPAhead: From Inpainting to Causal Forecasting for Urban Driving
papers.abstract: We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.
papers.summary: The authors fine-tune a pre-trained `V-JEPA` predictor, keeping its encoder frozen, to switch from filling in masked video regions to forecasting the future from past frames without action inputs, predicting sixteen future frames in one forward pass. On `CARLA` Town12 driving data, the model **retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates 69.0% of the time, versus 55.3% for a baseline that assumes the scene stays unchanged**, with larger gains at longer horizons. Probes show that the predicted features carry driving-relevant semantic information. Pixel-space quality improves only modestly, and usefulness for downstream driving tasks has not been tested.

papers.title: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
papers.abstract: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. To address this, we compare a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, holding the rest of the scaffold fixed. We evaluate both architectures on two models, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B, with three independent runs per architecture $\times$ model configuration. Crucially, to distinguish interface specialization from expanded coverage under repeated sampling, we introduce pass$_X$@$k$, a cross-agent pass@$k$ that provides an unbiased estimator of the probability that at least one of $k$ agents is successful. Although the bash and debugger agents solve partially disjoint subsets of the benchmark in any single pair of runs, our pass$_X$@$2$ estimator reveals that this is largely due to run-to-run variance rather than tool complementarity. Across both models, we find that two bash rollouts outperform the combination of one bash and one debugger rollout. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic variance in evaluating agent and tool diversity, and we hope that pass$_X$@$k$ will serve as a useful framework for the community.
papers.summary: Coding agents usually debug by editing code, running it and reading output in the shell rather than stepping through an interactive debugger. To isolate the debugger's contribution, the authors compare an agent that can only use a debugger with one that can only use bash, keeping the rest of the scaffold fixed, on all 500 `SWE-bench Verified` instances with `GPT-OSS-120B` and `Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B`. They introduce `pass_X@k`, an unbiased estimator of the chance that at least one of k different agents succeeds. The two agents appear to solve partly different problems, but this turns out to be mostly run-to-run variance: **two bash rollouts outperform one bash plus one debugger rollout** on both models.

papers.title: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.
papers.summary: Drafters for speculative decoding involve a trade-off: autoregressive drafters slow down as drafts get longer, while diffusion drafters predict each position independently. `ChainFlow` is a drafter based on flow matching, conditioned on the target model's hidden states, that needs only one or two flow steps. A variational autoencoder compresses those hidden states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore dependencies between tokens, and tree drafting raises acceptance rates. On `Qwen3.5` models served in `vLLM`, with matched drafter size and training data, it **outperforms `EAGLE-3` by 39% and `DFlash` by 11%**, and the code and drafters are open-sourced.
papers.highlight_summary:
Speculative decoding drafters face a tradeoff. Autoregressive drafters like `EAGLE-3` model dependencies between tokens, but their cost grows with draft length. Parallel and diffusion drafters produce a whole block at once, but they start each round from noise or masks and predict each position independently. `ChainFlow` treats drafting as a short flow-matching transport over the target model's own compressed hidden states. It starts from an extrapolation of the recent hidden-state trajectory, so a single Euler step is enough to draft 8 positions.

- A VAE compresses the target's final hidden states into a narrow latent, and two "chunk expert" transformers transport the extrapolated latents onto the next 8 future latents by cross-attending to the context; the target's frozen `lm_head` decodes the result, and a rank-256 Markov head plus a path-conditioned residual restore dependence on earlier draft tokens, with no second flow pass, before beam search emits a chain or an 8×4 tree.
- Pooled over eight English domains on `Qwen3.5-4B`, the 8×4 tree reaches **1.87×** speedup in `vLLM` versus **1.69×** for `DFlash` and **1.35×** for `EAGLE-3` (**1.11×** and **1.39×** faster at matched drafter size and training data), while the chain-only variant trails both baselines at 1.23×.
- Because flow cost depends on the latent width rather than the target's size, drafting stays at **0.30–0.38 ms** while the target's autoregressive step grows from 3.1 to 11.2 ms, so speedup peaks at `Qwen3.5-27B` with **2.12×** pooled and **3.23×** on math.
- Starting from the context instead of noise reaches 90% of the validation plateau in about 20 epochs versus 57, and it holds up with one integration step where noise collapses (τ 1.97 versus about 2.5); after sequential adaptation to Turkish, German and French, `ChainFlow` shows the largest gains in each new language, although without replaying about 20% earlier-language data it forgets 5–9× more than the baselines.
- Tree verification only pays off up to about 4 concurrent requests (0.94× at 8 and 0.45× at 128, while the baselines keep their gains), it requires a patched engine and greedy decoding, 4–13% of prompts produced outputs different from plain greedy decoding because of fp16 near-ties, and all experiments use only `Qwen3.5` targets.

papers.title: Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves at Least 0.361 of the Optimal Compression
papers.abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds a tokeniser by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols; its utility is the total reduction in string length achieved by $k$ merges. It was known that this greedy rule achieves at least a third of the optimal reduction. We prove that it always achieves at least 0.361 of the optimal reduction in string length, for every string, every budget and every tie-breaking rule; this is the first improvement of the bound one third. We also explain why one third was a barrier: the pair-packing relaxation behind it is tight, so a better bound must use more of the optimum's structure. When greedy destroys three of the optimum's merge points at once, one of them can usually be moved next door, because all copies of a rule of the optimum look alike; the remaining cases are paid for later. Along the way we determine the worst-case ratio for two merges exactly, bound it for three, and isolate a single inequality that would settle the problem.
papers.summary: Byte-Pair Encoding (`BPE`) builds a tokenizer by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols, and it was known to achieve at least one third of the best possible length reduction. The authors prove that **greedy `BPE` always achieves at least 0.361 of the optimal reduction**, for every string, merge budget and tie-breaking rule, which is the first improvement on the one-third bound. They show why one third was a barrier: the relaxation behind it is tight, so a better bound must use more of the optimal solution's structure. They also determine the worst-case ratio exactly for two merges, bound it for three, and isolate a single inequality that would settle the problem.

papers.title: Transporting the Past: An Optimal Transport View of Backtracking Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: We study backtracking counterfactual inference for Structural Causal Models (SCMs) through the lens of optimal transport. In SCMs, a factual observation generally induces a posterior distribution over exogenous variables, making counterfactual inference inherently distributional. We introduce two complementary frameworks that transport this posterior onto the set of exogenous configurations satisfying a desired counterfactual query. The first constructs a natural pointwise projection and is suitable when the transported exogenous distribution can be used directly. The second enforces mutual independence among counterfactual exogenous variables, so that the transported variables remain interpretable as genuine exogenous noises of the same SCM. We show that both frameworks are consistent with the original backtracking counterfactual principle, and we propose marginal, penalty-based, and hard-constrained solvers for finite-posterior settings. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs illustrate the geometry of the problem and reveal trade-offs among transport cost, counterfactual constraint satisfaction, and preservation of exogenous independence.
papers.summary: Backtracking counterfactuals in structural causal models (SCMs) answer what-if questions by revising the unobserved exogenous variables rather than intervening on the model. The authors frame this as optimal transport, moving the posterior over exogenous variables onto the set of configurations that satisfy the counterfactual query. They propose two frameworks: a pointwise projection, and a version that keeps the counterfactual exogenous variables mutually independent so they remain valid noise terms of the same SCM. **Both are shown to be consistent with the original backtracking principle**, and the authors provide solvers for finite posteriors. Synthetic experiments show trade-offs among transport cost, constraint satisfaction and preserving independence.

papers.title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
papers.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language. However, output predictions alone do not reveal how fine-grained emotion distinctions are organized internally. We study seven LLMs on GoEmotions, an English Reddit dataset annotated with 27 fine-grained emotion categories plus neutral. We compare model predictions and emotion-prompted final-token representations with the 28 GoEmotions categories and with coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings.
  We find a consistent pattern of $\textit{overcompression}$ relative to the fine-grained GoEmotions taxonomy. Under the tested KMeans protocol, when we cluster their hidden representations without using emotion labels, the clearest split is into two groups that largely separate positive from negative emotion. Coarser emotion groupings are also recovered with fewer clusters than the full 28-category taxonomy. Yet linear probes retain substantial fine-grained predictive information. These results suggest that fine-grained emotion information remains accessible even though broader affective structure more strongly organizes the unsupervised geometry.
papers.summary: To see how LLMs organize fine-grained emotions internally, the authors analyze seven models on `GoEmotions`, an English Reddit dataset labeled with 27 emotions plus neutral. They compare predictions and hidden representations against the full taxonomy and against coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings. When the representations are clustered without labels, **the clearest split is simply positive versus negative**, and the coarser groupings are recovered with fewer clusters. Linear probes still retain substantial fine-grained information, suggesting that detailed emotion distinctions remain accessible even though broad sentiment dominates the representation geometry.

papers.title: Cancellation Is Not Enough: What Retries Leave Behind in an Overloaded LLM Engine
papers.abstract: Clients and proxies in front of an LLM engine retry calls that time out. After a transient overload, these retries can keep the engine from recovering even when calls arrive below its capacity. Since the engine may keep computing for clients that have left, propagating cancellation looks like the natural remedy. In this paper, we test it on vLLM with overload experiments on three open models, and with scheduler traces of one that follow each client attempt to the execution it creates in the engine. We find that with retries on, cancellation alone did not restore service in any run, and only 12-38% of the calls that arrived after the overload were delivered. The traces suggest why: retries that vLLM ran typically started prefill less than half a second before they timed out. Executions that vLLM later aborted took 79-85% of the prompt tokens it computed, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed a third to half of all computed prompt tokens. A retry budget restored service by shedding retries but left many of the overload's calls undelivered. Request coalescing delivered every call from the overload onward, some late, unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution. Overload controls should thus be judged by the executions that retries add and the calls that clients receive.
papers.summary: Clients and proxies that retry timed-out calls can keep an LLM serving engine from recovering after a brief overload, even once traffic falls below capacity. In overload experiments on `vLLM` with three open models, plus scheduler traces linking each client attempt to the work it creates in the engine, **propagating cancellation alone never restored service when retries were on**, and only 12–38% of calls arriving after the overload were delivered. Retried requests typically started prefill less than half a second before timing out, aborted executions took 79–85% of the prompt tokens the engine computed, and `vLLM`'s prompt-token counter missed a third to a half of them. A retry budget restored service but left many overload-era calls undelivered, while request coalescing delivered every call unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution.

papers.title: Compressed Per-Player Local Methods for Multiplayer Federated Learning: Exact Convergence via Increment Sharing
papers.abstract: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL), introduced by Yoon et al. (2025), extends classical federated learning to settings where clients are rational players in a game with individual objectives and strategies, seeking an equilibrium. A natural baseline is Per-Player Local SGD (PEARL-SGD), where each player performs several local SGD steps before exchanging strategies through a central server. However, the original PEARL-SGD formulation does not extend cleanly to compressed communication. Directly compressing the players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium, even with deterministic gradients. To address this issue, we reformulate PEARL-SGD so that players communicate local strategy increments rather than the strategies themselves. Without compression, the two formulations are equivalent, but with compression, increment sharing preserves exact convergence, allowing us to design the communication-efficient compressed PEARL-SGD (C-PEARL-SGD). Beyond compression, we also consider variance reduction as another axis of improvement, introducing PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG. Under the original MpFL assumptions, we establish convergence guarantees for all variants through a unified parametric inequality. Numerical experiments, including distributed spectrum sensing, demonstrate the practical benefits of our methods over vanilla PEARL-SGD.
papers.summary: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL) treats federated clients as rational players in a game, each with its own objective and strategy, who are trying to reach an equilibrium. The baseline method, Per-Player Local SGD (`PEARL-SGD`), breaks down under compressed communication: compressing the players' strategies directly can stop convergence even when gradients are exact. The authors have players send local strategy increments instead of full strategies, a change that is equivalent without compression but **preserves exact convergence under compression**, which yields `C-PEARL-SGD`. They also add variance-reduced variants (`PEARL-SVRG`, `C-PEARL-SVRG`), prove convergence for all of them through a single unified inequality, and show gains over vanilla `PEARL-SGD` in experiments that include distributed spectrum sensing.

papers.title: Enabling Retraining-Free Accurate Inference in Analog Compute in Memory Accelerators
papers.abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators compute matrix-vector products directly inside memory arrays, eliminating weight movement and promising order-of-magnitude gains in inference efficiency. However, converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on these arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly. We enable retraining-free, accurate inference of pretrained models on simple analog arrays with low-cost, shared calibration. Our key observation is that analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and that this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. We center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, which keep shared reference errors spread and confine input mixing to each array. Across CNNs, vision transformers and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, the method brings vision models and larger LLMs within a few points of floating-point accuracy and matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights. On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, it restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.
papers.summary: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators run matrix-vector products inside memory arrays, but converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on them, and hardware-aware retraining is expensive. The authors observe that analog error depends on how a layer is laid out on the array, and that this layout can be changed offline without changing what the layer computes. They center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, then add a cheap shared calibration step. Across CNNs, vision transformers, and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, no weights are retrained, and on ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs the method **restores `ViT-B/16` from 37.4% to 82.9% and `Phi-4` from 27.0% to 72.2%**, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.

papers.title: FoleyForge: Free-form, Controllable, Rectified-flow Editing of Sound Effects
papers.abstract: We present FoleyForge, a generative model for instruction-based editing of sound effects. Given an input clip and a free-form instruction describing the desired change, it applies the edit while preserving the input's identity. A single model handles semantic, stylistic, and DSP-like changes. We introduce a data pipeline that guides an audio language model to author both DSP-based acoustic edits and similarity-preserving semantic edits, thus addressing the lack of publicly available audio editing data. Such data is then used to fine-tune a rectified-flow audio generation model, which we extend to expose attribute controls for loudness change, edit strength, and an input-derived contour envelope, each tunable via classifier-free guidance, yielding a more expressive editing model. FoleyForge achieves state-of-the-art instruction adherence at competitive audio quality and source faithfulness.
papers.summary: `FoleyForge` edits sound-effect clips from free-form text instructions while keeping the identity of the input sound, and a single model covers semantic, stylistic, and DSP-like (signal-processing) changes. Public audio-editing data is scarce, so the authors built a pipeline in which an audio language model writes both DSP-based acoustic edits and similarity-preserving semantic edits. They use this data to fine-tune a rectified-flow audio generator and add controls for loudness change, edit strength, and an envelope derived from the input, each adjustable through classifier-free guidance. The model reports **state-of-the-art instruction adherence** with competitive audio quality and faithfulness to the source.

papers.title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies
papers.abstract: Execution algorithms are calibrated asset by asset, because the queues, trade rates and bid-ask spreads they face differ by orders of magnitude across assets. For reinforcement learning this is zero-shot generalisation across contexts of very different scales, and microstructure invariance proposes a normalisation fixed by theory: measured in each asset's own units of time, size and price, markets look alike. In an exact order-by-order replay of public Nasdaq data, we train policies once, on 954 stocks in 2019, to choose between waiting in the queue and crossing the spread, and evaluate them unchanged on 1,964 unseen stocks in 2020-21, 2,629 stocks in 2025-26, crypto pairs and a second exchange. First, a policy that sees a stock only through its recent trade rate, trade size, spread and price increment (tick) costs within 0.015 spreads per share (a fifth of what learning saves) of a policy whose training data included the stock, and the stock's own history does not help it; it comes within a similar margin of policies trained on the second exchange when every episode counts equally, and within a wider one on crypto. Second, in mean cost before fees, invariant units beat raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors, but by under a basis point: most of their advantage is information and a common cost scale that a learner can also take as plain inputs, and none of the representations tested extrapolates to unseen spread regimes. Third, a near-zero transfer gap to a pooled comparator is weak evidence that a representation is right: we show that such a comparator detects only a small share of what a poor representation loses, and confirm it in synthetic markets and on pendulums.
papers.summary: Trade-execution algorithms are usually calibrated one asset at a time, and the authors test whether the normalization proposed by microstructure invariance theory lets reinforcement-learning execution policies transfer zero-shot. They train policies on 954 Nasdaq stocks from 2019 in an exact order-by-order replay, then evaluate them unchanged on thousands of unseen stocks from 2020-21 and 2025-26, on crypto pairs, and on a second exchange. A policy that sees each stock only through its trade rate, trade size, spread, and tick size comes **within 0.015 spreads per share of a policy trained on that stock**. Invariant units beat raw units and z-scores by less than a basis point, none of the representations extrapolates to unseen spread regimes, and the authors show that a near-zero transfer gap against a pooled comparator is only weak evidence that a representation is correct.

papers.title: Foundation-Model Residuals as Signals of Urban Bus Irregularity
papers.abstract:
Pretrained trajectory models encode mobility patterns learned across cities, but their errors when transferred to a new city are usually treated only as performance limitations. We instead ask whether these residuals reveal systematic local conditions. Architectures such as UniTraj and TrajFM learn transferable trajectory representations, although cross-context transfer remains challenging. Using the NetMob26 bus location, ticketing, weather, network, and socioeconomic data for Niteroi, we analyze spatial and travel-time residuals of these recent trajectory foundation models. We test whether high residuals concentrate spatially, whether spatial and travel-time residuals overlap, and which urban-context variables explain their distribution.
  We interpret high residuals as candidate proxy signals of transit irregularity rather than direct evidence of service disruption, and analyze their contextual associations using Explainable AI (XAI). Insights into such varied environments are increasingly valuable for evaluating new urban paradigms; for instance, the 15-minute-city perspective serves as a key motivation for our approach, guiding our methods and expanding the analysis beyond standard mobility metrics.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether the prediction errors of pretrained trajectory foundation models, when transferred to a new city, can serve as signals of local transit irregularity rather than being treated only as performance limits. Using the `NetMob26` bus location, ticketing, weather, network, and socioeconomic data for Niterói, they analyze spatial and travel-time residuals from `UniTraj` and `TrajFM`. They test whether high residuals cluster in space, whether the two kinds of residual overlap, and which urban-context variables explain them, using Explainable AI (XAI) methods. High residuals are presented as **candidate proxy signals of transit irregularity**, not as direct evidence of service disruption, and the analysis is motivated by the 15-minute-city planning perspective.

papers.title: Contextuality and Contradictions: Exploring Real-World Identifications of AI-Generated Writing
papers.abstract: As AI-generated content spreads into nearly every domain of human interaction, practices and discourses of AI detection, both formal and informal, have become an everyday part of how people interact with text and with each other. In this paper, we explore the real-world practices and discourses of AI identification that have emerged in response to a shifting discursive landscape where the human provenance of a text can no longer be taken for granted. We pair qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives on language and communication, to investigate AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students. We find that these identifications draw on a diversity of evidentiary types, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character, and that they are contradictory, dynamic, and contextually dependent. In practice, what often motivates an AI identification is not the presence of any specific textual element, but pragmatic infelicity: a perceived mismatch between the elements present and those deemed appropriate within the text's particular context. Consequently, real-world identifications of AI-generated writing do not merely neutrally point out the perceived presence of "AI-like" features, but can be leveraged as a discursive resource to maintain and define sociolinguistic norms: what can be said in a given context, what is appropriate, and, ultimately, what is human. Further, the design and implementation of systems and tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may therefore inherit, and enforce at scale, the norms of whichever contexts they were trained on.
papers.summary: The authors study how people actually decide that a piece of writing was AI-generated, focusing on English Wikipedia editors and students. They combine qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, drawing on linguistic anthropology. The judgments rest on very different kinds of evidence, from specific textual features to circular reasoning and assumptions about the author's moral character, and they are contradictory and depend on context. The central finding is that identifications are usually triggered by **pragmatic infelicity, a perceived mismatch between the text and what fits its context**, rather than by any specific feature, so detection tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property may enforce the norms of whatever contexts they were trained on.

papers.title: Dual-Stream LLM-Guided Reward Design for Reject-Inference-Aware Reinforcement Learning in E-Commerce Payment Fraud Detection
papers.abstract: Production fraud-detection models learn from a censored slice of their own traffic: transactions a legacy system blocked never receive fraud labels, so models train on a biased, approved-only distribution. We extend LLM-guided reward design, the framework of Qu et al. (2025) in which an LLM evolves the reward of a two-step REINFORCE fraud-blocking policy, to attack this reject-inference problem inside the reward. A single LLM designs a dual-stream reward: stream 1 applies the standard dollar-weighted precision objective to labeled transactions; stream 2 scores legacy-blocked, unlabeled transactions by contrasting the newest gradient-boosted risk signal against the legacy scores that drove the original block. Rather than prescribe which signals matter, we expose a superset of evidence and let the LLM decide for itself which to use, guided by evaluation feedback alone; because it writes the reward as code, that choice is directly auditable. On a held-out four-month out-of-time test, the dual-stream agent beats the prior labeled-only agent at every target recall, by +4.7, +2.4 and +3.0 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80%, 85% and 90% recall, and the production baseline by +6.8 points on average. The resulting policy is architecturally identical to that of Qu et al. (2025) and adds no inference cost.
papers.summary: Production fraud models are trained only on transactions that were approved, because transactions a legacy system blocked never receive fraud labels; this is the reject-inference problem. The authors extend an existing approach in which an LLM evolves the reward function of a two-step `REINFORCE` fraud-blocking policy. In their version, the LLM writes a dual-stream reward: one stream scores labeled transactions with dollar-weighted precision, and the other scores unlabeled blocked transactions by contrasting a newer gradient-boosted risk signal with the legacy scores that caused the block. On a four-month out-of-time test, the policy beats the earlier labeled-only agent at every target recall, including **+4.7 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80% recall**, with no added inference cost and a reward that can be audited as code.

papers.title: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model.
