To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at https://github.com/taikunudel/RL-ATTACK.
papers.summary: `RL-ATTACK` is a black-box adversarial attack on language models in which a reinforcement-learning attacker learns, from the target model's own responses, which text transformations to apply, instead of relying on external knowledge to guess them. On natural language inference it **drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries**, and it improves query efficiency and semantic preservation over baselines. Against generative question-answering models, the trained attacker consistently beats the untrained one and outperforms a strong optimization-based baseline in 4 of 6 settings. The authors also compare several reward designs and training settings and find that none is consistently best.

papers.title: An Educated Guess: Deriving Statistically Aligned Gradient Estimates for Zeroth-Order Optimisation
papers.abstract: As novel hardware architectures are explored for the purposes of machine learning, including neuromorphic chips, asynchronous systems, and ASICs, effective learning algorithms are highly desirable. While backpropagation is the standard for differentiation on standard hardware, its requirement for global synchrony and exact differentiability limits the exploration of exotic algorithms on non-traditional substrates and devices. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation methods, such as SPSA and weight perturbation, offer a compelling alternative by estimating gradients through inference-only passes; however, these methods have historically suffered due to the `curse of dimensionality', where random perturbations become increasingly misaligned with the true gradient in high-dimensional spaces. In this work, we move beyond blind random noise by deriving zeroth-order search directions from activation geometry available during the forward pass. This leads to a family of Spectral Zeroth-Order methods, SZO-$\kappa$, whose directions solve local response-based gradient-guessing objectives under explicit stochastic assumptions. These methods explore feature-supported directions that are more likely to produce informative loss responses. Using multilayer and convolutional networks, we analyse gradient alignment, bias-variance structure, and training stability of these methods relative to standard perturbation baselines and backpropagation.
papers.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimizers such as `SPSA` and weight perturbation estimate gradients using only forward passes, which makes them attractive for neuromorphic chips, asynchronous systems, and other hardware where backpropagation is hard to run. Their random perturbations, however, become increasingly misaligned with the true gradient as dimensionality grows. The authors derive the search directions from activation geometry available during the forward pass instead, producing a family of Spectral Zeroth-Order methods (`SZO-κ`) that solve explicit gradient-guessing objectives under stated statistical assumptions. On multilayer and convolutional networks, they analyze how these **feature-supported directions** compare with standard perturbation methods and backpropagation in gradient alignment, bias and variance, and training stability.

papers.title: Patching the Blind Spots: Reversible LLM Rule Overlay for Frozen Fraud Detectors
papers.abstract: In industrial tabular fraud classification, gradient-boosted trees remain state-of-the-art, but even a well-trained model has blind spots, and retraining the deployed model is not always safe. We propose a framework that patches such a model without modifying it: LLMs propose rules anchored on features the model underweights by SHAP, and the resulting noisy pool is screened for empirical support and calibrated into an additive, reversible log-lift overlay that runs at the production cut-off. Single-LLM benefit is high-variance and inverts between datasets, so we pool three diverse backbones by equal-weight logit averaging, trading peak gain for a bounded worst case. On a real-world e-commerce fraud detector trained on selection-biased data, continued training regresses even when carefully tuned, whereas the overlay gains on average +2.26% recall at equal precision ($\Delta$R@P) and +1.60% precision at equal recall ($\Delta$P@R) over production cut-offs spanning 30-57% precision and 23-63% recall. On a public benchmark of seven designed bias-shift variants it raises $\Delta$P@R on every variant and keeps $\Delta$R@P near neutral. Each amendment is a readable predicate naming the fraud pattern it covers.
papers.summary: Deployed gradient-boosted fraud classifiers have blind spots, and retraining them in production is not always safe. The authors leave the model unchanged and patch it from outside: LLMs propose rules built on features the model underweights according to SHAP, the rules are screened for empirical support, and the survivors are calibrated into an additive, reversible log-lift overlay applied at the production cut-off. Because the benefit from any single LLM varies widely and can reverse between datasets, three different LLMs are combined by equal-weight logit averaging to bound the worst case. On a real e-commerce fraud detector, where continued training made results worse, the overlay gains on average **+2.26% recall at equal precision and +1.60% precision at equal recall**, and each added rule is a readable predicate naming the fraud pattern it targets.

papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
papers.summary: Conversational recommender systems typically treat each user session in isolation. The authors propose a multi-agent architecture in which LLMs act as orchestrators that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and the flow of the conversation, with long-term memory built in as a first-class component that shapes both routing and query formation. In experiments on the `Amazon Reviews` dataset, memory-enabled sessions recover up to 63% of the gap to sessions where users give explicit queries, and **supervisory orchestration raises user acceptance by 28.9 percentage points**. LLM reranking does not improve `Hit@K` but does improve semantic consistency and diversity, which the authors measure with a new Semantic Consistency Score (`SCS`).

papers.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Evaluating Timing and Omission in Longitudinal AI Mental Health Support
papers.abstract: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support commonly focus on the clinical appropriateness of individual responses, potentially overlooking failures that emerge across extended interactions. As AI assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances and prior disclosures, this raises an accountability question: Do AI chatbots provide appropriate support as users' needs evolve? We investigate by analyzing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, examining how a memory-equipped assistant responds to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles. We introduce the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, to assess the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. Advice was less aligned with users' readiness after a crisis than in matched control stretches of the same conversation, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and users' communication style changed how often and when the assistant gave recommendations. Although explicitly unproductive advice was rare, the assistant frequently omitted clinician-expected support such as follow-up and planning for next steps. These findings show the limits of single response-level safety evaluation and the need to assess timing, omission, and consistency across users when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.
papers.summary: Evaluations of LLMs for mental health support usually judge one response at a time, which can miss failures that only appear over long conversations with a memory-equipped assistant. The authors run 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, covering suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises, and score them with `CARE` (Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative), a framework developed with mental health professionals that assesses the timing of advice and what is left out. After a crisis, advice was **less aligned with users' readiness than in matched control stretches, mostly because it came too early**, especially when recovery stalled. Explicitly unproductive advice was rare, but the assistant often omitted support clinicians expect, such as follow-up and planning next steps.

papers.title: Structuring Survey Histories for LLM Digital Twins: A Controlled Study of Background, Decision Procedure, and Evaluation Profiles
papers.abstract: LLM-based digital twins aim to predict how individuals would respond in new settings from representations of their prior responses. Existing evidence that compression of survey histories need not reduce predictive accuracy suggests that representation structure, rather than information volume alone, may be an important design choice. We study BDE, a fixed representation that organizes each respondent's survey history into Background, Decision procedure, and Evaluation. We evaluate it on Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025) by predicting each respondent's held-out answers on 17 tasks. In a paired evaluation with 100 respondents, a fully inferred BDE profile improves overall accuracy over the raw survey transcript by 1.27 percentage points (pp) on gpt-5.4-nano (p < 0.01) and 1.19 pp on gpt-5.4-mini (p < 0.001). Three analyses then examine the schema, extraction depth, and component composition. Against a length-matched free-form profile written from the same transcript by the same extractor, BDE improves pricing accuracy on both simulators (2.15 pp on nano, p < 0.01; 1.38 pp on mini, p < 0.05), while its overall advantage is significant only on nano (1.05 pp, p < 0.05). Allowing deeper inference during extraction yields no statistically significant gain on either simulator. By contrast, adding Evaluation to a Background--Decision procedure profile improves overall accuracy by 1.44 pp on nano (p < 0.001) and 1.22 pp on mini (p < 0.001). These results indicate that the advantage over raw transcripts is not explained by compression or length alone, and attribute it primarily to profile composition rather than deeper extraction.
papers.summary: LLM-based digital twins predict how a person would answer new survey questions from a representation of their earlier answers, and the authors test whether the structure of that representation matters. `BDE` organizes each respondent's survey history into Background, Decision procedure, and Evaluation. On `Twin-2K-500`, predicting held-out answers across 17 tasks for 100 respondents, it improves accuracy over the raw transcript by **1.27 percentage points on `gpt-5.4-nano` and 1.19 on `gpt-5.4-mini`**. Ablations suggest the gain comes mainly from what the profile contains, especially the Evaluation component, rather than from compression, length, or deeper inference during extraction.

papers.title: On Differentially Private Mechanisms for Linear Regression
papers.abstract:
We study the classic least-squares linear regression problem under differential privacy (DP) in the batch and the continual observation setting. In the latter setting, the mechanism receives a stream of $n$ data points $(x_i,y_i)$ ($x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$) and must output an estimate of the optimal parameters at each time step $i$. Although differentially private linear regression has been extensively studied in the batch setting, the problem remains underexplored for the continual setting, with prior work being restricted to constrained linear regression and update time polynomial in $n$.
  In this work, we introduce ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual differential privacy. Our mechanism's suboptimality gap is proportional to $\sqrt{d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. It requires $O(d^2\log{n})$ space and $O(d^2\log{n}+d^{\omega})$ update time, where $d$ is the dimension of the input space.
  We also study fundamental limits of differentially private linear regression by showing the first lower bounds for the box-constrained least-squares linear regression problem. Our lower bounds are proportional to $\min(n,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log^{1.5}d})$ for $(1,O(\frac{1}{n}))$-DP, and $\min(n,\frac{d}{\epsilon})$ for $\epsilon$-DP, and are derived using a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem from [Peter et al., 2024], providing new insights into the inherent hardness of this canonical task.
  Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets shows that the accuracy of our continual observation mechanism clearly outperforms any other known differentially private mechanism for this problem such as rerunning the batch algorithm at each time step.
papers.summary: The authors study least-squares linear regression under differential privacy (DP), both in the batch setting and in the continual-observation setting, where a new estimate must be released after every incoming data point. They introduce `ContinualAdaSSP`, **the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual DP**; its suboptimality gap scales with the square root of the dimension times polylogarithmic factors in the stream length, and its space and update time grow only logarithmically with that length. They also prove the first lower bounds for box-constrained private linear regression, via a reduction from a fingerprinting-code problem. On real datasets, the continual mechanism outperforms existing private alternatives, including rerunning the batch algorithm at every step.

papers.title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference
papers.abstract: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.
papers.summary: Most LLM architectures fix their compute per token at training time. `AlterNet` combines a Mixture-of-Experts design using shallow experts with a dynamic-depth mechanism, so the model can decide how much computation each input needs and can be **scaled down after training without retraining** when inference has to be faster or cheaper. The design relies on iterative computation, sequence-level routing by depth controlled by a halting mechanism inside the experts, a depth encoding that tracks progress through the chain, and a regularizer that encourages efficient use of compute. Only initial benchmarks are reported, along with directions for future work.

papers.title: How are viral trends different from educational and commercial uses of LLM image generation and editing? A privacy-preserving descriptive analysis
papers.abstract: Gemini's Nano Banana models, first introduced in late 2025, led to a shift in the capabilities and use of image generation and editing. We utilize Urania, a Google-developed framework for generating insights about LLM chatbot interactions with rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees, to analyze use cases and intents, techniques and ways of prompting, without ever looking at a single image or individual prompt. We select a subsample of 2.1M conversations in early 2026 which utilized Nano Banana models, into roughly 800 clusters in five categories: (1) Social & Viral Sharing, (2) Brand & Marketing Collateral, (3) Educational & Technical Information Media, (4) Product Visualizations & E-commerce, and (5) Architectural & Spatial Designs. We then compare these clusters on 21 features of use, measuring aspects of prompts' (a) editing techniques, (b) artistic style requests, (c) composition, and (d) chatbot interactions. This allows us to describe a baseline of how people are using image generation and editing tools for different use cases---(including growing and emergent use cases which were not possible before Nano Banana)---in a privacy-preserving manner.
papers.summary: Using `Urania`, a Google framework that analyzes chatbot conversations with formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees and without anyone viewing individual prompts or images, the authors study how people use Gemini's `Nano Banana` image generation and editing models. They group 2.1M conversations from early 2026 into about 800 clusters across five categories: social and viral sharing, brand and marketing, educational and technical media, product visualization and e-commerce, and architectural and spatial design. The categories are then compared on 21 usage features covering editing techniques, style requests, composition, and how users interact with the chatbot. The result is a **privacy-preserving baseline of real-world image-generation use cases**, including emerging ones that earlier models could not support.

papers.title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning can make LLMs more resistant to jailbreaks, but it is costly and can erase existing capabilities, so recent defenses intervene on specific internal components instead. Earlier methods choose where to intervene and how strongly in separate steps. `AttentionSwitch` instead **jointly learns a sparse set of attention heads and query-conditioned scaling factors** inside a frozen LLM, attenuating or amplifying those heads' outputs without changing the direction of their representations. Across popular models and jailbreak attacks it outperforms existing defenses, especially when little training data is available.

papers.title: Random Symbolic Boosting: A Geometric Approach to Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Symbolic models offer interpretability, but their construction through generational evolution can be computationally expensive. This article presents Random Symbolic Boosting (RSB), a method that constructs explicit additive symbolic models via boosting over populations of randomly generated syntax trees, eliminating the need for generational evolution. The idea combines two observations: high-dimensional spaces can be spanned by enough linearly independent vectors, and the semantics of syntax trees can be directly manipulated as such vectors. It is shown that, for Ordinary Least Squares, the boosting process guarantees a monotonic reduction of the training error for both regression and classification. Furthermore, an adaptive geometric early stopping mechanism is introduced. It is based on the angle between the prediction and target vectors, is independent of the problems scale, and requires no adjustments across tasks. Evaluated on a standard benchmark for symbolic regression, the method is located at the Pareto-optimal point between predictive accuracy and training time, ranking first on the real-world datasets. Additionally, it was tested on a large tabular classification benchmark with 200 problems, achieving competitive results.
papers.summary: Random Symbolic Boosting (`RSB`) builds interpretable additive symbolic models by boosting over populations of randomly generated syntax trees, avoiding the costly generation-by-generation evolution that symbolic regression normally uses. It treats each tree's outputs on the data as a vector, relying on the fact that enough linearly independent vectors can span a high-dimensional space, and the authors show that with ordinary least squares the boosting process monotonically reduces training error. An early-stopping rule based on the angle between the prediction and target vectors needs no tuning across tasks. On a standard symbolic-regression benchmark, `RSB` sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus training time and **ranks first on the real-world datasets**, and it is competitive on a 200-problem tabular classification benchmark.

papers.title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.
papers.summary: `AtariBench` tests whether vision-language models (VLMs) can act in dynamic environments by having them play 20 Atari 2600 games from high-frame-rate gameplay streams, with game time decoupled from the model's inference speed. State-of-the-art VLMs show substantial gaps: they **often fail to infer object motion and direction**, make brittle sequential decisions, and lean on the text history of the interaction even when new visual feedback is appended. The authors also introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores reliably indicate competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting affect performance.

papers.title: Debate to Deceive: Poisoning LLM's Fact-Checking via Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Knowledge attacks on Large Language Models, such as manipulating fact-checking judgments, pose significant risks to AI reliability. Existing approaches -- adversarial suffix/template injection and single-agent self-reflection -- lack robustness across diverse defenses and are prone to confirmation bias and costly trial-and-error, respectively. We propose Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework grounded in human debate structure and rhetorical style, enabling agents to generate adversarial passages that are semantically coherent, rhetorically effective, and resistant to early confirmation bias. D2D formalizes the adversarial process as an evolutionary game in which agents adaptively evolve their rhetorical strategies (Logos, Pathos, Ethos) through competition. To manage the intractably large LLM output space, we decouple agent behavior into a strategic layer, which selects a rhetorical action from a compact strategy space via evolutionary-inspired learning dynamics, and a generation layer, where the LLM produces a concrete passage conditioned on that strategy and the debate context. On four fact-checking benchmarks (FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact), D2D substantially outperforms existing attacks and evades most defenses.
papers.summary: `D2D` (Debate-to-Deceive) attacks LLM fact-checking by having multiple agents debate in order to produce adversarial passages that are coherent and rhetorically persuasive. Earlier suffix-injection and self-reflection attacks either fail against varied defenses or suffer from confirmation bias and costly trial and error. `D2D` models the attack as an evolutionary game: a strategic layer picks a rhetorical approach (appeal to logic, emotion, or credibility) from a small strategy space, and a generation layer has the LLM write the passage conditioned on that choice and the debate so far. On `FEVER`, `HealthVer`, `CLIMATE-FEVER`, and `SciFact`, it **substantially outperforms existing attacks and evades most defenses**.

papers.title: Goals as a Representational Layer for Human-AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: Goals are central to how people, teams, and organizations structure their work. Yet, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly operate across a worker's context, information about why a person is pursuing a task, beyond local prompts and interactions, is typically missing. We argue that goals should become an explicit representational layer mediating interactions among people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partially latent, and dynamically evolving, such a layer must be multidimensional, both grounded in human articulation and inferred from available evidence, and continuously updated. A goal layer could connect immediate requests to broader outcomes, improve the organization and retrieval of relevant context, support reflection and coordination, and provide a foundation for training, aligning, and evaluating AI systems in terms of human-centered outcomes. We highlight these opportunities while identifying open challenges involving goal inference, socio-cognitive frictions, alignment, privacy, and governance.
papers.summary: Generative AI systems increasingly work across a person's context, but they rarely know why the person is pursuing a task beyond the immediate prompt. The authors argue that goals should become an explicit representational layer between people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partly unstated, and change over time, they propose that **such a layer must be multidimensional, combine what people state with what is inferred from evidence, and be updated continuously**. They outline how this could improve context retrieval, coordination, and how AI is trained and evaluated against human-centered outcomes. They also list open problems in goal inference, social and cognitive friction, alignment, privacy, and governance.

papers.title: CrowdDirector: Runtime Orchestration of Crowd Simulation through Natural-Language Directives
papers.abstract: Natural language offers an intuitive way to direct a virtual crowd while a simulation is running. Handwritten rules execute efficiently but cannot respond flexibly to varied instructions, whereas asking a large language model (LLM) to control the crowd at every update introduces repeated latency, cost, and the risk of unsupported actions. We present CrowdDirector, a framework that uses an LLM only when the user adds or changes an instruction. The LLM translates the request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks whether the entities and actions it references exist in the current Unity scene. Accepted instructions are stored and remain continuously active as the simulation is running. At each simulation tick, a graph neural network uses the current scene state and active instruction to choose an available action and target for each agent, while Unity handles movement, interactions, and animation. The network is trained offline on simulated scenarios, with LLM guidance on how agents should respond to instructions. Our evaluations show the scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgements more often than the LLM's own assessment, and on a behavioural benchmark CrowdDirector follows user instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls. It therefore provides a practical middle ground between fixed rules and continuous LLM control.
papers.summary: `CrowdDirector` lets users steer a running crowd simulation with natural-language instructions without calling a large language model (LLM) at every update. An LLM is used only when an instruction is added or changed: it converts the request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks that the referenced entities and actions exist in the `Unity` scene. At each simulation tick, a graph neural network trained offline picks an action and target for each agent while `Unity` handles movement and animation. The scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgments more often than the LLM's own assessment, and **the system follows instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls**.

papers.title: MEDALLION: Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON
papers.abstract: Dimensionality reduction is widely used to visualize high-dimensional data and guide scientific discovery, yet interpreting which original features contribute to low-dimensional representations remains challenging, particularly for black-box methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. We introduce \textbf{MEDALLION} (Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON), a novel framework for interpreting low-dimensional embeddings through knowledge distillation and neural feature attribution. MEDALLION distills any given embedding with a neural encoder which we explain via a broad range of existing neural feature attribution methods. Through experiments on MNIST and applications in single-cell transcriptomics, we show MEDALLION provides informative feature attributions that cast additional insights into the underlying embedding and compare its performance with existing interpretability approaches.
papers.summary: It is hard to tell which original features drive low-dimensional embeddings produced by black-box methods such as `t-SNE` and `UMAP`. `MEDALLION` (Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON) distills any given embedding into a neural encoder and then explains that encoder with standard neural feature-attribution methods. In experiments on `MNIST` and single-cell transcriptomics data, the authors report that **the framework yields informative feature attributions that add insight into the underlying embedding**, and they compare it with existing interpretability approaches.

papers.title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. We formalise privilege escalation (PE) as the system-level security objective: an action may proceed only if every principal that influenced it would allow it. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. Its kernel, ITES, derives authority from provenance and the organisation's existing access-control system and intersects the permissions of every influencing principal. We prove a conditional authority-confinement theorem: under complete mediation, no-laundering provenance, a known non-empty decision context, fresh permission checks, and action binding, the kernel admits no action that escalates privilege with respect to any recorded influencing principal. The theorem covers the represented value-influence fragment; control influence from tool, branch, recipient, or plan-step selection remains a refinement obligation. Conflux extends the kernel with independent policy ports, argument-aware authorisation, disclosure, consent, delegation, restriction, and exposure planning. We describe two system- level evaluators. SLED is a black-box evaluator: it exhaustively explores a declared finite model of a defence up to a bound. SLED-V is a white-box evaluator: it checks a serialisable intermediate representation against security and provenance properties. The evidence is bounded and partial. The appendix reports retained AgentDojo, SLED, and SLED-V results, including the limits of those runs. No result in this paper is an unbounded deployment guarantee.
papers.summary: LLM agents combine input from several principals (the users, services, and data sources whose instructions or content reach the agent) and act on it, which creates a risk of privilege escalation. The authors define the security goal as allowing an action only if every principal that influenced it would permit it, and they argue that enforcement must sit outside the model's judgment. `Conflux` uses a kernel, `ITES`, that derives authority from provenance and the organization's existing access controls and intersects the permissions of all influencing principals. Under stated conditions, including complete mediation and fresh permission checks, they prove that **the kernel admits no action that escalates privilege relative to any recorded influencing principal**, though influence through tool or plan-step selection is not covered. Two bounded evaluators, the black-box `SLED` and the white-box `SLED-V`, plus `AgentDojo` runs provide partial evidence; the authors state that no result is an unbounded deployment guarantee.

papers.title: Federated training performs as well as centralized for 3D Latent Diffusion for Diagnosis-Conditioned Brain MRI Synthesis
papers.abstract: Generative models of brain MRI are useful to understand brain conditions, and to enrich scarce and imbalanced neuroimaging data. However, training these models requires large, multi-site training sets, which is challenging. Federated learning (FL) allows for training deep learning models without sharing data. We show that training a 3D conditional latent model federatedly (where data is kept private at each site) performs similarly to centralized training (where all the data have been copied to a single site). We evaluate three metrics: conditional fidelity (how well generated MRIs perform in classification), diversity (how the generated images match the real data distribution, using MultiScale-SSIM), and realism (how close generated images are to real images, using Fr\'{e}chet Inception Distance). Our results show that federated training is a viable route to develop multi-site generative models of brain MRI.
papers.summary: Generative models of brain MRI need large multi-site training sets, but medical data is hard to share. The authors train a 3D latent diffusion model conditioned on diagnosis using federated learning (FL), which keeps each site's data private, and compare it with centralized training on pooled data. They measure conditional fidelity through downstream classification, diversity with `MultiScale-SSIM`, and realism with Fréchet Inception Distance (`FID`). **Federated training performed similarly to centralized training on all three metrics**, which suggests FL is a workable way to build multi-site generative models of brain MRI.

papers.title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
papers.abstract: Can a network look stable at every layer and still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a basic stability quantity appearing in optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates. Deep networks naturally admit two such notions, input Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to data perturbations, and parameter Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to weight perturbations. We prove that, for deep networks with normalization layers, with batch normalization as the canonical example, both Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth and hence with parameter dimension, even under strong per-layer norm control such as $\|W_\ell\|_2\le 1$, and already for linear activations. Thus, a mechanism widely used to stabilize training can create severe worst-case instabilities that are invisible locally, i.e., from layerwise norm bounds alone. Parameter-Lipschitz explosion turns Lipschitz-dependent nonsmooth optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds for deep normalized networks, while input-Lipschitz explosion makes worst-case Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates vacuous. The latter also yields a concrete rank-separation mechanism for adversarial vulnerability. The theory predicts that perturbations introducing new singular directions should be amplified much more strongly than perturbations at the same noise level that remain within the input's original singular subspace. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support this prediction, showing that rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than same-subspace perturbations.
papers.summary: The authors examine whether networks with normalization layers can look stable at every layer yet be unstable as a whole. They prove that, for deep networks with normalization such as batch normalization, **both input and parameter Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth even when every layer's weight norm is at most 1 and activations are linear**. As a result, Lipschitz-based optimization guarantees become exponential in dimension, and Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates become vacuous. The theory also predicts that perturbations that add new singular directions should be amplified much more than perturbations of the same size within the input's existing subspace. Experiments on `MNIST`, `Fashion-MNIST`, and `CIFAR-10` support this, with rank-creating perturbations causing sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins.

papers.title: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
papers.abstract: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.
papers.summary: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) gives one score per document pair, so when several sources contribute to a target it cannot separate each source's own contribution from vocabulary they share. Semantic Conditional Similarity (`SCS`) compares two documents after removing semantic elements they share with a third document, using set operations. This makes comparisons directional and asymmetric, and **it splits shared and residual content without needing a similarity threshold**. The framework is developed for many sources and one target, extends to other source-target configurations, and its scores are meant to be read as rankings rather than absolute measurements.

papers.title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
papers.abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.
papers.summary: Persistent-memory systems for language models decide not only what to retrieve but which stored information is allowed to change current outputs. Jacobian-causal memory control (`JCMC`) represents each permitted memory intervention by a predicted influence signature, chooses interventions that hit a target effect within a side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects to decide whether to keep or roll back the change. Under smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, the authors prove bounds on local approximation error, reachable effects, selection regret, and interactions between simultaneous memories. **The paper reports no benchmark results**; it instead defines an estimator and an evaluation protocol against relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines.

papers.title: Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
papers.abstract: The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. Fine-tuning promises high-performing models at a fraction of the cost of training a base model, but it can also produce unintended behavioral changes. Multiple studies have shown that safety guardrails can erode with fine-tuning, yet large-scale studies across model architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methodologies remain limited. Where prior work in this space has studied value-centric refusal, this work focuses on knowledge-centric abstention. We audit 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned large language models against 11 paired base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge-centric abstention. We find that defined appropriate abstention measured by these benchmarks, already low in base models (median 8.3% on MedAbstain), falls further after fine-tuning (median 4.2%, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs on MedAbstain), and that the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs. These results motivate fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a model for a domain can weaken its safety behavior. This study looks at knowledge-centric abstention, meaning declining to answer when the model lacks the knowledge, rather than refusals based on values. The authors audit 25 biomedical fine-tuned models against 11 matching base checkpoints on `MedAbstain` and `ClinDet-Bench`. Appropriate abstention is already rare in base models (median 8.3% on `MedAbstain`) and **falls further after fine-tuning to a median of 4.2%, dropping in 21 of 25 pairs**. The size and direction of the change vary across pairs.

papers.title: Aligning, Fast and Slow: A Control-Theoretic Oversight Framework for Long-Horizon Trajectories and Maintained Deployments
papers.abstract: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while retaining memory or code changes that alter their later behavior. We introduce a control-theoretic framework that couples a fast loop controlling proposed actions with a slow loop reviewing persistent changes and reassessing configurations after model or tool updates. When measurement errors and changes between checks are bounded and controllers can enforce their decisions, we derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort. In simulation, dividing a fixed review budget between both loops reduces mean maximum departure from intended behavior roughly twelvefold compared with review confined to individual runs. In coding stress tests with authored memories and five matched seeds, combined controls reduce mean severity on a 0-3 scale from 0.325 without gates to 0.117, resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates; in trading stress tests, combined controls reduce mean shortfall in low-emission purchases from 0.892 without gates to 0.107. The overall framework helps developers and auditors compare and enforce oversight designs, while the agent studies test component controls rather than the full deployment-level guarantee.
papers.summary: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while keeping memory or code changes that alter their later behavior. The authors propose a control-theoretic oversight framework with a fast loop that reviews proposed actions and a slow loop that reviews persistent changes and re-checks configurations after model or tool updates. Assuming bounded measurement error and enforceable decisions, they derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort between the loops. In simulation, **splitting a fixed review budget across both loops cuts the mean maximum deviation from intended behavior about twelvefold** compared with reviewing only individual runs. In coding stress tests, the combined controls reduce mean severity from 0.325 to 0.117 while resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates, and trading stress tests show a similar reduction in shortfall.

papers.title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles
papers.abstract: Low-rank approximation is a basic tool for inference from large and noisy data matrices. However, when noise variances differ across entries, a setting known as heteroskedasticity, the noise can distort the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals. To address these challenges, we develop BRINE (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer), a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize the average noise variance across both dimensions. Under suitable conditions, this procedure restores the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and can amplify signal components without prior knowledge of the signal or noise structure. A key idea underlying our approach is to equalize the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. At the population level, we identify a potential function that characterizes this equalization and motivates an iterative minimization procedure. We prove convergence of the iterations to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. The updates can be estimated directly from noisy data, and we establish probabilistic error bounds for the scaling factors. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.
papers.summary: When noise variances differ across the entries of a large data matrix, a setting called heteroskedasticity, low-rank approximation can produce spurious components and miss weak signals. `BRINE` (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer) iteratively rescales rows and columns so that average noise variance is equal along both dimensions, using the diagonal of the data resolvent (a matrix function of the data) as a stand-in for the unknown variances. The authors prove that **the iterations converge to the true equalizer for any positive variance profile**, at a geometric rate under mild conditions, and give error bounds for the scaling factors estimated from data. Simulations and experiments on several types of biological data illustrate the method.

papers.title: Learning from How Users Interpret: Personalizing Recommendation Explanation Order
papers.abstract: Personalized explanations typically adapt their content or presentation based on preferences, interaction histories, or other user characteristics. We examine whether regularities inferred from prior textual interpretations can support personalization of explanation organization. In a controlled within participant study with 122 participants, prior interpretations were represented along three dimensions: information selection, relative salience, and relational organization. The relational dimension was partially operationalized through co mobilization. These representations were aggregated into fixed historical profiles and used to organize otherwise identical explanation sentences. Participants encountered four organization procedures: the OWN historical profile, the DONOR historical profile, a population profile called POP, and a language model procedure using the historical profile called PROFILE LLM. Post exposure objective comprehension was the primary outcome. OWN achieved 86.5 percent correct responses, compared with 66.0 percent for DONOR, 63.9 percent for POP, and 73.0 percent for PROFILE LLM. Mixed effects analyses showed higher comprehension with OWN than with each alternative procedure. No reliable overall condition effect was detected for recommendation acceptance. These findings indicate that historical profiles derived from prior interpretations can provide an actionable signal for personalizing explanation order while keeping explanatory content and wording fixed.
papers.summary: Personalized explanations usually adapt their content. This study tests whether the order of explanation sentences can be personalized based on how a user interpreted earlier texts. In a within-participant study with 122 participants, the same explanation sentences were ordered using the participant's own historical profile (`OWN`), another person's profile (`DONOR`), a population profile (`POP`), or a language-model procedure using the profile (`PROFILE LLM`). **`OWN` reached 86.5% correct comprehension answers versus 66.0%, 63.9%, and 73.0% for the alternatives**, while acceptance of the recommendations showed no reliable difference between conditions.

papers.title: Training Stability under Adaptive Curricula
papers.abstract: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approaches train reinforcement learning (RL) agents on diverse curricula that may evolve with their capabilities. While prior work has largely focused on how these curricula are constructed, we study whether their students remain trainable under the resulting distributions. Across multiple UED mechanisms, environment complexities, and extended training horizons, we identify recurring learner-side pathologies, including parameter growth, degraded value--outcome ordering, and loss of representational diversity, that accompany stagnation and performance degradation. These findings connect limitations in UED to optimization failures previously identified in conventional deep RL, while showing how adaptive curricula couple the learner's optimization state to its future training distribution. Controlled interventions show that mitigating selected pathologies improves learning. Stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule or increasing environment interaction. Our results establish learner trainability as a complementary design principle for UED. Effective curricula require students that remain capable of learning from the distributions they produce.
papers.summary: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) trains reinforcement learning (RL) agents on curricula that change as the agent improves, and prior work has focused mainly on how those curricula are built. This study asks whether the agents being trained stay trainable. Across several UED methods and long training runs, the authors find recurring problems in the learner, including parameter growth, value estimates that no longer rank outcomes correctly, and loss of representational diversity, which accompany stagnation and decline. They link these to known optimization failures in deep RL. **Stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum or adding environment interactions**.

papers.title: Not All Latents Are Equal: Importance-Weighted Latent Graph Generation
papers.abstract: Graph generation has shown tremendous effectiveness in modeling complex scientific tasks ranging from molecule generation to optimized circuit design. Most recent advancements have developed models that learn to denoise noisy graphs using either discrete diffusion or flow matching. However, discrete graph diffusion scales quadratically with the number of nodes, making it difficult to use such models on larger graphs. On the other hand, latent graph generation instead seeks to denoise noisy graph latents, which scale better to more nodes due to their lower dimension. However, in practice, latent graph generation models lag behind their discrete counterparts in performance. We study this problem, finding that it is caused by the unequal distribution of that different latent dimensions have on graph reconstruction. the impact. We observe that the vast majority of impact is contained in only a smaller number of latent dimensions. Since equal emphasis is placed on reconstructing the entire latent in the loss function, existing models are optimized to reconstruct information irrelevant to the downstream task. To tackle this problem, we propose Latent Importance Reweighting ({\bf LIR)} which weights each latent dimensions via it's importance to final graph reconstruction. Importance is calculated as the relative influence of a single latent unit on graph reconstruction, which is represented via the Jacobian of the decoder relative to the latent. Our method is model-agnostic and requires no additional model parameters or hyperparameters. Experiments show that LIR can boost performance and lead to faster training convergence when applied to two different autoencoders on various benchmark datasets. Code: https://github.com/biraaj/GraphGenLatentReweight
papers.summary: Latent graph generation scales better than discrete graph diffusion, whose cost grows quadratically with node count, but it usually performs worse. The authors trace this gap to the fact that **most of the impact on graph reconstruction is concentrated in a small number of latent dimensions**, while standard losses weight all dimensions equally. Latent Importance Reweighting (`LIR`) weights each latent dimension by its influence on reconstruction, computed from the decoder's Jacobian, and adds no parameters or hyperparameters. Applied to two different autoencoders on several benchmarks, `LIR` improves generation quality and speeds up training convergence.

papers.title: TopoSHAP: Shapley for Explainable and Efficient Topological Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) extends learning on graphs, such as molecules or social networks, to higher-order structures, such as rings in a molecule or groups in a social network. Explaining which of these structures drive a model's predictions, and which architectural components matter most for its performance, remains challenging. We introduce TopoSHAP, an efficient and general explanation framework that addresses both questions across topological domains and model architectures. TopoSHAP-cell assigns Shapley values to topological data cells and extracts compact explanations. These explanations match or outperform graph-based counterparts on GraphXAI benchmark data while running up to 112$\times$ faster. They also reveal advantageous topological feature design, leading to measured improvements in explanation recovery and predictive accuracy. On the architecture side, TopoSHAP-neighbor explains how neighborhoods contribute to model performance, and turns these evaluations into a backward-elimination search that identifies smaller, competitive architectures early in training. This is up to $11.3\times$ cheaper than traditional TDL training sweeps.
papers.summary: Topological deep learning (TDL) extends graph learning to higher-order structures such as rings in molecules or groups in social networks, but it is hard to explain which structures and architectural components drive results. `TopoSHAP-cell` assigns Shapley values to topological cells and produces compact explanations that match or beat graph-based methods on `GraphXAI` benchmarks while **running up to 112 times faster**. `TopoSHAP-neighbor` scores how each neighborhood type contributes to performance and uses those scores to prune architectures early in training, which costs up to 11.3 times less than standard TDL training sweeps.

papers.title: SteerGR: Steering Generative Recommendation via Sparse Autoencoders for Controllable Game Discovery
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation aims to predict item identifiers from user interaction histories, but explicit control over the properties of recommended items remains underexplored. A key challenge is to connect human-readable concepts to internal features whose interventions effectively change the recommended items. To address this, we propose Steerable Generative Recommender (SteerGR), a framework that uses sparse autoencoders for concept-level control in game discovery. SteerGR proceeds through three stages: (i) Concept Definition and Grounding for defining play concepts with an LLM; (ii) Feature Discovery and Selection for discovering candidate features by their concept associations and selecting one by its steering effect; and (iii) Sparse Feature Intervention for amplifying or suppressing selected features to steer recommendations without retraining the recommender. Extensive experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that the selected features successfully steer recommendations toward or away from target concepts. We believe this work takes a first step to extend SAE-based steering from LLMs to industrial generative recommendation.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders predict item identifiers from a user's history, but they offer little direct control over what kind of items they recommend. Steerable Generative Recommender (`SteerGR`) uses sparse autoencoders to connect human-readable play concepts, defined with an LLM, to internal features of the recommender. It then amplifies or suppresses those features to steer recommendations without retraining. In experiments with two industrial generative recommenders on a real-world game dataset, **the selected features steered recommendations toward or away from target concepts**.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction
papers.abstract: Reward models used for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are commonly selected using held-out data. When sample size and context dimension grow proportionally, the difference in test risk between models fitted on the full sample and on a fixed fraction of it need not vanish. Held-out evaluation can therefore consistently estimate the test risk of the model trained on the smaller sample, but because the relative ranking of candidate reward models can change after full-data refitting, held-out selection can be suboptimal. We develop an Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion that estimates the full-data reward model's out-of-sample risk under the target policy using only its training observations. This enables early stopping along the full-data gradient-descent trajectory without sample splitting. For neural networks with fixed depth and hidden width under Gaussian contexts, single-index rewards, context-dependent multi-index target policies, and known context-independent logging, we prove uniform consistency of our criterion over a fixed finite set of gradient-descent iterates and a near-oracle guarantee for the selected reward model. The same correction yields a doubly robust estimator that consistently estimates the true policy value without sample splitting, even when reward-model prediction error does not vanish. Experiments show decreasing risk-estimation error as dimension grows at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, and improved reward-model selection relative to held-out baselines. Empirically, our correction also reduces the root mean squared error of doubly robust value estimates computed from the same data used to fit and select the reward models.
papers.summary: In off-policy evaluation (OPE), reward models are usually selected on held-out data, but when sample size and context dimension grow together, the model trained on a subset can rank differently from the model refit on all the data. The authors develop an Onsager-corrected criterion, weighted by the target policy, that estimates the out-of-sample risk of the full-data model from its own training observations. This allows early stopping along gradient descent without splitting the sample. For fixed-size neural networks under Gaussian contexts and related assumptions, they prove consistency and a near-oracle guarantee. The same correction also gives **a doubly robust policy-value estimator that stays consistent without sample splitting**, and experiments show better reward-model selection and lower estimation error than held-out baselines.

papers.title: MotionDecipher: LLM-Assisted Clinical Interpretation of Human Motion Signals for Efficient Gait Analysis
papers.abstract: Clinical gait and motion analysis is widely used to guide targeted interventions for patients with neurological disorders, the outcome of which is typically a report with descriptions of joint movements and forces. Current practices rely on experts' manual effort, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide opportunities to address this problem, but translating human motion into clinical gait descriptions remains challenging because the quality of the context directly affects LLMs' reasoning capability over continuous motion signals. To tackle this, we introduce MotionDecipher, a novel framework bridging the semantic gap between motion data and clinical interpretations. Specifically, we made 3 key advancements: 1) a Human Motion Tokenizer that converts motion signals into domain-specific tokens for time- and frequency-informed gait interpretation; 2) a Meta Feature Selector that transforms tokens into Structured Representations; and 3) a Hybrid Context Constructor to determine the optimal demonstration-based prompt for In-Context Learning. We evaluated MotionDecipher on data collected at an accredited gait lab from 122 patients and 46 controls. Results show that MotionDecipher achieves 0.91 BERTScore (13% over GPT-5), while expert evaluation ranks MotionDecipher highest in Correctness, Completeness, and Conciseness compared to baselines, highlighting its promise for efficient gait analysis.
papers.summary: Clinical gait analysis ends in expert-written reports describing joint movements and forces, which takes a lot of manual effort. `MotionDecipher` helps LLMs write these descriptions in three steps: a motion tokenizer converts motion signals into domain-specific tokens that capture time and frequency information, a feature selector turns the tokens into structured representations, and a context constructor picks the demonstration examples for in-context learning. On data from 122 patients and 46 controls at an accredited gait lab, **it reaches a `BERTScore` of 0.91, 13% higher than `GPT-5`**, and expert reviewers ranked it highest for correctness, completeness, and conciseness.

papers.title: MotionBench-XAI: Benchmarking What Shapes Shapley Explanations in Spatiotemporal Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Predicting outcomes from spatiotemporal data, such as assessing Parkinson's severity from human motion, often requires explainability in addition to accuracy. Practitioners need to know what drove the prediction, whether it be spatial (a body joint), temporal (a specific window), or both. Shapley values are attributions computed by treating input features as players in a cooperative game and measuring how the model output changes as coalitions of players are removed. Computing them involves choosing what counts as players, how absent players are imputed, and how the game is evaluated. How these choices affect explanation quality is poorly understood for spatiotemporal data, and real data carries no ground-truth attributions to check against. We present MotionBench-XAI, a benchmark built on i) five synthetic spatiotemporal datasets with exact ground-truth Shapley values, ii) three real datasets across clinical gait, electrocardiogram, and audio, iii) ten attribution methods across three player sets, and iv) three trained architectures. We show that grouping features into players, across time, space, or both, matters more than the choice of imputer. Generative imputers improve explanations only when their conditional models are accurate. On real data, the standard proxy metrics select contradictory best methods. We distill these findings into practical insights and provide an open-source pipeline.
papers.summary: Computing Shapley value explanations requires several choices: what counts as a player, how missing players are filled in (imputed), and how the game is evaluated. How these choices affect spatiotemporal data such as human motion was poorly understood. `MotionBench-XAI` combines five synthetic datasets with exact ground-truth Shapley values, three real datasets covering clinical gait, electrocardiogram, and audio, ten attribution methods, and three model architectures. **How features are grouped into players, across time, space, or both, matters more than which imputer is used**, and generative imputers help only when their conditional models are accurate. On real data, the standard proxy metrics pick contradictory best methods.

papers.title: The Matthews Correlation Coefficient: Fifty years
papers.abstract: Fifty years after its introduction, the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) remains central -and debated- in binary classification. This survey offers a comprehensive retrospective and an in-depth analysis of MCC, covering its historical development, mathematical foundations, and implications for practice. We clarify long-standing misconceptions, formalize its equivalences (to Pearson's correlation and to Chi2 in 2x2 tables), and examine its behavior under class imbalance. Beyond MCC, we develop analytical (derivatives) and graphical (contour plots) frameworks that generalize to any confusion-matrix-based metric. These frameworks expose structural properties -bias, robustness, sensitivity- that scalar summaries conceal, and they provide actionable guidance for selecting and interpreting performance measures in applications where reliability and fairness matter. Together, our results position MCC within a broader toolkit while clarifying when it is informative -and when alternatives may be preferable.
papers.summary: This survey looks back on 50 years of the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (`MCC`), a widely used and debated metric for binary classification. It covers the metric's history and mathematical foundations, corrects long-standing misconceptions, formalizes its equivalence to Pearson's correlation and to the chi-squared statistic for 2x2 tables, and examines how it behaves under class imbalance. The authors also develop **analytical (derivative-based) and graphical (contour-plot) tools that apply to any metric computed from a confusion matrix**. These tools reveal properties such as bias, robustness, and sensitivity, and they help clarify when `MCC` is informative and when other metrics may be better.

papers.title: On the Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision-Language Models: A Few Gradient Signs Are All You Need
papers.abstract: The limited supervision available for the few-shot adaptation of vision-language models makes gradient estimation particularly noisy. We find that the gradient magnitudes are severely miscalibrated, while the signs of a small top-magnitude subset remain informative. This motivates SignSparseSGD and DynSignSparseSGD, two state-free optimizers that use gradient magnitudes only to select where to update and fixed-magnitude signs to decide how to update. The static variant fixes the support after the first minibatch. The dynamic variant refreshes it at every step. Across 11 datasets, three CLIP backbones, and five shot levels, the proposed methods are competitive with or outperform parameter-efficient and optimization-based baselines on average, while exhibiting markedly lower sensitivity to long training schedules. They introduce no task-specific modules, maintain no first- or second-moment optimizer states, and use one shared configuration across datasets, backbones, and shot levels. Our code is included in the supplementary materials and will be released upon publication.
papers.summary: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models gives very little supervision, so gradient estimates are noisy. The authors find that gradient magnitudes are badly miscalibrated in this setting, while the signs of a small subset of the largest-magnitude gradients still carry useful information. They propose `SignSparseSGD` and `DynSignSparseSGD`, two optimizers that keep no optimizer state. Both use gradient magnitude only to choose which parameters to update, then apply fixed-size sign steps. The static variant fixes that choice after the first minibatch, and the dynamic variant refreshes it at every step. Across 11 datasets, three `CLIP` backbones and five shot levels, the methods match or beat parameter-efficient and optimization-based baselines on average with **one shared configuration**, and they are much less sensitive to long training schedules.

papers.title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). We first evaluate the effectiveness of static thought-injection prompts under different styles as well as tagged and untagged conditions and find that the effects of thinking tags and payload styles are all properties of the specific target model. In the second study, we exploit this model-specificity in a containerized agentic cyber range, using indirect injection prompts styled in the form of the target model's own reasoning traces to achieve attack success rates (ASR) up to 50% on operational objectives such as reverse-shell exfiltration and repository backdooring. We also find that the same malicious objective in standard prompt injection user voice never succeeds, and thinking tags suppress the agent's tendency to disclose the injection. Our results show that imitating a reasoning model's own thought style is effective for this style of attack, and that tag stripping is an unreliable defense.
papers.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce an explicit chain of thought, which opens a 'thought injection' attack: untrusted text written to look like the model's own reasoning is fed back to it. The authors test static injection prompts against production-class open-weight models such as `GLM-5.3`, `MiniMax-M2.5` and `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next`. They find that how well thinking tags and payload styles work depends on the specific target model. In a containerized agentic cyber range, indirect injections styled after the target's own reasoning traces reach **attack success rates of up to 50%** on goals such as reverse-shell exfiltration and backdooring a code repository. The same goals never succeed when written as ordinary user-voice prompt injection, and the authors conclude that stripping thinking tags is an unreliable defense.

papers.title: Global Solar Siting from Geospatial Embeddings
papers.abstract: Global solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity is rapidly growing, helping decrease our emissions and dependence on fossil fuels. However, optimally siting a solar plant remains challenging, requiring anticipation of geographical, urban, and infrastructure needs. Current methods rely on multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) using hand-picked geophysical layers and solar-resource products, however these strategies are not geographically transferable and do not capture the practical requirements of solar sites. We use geospatial embeddings, dense vectors representing geophysical properties of a location, to analyse 38,591 existing solar sites and the land they were built on to learn the latent solar suitability signal. We assess a set of linear and non-linear models and select a soft-voting ensemble of a random forest and a multilayer perceptron (RF+MLP ensemble), chosen for accuracy and large scale deployability. Validated against future installations in thirteen countries, the ensemble separates existing solar sites from random land with a median ROC-AUC of 0.90. Compared with published MCDA strategies, the ensemble increases ROC-AUC by 0.06-0.30 in every country. The ranking also concentrates real deployment: the most-suitable 20% of land holds 84% of estimated generation (annual energy yield) and 67% of installed capacity (potential power output). After applying standard siting constraints, 5.6% of global land (9.8% if cropland is permitted) remains highly suited to solar. The global 10 m resolution solar suitability dataset and code can be found here: https://github.com/Abdullahr29/Global-Solar-Siting.
