papers.summary: Choosing sites for solar photovoltaic (PV) plants usually relies on multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) over hand-picked geophysical layers, and these methods transfer poorly between regions. The authors instead train models on geospatial embeddings, dense vectors that describe a location, using 38,591 existing solar sites. They select an ensemble of a random forest and a multilayer perceptron (`RF+MLP`). Tested against later installations in thirteen countries, the ensemble separates solar sites from random land with a **median ROC-AUC of 0.90** and beats published MCDA approaches by 0.06 to 0.30 AUC in every country. After standard siting constraints are applied, it estimates that 5.6% of global land is highly suitable for solar, and the authors release a global suitability map at 10 m resolution.

papers.title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology
papers.abstract: In the lower-star filtration (LSF), simplices are assigned filtration values according to the maximum-vertex rule, with each simplex entering the filtration when its highest-valued vertex appears. A limitation of this construction is that some higher-dimensional simplices may enter simultaneously with their boundary faces, causing certain topological features to be filled immediately upon formation and thus not appear in the resulting persistence diagram. To address this limitation, we propose three alternative filtration methods: the \(\varepsilon\)-lower-star filtration (ELSF), the \(L_p\) filtration (LpF), and the softmax filtration (SMF). {ELSF introduces a dimension-dependent delay to the maximum-vertex rule,} allowing higher-dimensional simplices to enter the filtration after their boundary faces, whereas {LpF and SMF use aggregation functions that depend on all vertex values rather} than solely on their maximum. By modifying how filtration values are assigned, these methods allow simplices to enter the filtration more progressively, so that topological features such as loops and voids may persist over longer filtration intervals rather than being filled immediately. Consequently, the resulting persistence diagrams may include persistence features that are not observed under LSF, potentially providing useful information for distinguishing data populations. Experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed filtration methods are computationally efficient and can provide greater sensitivity to structural differences in the data than LSF.
papers.summary: In persistent homology, the standard lower-star filtration (LSF) assigns each simplex the value of its highest vertex. As a result, some higher-dimensional simplices enter at the same moment as their boundary faces, so certain loops and voids are filled immediately and never show up in the persistence diagram. The authors propose three alternatives. The `ε-lower-star filtration` adds a delay that depends on dimension, while the `L_p` and `softmax` filtrations aggregate over all vertex values instead of taking only the maximum. On simulated and real-world data, the new filtrations are computationally efficient and **more sensitive to structural differences** between data populations than LSF.

papers.title: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks
papers.abstract: Specialized prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but no false positive rate has been published for any of them on legal contracts. We measure eleven open-weights guards on two corpora of legal contracts and find that existing guards struggle: document-level false positive rates are as high as 92.39%; two guards fall below chance on paired AUC; and a five-regex baseline is not Pareto-dominated by any guard in the panel. Controlled probes locate model-specific as well as general failure modes. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including a second threat category (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascaded LLM solution, where the positives of a mid-tier model are verified by a frontier model, is 6.5x cheaper than using exclusively a frontier model and approaches its performance.
papers.summary: Prompt injection guards are placed in front of document-analysis systems, but no false positive rate had been published for any of them on legal contracts. The authors measure eleven open-weights guards on two contract corpora. Document-level false positive rates reach **as high as 92.39%**, two guards fall below chance on paired AUC, and a baseline of five regular expressions is not Pareto-dominated by any guard. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including unauthorized scope claims, a threat category on which every guard scores zero. A cascade in which a frontier model verifies a mid-tier model's positives costs 6.5x less than using the frontier model alone and comes close to its performance.

papers.title: Solver-Admitted Metamorphic Testing of Learned Network Optimization Surrogates
papers.abstract: Equivalent encodings of an optimization problem can produce different learned predictions. Interpreting these differences requires accounting for numerical error and multiple optima. We construct metamorphic tests for optimization solver surrogates with explicit eligibility conditions, output alignment, and numerical thresholds. Reference-solver agreement and independent constraint checks determine which sampled pairs enter the audit. We study alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF), the traveling salesman problem (TSP), the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), and maximum independent set (MIS). Across five grids, GridSFM-Open violates each of 13 relations on at least one grid, and 12 by more than twice the threshold. Randomly initialized copies of the grid models fail nearly the same relations, so the failures do not require training. Source patches and input canonicalization remove selected discrepancies, but no intervention establishes preserved accuracy and feasibility within the declared margin on every grid. In routing, Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO) has a single-pass rotation/reflection violation rate that rises from 12.7% to 89.5% between 20 and 100 cities. Graph-Based Diffusion Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization (DIFUSCO) violates the MIS disjoint-union relation on 35.6% of draws. Post hoc normalization within connected components removes these violations on the tested graphs. These findings support reporting metamorphic consistency alongside optimality, feasibility, and accuracy, and validating repair quality separately from consistency.
papers.summary: Learned surrogates for optimization solvers can give different predictions for mathematically equivalent encodings of the same problem. The authors build metamorphic tests that state explicit eligibility conditions, output alignment and numerical thresholds, and they use a reference solver and independent constraint checks to decide which test pairs count. They apply the tests to AC optimal power flow, the traveling salesman problem, capacitated vehicle routing and maximum independent set. `GridSFM-Open` violates all 13 relations on at least one grid, and randomly initialized copies fail almost the same relations, which shows the failures do not come from training. `POMO`'s rotation and reflection violation rate **rises from 12.7% to 89.5%** as instances grow from 20 to 100 cities, and `DIFUSCO` violates the disjoint-union relation for maximum independent set on 35.6% of draws.

papers.title: Functional Dependency beyond Similarity: Hierarchical Decomposition of Training Data Attribution in Music Generative Models
papers.abstract: Copyright analysis focuses on the similarity between two works. However, generative AI models learn from training data through functional relations beyond similarity. Training Data Attribution (TDA) estimates the influence of each training instance on a generated output and may serve as a basis for remuneration. However, prior studies find global influence, where a few training instances rank as the most influential for almost every generation. Used directly, TDA scores would distribute part of every remuneration to these instances regardless of what was generated. To address this, we propose a new approach in which TDA scores are decomposed into three levels of influence, namely global indicating the influence of a training data to a trained model, group for its influence on a group of generated outputs (that could be clustered together), and specific for its influence on a single generated output. Our study finds that, across several music generative models and TDA methods, global- and group-level influence is non-negligible in every case. Based on these observations, we propose the term functional dependency for the relation of training data to a trained model or to its outputs. This notion both encompasses and distinguishes dependencies of different scopes, allowing TDA scores to be interpreted as distinct forms of contribution in legal, economic and ethical discussions on remuneration.
papers.summary: Training Data Attribution (TDA) estimates how much each training example influenced a generated output and could serve as a basis for paying rights holders. However, earlier work found that a few training examples rank as highly influential for nearly every generation. The authors split TDA scores into three levels: global influence on the trained model, group influence on clusters of similar outputs, and specific influence on a single output. Across several music generative models and TDA methods, **global and group influence are non-negligible in every case**. The authors propose the term 'functional dependency' so that these different kinds of contribution can be treated separately in legal and economic discussions of remuneration.

papers.title: What Matters for LLM Persona Simulation: Signal Form in Cold-Start E-Commerce Advertising
papers.abstract: Estimating advertising performance in cold-start settings is challenging because historical logs are unavailable before launch. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential alternative by simulating persona-conditioned user responses, but it remains unclear which design choices actually drive LLM-based persona simulation. Using real Google Ads e-commerce campaign data across five demographic segments, we identify three signal-form dimensions that affect simulation quality: (i) a demographic anchor without noisy rich attributes, (ii) a relative qualitative banner-blindness signal rather than quantitative anchors, and (iii) prompt phrasing. On this campaign, our method attains an MAE of 24.9 and a MAPE of 26.1%, a 51.3% lower MAE than the best tested non-LLM baseline and 77.3% lower than an LLM configuration using explicit CTR anchors. Systematic ablations show that minimal demographic descriptions achieve lower mean error than richer persona configurations, while relative qualitative cues substantially outperform the tested quantitative anchors. We additionally compare these configurations with direct-prior and rule-based baselines and with alternative LLM configurations.
papers.summary: Predicting ad performance before launch is hard because no historical logs exist yet. The authors test LLMs that simulate how users with given personas would respond, using real `Google Ads` e-commerce campaign data across five demographic segments. Three choices about how the persona signal is phrased matter most: a minimal demographic anchor without noisy extra attributes, a relative qualitative cue for banner blindness instead of numeric click-through-rate anchors, and the prompt wording. The best configuration reaches an MAE of 24.9, **51.3% lower than the best non-LLM baseline** and 77.3% lower than an LLM given explicit click-through-rate anchors.

papers.title: When F1 Is Not Enough: Auditing Codebooks for LLM-Assisted Annotation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text annotation in social science, but standard performance metrics do not explain why errors occur. Low F1 may reflect limitations of the annotation system, defects in the written codebook, or inconsistency in reference labels. We propose a pre-deployment codebook audit for LLM-assisted annotation. The audit uses class-specific metrics and confusion matrices to identify problematic classes and boundaries, structured document-level review to attribute error sources, and targeted codebook revision followed by held-out evaluation. We apply the audit to two published multi-class codebooks from distinct domains. In both applications, the audit identifies under-specified or conflicting coding rules, and targeted revisions reduce the diagnosed errors on held-out data. Analyses with two LLM annotators show that some problematic boundaries and codebook revisions transfer across models, whereas other revision effects are annotator-specific. The results show that LLM annotation errors can help identify weaknesses in the written measurement instrument, not only in the model. Codebook auditing complements prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning by clarifying whether persistent errors call for model improvement, codebook revision, or renewed scrutiny of reference labels.
papers.summary: When LLMs annotate text for social-science research, a low F1 score does not reveal whether errors come from the model, a flawed written codebook, or inconsistent reference labels. The authors propose a pre-deployment codebook audit. It uses per-class metrics and confusion matrices to find problem boundaries, reviews individual documents to attribute errors, and then revises the codebook and evaluates on held-out data. Applied to two published multi-class codebooks, the audit finds under-specified or conflicting rules, and **targeted revisions reduce the diagnosed errors on held-out data**. With two different LLM annotators, some problem boundaries and fixes carry over between models and others are specific to one annotator.

papers.title: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
papers.abstract: A source who has been right before deserves attention, but about what? We ask how far a demonstrated record of reliability travels in language models when the new claim cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models approach the question from three angles. Study 1 adapts the Einstein-effect paradigm and finds that models, unlike the human sample, favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for the same obscure statement, and that the preference largely reverses when the statement is reworded in the vocabulary of physics. Study 2 adapts a paradigm in which a trusted expert calls a scientific or religious explanation unknown or a mystery; models reproduce the human domain asymmetry in exaggerated form. Study 3, the central test, gives two fictional informants different records on checkable river forecasts and then has them endorse matched claims about hidden natural and spiritual causes of the same village events. Most models carry the record to natural causes and barely at all to spiritual ones; one model transfers it weakly to either. Telling the model that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance rather than by measurement lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model and produces no comparable gain on spiritual claims in any. Demonstrated reliability thus has a scope in these models, and the account a source gives of how they came to be reliable can narrow it. Whether this reflects a judgment about relevance or the low prior credence of spiritual claims is the question the design leaves open, and we outline the experiment that would settle it.
papers.summary: The authors ask how far a source's demonstrated reliability carries over, in language models, to claims that cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models adapt paradigms from human psychology. In the central study, two fictional informants build different track records on river forecasts and then endorse hidden natural or spiritual explanations for village events. Most models **carry the reliability record over to natural claims but barely to spiritual ones**. Saying that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model. The authors note that the design cannot yet tell whether this reflects a judgment about relevance or simply low prior belief in spiritual claims.

papers.title: STRIDE: Learning Humanoid Locomotion in Minutes with Acceleration-Based Rewards
papers.abstract: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap. However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator. This is why we introduce \method{}, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile. To learn efficiently from this reward, we use the off-policy RL algorithm XQC and combine a high gain setting for the joint position controllers with left-right symmetry augmentation. In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples. Compared to learning without these two components, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while without them the robot learns only in over an hour.
papers.summary: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot avoids the gap between simulation and reality. However, typical reinforcement learning (RL) rewards track base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without motion capture or a well-calibrated state estimator. `STRIDE` instead rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile, which needs only the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). It combines the off-policy `XQC` algorithm with high-gain joint position control and left-right symmetry augmentation. In simulation it learns to walk on the `Unitree G1` and `Booster T1` humanoids **within 14 minutes of samples** and cuts falls during training by 81%, while learning without these two components takes over an hour.

papers.title: Mind the Divergence: Divergence-Guided Reliability-Aware Fusion and Adaptive LLM Prompting for Conversational Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) integrates textual, acoustic, and visual cues to identify utterance-level emotions. However, existing approaches generally do not explicitly adapt multimodal processing to the degree of inter-modal predictive disagreement. In real conversations, semantic incongruity, concealed emotion, noisy observations, and ambiguity can affect modality-specific emotional evidence differently, while the reliability of individual modalities varies across samples. Rather than identifying each source of inconsistency separately, we model their common consequence for emotion recognition as predictive disagreement among unimodal emotion distributions over the same emotion-label set. Such disagreement makes indiscriminate fusion prone to propagating unreliable or competing evidence. Inspired by the Brunswik Lens Model, we propose MiD-ERC, a divergence-centric framework that quantifies inter-modal predictive disagreement using a normalized divergence score and estimates sample-specific modality reliability. MiD-ERC uses these signals to coordinate divergence-guided cross-modal gating, divergence-modulated reliability weighting, and divergence-conditioned adaptive LLM prompting. The framework is trained end-to-end using only standard emotion annotations, without requiring additional conflict labels, auxiliary data construction, or external retrieval modules. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD demonstrate that MiD-ERC achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly pronounced improvements on high-divergence samples.
papers.summary: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) combines text, audio and visual cues, but existing methods do not adjust how they fuse modalities when those modalities disagree. Drawing on the Brunswik Lens Model, `MiD-ERC` computes a normalized divergence score between the emotion predictions of each modality and estimates how reliable each modality is for a given sample. It uses these signals to drive cross-modal gating, reliability weighting and adaptive LLM prompting. It is trained end to end on standard emotion labels only, with no extra conflict labels. It reports state-of-the-art results on `IEMOCAP` and `MELD`, with **the largest gains on samples where the modalities disagree most**.

papers.title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while smoothing the arrival of generated samples at the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. Within ASP, scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. ASP also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to about two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.
papers.summary: In asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for LLMs, the rollout stage wastes compute on padding, long-tail outputs, and uneven filling of the training queue. The Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (`ASP`) addresses all three with a single offline preprocessing pass. This allows rollouts to run across multiple inference instances inside an architecture that separates rollout from training and keeps policy lag bounded. `ASP` delivers **up to 3.22x end-to-end throughput** and up to 76.8% lower iteration time than `MindSpeed-RL`, and up to 62.5% lower iteration time than `verl`, with no visible degradation in convergence. In an internal telecom-domain post-training workflow it cut training time from more than three months to about two.

papers.title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective
papers.abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents that call tools over many steps accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, which steadily inflates their context. Existing compression methods rank text by importance or truncate by fixed rules, so they can drop information that a later step depends on. `WAAC` learns reusable compression patterns from successful past trajectories and runs a backward dependency analysis during execution to decide what each piece of history must keep. It then picks a compression strategy for each type of information. On `PinchBench` and `Odysseys` it reaches an overall score of 87.6 and a 19.0% perfect completion rate respectively, while **cutting execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1%** compared with the strongest baselines.

papers.title: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference
papers.abstract: Fine-tuned (FT) derivatives of large language models (LLMs) are now released in large numbers, yet their provenance relies on self-reports and cannot be verified. Misattributed lineage leaves a verifier unable to audit outsourced fine-tuning, confirm license compliance of derived models, or trace vulnerabilities that a parent passes to its children. All three require the direction of derivation, not merely its presence. Existing output-only methods are limited to pairwise derivation tests or undirected lineage estimation, while recovering a directed tree requires white-box access to model weights. We formalize the problem of reconstructing a directed model tree, including internal nodes, under gray-box access, where only teacher-forced log-likelihoods are observed and weights are never inspected. Fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of the training data, and a child inherits this increase from its parent. Building on this property, we define an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between any two models as a trace of fine-tuning history, and derive from it an edge weight for each ordered pair of models. We propose TRACE-Edge, which exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree under these edge weights, with neither hyperparameters nor tree-structure constraints. We evaluate it on five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks. TRACE-Edge achieves a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 when probed with the fine-tuning examples, and on average outperforms an output-similarity baseline even with held-out probes drawn from the same distribution as the training data.
papers.summary: Fine-tuned derivatives of LLMs are released in large numbers, but their claimed lineage cannot be verified. That blocks license checks, audits of outsourced fine-tuning, and tracing vulnerabilities that pass from parent to child models. The authors reconstruct a directed tree of models, including intermediate nodes, using only teacher-forced log-likelihoods and never inspecting weights. Their method relies on the observation that fine-tuning raises the likelihood of the training data and that children inherit this increase from their parents. `TRACE-Edge` builds asymmetric edge weights from these likelihood shifts and solves exactly for the maximum spanning directed tree, with no hyperparameters. Across 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks, it reaches **0.74 parent-match accuracy** when probed with the fine-tuning examples and on average beats an output-similarity baseline even with held-out probes.

papers.title: Extending Grid Foundation Models for Phasor-Domain Dynamic Simulation
papers.abstract: Grid Foundation Models (GridFMs) are emerging as a powerful framework for learning and transferring knowledge across power grids and grid analysis tasks. This work extends GridFMs from steady-state analysis to dynamic simulation. We present DynGridFM, which uses component-wise tokenization and a structured latent operator to learn shared dynamic representations across heterogeneous grids and enable transfer to unseen systems. Pretrained on nine grids, DynGridFM is adapted to a held-out 48-machine grid, where fine-tuning on 64 trajectories achieves accuracy comparable to training from scratch on 128. On a single GPU, it achieves 924x to 1232x speedup over numerical simulators on one CPU core.
papers.summary: Grid Foundation Models (GridFMs) learn knowledge that transfers across power grids, but so far they have covered only steady-state analysis. `DynGridFM` extends them to dynamic simulation by tokenizing each grid component separately and using a structured latent operator to learn representations shared across different grids. Pretrained on nine grids and adapted to a held-out 48-machine grid, it matches training from scratch on 128 trajectories after fine-tuning on only 64. On a single GPU it runs **924x to 1232x faster** than numerical simulators on one CPU core.

papers.title: Reweighting for Transfer Classification: Exact Risk Conversion and Minimax Adaptation
papers.abstract: A source can make a training mixture easier to learn while making its accuracy less valuable for the target. We study how the training problem a source creates and the finite-sample error of learning it jointly determine target-risk guarantees under reweighting. For binary classification, for each pair of laws and each positive target weight, we derive the sharpest target excess hinge-risk bound implied by mixture excess alone, uniformly over clipped predictors. This exact conversion curve is determined by density-weighted local votes. A two-sample oracle inequality for weighted support vector machines supplies the mixture excess, and the composition becomes explicit for Gaussian kernels. On a tilted-boundary class, we establish the all-procedure minimax classification rate $[n+s_+^2/(m^{-1}+\tau^2)]^{-1}$ in the transferable strength $s_+$ and the tilt $\tau$, separating source sampling uncertainty ($m^{-1}$) from relation uncertainty ($\tau^2$). A target-checked Gaussian-SVM selector adapts to unknown $s_+$ and $\tau$ up to a logarithmic factor for fixed dimension, and retains the target-only rate up to the same factor against arbitrary independent sources under the stated target model. On a separate smooth opposition class, the minimax risk within the family of exact Gaussian SVMs fitted to the original labels with nonnegative weights is exponentially larger than the unrestricted minimax risk whenever the target sample is at most half the source sample, despite arbitrary data-dependent weighting and tuning. The value of a source thus depends on the training problem it creates, on what accuracy there means for the target, and on whether the permitted use of the source can implement the needed correction.
papers.summary: The authors study when reweighting a source dataset helps binary classification on a target distribution. A source can make the combined training problem easier to learn while making accuracy on it less meaningful for the target. They derive the tightest target excess hinge-risk bound implied by the mixture's excess risk alone, combine it with an oracle inequality for weighted support vector machines, and establish a **minimax classification rate** that separates source sampling uncertainty from source-target mismatch. A target-checked Gaussian-kernel `SVM` selector adapts to unknown transfer strength up to a logarithmic factor. On a separate class of problems, any nonnegatively weighted Gaussian `SVM` fitted to the original labels is exponentially worse than the unrestricted optimum.

papers.title: The Relational Capacity Framework: A Lens for AI-Mediated Relationality
papers.abstract: A growing literature examines the impact of engaging with AI chatbots on our relationality: our ability to form relationships with others, maintain them through life's changes, and exit when needed. Currently, substantial work focuses on purpose-built AI companions (e.g. Replika, Character.AI), with less work investigating socioemotional uses of the more widely-used general-purpose chatbots. In this paper, we present a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs. Participants' AI uses varied, from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information as they navigated their social contexts. To explain this heterogeneity, we provide 8 states that describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth, and information. We then present a unified conceptual model for the role of technology in mediating human relationality, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline future research designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.
papers.summary: Most research on how AI chatbots affect human relationships focuses on purpose-built companion apps rather than general-purpose assistants. The authors study 100 people who use general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs, such as practicing social skills, getting extra bandwidth, or gathering information while navigating their social lives. To explain how varied these uses are, they define **8 states in which AI expands or contracts a person's capacity for relationships**, depending on that person's skills, bandwidth and information. They combine these states into a conceptual model, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline research on the role AI should play in human connection.

papers.title: Learning to Restart: Differentiable Restart Policies for Optimization Dynamics
papers.abstract: Adaptive restart mechanisms, which reset the momentum or other auxiliary state of an iterative optimizer, play a central role in the empirical performance of accelerated first-order methods, yet existing restart rules remain almost entirely hand-designed. The obstruction to learning restart policies is that, unlike the typical Learning to Optimize (L2O) setting, the discrete restart events make the resulting trajectory non-differentiable in the algorithm parameters and thus block gradient-based optimization of the restart policy. We resolve this obstruction by developing a differentiable framework for restart policies through their continuous-time limit. We introduce surrogate gradients for the restart events and optimization trajectories that are efficient to compute and provably converge to their continuous-time counterparts. We validate the effectiveness of our surrogate gradients in L2O settings, training restart policies that improve upon standard handcrafted adaptive restart criteria on quadratic and linear programs, and that transfer zero-shot from synthetic quadratics to logistic regression on real datasets.
papers.summary: Accelerated first-order optimizers rely on restart rules that reset momentum, but these rules are designed by hand. They are hard to learn because the discrete restart events make the optimization trajectory non-differentiable, which blocks the gradient-based training used in learning-to-optimize (L2O). The authors make restart policies differentiable through the continuous-time limit of the optimizer and introduce surrogate gradients that are cheap to compute and **provably converge to their continuous-time counterparts**. Learned restart policies outperform handcrafted adaptive restart criteria on quadratic and linear programs, and they transfer zero-shot from synthetic quadratics to logistic regression on real datasets.

papers.title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization
papers.abstract: The abundance of user-generated conversational data makes the question of how to responsibly derive insights from confidential data without putting the individuals in it at risk ever more important. However, the majority of existing differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation (SDG) and anonymization approaches ignore the context of the data's downstream usage, which results in loss of important information. DP-SDG provides the same guarantee regardless of the recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories. They both ignore the observation that an attribute that is harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another, and each audience typically needs only some attributes preserved. We propose Ext-Classify-Priv, a framework that (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP approaches. On Reddit data with 3 audiences, our audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, our SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1 and on the proprietary real estate data, our anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.
papers.summary: Differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation and anonymization give the same protection no matter who receives the data, even though an attribute that is harmless for one audience may be sensitive for another. `Ext-Classify-Priv` first extracts the types of information present in a corpus. It then uses the contextual integrity framework to classify which types are private for a given audience, and protects only those types through anonymization or feature-level DP synthesis. On Reddit data with three audiences, releases tailored to each audience are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release. On bioRxiv data the synthesis method **improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420** at epsilon=1.

papers.title: Richness Is Not Evenness: Ordered Renyi Crossings under Self-Training
papers.abstract: Recursive self-training of language models, a setting studied in model collapse, can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words, mostly function words, less dominant. We fine-tune English GPT-2 on its own output for nine generations, vary the training-data sampling temperature, and measure every model with one fixed sampler. As training temperature rises, Renyi entropy changes turn from loss to gain at distinct temperatures: min-entropy first, then collision entropy, Shannon entropy and observed richness. Between the outer crossings, word types fall while the most-common word becomes less dominant. Untruncated training at T = 1 lies in this interval: at 13,000 words, generation 9 has 24% fewer types than generation 0 yet collision entropy is 0.91 bits higher. The ordering persists with a finer grid, different measurement samplers, a fixed word budget and five fresh training seeds. Min-entropy again crosses before richness in four further settings (in Hindi only at interpolated roots) and in 12 of 13 distinct measurements under eight text representations. Next-token identities and a categorical simulation isolate decoding and sampling effects; the crossing order remains empirical. Fine-tuning on human text can produce the same split while likelihood improves, and no single order's sign reliably identifies worse likelihood across the tested settings. We recommend reporting entropy profiles at stated budgets with an independent quality measure.
papers.summary: Recursive self-training of language models, the setting studied as model collapse, can shrink vocabulary while making the most frequent words less dominant. The authors fine-tune `GPT-2` on its own output for nine generations, vary the sampling temperature used to make training data, and measure every model with one fixed sampler. As training temperature rises, different Rényi entropy orders switch from loss to gain at different temperatures, starting with min-entropy and followed by collision entropy, Shannon entropy and vocabulary richness. At T = 1, **generation 9 has 24% fewer word types than generation 0 but 0.91 bits higher collision entropy**. The authors recommend reporting full entropy profiles at stated budgets together with an independent quality measure, because no single entropy order reliably signals worse likelihood.

papers.title: From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills
papers.abstract: As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. Existing agent systems provide mechanisms for controlling tools and execution environments, but do not directly specify the resources required by each delegated subtask. Moreover, task outcomes and execution trajectories alone provide limited supervision for determining whether a subagent has received appropriate permissions. We observe that Agent Skills encode procedural knowledge describing the operations, tools, and files required at each step, providing a natural source of supervision for authorization. Building on this observation, we synthesize tasks and step-by-step procedures from Skills, execute them through subagent delegation in interactive environments, and use verified trajectories to construct training data for task execution and authorization. On ClawArena-Team, our method improves tool permission precision by 13.4 percentage points and workspace permission precision by 24.1 percentage points, while increasing overall task success by 11.6 percentage points for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, our method remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis approaches. These results show that the procedural knowledge embedded in Agent Skills provides a source of supervision for precise subagent orchestration that task outcomes alone cannot provide.
papers.summary: When language agents hand work to subagents, they must decide which tools and workspace resources each subagent may access, and task outcomes alone say little about whether those permissions were right. The authors observe that `Agent Skills` describe the operations, tools and files each step needs. They use these skills to synthesize tasks and step-by-step procedures, run them through subagent delegation, and turn verified trajectories into training data for both task execution and authorization. On `ClawArena-Team` with `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`, the method **raises tool-permission precision by 13.4 points and workspace-permission precision by 24.1 points** and improves task success by 11.6 points, while staying competitive on `Terminal-Bench 2.1` and `SkillsBench`.

papers.title: Toward LLM Self-Play Under Data Scarcity: Effectiveness, Generalizability, and Trustworthiness
papers.abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has been driven largely by scaling model size and human-curated training data, yet this paradigm is increasingly constrained by data scarcity and diminishing returns from human supervision. Self-play offers a promising pathway for autonomous data generation and improvement, but current frameworks remain unsatisfactory due to a lack of a data-centric perspective, limited cross-domain generalization, and growing trustworthiness and security concerns. In this paper, we argue that real-world LLM self-play systems should achieve effectiveness, generalizability, and trustworthiness under data scarcity. To address these challenges, we outline three blue-sky research directions for future self-play systems: (1) data-centric self-play for effective experience generation, (2) generalizable self-play for open-world and unverifiable tasks, and (3) trustworthy self-play for reliable self-evolution. We further discuss research opportunities and solutions within each direction. This paradigm shift will establish a sustainable and safe AI ecosystem by transforming finite human knowledge into inexhaustible high-quality experience through self-play architectures.
papers.summary: This position paper argues that scaling large language models (LLMs) on human-curated data is running into data scarcity, and that self-play, where models generate their own training experience, is a way forward. The authors say current self-play frameworks lack a data-centric perspective, generalize poorly across domains, and raise trustworthiness and security concerns. They propose **three research directions: data-centric self-play for effective experience generation, generalizable self-play for open-world and unverifiable tasks, and trustworthy self-play for reliable self-evolution**, and they outline open problems and candidate solutions for each.

papers.title: Geometry-Aware Score-Repellent Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: The recently proposed Score-Repellent Monte Carlo (SRMC) method improves MCMC sampling by tilting the target density $\pi$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the factor $\exp(-\alpha\,\theta_n^\top s(x))$, where the score function $s(x) = \nabla_x \log \pi(x)$, and $\theta_n$ is the score average from past samples. However, a single scalar repellence strength $\alpha\ge0$ cannot handle both the steep and the flat directions in anisotropic energy landscapes at once. We introduce \emph{Geometry-Aware SRMC} (GA-SRMC), which generalizes the Euclidean alignment to $\theta^\top M s(x)$ for any symmetric positive-definite matrix $M$. A stochastic-approximation central limit theorem under a trace constraint on $M$ identifies the trace-normalized inverse Fisher $M_{\rm opt}\propto S^{-1}$ as the unique minimizer of the worst-direction covariance bound, elevating the Fisher information $S=\text{Cov}_\pi(s,s)$ from a proposal-side preconditioner (e.g., FisherMALA, natural gradient) to the bound-optimal repulsion-side matrix, with a single online estimate $\widehat S_n$ serving both roles at no additional computational cost. The full-Fisher online metric $M_n$ converges almost surely to $M_{\rm opt}$ and satisfies a CLT, providing a theoretical guarantee for the online implementation of the GA-SRMC framework. On an $8$-target simulation spanning the condition number $\kappa\in[1.3,100]$ and dimension $d\in[2,785]$, GA-SRMC dominates SRMC in ESS by $\boldsymbol{4.3\times}$ on anisotropic Gaussian ($\kappa=100$) and $\boldsymbol{6.8\times}$ on MNIST under the MALA baseline, by $\boldsymbol{16\text{--}32\%}$ on three well-conditioned logistic-regression posteriors, and by up to $\boldsymbol{+48\%}$ under FisherMALA; gains peak on the most anisotropic targets, and posterior-mean MSE is lower than with SRMC in all $16$ full-Fisher implementations.
papers.summary: `Score-Repellent Monte Carlo` (`SRMC`) improves Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling by pushing new samples away from the average score seen so far, but its single scalar repulsion strength cannot handle steep and flat directions at the same time. `GA-SRMC` replaces this with a matrix-weighted alignment and proves that the trace-normalized inverse Fisher information is the unique optimal choice of matrix under a worst-direction covariance bound. One online Fisher estimate can then serve as both proposal preconditioner and repulsion matrix at no extra cost, with almost-sure convergence and a central limit theorem. Across eight targets, `GA-SRMC` improves effective sample size over `SRMC` by **4.3× on an ill-conditioned Gaussian and 6.8× on `MNIST`**, with smaller gains on well-conditioned logistic-regression posteriors.

papers.title: Task-Contribution Dynamics of Adam in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Slow-Manifold Analysis and Gradient Modulation
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often suffer from imbalanced optimization of competing loss components, particularly when approximating solutions with high-frequency or multiscale features. Although existing balancing strategies have proven effective in alleviating this difficulty, the mechanisms governing the evolution of individual task contributions to Adam's parameter updates remain insufficiently understood. We introduce task-wise indicators to characterize this evolution and identify three distinct training regimes: smooth variation, intermittent spikes, and persistent oscillations. Focusing on the early smooth regime, we combine discrete-time analysis with a continuous-time singular perturbation framework under the full-batch setting and the parameter regime $(1-\beta_2)/(1-\beta_1)\ll1$. A first-order approximation of the locally attracting slow manifold reveals two factors governing the step-to-step redistribution of task contributions: curvature-related alignment disparities and differences in the coordinatewise distributions of preconditioned task gradients. Both factors involve Adam's shared second-moment estimate. Inspired by AdaTask, we propose Gradient-Modulated Adam (GMAdam), which modulates incoming task gradients using task-specific second-moment estimates. Numerical experiments on high-frequency Poisson and wave equations, the Allen-Cahn equation, and two-dimensional lid-driven cavity flow ($Re=100,400$) demonstrate consistent improvements in predictive accuracy over AdaTask at comparable computational cost.
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often train poorly because their competing loss terms are optimized unevenly, and it is not well understood how each term's contribution to Adam's updates changes during training. The authors define task-wise indicators, identify three training regimes (smooth variation, intermittent spikes and persistent oscillations), and analyze the early smooth regime with a singular-perturbation slow-manifold approximation. The analysis traces the redistribution of task contributions to curvature-related alignment differences and to the shared second-moment estimate in Adam. Building on `AdaTask`, they propose `GMAdam`, which uses task-specific second-moment estimates, and report **consistently better accuracy than `AdaTask` at comparable cost** on Poisson, wave, Allen-Cahn and lid-driven cavity flow problems.

papers.title: SSF-Net: A Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network for Accurate PDE Operator Learning
papers.abstract: Machine learning methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) significantly improve computational efficiency over traditional numerical solvers such as finite element method (FEM). However, PDE dynamics inherently span both local and global dynamics: disturbances propagate and decay gradually through the domain, while global coupling effects can influence the whole system simultaneously. Capturing both types of dynamics with a low complexity model remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose the Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network (SSF-Net), built around a dual-branch Spatial-Spectral Fusion (SSF) block comprising a spatial branch and a spectral branch. The spatial branch employs a multi-directional Mamba, which mitigates its inherent causal, single-direction scanning bias and capture local interactions with reduced directional bias at linear complexity. The spectral branch leverages a Fourier transform with a block-diagonal MLP to efficiently capture global spectral features with reduced parameter count and complexity. The SSF block is embedded in a multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder, which extracts multi-scale features. We evaluate SSF-Net on a comprehensive PDE benchmark spanning multiple task types and assess its long-horizon stability. Compared with attention-based and convolution-based baselines, SSF-Net achieves lower prediction error with fewer parameters while retaining near-linear asymptotic complexity in the number of spatial tokens.
papers.summary: Neural solvers for partial differential equations (PDEs) need to capture both local propagation and global coupling while keeping computational cost low. `SSF-Net` uses a dual-branch block in which a multi-directional `Mamba` spatial branch captures local interactions in linear time and reduces Mamba's single-direction scanning bias, while a Fourier-transform spectral branch with a block-diagonal MLP captures global features with few parameters. These blocks sit inside a multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder. On a broad PDE benchmark, including long-horizon rollouts, **`SSF-Net` achieves lower prediction error with fewer parameters** than attention-based and convolution-based baselines, at near-linear complexity in the number of spatial tokens.

papers.title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
papers.abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.
papers.summary: Home robots driven by vision-language models (VLMs) will need to work with existing cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices and wearables, and to reason about ambiguous alerts, such as a smoke alarm that could mean a fire, normal cooking or a faulty sensor. `HomeLoop` is an `Isaac Sim` framework and benchmark that combines robot bodies, networked devices, simulated residents, faulty sensors and evolving hazards. It has 20 tasks scored by temporal-logic checks on both outcomes and intermediate actions, with a cost attached to every action. Across six VLMs, the best reaches a 61.9% family-balanced score, and **models over-react: failures from prohibited interventions outnumber missed required interventions by more than two to one**, for example shutting off the stove before checking why the alarm went off.

papers.title: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability
papers.abstract: We study the problem of causal effect identification from an arbitrary set of observational and/or interventional distributions, which we call Universal Identifiability (uID). The uID problem generalizes existing classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems, which considered the identification problem from either mere observational distributions or a specific type of interventional distributions. Prior research has established graphical criteria to determine when a causal effect is identifiable in ID and gID problems. Moreover, algorithms that leverage do-calculus and basic probability manipulations have been proposed to compute these effects. Consequently, it has been shown that do-calculus is both sound and complete in these problems. Despite these well-established results, a formal definition of what it means for the do-calculus to be complete does not exist. We propose a rigorous formalization for the completeness of the do-calculus and show that the completeness results in previous work remain valid. However, for more general problems, such as uID, the rules of do-calculus are no longer complete. This is perhaps the reason why the uID problem has remained open thus far.
papers.summary: The authors study Universal Identifiability (uID), the problem of identifying a causal effect from an arbitrary set of observational and interventional distributions, which generalizes the classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems. Although do-calculus has been described as complete for ID and gID, no formal definition of that completeness existed. The authors provide one and confirm that the earlier completeness results still hold. They then show that **do-calculus is not complete for uID**, which they suggest may explain why the problem has stayed open.

papers.title: Composable Causality: A Toolkit for Systematic Time-Series Causal Discovery and Treatment-Effect Benchmarking
papers.abstract: Real-world multivariate time series rarely come with verified ground-truth causal structure, so research on time-series causal discovery and treatment-effect estimation depends on synthetic data. Existing tools are either fixed datasets that cannot be modified after release or script-based generators in which each script fixes one combination of mechanism, confounding, and missingness. Neither supports controlled experiments that vary a single property, such as sparsity, noise distribution, or missingness mechanism, while holding the others fixed. Counterfactual evaluation has the same gap, since existing simulators are built per paper with hardcoded mechanisms or produce observational data only. We introduce DTCD (Datasets and Toolkit for Causal Discovery), a data generation library that produces multivariate time series with ground-truth contemporaneous and lagged adjacency matrices. Topology, mechanism, noise, observational mask, and intervention policy are independent components that compose through configuration alone. Paired counterfactual twins, produced by caching the stochastic realization during the factual rollout and re-injecting it during the interventional rollout, recover individual treatment effects to numerical precision. A reference benchmark of eight discovery algorithms on eighty-one configurations and four treatment-effect estimators on eighteen configurations exposes failure modes that aggregate metrics hide. These include the inability of standard discovery methods to handle missing values, regardless of whether the missingness mechanism is informative, and a marginal-variance shortcut (varsortability) that we measure and remove by standardization. Code and data: https://github.com/hferdous/Composable_Causality
papers.summary: Research on time-series causal discovery relies on synthetic data, but existing generators are fixed datasets or scripts that hard-code one combination of properties, so controlled single-factor experiments are hard to run. `DTCD` is a library in which topology, mechanism, noise, missingness mask and intervention policy are independent components combined through configuration, producing ground-truth contemporaneous and lagged adjacency matrices. It produces paired counterfactual twins by caching and re-injecting the random noise, which recovers individual treatment effects to numerical precision. A reference benchmark of eight discovery algorithms and four treatment-effect estimators shows that **standard discovery methods cannot handle missing values, whatever the missingness mechanism**, and measures and removes a variance-based shortcut known as varsortability.

papers.title: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation
papers.abstract: Many professional reports reuse the structure of prior editions while updating the content. We formalize this setting as form-restricted report generation: given a sample report and new grounding documents, generate a report that preserves the sample's form while accurately reflecting the new evidence. We introduce FRAME, a benchmark of 120 EDGAR- and arXiv-derived instances across Financial Quarterly, Financial Annual, Academic Simple, and Academic Complex categories, built with a temporal three-snapshot pipeline. We evaluate outputs with three human-validated metrics: structural similarity via semantic tree-edit distance, coverage via information unit recall, and faithfulness via claim-level grounding verification. Across five LLMs, open-source models nearly match proprietary models on structure but lag on coverage and faithfulness; all models perform better on financial than academic reports, and performance declines with longer outputs and more complex grounding.
papers.summary: Many professional reports keep the structure of earlier editions while updating the content, a task the authors formalize as form-restricted report generation from a sample report and new grounding documents. `FRAME` provides 120 instances drawn from EDGAR financial filings and arXiv papers, evaluated with human-validated metrics for structural similarity, information coverage and claim-level faithfulness. Across five large language models (LLMs), **open-source models nearly match proprietary ones on structure but trail on coverage and faithfulness**. All models do better on financial reports than on academic ones, and performance drops as outputs get longer and grounding gets more complex.

papers.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data
papers.abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.
papers.summary: Automated clinical discovery tools usually extract predefined phenotypes, which limits which associations they can find. Foundation models trained on clinical data may encode features nobody has defined yet, but those features are hard to interpret. `Glyph` extracts features from multimodal clinical data with foundation models and sparse autoencoders, maps them to coded clinical concepts, and tests whether they are useful for discovery. Applied to abdominal CT scans, radiology reports and lab values from 41,628 patients, it found **397 predictive concepts backed by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations**, most of which reproduced automatically in held-out cohorts from other sites and added predictive power to literature-derived markers.

papers.title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training
papers.abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.
papers.summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) gives the most accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but AdamW stores two dense FP32 optimizer states per weight matrix. The authors find that low-rank optimizers such as `GaLore` and `LDAdam` degrade in QAT because much of the momentum lies outside the top singular subspace, and that this residual is still useful when only its sign is kept. `ResQAdam` keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only within the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update from the residual. Across two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines with weights down to 2 bits, it **cuts optimizer-state memory by 71–74% relative to AdamW** while staying close to AdamW accuracy in most settings and losing less than 2% throughput.

papers.title: Grid-Oriented Probabilistic Load Forecasting for AI Data Centers
papers.abstract: Probabilistic load forecasts for AI data centers need to represent both uncertainty under changing workloads and temporal dependence to support grid operations. This paper develops an open, grid-oriented benchmark using measured GPU power from a 448-GPU AI cluster. Forecasts are evaluated through four stages: probabilistic prediction, online uncertainty calibration, temporal scenario generation, and horizon-wide reserve sizing. Following a change in cluster utilization, a quantile LightGBM forecast achieves only 63.4% coverage for a nominal 90% interval, while online regime-conditioned calibration increases coverage to 87.3%. Even with well-calibrated marginal forecasts, independent sampling produces unrealistic ramp distributions and excessive reserve procurement. Reconstructing temporal dependence from historical forecast errors reduces the discrepancy in ramp statistics and lowers realized reserve cost by 7.4-10.6% across three forecasting tasks. These findings show that marginal forecast quality alone is insufficient for operational decisions and motivate joint evaluation of calibration, temporal structure, and decision outcomes.
papers.summary: Grid operators need probabilistic load forecasts for AI data centers that capture both uncertainty under shifting workloads and dependence over time. Using measured GPU power from a 448-GPU cluster, the authors build an open benchmark covering probabilistic prediction, online calibration, scenario generation and reserve sizing. After a utilization shift, a quantile `LightGBM` forecast covers only 63.4% of outcomes with a nominal 90% interval, and online regime-conditioned calibration raises this to 87.3%. Even well-calibrated forecasts give unrealistic ramp behavior when sampled independently, while **rebuilding temporal dependence from past forecast errors lowers reserve cost by 7.4–10.6%**.

papers.title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle
papers.abstract: Can frontier general-purpose agents understand client intent, explore creative directions, execute revisions, and prepare production deliverables? We introduce DRAFT-Bench (Design Reliability Across Feedback and Tasks), a lifecycle-oriented evaluation of requirement elicitation, creative exploration, constrained editing, iterative revision, and production handoff. Its Requirement-to-Artifact framework links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions, and delivery obligations. We compare native Codex/Astra and Claude Code across 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, alongside a separate 40-scenario RFQ track. Astra completes 43/43 design conditions and Claude 35/43. All scored core runs receive full structural credit, yet on the 28 core conditions scored for both systems, semantic checks flag violations in 11 for Astra and 5 for Claude; these are model judgments, not expert-confirmed failure rates. RFQ coverage is high, but success ordering changes across cohorts. SKU expansion, revision dependencies, and White ink files expose ambiguity among unmet obligations, missing inputs, and evaluator interpretations. These findings separate execution, requirement compliance, and professional acceptance. Unpaired tracks and different tools preclude claims of RFQ-to-delivery success, factory acceptance, or a pure model ranking.
papers.summary: `DRAFT-Bench` tests whether general-purpose frontier agents can handle the full professional design lifecycle: eliciting requirements, exploring creative directions, making constrained edits, revising iteratively and preparing production deliverables. It links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions and delivery obligations, and compares `Codex`/`Astra` with `Claude Code` across 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, plus a separate 40-scenario request-for-quote track. `Astra` completed all 43 conditions and `Claude Code` completed 35, and every scored run received full structural credit. However, **model-based semantic checks flagged requirement violations in 11 of 28 shared conditions for `Astra` and 5 for `Claude Code`**, which separates task completion from requirement compliance; the authors note these are model judgments, not expert-confirmed failures.

papers.title: Ordered Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.
papers.summary: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) clips importance ratios with one fixed range for every sample, so it cannot tell harmful extreme ratios apart from large but tolerable ones. A case study shows that stable updates depend on controlling the extreme tail of the ratio distribution rather than on keeping each ratio inside a fixed interval. `Ordered Policy Optimization` (`OPO`) sorts the ratios in each minibatch and gives the most extreme ones adaptive per-sample clipping radii derived from a target tail profile, using only a sort and a modified loss. On `MuJoCo` and `Atari` benchmarks, **`OPO` performs strongly against established baselines**.

papers.title: Surrogate Quality Score: A Novel Composite Performance Metric for Model Selection
papers.abstract: The growing reliance on high-fidelity, state-of-the-art machine learning based models for engineering decision-making necessitates robust and systematic approaches for model selection. While high predictive accuracy at untrained points is a necessary trait in the final model, other attributes such as model complexity, forecastability, explainability, scalability, and physics-awareness may be equally important or relevant criteria depending on application context and user requirements. In this work, we propose a novel composite performance metric, Surrogate Quality Score (SQS) for model selection based on predictive accuracy and model complexity simultaneously. SQS heuristically integrates these two attributes through a weighted product of normalized measures, yielding a unified score to reflect overall model quality. A user-specified parameter in SQS enables explicit control over the accuracy-complexity trade-off, thereby incorporating human judgement and preference in the model selection process. We extensively discuss and justify the formulation of SQS and demonstrate its utility through an illustrative example. By combining predictive accuracy and model complexity, SQS offers a systematic and objective approach for model selection based on both attributes.
papers.summary: Choosing a machine-learning surrogate model for engineering decisions often requires balancing predictive accuracy against other properties such as model complexity. The authors propose `Surrogate Quality Score` (`SQS`), **a composite metric that combines normalized accuracy and complexity as a weighted product**, with a user-set parameter that controls the trade-off between the two. They justify the formulation and demonstrate it on an illustrative example.

papers.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
papers.abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.
papers.summary: How well an agent performs depends on its harness (its prompts, tools, memory and control loop) as well as on its model, yet most benchmarks keep the harness fixed. `Flex-RSI` measures recursive self-improvement on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round an executor improves the solution, which is kept only if held-out validation improves, and an improver then rewrites the harness, including itself. Across closed and open-weight models, self-improvement helps most when agents build their own solutions, success-or-failure-only feedback holds back open-weight models, and open-weight models fall furthest behind on strict physical-stability or exact-correctness checks. **Paired runs show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.**
papers.highlight_summary:
Agent performance depends on the harness (the prompts, tools, memory and control loop around the model) as much as on the model itself, yet most benchmarks hold the harness fixed. `Flex-RSI` measures whether frontier agents can improve both their task solution and their own harness on vision and robotics tasks, under a fixed budget and starting from a shared general-purpose harness.

- Each round, an executor edits the solution using development data, and the edit is kept only if it beats the current solution on hidden validation data by a noise margin; an improver then rewrites the executor's prompts, tools and workflow, along with its own instructions and lessons, and the final solution is scored once on a hidden test split.
- Across **24 tasks** in six areas (action, reasoning, creation, reconstruction, perception and infrastructure) and **18 models**, self-improvement raised the validation score in **150 of 177 runs (85%)** by a median of **10.4 points**; closed-source models improved more often and by more than open-weight ones (**94% of runs, median +14.9** against **76%, median +8.5**), and `Claude Opus 5.5` led overall with the best test score on 11 of 20 tasks.
- Gains are largest when the agent must build the solution from a weak starter, as on `3D Tracking`, where the median validation score rose **from 19.4 to 62.2**; they are near zero where the starter already scores high, as on `ARC-AGI-1/2`, and when feedback only records success or failure, open-weight models' median gain drops to **1.6 points** against **16.9** for closed models.
