- Open-weight models fall furthest behind on strict physical or exact-correctness checks; on `Scene from Video`, for example, **none of the objects they place stay stable in simulation**, while **70.7%** of those placed by `Opus` do, and token spend is essentially uncorrelated with score (rank correlation **−0.05**).
- Letting the improver edit the harness raised the test score in **6 of 7 paired runs**, such as `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` on `Active Search` going **from 21.0 to 59.3**, but that ablation is small, each model was run only once per task, and coverage is uneven, since several models were evaluated on only a subset of tasks and four tasks have just two models so far.

papers.title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
papers.abstract: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4% fewer tokens, remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural modification.
papers.summary: Translating parallel scientific code between high-performance computing frameworks is laborious, and existing language-model pipelines use fixed sequential steps with generic repair. The authors split the work among three agents for translation, compilation diagnosis and execution validation, coordinated by an orchestrator that sends each failure to a targeted repair skill. An automated output check drives self-correction, and an offline LLM-based verification catches false positives that pass compiler and runtime checks. On 30 `HeCBench` kernels translated in both directions among `CUDA`, `OpenMP` and `SYCL` with three open-source models, **the framework beats a state-of-the-art baseline on verified correctness in all 18 model-direction combinations while using up to 52.4% fewer tokens**.

papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Value: Choosing Weak Supervisors by What the Student Inherits
papers.abstract: Weak supervisors are usually judged by their own errors, but what matters is what a student learns from them. For squared loss and any linear learner shared by all supervisors, we show that a supervisor's value is determined by its errors after they pass through the student's learning operator. Consequently, the inner products of the supervisors' raw errors can be compatible with every feasible value of the student's risk, and weighting supervisors by them can be arbitrarily worse than the best weighting in relative excess risk. This student-relative value is not identifiable from unlabeled data, but what is missing is small: one finite-dimensional projection of the target decides whether training on a weak aggregate helps, another decides how to weight the supervisors. Known teacher training rules, or a label-model condition stated in student-relative form, shrink it further. Clean labels close the remaining gap at a cost set by the geometry of the unresolved directions rather than by the dimension of the student's representation, with matching worst-case lower bounds. In Gaussian designs we also quantify when exact teacher structure beats ordinary stacking and when weak supervisors, combined with clean labels, beat every procedure that uses the clean labels alone. The guarantees extend to fitted ridge students and finite unlabeled data.
papers.summary: Weak supervisors are usually judged by their own error rates, but what matters is what a student model learns from them. For squared loss and linear students, the authors show that a supervisor's value depends on its errors after they pass through the student's learning operator, so **weighting supervisors by raw error statistics can be arbitrarily worse than the best weighting**. This student-relative value cannot be identified from unlabeled data alone, but the missing information is small: two finite-dimensional projections of the target, which a few clean labels can resolve at a cost set by the geometry of the unresolved directions, with matching lower bounds. The results extend to ridge students and finite unlabeled data.

papers.title: Concordance-Optimal Continuous Music Emotion Estimation: Variance Decomposition, Dual-Branch Temporal Fusion, and Conformal Prediction Intervals
papers.abstract:
Continuous music emotion recognition (MER) estimates how Arousal and Valence evolve within a song, yet the field's standard metric, pooled frame-level correlation, is dominated by between-song differences and cannot distinguish a model that tracks emotional dynamics from one that only ranks songs by their average level. We decompose annotation variance into between- and within-song components and show that mean squared error (MSE) targets the former, while windowed Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC = $r \cdot C_b$) targets the latter by penalising the variance compression MSE induces. A single weight $\lambda$ controls the trade-off: on 1,764 DEAM songs, raising $\lambda$ from 0 to 1 lowers pooled Arousal $r$ from 0.843 to 0.810 while raising mean within-song $r$ from 0.204 to 0.368.
  Building on this objective, we present MMAS (Multimodal Music Analysis System), an open-source model that predicts Arousal and Valence every 0.5 s from raw audio. It fuses frozen MERT-v1-95M embeddings with ten symbolic features from automatic transcription through a dual-branch temporal convolutional network with cross-modal attention. Because both branches are audio-derived, one model trains jointly on DEAM and PMEmo without domain conditioning. Under song-grouped 5-fold cross-validation (2,531 songs), pooled $r$ reaches 0.801/0.685 (Arousal/Valence) on DEAM and 0.742/0.746 on PMEmo. Against a ridge baseline on identical features, within-song Arousal $r$ roughly triples (0.344 vs. 0.125; $n = 353$ songs, Wilcoxon $p = 1.7 \times 10^{-21}$, $d = 0.56$). Complete transcription failure costs at most 0.04 pooled $r$. Split-conformal intervals attain 93.7% (Arousal) and 90.0% (Valence) marginal coverage at a 95% target, with the shortfall traced to within-song dependence. MMAS is released as a pip-installable package.
papers.summary: The standard metric for continuous music emotion recognition (MER), pooled frame-level correlation, mostly reflects differences between songs and does not show whether a model tracks how emotion changes within a song. The authors decompose annotation variance into between-song and within-song parts and show that a windowed concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) loss targets within-song dynamics while mean squared error targets song-level averages. Their open-source `MMAS` model fuses `MERT-v1-95M` audio embeddings with features from automatic transcription and trains jointly on `DEAM` and `PMEmo`. **It roughly triples within-song Arousal correlation over a ridge baseline (0.344 vs. 0.125)**, and split-conformal intervals reach close to the target coverage.

papers.title: Using an LLM to Tackle Difficult Cases in NER for Nepali Tweets
papers.abstract: Named entity recognition (NER) is challenging for social media data in a low-resource language. LLMs often lag behind pretrained language models (PLMs) in NER performance, but they show promise in handling cases that PLMs struggle with. Using a dataset of Nepali tweets, we split the test set into "easy" and "hard" cases using token probabilities from a fine-tuned pretrained language model (PLM). We then evaluate an LLM on the hard test cases using 16 different prompt configurations. We find that selecting examples based on semantic similarity and increasing the number of examples improves F1 score by almost 10 points from the baseline configuration. Although the LLM underperforms the PLM on the full and easy test sets, it surpasses the PLM on the hard test set, resulting in an improved score when the two models are combined.
papers.summary: Named entity recognition (NER) on social media text in low-resource languages is difficult, and large language models usually trail fine-tuned pretrained language models (PLMs) on it overall. Using a dataset of Nepali tweets, the authors use token probabilities from a fine-tuned PLM to split the test set into easy and hard cases, then test an LLM on the hard cases with 16 prompt configurations. Choosing in-context examples by semantic similarity and using more of them improves F1 by **almost 10 points** over the baseline prompt. The LLM does worse than the PLM on the full and easy sets but better on the hard set, so combining the two models gives a higher overall score.

papers.title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals
papers.abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.
papers.summary: `PhysioWave-T` is a family of wavelet-based foundation models for EEG, ECG, and sEMG biosignals. To keep sequences short, it uses dynamic scale folding, which merges wavelet subbands before tokenization. Learned channel-name embeddings and route-specific front ends let one Transformer per modality handle different electrode layouts and sampling rates. Scale folding cuts Transformer latency by **4.0 to 7.2 times** and peak memory by 6.8 to 12.7 times with no accuracy loss, and the 30M-parameter EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against `BENDR`, `BIOT`, `LaBraM`, and `EEGPT`. A reliability-aware latent fusion method (`RALF`) combines separately pre-trained encoders and raises seizure event sensitivity on `SeizeIT2` from 61.4% to 74.4%.

papers.title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems often combine judgments from several model instances, but the agents' reasoning about each other can itself cause errors. The authors identify phantom consensus: agents change their public decisions after ambiguous social signals and misreport what the others privately believed, even when the recorded private judgments do not support that consensus. Their benchmark, `PHANTOM-Bench`, separates private judgments, public decisions, estimates of group belief, and recovery when private votes are revealed. Across nine models, public accuracy drops by **up to 47.8 percentage points**, and showing agents each other's recorded private decisions fixes many of these failures, though recovery varies by model.

papers.title: Beyond Truncation? Entailment-Licensed Elision and the Limits of Semantic Preservation in LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) answer at greater length than a request needs. We ask whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that surplus while preserving content, judged against the simplest possible baseline: truncating the model's own answer to the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore non-inferiority margins, yet we prove and confirm by audit that its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer: the saving is truncation. A survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that selects content better than truncation without oracle labels. We therefore introduce Entailment-Licensed In-Decoding Elision (ELIDE), which, at each sentence boundary, withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, while leaving the model's generation unchanged. ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, but reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows that 59% harm the answer, a failure that no automatic measure detects. Scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one elision in ten on two fresh tests.
papers.summary: Instruction-tuned LLMs often write longer answers than a request needs, and the authors test whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that excess better than simply cutting the answer off at the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 20 to 35% of tokens within pre-registered `BERTScore` margins, but they prove and confirm that its output is always a prefix of the original answer, so the saving is just truncation; a survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that beats truncation without oracle labels. They then propose `ELIDE`, which hides a sentence-level span only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by text already shown. `ELIDE` beats matched-length truncation on automatic metrics across three model families, but human reading shows **59% of its elisions harm the answer**, a failure no automatic measure detected; limiting each elision to its own discourse unit brings the harmful rate down to about one in ten.

papers.title: Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model
papers.abstract: Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345$\times$ less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.
papers.summary: Looped models refine their latent state by repeating a recurrent block, but they have no explicit measure of progress that tells them when to stop or how to improve. `Energy-Based Reasoners` (EBRs) learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and treat each loop step as gradient descent on that energy, so the energy both scores states and provides a stopping signal. An exploration-based training procedure finds additional modes to shape the energy landscape. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or beat prior recurrent reasoners, reaching 99.9% accuracy on `Sudoku-Extreme` with **345 times less inference compute** than the next-best model, and they reach state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions on multi-solution tasks.
papers.highlight_summary:
Looped reasoners refine a latent state over many iterations, but nothing explicit tells them whether they are making progress, when to stop, or which of several candidate answers is best. Energy-Based Reasoners (`EBR`s) learn a scalar energy over latent reasoning states and make each loop step a gradient-descent step on that energy, so a single learned function guides refinement, decides when to halt, and picks the best candidate.

- The energy is computed by a small Transformer backbone with a per-token scalar head, and states are updated by noisy, sphere-projected gradient descent; a convergence loss pushes correct predictions toward stationary points, and inference stops when the gradient norm falls below a threshold.
- A training scheme called state-based Explorative Modeling (`SXM`) runs K parallel descent trajectories per input and supervises only the trajectory–solution pair that matches best, which shapes the energy landscape to hold several valid solutions instead of collapsing them into one.
- With only **1.8M parameters**, `EBR` reaches **99.4%** single-sample accuracy on `Sudoku-Extreme` and **87.4%** on `Maze-Hard`, rising to **99.9%** and **88.3%** with 5 samples ranked by lowest energy; at comparable Sudoku accuracy it uses **345× fewer inference FLOPs** than `EqR`, and gradient-norm stopping alone cuts compute **10.8×** versus a fixed iteration budget.
- On multi-solution tasks, `EBR` gets near-perfect single-sample validity and raises 20-sample coverage of distinct solutions on 10×10 `N-Queens` from **57.5% to 92.0%** compared with `GRAM`, while ablations show that swapping energy descent for a directly learned transition drops Sudoku accuracy from 98.96% to 60.05%.
- Training requires second-order derivatives, custom GPU kernels and extra hyperparameters, `SXM` brought no gain on the small `Maze-Hard` training set, and every experiment is a structured algorithmic puzzle, so it remains untested whether the approach scales to language or general reasoning.

papers.title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
papers.abstract: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.
papers.summary: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are hard to run in real time on a robot, while small on-robot VLAs fail more often, and querying a server-hosted model for every action limits how many robots one server can support. The proposed VLA handover runs a small VLA locally and switches to a large server VLA only when a failure predictor expects the small one to fail. The switching is posed as minimizing request cost subject to a required success probability and is approximated with a heuristic framework that retrains neither model. In `LIBERO` simulations with `SmolVLA` and `π0.5`, handover raises success by 11 to 22 percentage points over the small model alone and sends **49 to 77% fewer server requests** than server-only control, at a 2 to 4 point lower success rate.

papers.title: LEF-JEPA: Denoising-Trained Latent Energy Fields for Spatial Representation Learning
papers.abstract: A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in its latent representations. We further observe that some existing methods improve spatial structure while also retaining rich variations in texture and color. However, preserving more low-level visual information does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. This raises a key question: how can we strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without over-encoding these details? We introduce LEF-JEPA, which learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead. To reduce the cost of energy optimization during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that allows low-energy-state search to be performed by specialized Ising solvers. On physical hardware, we validate the feasibility of achieving lower forward latency with fewer local updates. Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.
papers.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) that supervise prediction only at masked positions tend to capture object shapes and boundaries poorly in their latent representations. `LEF-JEPA` learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and passes this signal to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference cost. To make the energy optimization cheaper, the authors build a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that specialized Ising solver hardware can minimize, and they show lower forward latency on physical hardware. Under a `CIFAR-10` pretraining and frozen-encoder protocol, both variants **outperform `V-JEPA2.1`** on classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.

papers.title: Action-Centered Causal Bandits for Budget-Constrained Promotion Targeting
papers.abstract:
Web platforms select among costly interventions for each user to maximize incremental outcomes under a global budget. We formulate this problem as a budget-constrained contextual bandit with heterogeneous treatment effects. Although an action-independent outcome baseline cancels from treatment comparisons, modeling a nonlinear baseline can increase statistical complexity.
  We propose DR-CATE-CBwK, an action-centered causal bandit that directly learns treatment contrasts. Its online update remains valid under baseline-model misspecification without inverse-propensity weighting. It combines an offline doubly robust learner to warm-start treatment-effect estimates, an online action-centered estimator for sequential contrast learning, and a primal-dual controller with an affordable-action rule to enforce the effective-cost budget pathwise.
  For linear conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) in a stationary i.i.d. setting, we prove a high-probability (\widetilde{O}(Kd\sqrt{T})) regret bound, where K is the number of priced actions, d the context dimension, and T the horizon. We benchmark against the fluid linear program (LP) under the coverage-guaranteed action rule. We further show that the action-centered estimating moment remains unbiased under any predictable baseline estimate, whereas a specified separate-arm reward regression can exhibit asymptotic contrast bias under action-dependent logging and shared-baseline misspecification.
  On a semi-synthetic job-marketplace benchmark with real logged features and simulated outcomes, our practical Thompson-restricted variant achieves the lowest regret among evaluated budget-feasible methods in the operating regime. It reduces regret by approximately 20% versus the strongest reward-based baseline, outperforming raw-reward contextual bandits, BwK baselines, and a static offline policy, while never exceeding the effective-cost budget.
papers.summary: Web platforms choose among costly promotions for each user to maximize incremental outcomes under a global budget, which the authors frame as a budget-constrained contextual bandit with heterogeneous treatment effects. `DR-CATE-CBwK` learns treatment contrasts directly. It combines an offline doubly robust warm start, an online action-centered estimator that stays valid when the baseline model is misspecified, and a primal-dual controller that enforces the budget at every step. For linear conditional average treatment effects they prove an Õ(Kd√T) regret bound. On a semi-synthetic job-marketplace benchmark, a Thompson-sampling variant cuts regret by **about 20%** against the strongest reward-based baseline without ever exceeding the budget.

papers.title: Rethinking Optimization Methods for Hierarchical Feature Selection
papers.abstract: Rare-event forecasting often depends on interpretable conjunctions: a single keyword, location, or temporal cue may be weak, while their joint occurrence can identify a meaningful precursor. Hierarchical-Task Numerical conjunctive feature Learning (HTNL) selects Numerical Conjunctive Features (NCFs) through a structured sparsity objective. However, the resulting optimization problem is challenging, making optimization design critical to its practical performance. We give a unified diagnosis of four HTNL optimization families: original majorization-minimization (MM), variational quadratic form (VQF), alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), and weighted group lasso (WGL). Our analysis distinguishes three key factors that jointly determine HTNL optimization behavior. First, VQF and MM are algebraically equivalent under matched variational updates and optimize a squared-penalty formulation. Second, ADMM optimizes the unsquared objective through consensus splitting; we replace its truncated FISTA proximal solver with a scalar bisection update (ADMM-Bisect) for more accurate treatment of near-threshold blocks. Third, WGL targets the same unsquared objective, while all methods face rapidly decaying active-set admission scores. Across two synthetic datasets and 11 civil-unrest and flu-surveillance tasks, VQF achieves the highest mean AUC with the most compact non-collapsing supports. ADMM-Bisect reduces measured runtime, while calibrated WGL avoids the empty-support failures of its original scale. Synthetic results further show how proximal accuracy, pruning, and search budget affect candidate recovery, especially for longer conjunctions. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.
papers.summary: Hierarchical-Task Numerical conjunctive feature Learning (`HTNL`) selects interpretable feature conjunctions for rare-event forecasting through a structured sparsity objective that is hard to optimize. The authors analyze four optimization families: majorization-minimization (MM), variational quadratic form (VQF), ADMM, and weighted group lasso. They show that VQF and MM are algebraically equivalent and introduce `ADMM-Bisect`, which replaces a truncated proximal solver with a scalar bisection update. Across synthetic data and 11 civil-unrest and flu-surveillance tasks, **VQF achieves the highest mean AUC** with the most compact supports, while `ADMM-Bisect` reduces runtime.

papers.title: Enforcing Symmetries on Pre-trained ML Models for Physics
papers.abstract: Post-hoc group averaging (or test-time augmentation) is a simple way to impose symmetry on a trained predictor without changing its architecture or retraining it. For finite and compact groups, averaging over a normalized Haar measure on the group gives the Reynolds operator: a canonical projection onto invariant or equivariant predictors with known non-increasing risk guarantees under certain assumptions. This paper provides numerical experiments on physics emulation models that demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in this setting. We then extend this framework to non-compact group symmetries. For non-compact groups, the Haar measure cannot be normalized, so group averaging cannot be defined in the same way. We replace it with three alternatives: the Weyl unitary trick (which requires complexifying the space and extending the predictor), a data-dependent orthogonal projection (which involves a non-trivial optimization on the space of invariant or equivariant functions), and a frame averaging approach (which involves mapping each point to a set of orbit representatives). We illustrate the constructions theoretically and empirically on the unit-rescaling group and the Lorentz group. Our results show that in the non-compact case, the Weyl trick and frame averaging do not provide a consistent improvement over the baseline, except where the test data is out-of-distribution (an orders-of-magnitude improvement in this case) and, for the Weyl trick, in low-data regimes. The orthogonal projection can provide improvements in-distribution and out-of-distribution. We also observe that models trained directly on invariant features matched or beat the projection of an unconstrained one. We conclude that post-hoc symmetrization extends to non-compact groups, but it does not consistently outperform training a symmetric model.
papers.summary: Averaging a trained predictor's outputs over a symmetry group, also called test-time augmentation, imposes the symmetry without retraining. For compact groups this has known risk guarantees, and the authors confirm that it works on physics emulation models. They extend the idea to non-compact groups such as unit rescaling and the Lorentz group, where ordinary averaging is undefined, using three substitutes: the Weyl unitary trick, a data-dependent orthogonal projection, and frame averaging. The Weyl trick and frame averaging help mainly on out-of-distribution data, where gains reach orders of magnitude, while the projection helps both in and out of distribution. Even so, **models trained directly on invariant features match or beat post-hoc symmetrization**.

papers.title: When2What: A Timing-Conditioned Framework for Long-Horizon Forecasting of Continuous Cardiovascular Waveforms
papers.abstract: Long-horizon forecasting of quasi-periodic cardiovascular waveforms, such as the electrocardiogram (ECG), arterial blood pressure (ABP), and photoplethysmogram (PPG), requires predicting both when future cardiac events will occur (beat timing) and what the local structural pattern looks like around each event (beat morphology). However, standard sequence forecasters trained with pointwise mean squared error (MSE) average across uncertain future heartbeat phases, flattening sharp R peaks and pulse upstrokes into featureless baselines. Our analysis of intraoperative ECG reveals a clear temporal asymmetry: beat-time predictability from history decays within seconds due to stochastic heart-rate variability, whereas local beat morphology aligned at true beat times remains stable over several minutes. Guided by this insight, we introduce When2What, a timing-conditioned framework comprising three stages: Predict, Commit, and Generate. Given a 120-s history, When2What predicts a dense 60-s timing map, selects and sharpens discrete beat events into unit-height Gaussian impulses, and conditions a neural waveform generator on both these committed events and the observed history. Across intraoperative ECG, When2What substantially outperforms existing time-series and physiological forecasters, achieving a near-term waveform event skill of 0.644 and reproducing 95.62% of its predicted heartbeats in the generated waveform where direct long-horizon forecasters collapse into flat baselines. Furthermore, When2What transfers zero-shot to external hospital and atrial fibrillation cohorts, extends effectively to ABP and PPG pulse waveforms, and is supported by ablations and synthetic analyses that establish explicit timing conditioning as an effective paradigm for quasi-periodic long-horizon waveform forecasting.
papers.summary: Long-horizon forecasting of cardiovascular waveforms such as ECG, arterial blood pressure, and photoplethysmogram requires predicting both when heartbeats occur and what each beat looks like, but forecasters trained with mean squared error average over uncertain beat timing and flatten the signal. The authors observe that beat timing becomes unpredictable within seconds, while beat shape stays stable for minutes. `When2What` therefore predicts a dense timing map for the next 60 seconds, commits to discrete beat events, and conditions a neural waveform generator on those events and the observed history. On intraoperative ECG it reproduces **95.62% of its predicted heartbeats** in the generated waveform, where direct forecasters collapse to flat baselines, and it transfers zero-shot to external hospital and atrial fibrillation cohorts.

papers.title: Same Facts, Different Remedy: Linguistic Profiling and Arbitrariness in LLM and System One Decisions
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to resolve consumer complaints, and the way complainants write varies with age, education and socioeconomic status (SES). We audit three remedy-decision systems using sociolinguistic rewrites of US consumer financial complaints that are instructed to preserve every fact: two generative LLMs that return a single label (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini) and a probabilistic "System One" model that returns a distribution over remedies (Jev). Using pre-registered hypotheses tested once on held-out complaints, we separate two phenomena that single-label audits conflate. At the group scale, older, college-educated and higher-SES styles receive slightly more generous remedies; these effects replicate but are small, with every monetary-remedy gap within 0.5 percentage points. At the individual scale, two style versions of the same complaint receive different monetary decisions 2.6-6.3% of the time. In a variance-component analysis of the probabilistic model, persona components shared across the two rewrite models account for about 1.6% of within-complaint variation. The persona gaps are associated mainly with delivery (vocabulary, grammar, politeness) rather than content. Positive controls show that all three systems respond 49-387 times more strongly to remedy-relevant facts than to style. Rewriting every complaint into one standard style reduced GPT-4o-mini's education and SES gaps by 94% and 87% while retaining fact sensitivity, but reversed two of the probabilistic model's gaps and did not make individual decisions more stable. Independent LLM auditors flagged material fact changes in 3.3% and 11.7% of rewrites, and instability persisted among unflagged rewrites. Fairness audits of LLM decision systems should report group disparities and individual instability as separate outcomes.
papers.summary: LLMs are increasingly used to resolve consumer complaints, and complainants' writing style varies with age, education, and socioeconomic status. The authors audit `GPT-4o-mini`, `GPT-5-mini`, and a probabilistic remedy model using fact-preserving sociolinguistic rewrites of US consumer financial complaints, with pre-registered hypotheses. At the group level, older, college-educated, and higher-status styles get slightly more generous remedies, with all monetary gaps within 0.5 percentage points. At the individual level, **two style versions of the same complaint receive different monetary decisions 2.6 to 6.3% of the time**. All systems respond 49 to 387 times more strongly to relevant facts than to style. Rewriting complaints into one standard style shrinks some group gaps but does not make individual decisions more stable, so the authors argue that audits should report group disparity and individual instability separately.

papers.title: Calibrating your confidence requires thinking of all the ways you could be wrong
papers.abstract:
A primary limitation of modern deep learning is the miscalibration of model confidence; traditional architectures fundamentally lack a mechanism to quantify their own uncertainty. Larger models and larger datasets mitigate this issue, but they do not resolve the underlying structural deficiency. Bayesian methods offer a principled uncertainty-aware learning framework through stochastic parameters. Yet, despite the established benefits, the inherent computational overhead often compromises either scalability or quality. This trade-off currently prevents the widespread adoption of Bayesian methods.
  This Thesis bridges the gap between high-quality and low-complexity by introducing a novel distribution on parameter space: a degenerate Gaussian whose covariance is a projection matrix aligned with the null space of the Fisher information matrix. We demonstrate the scalability of this Bayesian posterior through two numerically efficient algorithms: one for posterior sampling and another for the direct computation of predictive confidence. Empirically, we show State-Of-The-Art confidence calibration and out-of-distribution detection for large models.
  We provide theoretical grounding for this approach. We study the degeneracies inherent in Amari's information geometry and highlight its most relevant component: the split of parameter's perturbations into two orthogonal subspaces. From this perspective, our posterior naturally emerges as the simplest choice that captures this split, assigning unitary variance to one subspace and zero variance to the other. Moreover, through the tools of differential geometry, we utilize this split to identify and rectify a critical misalignment issue of the non-linearized Laplace Approximation. Finally, with a focus on PAC-Bayes generalization bounds, we pave the way for a deeper understanding of the learning capabilities of overparametrized models.
papers.summary: Deep networks are often miscalibrated, and Bayesian methods that fix this are usually either too expensive or too low-quality to scale. This thesis introduces a degenerate Gaussian posterior over parameters whose covariance is a projection onto the null space of the Fisher information matrix, together with efficient algorithms for posterior sampling and for computing predictive confidence directly. The authors report **state-of-the-art calibration and out-of-distribution detection for large models**. On the theory side, they derive the posterior from information geometry as the simplest choice that separates parameter perturbations into two orthogonal subspaces, use this to correct a misalignment in the non-linearized Laplace approximation, and connect the approach to PAC-Bayes generalization bounds.

papers.title: Seeing vs. Counting: Complexity Twins Show Where Multimodal LLMs Fail on Diagrams
papers.abstract: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, does it fail at seeing or at counting? Existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together, confounding the two. We pair counting questions about the same drawing that sit in different counting-complexity classes, such as its spanning trees (a determinant) and its simple paths (#P-complete), and use a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. We test Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models; for the Gemini models, the answer depends on how the model computes. In chain of thought, most of them read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class (for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of the answer). Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, and a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, against 57/96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.
papers.summary: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, it is unclear whether it misread the image or miscomputed the count, because existing benchmarks change visual density and algorithmic difficulty together. The authors pair counting questions on the same drawing from different complexity classes, such as spanning trees and simple paths, and use a transcription probe and text-only controls to separate reading from computing. Testing `Gemini`, `Gemma`, and `Qwen3-VL` models, they find that with chain of thought most `Gemini` models read small drawings correctly but then miscount, with errors driven more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class. Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, which makes reading the bottleneck; a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks transcribes **86 of 96 large grids exactly**, against 57 when the upright reading is simply repeated.

papers.title: Capital Efficiency, Isolation, Risk, and Ruin in Generative AI Inference Serving Infrastructure
papers.abstract: Generative AI serving is an extremely capital-intensive endeavor that demands rapid, step-change improvements in capital efficiency to prevent industry wide increases in the cost of capital from limiting growth plans. Keeping pace with the economic necessities will increasingly require infrastructure providers to confront operationally-inconvenient realities of production serving, including the extreme heterogeneity of generative AI request costs. We have explored workload isolation as a foundational, fleet-level lever for increasing capital efficiency. Isolation is the practice of intelligently grouping "like" requests before execution. Rather than exposing every replica to the full heterogeneous workload distribution, isolation deliberately reshapes the workload presented to the hardware by assigning requests with different cost characteristics to different portions of the fleet. Workload isolation on its own does not make expensive requests cheaper; it prevents a costly portion of the workload from unnecessarily determining the operating point and capital efficiency of the entire fleet. It additionally lays the foundational groundwork that can serve as a launching point for compounding gains via narrow-band optimizations (tailoring) and custom silicon designs while also informing up on pricing policy. This paper uses representative production data and experience to convey the motivation behind isolation as a fleet-level lever for increased capital efficiency.
papers.summary: Generative AI serving is very capital-intensive, and request costs vary enormously, so expensive requests can set the operating point for an entire fleet. Drawing on representative production data and experience, the authors argue for workload isolation: grouping similar requests and routing requests with different cost profiles to different parts of the fleet. Isolation does not make expensive requests cheaper, but it **keeps the costly part of the workload from setting the capital efficiency of the whole fleet**. The authors present it as groundwork for further gains from narrow-band tuning, custom silicon, and pricing policy.

papers.title: FoundaRF: A Physics-Informed Foundation Model Framework for Radio-Frequency Passive Components
papers.abstract: Designing RF/mmWave passive components is a time-consuming process that relies heavily on expert knowledge and iterative EM simulations. Although recent ML surrogate models have shown great promise in accelerating passive design, they remain task-specific and lack generalization. This paper presents FoundaRF, a foundation model framework that unifies passive layout modeling across diverse layout structures and technologies. It combines a self-supervised encoder with adaptive layout processing and physics-aware decoders to enable few-shot transfer. Experiments across four semiconductor technologies show strong generalization to unseen structures, outperforming baselines with up to a 3.3x reduction in prediction error, reducing labeled-data requirements by up to fourfold, and substantially shortening design turnaround. FoundaRF establishes a scalable and data-efficient solution for RF/mmWave passive design automation.
papers.summary: Designing RF and millimeter-wave passive components relies on expert knowledge and repeated electromagnetic simulation, and existing machine-learning surrogate models are task-specific. `FoundaRF` is a foundation model framework that combines a self-supervised encoder, adaptive layout processing, and physics-aware decoders, allowing few-shot transfer across layout structures and semiconductor technologies. Across four technologies it generalizes to unseen structures, cuts prediction error by **up to 3.3 times** relative to baselines, and needs up to four times less labeled data.

papers.title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning Market Making: Lessons from Loss Function Experimentation
papers.abstract: Market makers play a vital role in ensuring efficient trade within financial markets. Recent literature has delved into training market-making systems using reinforcement learning. This paper delves into the impact of various loss function formulations on risk management behavior within reinforcement-based market making. Through empirical evaluation, we contrast profit-maximizing strategies with risk-averse approaches, finding that penalties for inventory and cash management foster more resilient and adaptable market-making strategies. Our results underscore the significance of striking a balance between profit maximization and risk management in algorithmic trading, providing actionable insights for refining strategies in practical settings.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning has been used to train market-making agents, and this study examines how the choice of loss function shapes their risk behavior. The authors compare profit-maximizing objectives with risk-averse ones in empirical experiments. They find that **adding penalties for inventory and cash positions produces more resilient and adaptable strategies**, which they present as evidence that profit and risk management need to be balanced in algorithmic trading.

papers.title: KnowEvo: Knowledge Evolution for Protein Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in scientific discovery, yet systematically accumulating and refining reusable scientific knowledge remains challenging. Existing approaches primarily improve LLM-based problem solving through parameter optimization or feedback-driven refinement of prompts, programs, and solution trajectories, leaving acquired expertise either embedded in model weights or scattered across iterative problem-solving processes. As a result,knowledge is difficult to systematically inspect, evaluate, and refine. We propose KnowEvo, a framework that treats externalized knowledge itself as the optimization target. Our key insight is that scientific knowledge is inherently modular: multiple interacting mechanisms jointly determine the design outcomes. This makes knowledge evolution fundamentally challenging, as improvements cannot be attributed to individual components in isolation. To address this, KnowEvo represents knowledge as executable expertise blocks and organizes their refinements into strategy mutation trees, enabling structured exploration over a combinatorial knowledge space. The framework combines a Thompson-style forward allocation strategy that adaptively distributes evaluation budgets across strategy variants with a backward revision process, in which a code agent operates in an isolated sandbox to translate rollout evidence into localized program updates. This design enables persistent accumulation, evaluation, and refinement of mechanistic expertise across iterative experimentation. We evaluate KnowEvo on protein optimization tasks including stability and solubility. Results show that knowledge evolution consistently improves over initial strategy blocks and outperforms monolithic program evolution and prior LLM-guided evolution baselines across metrics such as pass@k, MRR, MAP,and NDCG@5. Code is available at https://github.com/recynie/KnowEvo.
papers.summary: LLM-driven scientific discovery tends to leave acquired expertise buried in model weights or spread across problem-solving traces, where it is hard to inspect or refine. `KnowEvo` makes externalized knowledge the optimization target: it represents expertise as executable blocks and organizes their refinements into strategy mutation trees. A Thompson-style allocation step distributes evaluation budget across strategy variants, and in a backward revision step a code agent working in an isolated sandbox turns rollout evidence into localized program updates. On protein stability and solubility optimization, knowledge evolution **outperforms monolithic program evolution and prior LLM-guided evolution baselines** on pass@k, MRR, MAP, and NDCG@5.

papers.title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
papers.abstract: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.
papers.summary: Earlier work tests LLM introspection by injecting a concept direction into a text-only model's activations and asking whether it notices. Vision-language models (VLMs) must additionally keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see, a problem cognitive psychology calls reality monitoring. The authors vary the image and the injected concept independently and ask models what they see, whether a thought was injected, and what it was. Across six VLMs, only `Gemma-3-27B` reliably identifies injected concepts (35% versus 3% for steering alone), and its source attributions are fragile: strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen. In ordinary captioning, **injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions** of real photographs.

papers.title: SIMBAD: Spatio-Temporal Traffic Forecasting Robust to Aperiodicity
papers.abstract: Accurate traffic prediction is essential for urban planning but remains challenging due to the irregular patterns caused by unexpected events. While Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) effectively model periodic data, they often struggle with these aperiodic fluctuations. To address this, we propose SIMBAD, which improves generalization irregular patterns via two key mechanisms: 1) adaptive regulation of periodic signals to prioritize recent signals, and 2) dynamic spatial modeling that adjusts influence between connected nodes based on contextual relations. Built upon simple similarity metrics to adapt to aperiodic patterns, SIMBAD outperforms existing methods on real-world benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior performance in predicting unseen and irregular traffic events.
papers.summary: Spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs) model periodic traffic patterns well but struggle with irregular fluctuations caused by unexpected events. `SIMBAD` addresses this with two similarity-based mechanisms: adaptive regulation of periodic signals that gives more weight to recent observations, and dynamic spatial modeling that adjusts the influence between connected road nodes based on context. On real-world benchmark datasets it **outperforms existing methods**, particularly on unseen and irregular traffic events.

papers.title: Optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming: Complexity and Implementations
papers.abstract: Probabilistic Answer Set Programming (PASP) extends Answer Set Programming with the possibility of representing uncertain data. Among the possible available semantics, we focus here on the credal semantics. In this setting, prior work has focused exclusively on plain ASP programs, i.e., programs without optimization constructs. However, many real world tasks define optimality criteria over the possible solutions, which cannot be conveniently modeled with existing probabilistic ASP frameworks. In this paper, we close this gap and propose optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming, which extends PASP by also allowing weak constraints, which are the standard optimization construct of ASP. We define the semantics of such programs, study the computational complexity of the inference and most probable explanation tasks, and propose practical implementations based on Algebraic Model Counting and Answer Set Programming with Quantifiers. An empirical evaluation of the proposed approach on three real world tasks confirms the applicability of our framework.
papers.summary: Probabilistic Answer Set Programming (PASP) adds uncertain facts to Answer Set Programming (ASP), but under the credal semantics prior work covered only programs without optimization constructs. This work extends PASP with weak constraints, ASP's standard way to state optimality criteria, and defines the semantics of the resulting optimal PASP programs. It analyzes the computational complexity of inference and most probable explanation tasks, and gives implementations based on `Algebraic Model Counting` and `ASP with Quantifiers`. **Experiments on three real-world tasks show that the framework is practical to apply**.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation from Neural Networks to Differentiable Logic Networks
papers.abstract: Differentiable logic networks (DLNs) are interpretable, edge-friendly classifiers that learn both their logic operators and their connections through gradient descent, achieving accuracy competitive with multi-layer perceptrons at orders-of-magnitude lower inference cost. Their accuracy, however, is bounded by the problems of vanishing gradients, scalability, and lack of an ecosystem, leaving a gap relative to conventional neural networks on several datasets. We introduce knowledge distillation for DLNs to narrow this gap. We distill from a trained multi-layer perceptron teacher into a DLN student, integrating the distillation objective into a two-phase training loop without altering the architecture or the inference procedure. The teacher is discarded after training. Hence, the distilled model retains the interpretability, sparsity, and inference cost of a conventionally trained DLN. We investigate this approach through four variants: a joint hyperparameter search that optimizes the distillation weight and temperature alongside the architecture, a grid search over these two hyperparameters with the architecture fixed, and two single-phase variants that employ distillation during only the neuron-function or only the connection phase. On 20 public tabular classification tasks, distillation improves balanced-class accuracy at negligible cost to gate-level operation counts and model size, though the benefit varies by dataset. Performance improvements of up to 15% are observed, in some cases surpassing the teacher itself.
papers.summary: Differentiable logic networks (DLNs) learn both their logic gates and their wiring by gradient descent, and they are interpretable classifiers that are cheap to run on edge devices. Their accuracy still lags behind standard neural networks on some datasets. The authors distill a trained multi-layer perceptron teacher into a DLN student during the DLN's two-phase training loop, leaving the architecture and the inference procedure unchanged, and compare four variants of where and how distillation is tuned and applied. Across 20 tabular classification tasks, distillation improves balanced-class accuracy by **up to 15%**, sometimes beyond the teacher, with negligible change in gate counts or model size, though the gain varies by dataset.

papers.title: Language, Not Code Abstraction: Natural-language Training Shapes Brain-aligned Geometry
papers.abstract: Code-trained language models produce positive brain scores, which raises the question of whether abstract structure learned from programming languages can substitute for natural-language training. We trained 25 GPT-2-small models on TinyStories, Python, C functions, x86-64 assembly, and the corresponding machine code, and scored them using a shared tokenizer and encoding procedure against matched random-weight models. On Pereira-243 and Tuckute2024, TinyStories exceeds the mean of the four code models by $\Delta r = 0.053$ and $0.059$ (Holm-corrected $p<0.001$), while code training leaves alignment near the random-weight level. The language advantage is benchmark-specific: Blank2014 shows no corrected language-code difference, and Fedorenko2016 shows no language benefit. Geometry tracks the encoding result on Pereira-243: TinyStories seeds converge on the most similar representations, and its fit-free correspondence with neural dissimilarity peaks at $\rho = 0.14$, twice the code and random-weight levels. Binary-trained models have about three effective dimensions, so seed agreement alone does not imply neural correspondence. Updating only the embedding matrix on English improves mean-over-depth alignment for every code model more than an equal update on its own corpus. Within this architecture and training setup, natural-language training produces a distinct representational geometry with closer neural correspondence on Pereira-243
papers.summary: Language models trained on code also show some alignment with human brain recordings, which raises the question of whether abstract structure learned from programming languages can stand in for natural-language training. The authors trained 25 `GPT-2-small` models on `TinyStories`, Python, C, x86-64 assembly, and machine code, and scored each against random-weight baselines on several neural benchmarks. On `Pereira-243` and `Tuckute2024`, the language-trained models beat the code models by about 0.05-0.06 in correlation, while **code training leaves brain alignment close to the random-weight level**. The advantage depends on the benchmark: `Blank2014` and `Fedorenko2016` show no language benefit. Updating only the embedding matrix of a code model on English text improves its alignment.

papers.title: Scout Before You Route: Predicting Task Success and Token Count from a Small LLM Prefill
papers.abstract: Routers typically choose a model per query by trading predicted correctness against cost. Most price each model at a fixed cost, as if every query used the same number of output tokens, but the output length of reasoning models varies by an order of magnitude across queries. When is per-query cost worth predicting? What factors drive cost? How cheaply can predictions be made? We predict both the success probability and the output length of candidate models from the prefill activations of a single small frozen LLM, the scout. With reasoning candidates, perfect per-query cost knowledge would save 29-61% of spending on eight of nine datasets, and much less with non-reasoning candidates on the same problems. On those eight datasets, our predicted costs save 9-33% at matched accuracy relative to median-length pricing, up to 69% of what perfect knowledge would save. They are significantly cheaper than each estimator we reimplemented or adapted from published work, including ZeroRouter and a MixLLM-style predictor, on a majority of datasets. Output length depends mostly on the problem. On most math and code datasets, harder problems are longer, so predicted success alone prices cost nearly as well. On knowledge and mixed-format datasets they are not, and predicted success falls well behind a probe trained on length. The probe keeps most of its saving with 20 labelled problems and transfers without labels to four of seven new benchmarks. On a mixture of all nine benchmarks, it saves 22% beyond pricing each benchmark at its own median length. Savings stop growing at about a 2B scout, so above 4B a larger scout costs more than it adds.
papers.summary: LLM routers usually assign each candidate model a fixed cost per query, even though the output length of reasoning models can vary tenfold from one query to the next. The authors use the prefill activations of a single small frozen LLM, the scout, to predict both each candidate's chance of answering correctly and the number of tokens it will produce. With reasoning candidates, the predicted costs **save 9-33% of spending at matched accuracy** compared with median-length pricing, which beats reimplemented baselines such as `ZeroRouter` and a `MixLLM`-style predictor on most datasets. The length probe needs only about 20 labelled problems, often transfers to new benchmarks without labels, and gains stop growing at about a 2B-parameter scout.

papers.title: A Controlled Study of Models, Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum in Agentic Robotics
papers.abstract: Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update. Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.
papers.summary: Agentic robotics uses coding agents to write and iteratively improve robot control policies from the results of physical interaction. This controlled simulation study covers nine manipulation tasks, 631 experiment configurations, and 28K coding-agent rollouts, and it systematically varies model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The results suggest that **the bottleneck is usually not access to information but turning that information into the right policy update**. Self-improvement works best when agents correctly attribute failures, reason about the task's spatial and geometric structure, and make selective rather than wholesale changes to the code.

papers.title: ToolDex: An Ego-Exo Human Demonstration Dataset for Creative Physical Tool Use
papers.abstract:
Creative tool use is a fundamental human capability and an important step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. It requires agents to reason about object affordances, physical constraints, and manipulation strategies, especially when standard tools are unavailable. However, progress in this area is limited by the lack of real-world datasets that capture human tool-use behavior with sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, focus on simplified interactions, or lack detailed observations and annotations.
  We introduce ToolDex, a large-scale egocentric-exocentric (ego-exo) human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use. ToolDex captures scenarios in which humans select, adapt, and repurpose available objects as tools. Using synchronized egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras, the dataset provides high-fidelity multi-view observations and rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. Beyond data collection, we establish a benchmark suite characterizing three core capabilities: physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning. ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and developing embodied agents that can adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments.
  Dataset visualizations and benchmarking results are available at https://tooluse-dataset.github.io/.
papers.summary: Research on creative tool use, where agents repurpose available objects when the standard tool is missing, is held back by a lack of realistic, large-scale data. `ToolDex` is a human demonstration dataset recorded with synchronized egocentric (first-person) cameras and eight exocentric (external) cameras, showing people selecting, adapting, and repurposing objects as tools. It includes detailed annotations of hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. The dataset comes with **a benchmark suite covering physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning**.

papers.title: Function-Space Certification for Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Certifying the robustness and physical consistency of scientific machine-learning models ensures that their predictions remain reliable beyond the test set. For neural operators, which learn PDE solution operators by mapping infinite-dimensional function spaces, certification means establishing rigorous, domain-wide guarantees for their output functions. However, standard neural network (NN) verification methods are fundamentally designed for vector-to-vector mappings, and they can only certify neural operators at fixed grid resolutions and provide no guarantees over the entire domain or across another resolution. We close this gap by introducing a function-space certification framework that verifies neural operators across the entire continuous domain. We formulate interval bound propagation (IBP) and CROWN in function space, propagating upper and lower bound functions through each layer using rigorous numerical integration. In addition, we extend bound propagation to higher-order derivatives to certify PDE residuals and solution error bounds. Experiments across several neural operator architectures and scientific problems, including the 572.5-million-parameter spherical Fourier neural operator for global weather forecasting, show that our method produces tight, domain-wide guarantees efficiently, providing a foundation for trustworthy operator learning.
papers.summary: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces to solve partial differential equations (PDEs), but standard neural-network verification works only on fixed-size vectors and therefore certifies these models only at a single grid resolution. The authors reformulate interval bound propagation (`IBP`) and `CROWN` in function space, propagating upper and lower bound functions through each layer with rigorous numerical integration. They also extend bound propagation to higher-order derivatives so that PDE residuals and solution error bounds can be certified. The method gives tight, domain-wide guarantees efficiently across several architectures, **including a 572.5-million-parameter spherical Fourier neural operator used for global weather forecasting**.

papers.title: Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection for Reasoning Distillation
papers.abstract: Training smaller language models on reasoning solutions generated by a larger teacher model is the prevailing approach for transferring mathematical reasoning capabilities. However, the student tends to overfit the output distribution of the teacher and generalizes poorly when its own behavior at inference time deviates from the training data. Recent methods attempt to bridge this gap by incorporating error data, yet the corrective trajectories still reflect the reasoning patterns of the teacher, which the student cannot reliably reproduce, leaving the distribution mismatch largely unresolved. We propose a method, Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), built on the insight that effective training data should be jointly determined by what the student fails on and what it can realistically learn. Our method first profiles the failure behavior of the student on each problem through repeated sampling, characterizing it in terms of error rate and error consistency to reveal qualitatively distinct failure modes. Each mode demands a fundamentally different training signal. The diagnosed mode then guides candidate generation from the teacher via distinct prompting strategies tailored to each failure type. Among the correct candidates, our method selects the one whose initial reasoning steps after the point of divergence are most reproducible by the student. These first corrective steps constitute the primary bottleneck, while the remaining steps follow an already corrected context and can therefore be continued more readily. This contrasts with standard reranking approaches, which score the trajectory as a whole and thereby dilute the signal at the critical reasoning transition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves the SOTA performance across the five benchmarks on both student backbones.
papers.summary: Small models trained on a larger teacher's math solutions tend to overfit the teacher's reasoning style and then struggle when their own outputs drift from it. Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (`FPRT`) first samples the student repeatedly on each problem and classifies its failure mode by error rate and error consistency. It then prompts the teacher with a strategy tailored to that failure mode. Among the correct candidates, it keeps the one whose first corrective steps after the point of divergence the student can most easily reproduce, rather than scoring whole trajectories. The method reports **state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks with two student backbones**.

papers.title: When Can You Trust Neural Critics? Auditing Mutual Information Estimates of Higher-Order Epistasis in Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Mutual information (MI) estimation is used to probe what neural representations encode, including in protein language models, but variational MI estimators have variance that scales at least exponentially in the true MI. We audit a prior neural-MI study of order-resolved epistasis in ESM-2 on the four-site GB1 landscape. Run-to-run differences show no systematic bias and a magnitude comparable to ordinary cross-seed retraining variability, and the evaluation-pairing scheme shifts scores substantially. At the original dimensionality, two of three alternative estimator families stabilize the estimate across seeds and one does not. In a synthetic calibration at the representation dimensionalities of two other protein language models (a Gaussian channel with known MI; no model representations), all three families recover materially less signal than required, despite correct signal ordering and stable seeds. A control critic given the true signal direction, which also reduces its input to one dimension, recovers 93.3% and 98.7% of the analytic MI at gain 1.5 (at 5,120 and 4,096 dimensions), so the signal is recoverable with privileged information, but the control does not identify why blind estimation fails. We package the checks into a reusable diagnostic protocol and conclude that even a stabilized estimator is not currently sufficient for order-resolved dependence claims made under blind search at this dimensionality and sample size.
papers.summary: Neural mutual information (MI) estimators are used to probe what learned representations encode, but their variance grows rapidly as the true MI increases. The authors audit a prior study that measured higher-order epistasis in `ESM-2` on the four-site `GB1` protein landscape. They find that run-to-run differences are as large as ordinary retraining noise and that the choice of evaluation pairing shifts scores substantially. In synthetic calibrations with known MI at the dimensionality of other protein language models, **all three estimator families recover materially less signal than needed**, even though they rank signals correctly. The authors package their checks into a reusable diagnostic protocol and conclude that current estimators cannot support order-resolved dependence claims at this dimensionality and sample size.

papers.title: LeanDojo-v2: A Comprehensive Library for AI-Assisted Theorem Proving in Lean
papers.abstract: Building on recent progress in machine learning for formal theorem proving in Lean, we introduce LeanDojo-v2: an end-to-end framework that unifies repository data extraction, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, AI autocompletion, and LLM-assisted theorem proving in a single software library. In addition, we provide Lean4Code, a lightweight IDE that integrates the various features of LeanDojo-v2 through a simple, mathematician-friendly UI. These tools will enable mathematicians and researchers to easily fine-tune language models on domain-specific Lean codebases and experiment with LLM-assisted theorem proving without a complex setup.
papers.summary: `LeanDojo-v2` is an end-to-end software library for AI-assisted theorem proving in the `Lean` proof assistant. It combines extraction of data from Lean repositories, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, AI autocompletion, and LLM-assisted proving in one library. It also ships with `Lean4Code`, a lightweight IDE that exposes these features through an interface designed for mathematicians. **The goal is to let researchers fine-tune models on their own Lean codebases and experiment with LLM-assisted proving without complex setup**.
papers.highlight_summary:
AI-assisted theorem proving in Lean is spread across separate research tools that are hard to maintain and require programming skill to set up. `LeanDojo-v2` combines repository data extraction, model fine-tuning, proof search and whole-proof generation in one Python library, and `Lean4Code` provides an editor built for Lean that lets mathematicians use these tools with a few clicks.

- The training pipeline extracts theorems, proofs and premises from any Lean repository, groups theorems into easy, medium and hard by proof length (cut at the 33rd and 67th percentiles), and trains progressively from easier repositories to harder ones, following `LeanAgent`.
- Any `HuggingFace` model can be fine-tuned to predict the next tactic from the current proof state, using SFT, `LoRA`, or reinforcement learning with `GRPO` or `PPO` and user-defined rewards such as proof success.
- Proving works either step by step, using `Pantograph` for DFS or MCTS search over a goal-tactic graph and a shortest-path pass to recover a minimal-length proof, or by generating the whole proof in one pass, including through hosted `DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B` via the HuggingFace API.
- Moving autocompletion to API inference removes the need for local C++ inference libraries like `CTranslate2`, which cuts setup time from **over ten minutes to a few seconds** compared with `LeanCopilot`.
- The paper reports no proving benchmarks or success rates, so the system's value is in its infrastructure and usability; `Lean4Code` also only supports the Lean version of the latest library release, and newer Lean versions often break backward compatibility.

papers.title: StreamTab: Training-Free Temporal Link Prediction with Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Temporal link prediction uses past interactions to predict whether two nodes will interact in the future. Temporal graph neural networks achieve strong results on this task, but they are trained separately for each graph. How a model should use interaction history also depends on the candidates it is compared with. A past interaction can distinguish a recurring link from a random pair that has never interacted, but when the negative candidates have also interacted before, other signals are needed.
