We propose StreamTab, a training-free framework built on a frozen tabular foundation model pretrained only on synthetic tables. StreamTab describes each candidate pair by statistics of its past interactions and shows the model recent observed interactions and sampled negative pairs as labeled examples, from which the model scores new candidates. Its central design, regime conditioning, samples the negative examples according to how the candidates are sampled, so the examples show the distinction the model must make. As new interactions arrive, StreamTab updates the statistics and refreshes the examples while the model parameters stay fixed. On thirteen datasets against 21 temporal graph baselines, StreamTab achieves the highest average precision on twelve datasets under historical sampling and eleven under inductive sampling, and ranks first or stays within one point of the best on seven datasets under random sampling. With the same features and model, regime conditioning raises average precision over examples with random negatives by a median of 12.6 points under historical sampling.
papers.summary: Temporal link prediction asks whether two nodes in a graph will interact in the future, and the strongest methods are temporal graph neural networks that must be trained separately for each graph. `StreamTab` instead uses a frozen tabular foundation model pretrained only on synthetic tables, describing each candidate pair with statistics of its past interactions and supplying recent positive pairs and sampled negative pairs as in-context examples. Its key design, regime conditioning, samples those negative examples the same way the test candidates are sampled, so the examples show the distinction the model actually has to make. Without any training, it achieves **the highest average precision on 12 of 13 datasets** against 21 baselines under historical negative sampling, and regime conditioning alone adds a median of 12.6 points of average precision.

papers.title: Equidistribution of Solution Gradients in Physics-Informed Neural Networks via Coordinate Transformations
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) often struggle to approximate solutions with sharp gradients due to optimization difficulties and spectral bias. Motivated by the principle of gradient equidistribution from the stretching approach in grid generation, which redistributes solution gradients to reduce functional complexity, we propose Coordinate Transformation PINNs (CTPINNs), which incorporate learnable coordinate transformations to map the physical domain into a computational domain where the physical solutions become approximately affine, making them easier for neural networks to learn. We propose two constructions of the transformation: an explicit construction based on Majorants and an implicit construction based on invertable neural networks. Experimentally, the explicit construction can improve accuracy for PDEs with available explicit coordinate transformations, and the implicit construction can be combined with other advanced PINN models as an efficient plug-in module to improve performance across a range of challenging PDE benchmarks.
papers.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) struggle to fit solutions with sharp gradients because of optimization difficulties and spectral bias, the tendency of networks to learn smooth functions first. Coordinate Transformation PINNs (`CTPINNs`) borrow the idea of gradient equidistribution from mesh generation: they learn a coordinate transformation that maps the physical domain into a computational domain where the solution is approximately affine and easier to learn. The transformation is built either explicitly from majorant functions or implicitly with invertible neural networks. The explicit version improves accuracy when a suitable explicit transformation exists, and **the implicit version works as a plug-in that improves other advanced PINN models** on challenging PDE benchmarks.

papers.title: Real-Time Short-Response Selection for Spoken Dialogue Systems
papers.abstract: To realize spoken dialogue systems that can interact naturally with users, it is important for the system to respond to user utterances at appropriate timings. To achieve such natural turn-taking, the system needs not only to predict appropriate response timings but also to mask delays caused by language generation and speech synthesis so that they are not perceived by the user. We propose a real-time short-response selection task that can be integrated with existing turn-taking models to mask generation delay. To address this task, the proposed model learns the mapping between dialogue context and short responses using contrastive learning. When a turn-taking event is detected, the system selects a response from a set of pre-generated candidates. The selected response is played while the main response is being generated. Experimental results show that the proposed method learns to select short responses based on dialogue context, outperforming random and LLM-based baselines. Moreover, integrating response selection maintained turn-taking prediction performance and added minimal processing overhead.
papers.summary: Spoken dialogue systems need to reply at natural moments, but generating language and synthesizing speech introduce delays that users notice. The authors propose a real-time short-response selection task. When a turn-taking model detects that the system should speak, a model trained with contrastive learning picks a fitting short reply from pre-generated candidates and plays it while the full response is generated. The selector **outperforms random and LLM-based baselines** at choosing context-appropriate replies, keeps turn-taking prediction performance intact, and adds minimal processing overhead.

papers.title: ProtoCouncil: Multi-Encoder Anatomical Prototypes for Prostate Cancer Detection in Micro-Ultrasound
papers.abstract:
Purpose: Micro-ultrasound ($\mu$US) is a promising modality for prostate cancer (PCa) detection, but identifying suspicious tissue depends heavily on clinical experience. Models trained on sparse, noisy core-level pathology offer little insight into their decisions and can fail under domain shift. Clinical use needs a traceable decision process and a flag for uncertain predictions.
  Methods: We introduce ProtoCouncil, in which three foundation encoders (MedSAM, DINOv3 and V-JEPA 2.1) learn case-based prototypes at three anatomical levels: whole gland, needle track and gland sectors. Prototypes are projected onto real training-core regions, and label-free fusion keeps every class logit as a bias plus an exact sum of prototype similarity contributions. Encoder disagreement triggers selective prediction.
  Results: In five-fold patient-level cross-validation (6,588 cores, 693 patients), ProtoCouncil reaches 82.9% AUROC for clinically significant PCa (csPCa, Grade Group $\geq$3), 4.3 points above the best previously published method. In zero-shot evaluation on two external cohorts, ProtoCouncil achieves higher all-cancer and csPCa AUROC than all previous methods. Nearest same-class exemplars match test-core tumor involvement better than random same-class cases. Externally, csPCa accuracy falls from 79% when encoders agree to 27% when two oppose the fused call. Abstaining on disagreement raises balanced accuracy by 7 and 15 points, while retaining 58% and 54% of the cores.
  Conclusion: ProtoCouncil grounds core-level predictions in exact similarity-based evidence from real, anatomically indexed training cases, which makes its reasoning interpretable. It achieves the highest csPCa AUROC across three cohorts and identifies unreliable predictions through encoder disagreement.
papers.summary: Detecting prostate cancer in micro-ultrasound depends heavily on clinical experience, and existing models are hard to interpret and break under domain shift. `ProtoCouncil` has three foundation encoders (`MedSAM`, `DINOv3`, `V-JEPA 2.1`) learn case-based prototypes at the whole-gland, needle-track, and gland-sector levels, so that each prediction decomposes exactly into similarities to real training cases. Disagreement between the encoders is used to flag predictions to abstain on. On 693 patients it reaches **82.9% AUROC for clinically significant cancer, 4.3 points above the best prior method**, leads on two external cohorts, and abstaining on encoder disagreement raises balanced accuracy by 7-15 points.

papers.title: Does Reasoning Improve Psychological Depth in Large Language Models?
papers.abstract: Benchmark gains from reasoning-enhanced large language models encourage the assumption that these models should broadly perform better on complex generative tasks, but this remains underexplored in open-ended, creative domains shaped by nuances of reader experience. We tested this assumption through the lens of psychological depth in short stories. We compared DeepSeek-R1 vs. DeepSeek-V3, our closest available contrast for reasoning-oriented post-training, and GPT-5 vs. GPT-4o, through 60 blinded pairwise evaluations in which seven human annotators and an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge rated prompt-matched story outputs. Human evaluations showed no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 was slightly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0-62.9% across two reasoning-effort settings), whereas DeepSeek-R1 fell behind DeepSeek-V3 (42.9%). Although this pattern was marked by low inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.070$), our annotation-quality checks suggested genuine evaluative subjectivity, plausibly reflecting distinct annotator decision schemes rather than annotation failure. In contrast, the LLM-as-a-Judge showed a strong pro-reasoning bias (98.3% of pairs vs. 55.2% of human votes), consistent across its five configurations and partly tracking sentence length. These findings suggest that, at the frontier, reasoning-related quality differences are small enough to be dominated by reader subjectivity, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators can obscure this subjectivity in nuanced creative-generation tasks.
papers.summary: This study tests whether reasoning-oriented LLMs write short stories with more psychological depth, comparing `DeepSeek-R1` against `DeepSeek-V3` and `GPT-5` against `GPT-4o` in blinded pairwise ratings from seven human annotators and an LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble. Human raters showed no consistent reasoning advantage: `GPT-5` was slightly preferred over `GPT-4o`, while `DeepSeek-R1` fell behind `DeepSeek-V3`, with very low agreement between annotators that appears to reflect genuine subjectivity rather than poor annotation. **The LLM judge preferred the reasoning model in 98.3% of pairs, compared with 55.2% of human votes**, a bias that partly tracked sentence length. The authors conclude that LLM judges can hide reader subjectivity in nuanced creative tasks.

papers.title: WearableBridge: Task-Guided Latent Transport for Free-Living Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Wrist-worn accelerometers make activity monitoring feasible at scale, but incidental arm motion, device orientation, and shifting context blur the signal that separates activities. Calibration studies supply higher-quality references such as concurrent thigh recordings or supervised laboratory wrist sessions, but they are expensive, cover few participants, and are rarely available at deployment. How can limited reference data improve recognition for participants who wear only a wrist device? We propose WearableBridge, which holds the reference encoder and classifier fixed and learns a task-guided transport map, the bridge, that carries each wrist feature into the region the classifier associates with its activity. Reference features or the classifier's predictions indicate the destination, and a classification loss penalizes wrist features that land in the region of another activity. We instantiate WearableBridge with three bridges: Mapper regresses onto reference features, Distillation matches the classifier's class probabilities, and MeanFlow learns a one-step flow from wrist toward reference features. On 40 held-out free-living PAAWS participants, all three bridges improve macro-F1 in every training run, and the strongest, MeanFlow, raises mean macro-F1 from 35.1% to 56.0% with concurrent thigh references (Thigh2Wrist), and from 54.0% to 63.5% with group-matched laboratory wrist references (Lab2Freeliving). Fitted only on PAAWS, MeanFlow also raises macro-F1 on the CAPTURE-24 cohort from 42.8% to 54.7%. The gains replicate on selfBACK, hold across four reference encoders, and grow with temporal context. A study can therefore collect reference recordings for a calibration subset and improve wrist-only recognition for every other participant, training only a bridge of 0.13 to 2.44 million parameters while the reference encoder and classifier stay unchanged.
papers.summary: Wrist-worn accelerometers make large-scale activity monitoring practical, but arm motion and device orientation blur the signal, and higher-quality reference recordings, such as a thigh sensor or supervised lab sessions, are available for only a few participants. `WearableBridge` keeps a reference encoder and classifier fixed and learns a small transport map, the bridge, that moves wrist features into the region the classifier associates with the correct activity. Three bridge variants are tested, and the strongest, `MeanFlow`, **raises macro-F1 from 35.1% to 56.0%** on held-out free-living `PAAWS` participants when thigh recordings are used as references. The gains carry over to the `CAPTURE-24` and `selfBACK` datasets, and the bridge needs only 0.13-2.44 million parameters.

papers.title: UniRGBA: Unifying RGB and Alpha in Pretrained Video Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have achieved remarkable photorealistic RGB synthesis, yet generating videos with a native alpha channel remains an open challenge. Existing approaches often rely on matting-style data and non-native RGBA designs, causing them to specialize in real-object scenes and to degrade severely on visual-effect content whose semi-transparency is spatially non-local and non-elliptical. We present UniRGBA, a unified framework whose key insight is that RGBA generation does not require a dedicated alpha encoder or complex latent-space restructuring---a minimal, targeted extension of the existing RGB pathway is sufficient. UniRGBA-VAE extends a causal video VAE to 4-channel RGBA via zero-initialized channel expansion, symmetric selective layer unfreezing (5% trainable), and a six-term progressive reconstruction loss anchored by a KL reference loss that prevents latent drift, followed by a two-stage schedule that introduces a lightweight GAN objective. We then apply standard DoRA to the pretrained DiT, reusing the unified 4-channel latent without any alpha-specific architectural changes. On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, UniRGBA substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction while preserving RGB fidelity. For generation, UniRGBA outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA text-to-video tasks and matches or surpasses the original pretrained Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics, demonstrating that native alpha support can be integrated without compromising the underlying RGB prior or the model's architectural versatility.
papers.summary: Video diffusion models produce photorealistic RGB video but generally cannot output a native alpha (transparency) channel, and existing approaches break down on visual-effect content with complex semi-transparency. `UniRGBA` shows that a minimal extension of the existing RGB pipeline is enough. Its VAE gains a fourth channel through zero-initialized channel expansion with only 5% of layers unfrozen, and the pretrained diffusion transformer is adapted with standard `DoRA` without any alpha-specific changes. The approach **outperforms `Wan-Alpha` on RGBA reconstruction and text-to-video generation while matching or exceeding the original `Wan2.1` backbone on RGB-only metrics**.

papers.title: Large Language Model Deployment on Resource-Constrained Edge Devices: A Practitioners Survey
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed many areas of artificial intelligence (AI), but their substantial resource requirements limit their deployment on mobile and edge devices. Although LLMs have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various applications, the next challenge is deploying these models on resource-limited edge devices. Recent innovations in software optimizations and specialized hardware have made it feasible to deploy LLMs on edge devices. Edge deployment offers benefits including local data processing, cost savings, reduced latency, and personalized responses. This paper reviews the latest techniques that make the deployment of LLMs on edge devices feasible.
papers.summary: This survey reviews techniques that make it feasible to run large language models (LLMs) on mobile and edge devices despite their heavy resource demands. It covers recent software optimizations and specialized hardware written from a practitioner's perspective. It frames **the benefits of edge deployment as local data processing, lower cost, reduced latency, and personalized responses**.

papers.title: GlobalPuzzle: Globally Informed Genetic Search for Eroded Jigsaw Puzzle Reassembly
papers.abstract: Jigsaw puzzle reassembly remains a highly challenging task, particularly when piece boundaries are irregularly eroded to simulate damage to cultural artifacts. On the GAP benchmark, existing methods achieve a perfect assembly accuracy of only 0.3% on $5 \times 5$ puzzles, whereas humans can solve jigsaw puzzles with remarkably high accuracy. Humans typically approach puzzle solving by identifying potentially adjacent pieces, evaluating the current assembly, and iteratively performing complex operations such as adding pieces, replacing incorrectly placed pieces, and moving entire connected groups of pieces. However, existing methods face a fundamental limitation: approaches that leverage global visual information typically predict piece arrangements directly, making it difficult to explicitly perform such complex iterative operations, while search based methods can rearrange pieces but primarily rely on pairwise boundary compatibility, lacking global visual information to evaluate and guide the search process. To bridge this gap, we propose GlobalPuzzle, a jigsaw puzzle reassembly framework that integrates global canvas level evaluation, action guidance, and genetic search. By incorporating global visual information into the evaluation and optimization of candidate assemblies, GlobalPuzzle aims to resolve ambiguous adjacency relationships that are difficult to determine from irregularly eroded piece boundaries alone, enabling flexible, globally informed reconstruction.
papers.summary: Reassembling jigsaw puzzles whose piece edges have been eroded, a setting that simulates damaged cultural artifacts, remains very hard: **existing methods perfectly assemble only 0.3% of 5x5 puzzles on the `GAP` benchmark**. Methods that use global visual context predict an arrangement directly and cannot iteratively refine it, while search-based methods can rearrange pieces but rely mostly on pairwise boundary matching. `GlobalPuzzle` combines genetic search with canvas-level evaluation of whole candidate assemblies and global action guidance. This lets it add pieces, replace misplaced ones, and move connected groups, much as people do when solving puzzles.

papers.title: BrainCoT: A Multi-Task Zero-Shot Brain Signal Foundation Model with Neurometric-Anchored Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.abstract: Brain signals exhibit substantial multi-center heterogeneity, strong inter-subject variability, and highly diverse task settings, which makes it difficult to build models that generalize beyond a single task. While recent brain signal foundation models leverage large-scale pretraining to learn generalizable representations, they often fall short in practice because they still require target-data-specific supervised adaptation, lack multi-task zero-shot capability, and rarely provide verifiable evidence to support their predictions. In this work, we present BrainCoT, a multi-task zero-shot Brain signal foundation model with neurometric-anchored Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. BrainCoT unifies heterogeneous tasks into an instruction-driven framework so that, after pretraining, a single model can be directly applied to multiple tasks in zero-shot settings without additional adaptation. It further introduces neurometric-anchored chain-of-thought grounded in neurometric evidence for verifiable reasoning, and adopts Decision-Consistent Rationale Training to keep process learning aligned with correct predictions. Across extensive evaluations, BrainCoT achieves an average ACC of 67.41% and AUC of 74.33% in zero-shot classification without downstream training data, outperforming the strongest linear-probing baseline trained with 1% labeled downstream data by 3.85% in ACC and 5.97% in AUC.
papers.summary: Brain-signal foundation models still usually need task-specific supervised fine-tuning and rarely provide evidence for their predictions. `BrainCoT` casts heterogeneous brain-signal tasks into a single instruction-driven format, so one pretrained model can handle multiple tasks zero-shot. It produces chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales grounded in neurometric evidence, and it uses Decision-Consistent Rationale Training to keep those rationales aligned with correct predictions. Without any downstream training data, it reaches 67.41% accuracy and 74.33% AUC, **beating the strongest linear-probing baseline trained on 1% of labelled data by 3.85 accuracy points**.

papers.title: Training-Free Active Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) is usually studied in a fully unsupervised regime, where adaptation relies on pseudo-labels, confidence scores, or entropy computed by the model itself. This is a severe restriction on hard shifted samples: the model is asked to repair its own uncertain predictions without any external evidence. At the other extreme, supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly train or correct the model. We study the intermediate deployment regime between these two extremes. In Active Test-time Adaptation for VLMs (Active VLM-TTA), a pretrained VLM may spend an explicit labeling budget on selected test samples, but the prediction for the current sample must be emitted before its label can be used; queried labels are therefore costed, delayed evidence for future samples rather than free correction for the present one. Under this future-only constraint, the central question is how to reuse sparse labels conservatively. We instantiate this setting with ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval (ACTOR), a training-free plug-in module that routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query, and memory-based correction using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/ACTOR.
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) of vision-language models (VLMs) usually runs with no supervision at all, so a model has to fix its own uncertain predictions on shifted data with no outside evidence. The authors study a middle setting, Active VLM-TTA. The model can pay to label selected test samples, but each label only arrives after the current prediction has been made, so it can help only with later samples. Their training-free plug-in, `ACTOR`, sends each uncertain sample to one of three paths: keep the base prediction, query a label, or correct the prediction from a memory of earlier labels when a consistency-and-reliability check passes. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and an `ImageNet`-based domain-transfer benchmark, `ACTOR` **consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines** on both ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead.

papers.title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed
papers.abstract: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.
papers.summary: Hundreds of millions of people type Indian languages in Latin characters, but romanized Indic text generation is missing from benchmarks. The authors show that the automatic metrics `BGE-M3` and `BERTScore` misjudge its quality for Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada. They tested `Claude Opus 4.8`, `GPT-5.5`, `Gemini 2.5-flash`, and `Qwen3.5-35B` on 142 `OpenAssistant` query-response pairs. On a diagnostic subset, native speakers rated `GPT-5.5` 1.43 points higher than `Claude Opus 4.8` on a 12-point rubric, while the two models' `BGE-M3` means **differ by only 0.004**. The study also found model-specific failures that the metrics miss, such as `Gemini` slipping into native script in 16.9% of Telugu responses and `Qwen` answering only in English in 16.2% of Kannada responses, and it proposes a failure-aware evaluation policy that scores such outputs as zero.

papers.title: When Routine Operations Break Architectural Pattern Relationships in LLM Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: LLM agent harnesses distribute tool mediation, state management and safety guardrails across native services, independently written plugins and configuration. Routine operations can change the runtime order or retained state that architectural pattern relationships require, without any code change. We study five relationships associated with the Guardrail Enforcement Point, Autonomy Controller and Blackboard patterns across five released harnesses, analysing a main sample of fourteen independently written plugins. Using PatternOps, our assessment procedure, we trace requirements from pattern descriptions, provider documentation and deployment profiles to the providers that realise them and the records that decide them. We then compare alternative allocations under supported operations. Such operations broke relationships silently: after a plugin was reapplied or an allow rule saved, policy stopped evaluating edits while every plugin stayed active, and a prohibited edit executed. Which alternatives qualified depended on the requirement. Allocations that kept the required order, or kept or rebuilt the needed state, held on their tested paths and operation sequences, while others prevented prohibited effects but missed edits rejected elsewhere. In these harnesses, a pattern relationship is a property of the running system and its history, so architects should evaluate it against the decision paths, state lifetimes and operation sequences their deployments use.
papers.summary: LLM agent harnesses spread tool mediation, state management, and safety guardrails across built-in services, third-party plugins, and configuration. The authors show that routine operations can silently break the relationships that architectural patterns depend on, without any code change. Using an assessment procedure called `PatternOps`, they studied relationships tied to the Guardrail Enforcement Point, Autonomy Controller, and Blackboard patterns across five released harnesses and fourteen independently written plugins. In one case, **after a plugin was reapplied or an allow rule was saved, the policy stopped evaluating edits and a prohibited edit executed** while every plugin still showed as active. Only designs that preserved the required ordering, or kept or rebuilt the needed state, held up on the tested paths, which leads the authors to argue that such properties must be checked against real operation histories.

papers.title: MARS: Training Multilingual Search Agents for Retriever-Free Evidence Acquisition
papers.abstract: Existing multilingual retrieval-augmented generation relies heavily on learned retrievers and similarity-based ranking from multilingual collections, which are vulnerable to cross-lingual retrieval errors and indexing overhead. In this paper, we explore retriever-free multilingual search, where the model directly interacts with raw corpora through executable shell commands. This paradigm shifts the bottleneck to multilingual search action generation, where exact search is sensitive to entity surface forms and outcome-only supervision provides limited guidance for multi-turn search. To address these challenges, we propose MARS, a multilingual search agent in direct corpus interaction (DCI) with reinforcement learning (RL). MARS introduces corpus-native entity grounding to recover reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence, mitigating failure to retrieve evidence. Meanwhile, we present a redundancy-aware search reward to encourage concise and effective search trajectories, addressing training collapse in RL of multilingual scenarios. Experiments show that \ours~consistently outperforms strong retrieval-based and DCI baselines, while demonstrating robust cross-lingual generalization and substantially reducing redundant corpus interactions.
papers.summary: Multilingual retrieval-augmented generation usually depends on learned retrievers, which make cross-lingual retrieval errors and require building an index. `MARS` replaces the retriever with an agent that searches raw corpora directly through shell commands, an approach called direct corpus interaction (DCI), and trains it with reinforcement learning (RL). Two additions handle the main difficulties: corpus-native entity grounding recovers the exact surface forms that appear in the corpus so lexical searches hit, and a redundancy-aware search reward discourages repetitive search trajectories, which keeps multilingual RL training from collapsing. `MARS` **consistently outperforms strong retrieval-based and DCI baselines**, generalizes across languages, and makes far fewer redundant corpus calls.

papers.title: TUGB: A Two-stage Uncertainty-aware Generative Auto-Bidding Framework
papers.abstract: Generative modeling, particularly Decision Transformers, shows promise in auto-bidding strategies. However, it struggles with limited exploration in static offline datasets, vulnerability to dynamic environmental shifts, and a reliance on heuristic return-to-go (RTG) specifications that may yield suboptimal performance on unseen traffic. To address these challenges, we propose the Two-stage Uncertainty-aware Generative Auto-Bidding (TUGB) framework. TUGB integrates generative sequence modeling with Reinforcement Learning (RL). It employs a two-stage pipeline where a pre-trained Generative Bidding Model is fine-tuned via an ensemble-based Uncertainty-aware Environment Model. This approach quantifies epistemic uncertainty to penalize high-risk trajectories and evolves the policy from RTG-conditioning to direct bidding optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TUGB significantly outperforms SOTA baselines. Notably, full-scale deployment on JD Search Ad achieved a 2.32\% increase in cost and 3.57\% in target cost, validating its industrial efficacy, while its successful adaptation to subsequent mechanism upgrades and JD Food Delivery Ad further validates TUGB's superior generalization capability.
papers.summary: Decision Transformer-style generative models for ad auto-bidding struggle with three problems: offline data offers little exploration, traffic conditions shift, and the return-to-go (RTG) targets that steer them are set by hand. `TUGB` (Two-stage Uncertainty-aware Generative Auto-Bidding) first pre-trains a generative bidding model, then fine-tunes it with reinforcement learning against an ensemble environment model. The ensemble estimates epistemic uncertainty so that high-risk trajectories can be penalized, and the fine-tuned policy moves from RTG conditioning to optimizing bids directly. A full-scale deployment on JD Search Ads produced a **2.32% increase in cost and 3.57% in target cost**, and the method also transferred to a later auction-mechanism upgrade and to JD Food Delivery Ads.

papers.title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering
papers.abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
papers.summary: Multimodal LLMs answering questions about long videos work under tight visual-token budgets, which forces a choice between broad temporal coverage and fine spatial detail. `AdaAlloc` treats this as an allocation problem and needs no training. It first plans how to split the budget between a sparse, low-resolution global overview and dense, high-resolution local frames. It then uses temporal grounding to find candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory, which the final answering model reasons over. Across `LVBench`, `MLVU`, `VideoMME`, and `LongVideoBench`, it beats uniform sampling at the same budget by **up to 10.5 percentage points** and outperforms the frame-selection and agentic methods it was compared against.

papers.title: AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for creative tasks such as writing, design, and idea generation. For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Novelty is one standard measure of creativity, and current creativity evaluations ask human experts or LLM judges to rate how novel an output is. However, these ratings have no fixed reference for what counts as novel (or, in other terms, departure from the familiar). Measuring this departure requires a task with known familiar defaults. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology is such a task. In this creativity test, people imagine a creature from another planet. The departure from features of Earth animals, such as bilateral symmetry and legs as mode of locomotion, is used as measure of creativity. We introduce AlienBench, a benchmark that adapts the structured imagination task to language models. Models describe alien creatures, and a panel of three LLM judges extracts ten biological features from the description and labels them as either Earth-typical or a departure. The sum of feature departures is the score of a description, from 0 to 10. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.
papers.summary: Creativity evaluations of LLMs usually ask experts or LLM judges to rate novelty, but those ratings have no fixed baseline for what counts as familiar. `AlienBench` adapts the structured imagination task from cognitive psychology, in which participants invent an alien creature. Three LLM judges extract ten biological features from each description and mark each one as Earth-typical or a departure, which gives a score from 0 to 10. Ten models each produced 180 descriptions under six prompt conditions, with mean scores ranging from 3.28 for `GPT-6 Luna` to 6.55 for `Ministral 3 14B`. **Open-weight models scored higher than proprietary ones (5.40 vs. 4.58)**, and under the baseline prompt the models departed from Earth defaults more often than 100 human participants on every feature.

papers.title: COMBIO: Automated Discovery of a Compact Composite Biomarker from Routine Laboratory Panels
papers.abstract: Machine-learning models based on routine laboratory panels can predict outcomes but can be difficult to interpret and operationalize. We present COMBIO, an automated pipeline that distils such a model into a compact closed-form biomarker. The composite is a product of laboratory measurements raised to integer powers from minus two to two. The sign of each exponent indicates whether higher values of the corresponding measurement increase or decrease the composite. Shapley additive explanation values from the gradient-boosted reference model rank five candidate measurements and guide eligible exponent signs. An exhaustive search over small integer exponents selects the formula on an inner validation set, before evaluation on the reserved test set. We evaluated COMBIO across six tasks: three National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey outcomes, liver-disease classification in the Indian Liver Patient Dataset, and Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV in-hospital mortality and sepsis case-finding, with external evaluation in the eICU Collaborative Research Database for the two hospital tasks. Across the six test sets, COMBIO's area under the receiver operating characteristic curve differed by at most 0.03 from logistic regression using the five candidate laboratory measurements. The hospital mortality composite had an area under the curve of 0.698 in the external database. A version restricted to widely available measurements in the source hospital database achieved an area under the curve of 0.786 in a cohort covering 92% of admissions. The multiplicative representation provides compactness rather than additional accuracy, and local validation and recalibration are required before clinical use.
papers.summary: Machine-learning models built on routine lab panels can predict clinical outcomes but are hard to interpret and put into practice. `COMBIO` distills such a model into a single closed-form biomarker: a product of lab measurements, each raised to an integer power between -2 and 2. Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) values from a gradient-boosted reference model pick five candidate measurements and constrain the exponent signs, and an exhaustive search chooses the formula on validation data. Across six tasks drawn from `NHANES`, the `Indian Liver Patient Dataset`, and `MIMIC-IV`, with external testing in `eICU`, the composite's area under the ROC curve (AUC) was **within 0.03 of logistic regression** on the same five measurements. The authors present the formula's compactness, not extra accuracy, as its benefit.

papers.title: PhoPunct: A Large-Scale Benchmark of Transformer Architectures for Vietnamese Punctuation Restoration
papers.abstract: Vietnamese punctuation restoration is often evaluated on relatively small benchmarks, limiting conclusions about how architectural choices scale with data volume. We present a controlled benchmark on News and Novels corpora containing 22.1 million labeled tokens (19.9M News and 2.2M Novels). We evaluate 17 architectures formed from four pretrained Transformer backbones and optional bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) and conditional random field (CRF) layers, together with a PhoBERT-large-Bi-LSTM-CRF model, PhoPunct. Every model is trained for eight epochs with the same learning rate and without architecture-specific tuning. Under this fixed budget, adding Bi-LSTM and CRF layers does not reliably improve macro F1: in seven of eight matched domain-backbone comparisons, a plain Transformer classifier matches or outperforms its Bi-LSTM-CRF counterpart. PhoPunct obtains the best News result (61.35), whereas XLM-R with a CRF obtains the best Novels result (50.18), exceeding PhoPunct (48.97). These results show that the value of recurrent and structured-prediction heads depends on their optimization regime and motivate explicit separation between architectural improvements and improvements due to architecture-specific tuning. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/aisia-research-lab/PhoPunct
papers.summary: Vietnamese punctuation restoration has mostly been evaluated on small datasets. This benchmark uses 22.1 million labeled tokens from news and novels and compares 17 architectures: four pretrained Transformer backbones, each with or without bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) and conditional random field (CRF) layers, plus a `PhoBERT-large`-Bi-LSTM-CRF model called `PhoPunct`. Every model was trained for eight epochs with the same learning rate and no architecture-specific tuning. Under that fixed budget, **a plain Transformer classifier matched or beat its Bi-LSTM-CRF counterpart in seven of eight comparisons**. `PhoPunct` scored best on news (61.35 macro F1), while `XLM-R` with a CRF scored best on novels (50.18).

papers.title: Authorization Drift in LLM Agents: Evaluating Boundary Compliance in Multi-Step Tool Use
papers.abstract: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.
papers.summary: LLM agents can overstep their authorization while pursuing a user's goal, even with no attacker involved. The authors call this authorization drift and define it along four dimensions: data, tool, scope, and time. The Authorization Drift Benchmark (`ADB`) contains 648 tasks across seven domains, each offering a compliant path and a tempting unauthorized shortcut. Tasks were validated with real agent rollouts through a pipeline called `SERS` (Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis). Across 13 LLMs, three frameworks, and 25,207 trajectories, **more capable models drifted more, with frontier models at drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61**, even though 86.18% of tasks had at least one observed clean, successful run. Most drift came from collecting too much data early in a task, and mapping drift points to the law in four jurisdictions made data minimisation the most frequently implicated provision.

papers.title: PathXAI: Evidence-guided structured pathology reporting by transferable tissue segmentation
papers.abstract: Pathology reporting requires translating tissue observations across regions and slides into specific diagnoses and supporting morphological descriptions. However, the use of explicit tissue-composition measurements to guide H&E-based report generation remains underexplored. Thus, we developed PathXAI, which combines segmentation-derived tissue information with H&E images and optional domain knowledge to guide diagnostic reasoning, targeted reinspection and structured report writing. Its segmentation component exceeded baselines in mean Dice on internal and external tests. In automated report evaluation on 1,200 public and 151 private cases, PathXAI achieved higher agreement with reference diagnoses and documented morphology than the H&E-based comparators. On the public evaluation cohort, PathXAI-Report exceeded Qwen + H&E in cancer family match rate by 4.4 percentage points and in finding F1 by 5.7 percentage points. PathXAI generates evidence-linked reports with a self-hosted pretrained vision-language model, without updating its weights.
papers.summary: Explicit measurements of tissue composition are rarely used to guide automated pathology reports generated from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained slides. `PathXAI` combines tissue information derived from segmentation with H&E images and optional domain knowledge to drive diagnostic reasoning, targeted re-inspection, and structured report writing, using a self-hosted pretrained vision-language model without updating its weights. Its segmentation component beat baselines on mean Dice in internal and external tests. On the public evaluation cohort, `PathXAI-Report` **exceeded `Qwen` + H&E by 4.4 percentage points in cancer-family match rate and 5.7 points in finding F1**.

papers.title: Finite-sample Calibration Guarantees for Binary Segmentation
papers.abstract: Machine learning based segmentation models are frequently miscalibrated, producing for each pixel a label prediction whose associated confidence does not accurately reflect the true underlying probability. This limitation is particularly critical in high-stakes applications such as medical image segmentation. Although several calibration methods have been proposed, only a small subset of them provides theoretical guarantees on the calibration error, i.e., they do not typically ensure that, with high probability, the model exhibits a low calibration error. In this work, we develop a post-hoc calibration method for which formal calibration guarantees can be established. To achieve this, we derive from standard concentration inequalities an improved theoretical bound that explicitly accounts for the spatial dependence inherent in binary segmentation outputs. We empirically demonstrate that the proposed calibrator satisfies the derived guarantee and outperforms existing post-hoc calibration approaches.
papers.summary: Segmentation models are often miscalibrated, meaning their per-pixel confidence does not match the true probability, and few calibration methods offer formal guarantees on calibration error. The authors build a post-hoc calibration method for binary segmentation with a high-probability guarantee. Starting from standard concentration inequalities, they derive a tighter bound that explicitly accounts for spatial dependence between pixels. Experiments show the calibrator **satisfies the derived guarantee** and outperforms existing post-hoc calibration approaches.

papers.title: Deep Learning Theory through the Lens of Statistical Physics: A Topical Review
papers.abstract: The recent success of foundation models and deep learning has far outpaced our theoretical understanding of how large-scale neural networks learn and generalize. Statistical physics provides a natural language for describing such high-dimensional, nonlinear, and strongly coupled systems, offering concepts such as mean-field theory, phase transitions, energy landscapes, and stochastic dynamics. In this topical review, we adopt a statistical-physics way of thinking -- from concepts including phases and criticality, and free-energy viewpoints, to methods such as kernel and Gaussian-process limits, mean-field and dynamical mean-field theories, random-matrix tools, and Fokker-Planck formalisms, and to a mindset emphasizing universality, scaling, and tractable limits with explicit validity regimes. We survey recent progress on understanding modern deep learning through this lens, including mean-field analyses of wide networks, spectral and geometric perspectives on loss landscapes, stochastic-gradient-based training viewed as a dynamical process, and phase-transition analogies that organize phenomena such as overparameterization, generalization, and representation change. Our goal is to synthesize these threads into a coherent framework that clarifies what each approximation explains, when it is expected to hold, and how apparently competing narratives relate or diverge. Together, these perspectives form a unified physical framework that views representation learning as a collective phenomenon in high-dimensional systems, bridging deterministic and stochastic regimes of gradient-based optimization.
papers.summary: This topical review surveys how statistical physics helps explain how large neural networks learn and generalize. It covers concepts such as phases, criticality, and free energy, along with tools including kernel and Gaussian-process limits, mean-field and dynamical mean-field theories, random-matrix methods, and Fokker-Planck formalisms. The survey spans mean-field analyses of wide networks, the spectral and geometric structure of loss landscapes, stochastic gradient descent viewed as a dynamical process, and phase-transition analogies for overparameterization and generalization. It aims to **clarify what each approximation explains and when it holds**, and frames representation learning as a collective phenomenon in high-dimensional systems.

papers.title: CARGO: Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Preventive Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving
papers.abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.
papers.summary: `CARGO` (Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative merging of on-ramp traffic into mixed traffic. It estimates how each vehicle's actions influence the others, uses those signed influences to shape a shared team reward, and assigns safety responsibility based on each agent's excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy, with a conditional diffusion model predicting future responses for risk estimation. Each agent's risk-reduction requirement is then set according to its local capacity within a policy trust region, and the authors give theoretical results on risk monotonicity. In high-density `highway-env` traffic, `CARGO` **raises success rate by 66.04% and cuts crash rate by 56.23%** relative to the best baseline on each metric.

papers.title: SPDMX: Large-Scale Open Stem Audio From Symbolic Music
papers.abstract: Large public datasets have driven recent progress in machine learning, from text and vision to speech and general audio. Music remains an outlier, as copyright blocks redistribution of training audio, while many modern tasks need individual stems rather than mixtures. Existing multitrack resources trade off realism, scale, and licensing, while synthetic alternatives rely on proprietary VSTs or naive open rendering that yields weak stems. We introduce SPDMX, a listening-guided rendering of public-domain PDMX scores into an openly-licensed stem corpus with aligned scores and an open render pipeline: $253{,}982$ songs, $490{,}159$ mono stems, and $5{,}469$ song-hours at $44.1$ kHz under CC BY 4.0, with paired MIDI and identifiers linking to PDMX metadata. $88{,}403$ songs ($34.8\%$; $2{,}734$ song-hours) provide multitrack supervision. To our knowledge, this is the largest openly-licensed synthetic multitrack subset by song-hours, enabling source separation, stem-conditioned synthesis, MIDI-to-audio, transcription, and joint symbolic-audio modeling. We release the corpus, metadata, and open pipeline for reuse on other symbolic collections. Demos and experimental notes are on the project page.
papers.summary: Copyright blocks the redistribution of music training audio, and many tasks need individual instrument stems rather than full mixes. `SPDMX` renders public-domain `PDMX` scores into an openly licensed stem corpus using a rendering pipeline tuned by listening tests and released openly. The corpus contains 253,982 songs, 490,159 mono stems, and 5,469 song-hours at 44.1 kHz under CC BY 4.0, with aligned MIDI. Of these, 88,403 songs (2,734 song-hours) are multitrack, which the authors describe as **the largest openly licensed synthetic multitrack collection by song-hours**, usable for source separation, transcription, MIDI-to-audio, and joint symbolic-audio modeling.

papers.title: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits, spike-based neuromorphic computing offers promising potential in high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications. Building on the latency-coding principles, this article proposes a framework for data-light condition monitoring that relies solely on three-phase AC current measurements. The AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are inherently compatible with spiking neural networks that can effectively facilitate the estimation of device parameters. Case studies are presented to validate the performances, while constraints and further optimizations are also evaluated and discussed, and future extensions of the methodology are provided.
papers.summary: The authors propose a condition-monitoring method for power electronics that needs only three-phase AC current measurements. Building on latency-coding principles, they encode the current signals as the membrane potentials of spiking neurons modeled as RC circuits, which feed directly into spiking neural networks that estimate device parameters. Case studies validate the approach, and the authors discuss its **energy-efficient, data-light design**, its constraints, and possible extensions.

papers.title: Learning Generative Dynamics for 3D Molecule Generation via Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constraints
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for generating 3D molecules. Despite showing remarkable promise, they learn atomic distributions implicitly from data, without explicitly encoding physicochemical rules into their generative dynamics. Consequently, generated samples can be statistically plausible yet chemically invalid. To address this problem, we propose Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constrained Diffusion (SensDiff), a framework that integrates symbolic rules into generative modeling, enabling the model to internalize scientific priors during training. Central to SensDiff is the observation that the diffusion trajectory of 3D molecule generation exhibits a coarse-to-fine evolution: valid molecules arise by first mitigating macroscopic geometric conflicts and then refining structures toward microscopic chemical consistency through iterative denoising. Accordingly, SensDiff mirrors this dynamic by sequentially enforcing constraints with adaptive weighting during training, progressively steering generation toward valid molecular geometries. Moreover, SensDiff translates domain knowledge into interpretable generative controls, grounding opaque neural denoising in scientific principles. Experiments on molecular benchmarks and real-world constrained generation tasks confirm that SensDiff consistently improves chemical validity while adhering to physicochemical rules and user-specified targets. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026_SensDiff.
papers.summary: Diffusion models for 3D molecule generation learn atomic distributions only implicitly, so they can produce molecules that look statistically plausible but are chemically invalid. `SensDiff` (Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constrained Diffusion) adds symbolic physicochemical rules to training. It is based on the observation that denoising moves from coarse to fine: large-scale geometric conflicts get resolved first and fine chemical consistency comes later. The method therefore applies constraints in sequence with adaptive weighting during training. Experiments on molecular benchmarks and real-world constrained generation tasks show **consistent gains in chemical validity** while respecting physicochemical rules and user-specified targets.

papers.title: Augmentron: Scalable Multi-View Visual Augmentation for Robot Learning
papers.abstract: Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations can become sensitive to environmental features that are unrelated to the task. Existing generative augmentation methods can introduce visual diversity, but processing every frame and camera view independently is computationally expensive and may produce inconsistent observations across cameras and timestamps. We introduce Augmentron, a geometry-aware pipeline that generates reusable scene representations and renders them through recorded camera poses. This produces temporally and multi-view consistent environ- ment and workspace variations while preserving the robot, task objects, actions, and annotations. Across three physical manipulation tasks, replacing half of the real world training dataset with Augmentron data improves model success across three tasks for both in out-of-distribution distractor objects, and out-of-distribution workspace variation evaluations. In a separate comparison against alternate augmentation techniques, Augmentron achieves the highest pooled success in all three conditions. The results show that introducing augmented data to a data training recipe can help policies generalize to dynamic real-world settings.
papers.summary: Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations can become sensitive to scene features that have nothing to do with the task, and generative augmentation that edits each frame and camera view separately is expensive and inconsistent across views. `Augmentron` builds reusable, geometry-aware scene representations and renders them through the recorded camera poses. The resulting environment and workspace variations stay consistent across time and camera views while keeping the robot, task objects, actions, and annotations intact. On three physical manipulation tasks, **replacing half the real training data with `Augmentron` data improved success** with unseen distractor objects and unseen workspace changes, and it achieved the highest pooled success against alternative augmentation methods.

papers.title: BMMS: Policy-Conditioned Measurement of Behavioral Compliance in Language Models
papers.abstract: Behavioral evaluation of language models fixes its dimensions in advance: hallucination, sycophancy, toxicity, over-refusal. An operator in a regulated industry needs a different question answered: does a system do what a particular rulebook requires? We introduce the Behavioral Misalignment Metric Suite (BMMS), which measures policy-conditioned misalignment by taking a policy corpus as an argument and returning a compliance profile over it, for any published policy and any system that answers in natural language. The Compliance Attainment Score (CAS) measures severity-weighted attainment over the obligations that bind the system, and the Compliance Robustness Margin (CRM) the share of that attainment surviving graded adversarial pressure; Behavioral Invariance (BIV) and the Behavioral Disposition Index (BDI) are specified and released with the suite. Dimensions enter only by passing a published admission test whose binding criterion is attribution: a quantity that moves when the judge changes, holding the target fixed, is measuring the instrument. Applying it excluded one of the quantities the suite itself reported. Across 1,003 obligations from eleven documents in five registers, the admission criterion holds 94.4% precision against blinded human judgment on vendor specifications and 50.0% on analytical guidance, extraction fidelity is 94.6%, and re-scoring under judges from two other providers leaves target ordering invariant while the absolute score of a single target spans up to 0.22. We apply it to the two most detailed published behavioral specifications. Own-specification advantage is not resolved from zero once document difficulty is subtracted, but absolute self-compliance is another matter: GPT-4o fails 70.7% of the hard constraints binding it in the Model Spec published by OpenAI, where the two Claude models fail 0.0% and 9.1% of theirs.
papers.summary: Behavioral evaluations of language models usually fix their dimensions in advance, such as hallucination or sycophancy, whereas regulated operators need to know whether a system follows a specific rulebook. The Behavioral Misalignment Metric Suite (`BMMS`) takes a policy corpus as input and returns a compliance profile. Its main metrics are a severity-weighted Compliance Attainment Score (`CAS`) and a Compliance Robustness Margin (`CRM`), which measures how much compliance survives adversarial pressure. A dimension is admitted only if it does not shift when the judge model changes. Across 1,003 obligations from eleven documents, model rankings stayed the same under judges from other providers, and **`GPT-4o` failed 70.7% of the hard constraints in OpenAI's own Model Spec**, while two Claude models failed 0.0% and 9.1% of theirs.

papers.title: Learning When to Think: Dual-Reference Offline Optimization for Adaptive VLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.
papers.summary: Making vision-language models reason step by step on every input wastes compute, so the goal here is a single model that answers simple inputs directly and reasons only when needed. Because fast answers and slow reasoning traces usually come from different sampling sources, a training objective with a single reference distribution misweights one of the two modes. `DR-BOLT` (Dual-Reference BOLT) separates the desired fast/slow mixture from the sampling distribution and corrects the mismatch during reward-weighted offline training. On `Qwen3-VL`, it improves the trade-off between score and response length on `ScienceQA` and three held-out benchmarks, using slow reasoning on 24.1% of inputs and training **2.90 times faster end to end than a reproduced `GRPO`** baseline.

papers.title: Evaluation of a Multi-Link Machine Learning Approach for Rainfall Detection Using Satellite Microwave Links
papers.abstract: The impacts of climate change have increased the need for reliable real-time rainfall monitoring systems. This study investigates rainfall detection using a network of opportunistic sensors based on satellite microwave links (SMLs) combined with machine learning (ML) classifiers. Two models, a random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network (CNN), were trained on aggregated SML data, including information from neighboring links. The results demonstrate that leveraging information from multiple links substantially enhances the detection of both wet and dry periods compared to single-link approaches. Moreover, the RF model consistently provides a more stable and reliable trade-off than CNN, improving rainfall detection and reducing misclassifications overall, with particularly strong performance during harsh weather conditions. The study spanned up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.
papers.summary: Satellite microwave links (SMLs), whose signals weaken when it rains, can serve as opportunistic sensors for real-time rainfall monitoring. The study trains a random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify wet and dry periods from aggregated SML data, including signals from neighboring links. **Using information from multiple links substantially improves wet- and dry-period detection compared with single-link approaches**, and the `RF` model gives a more stable trade-off than the `CNN`, with fewer misclassifications and especially strong results in harsh weather. The evaluation covers up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.

papers.title: Beyond the Grid: Continuous Dictionary Pursuit for Interpretable Signal Decomposition
papers.abstract: Deep learning models achieve high accuracy in signal processing but remain difficult to interpret. Classical matching pursuit and sparse coding offer better transparency but suffer from spectral leakage and grid mismatch when signal frequencies do not align with discrete dictionary atoms. We introduce Continuous Dictionary Pursuit (CDP), a framework for interpretable signal decomposition that learns the parameters of closed-form functions directly from data. CDP optimizes over a continuous manifold of differentiable atoms and, unlike prior continuous pursuit methods that operate on a single analytic family, searches a heterogeneous library spanning periodic, trend, transient, and discontinuous structures. The algorithm employs a greedy iterative strategy using data-driven priors and gradient-based optimization to isolate individual signal components, with discontinuous waveforms made differentiable through spectral sharpness annealing. To ensure a sparse atom set for reconstruction, the framework utilizes a stopping criterion based on a predefined atom budget and residual error convergence. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show that CDP removes the grid discretization error for atom families contained in its library, recovers generative parameters to within $1\%$ on stationary synthetic signals expressible in that library, and achieves the best sparsity-accuracy trade-off among classical, continuous-pursuit, and neural baselines in the sparse regime. Beyond decomposition, we demonstrate that the extracted atoms can serve as structured curriculum targets for training sequence models, improving forecasting accuracy over standard end-to-end training on most evaluated datasets. The method offers a glass-box alternative for signal decomposition by providing high reconstruction fidelity alongside direct physical interpretability.
papers.summary: Classical matching pursuit and sparse coding give interpretable signal decompositions, but they suffer from grid mismatch and spectral leakage when a signal's frequencies fall between the dictionary's discrete atoms. `Continuous Dictionary Pursuit` (`CDP`) instead fits the parameters of closed-form, differentiable atoms drawn from a mixed library of periodic, trend, transient, and discontinuous shapes. It extracts components greedily using gradient-based optimization and data-driven priors, and it anneals spectral sharpness so that discontinuous waveforms become differentiable. `CDP` removes discretization error for atom families in its library, **recovers generative parameters to within 1% on stationary synthetic signals**, gives the best sparsity-accuracy trade-off among the baselines, and its extracted atoms serve as curriculum targets that improve sequence-model forecasting on most datasets tested.

papers.title: FIND: Frequency Invariance Disentanglement for Test-Time Adaptation in LiDAR 3D Detection
papers.abstract: LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection (L3OD) is a fundamental 3D perception task, yet its performance is often compromised by domain shifts arising from diverse sensor configurations and environmental conditions. Existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods primarily leverage self-supervision in the spatial domain, yet they frequently confound semantic content with domain style due to the sparse, non-Euclidean nature of point clouds. To overcome this limitation, we propose FIND (Frequency INvariance Disentanglement), a novel TTA framework that precisely disentangles domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference within the frequency domain. Our methodology utilizes B-Spline fitting to construct locally adaptive filters integrated into a dual-stream architecture: an Invariant Stream extracts robust features to guide pseudo-labeling, while a Specific Stream enforces consistency against domain perturbations. By combining invariance-driven alignment with stability-guided regularization, our approach dynamically extracts robust domain-invariant features while suppressing domain-specific interference. Extensive experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and robust corruption benchmarks demonstrate that FIND significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/llldx03/FIND.
papers.summary: LiDAR-based 3D object detectors lose accuracy under domain shifts caused by different sensor setups and environmental conditions, and existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods that work in the spatial domain tend to mix up semantic content with domain style. `FIND` separates domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference in the frequency domain, using B-spline fitting to build locally adaptive filters inside a dual-stream architecture. An invariant stream extracts robust features that guide pseudo-labeling, while a specific stream enforces consistency under domain perturbations. On cross-dataset adaptation and corruption-robustness benchmarks, **`FIND` significantly outperforms state-of-the-art TTA methods**.

papers.title: TOFS: Feature Selection with Swap Supervision for Semantic Communication over Fading Channels
papers.abstract: Task-oriented semantic communication transmits task-relevant features to support receiver inference under limited communication resources and adverse channel conditions. For image classification, the usefulness of a feature depends on the other transmitted features and the distortion introduced by the wireless channel. Effective feature prioritization should therefore account for classification performance after transmission of the selected features. This paper proposes a Task-Oriented Feature Selection (\textit{TOFS}) framework and method, which evaluates feature replacements using receiver classification loss. Loss differences confirmed under independent transmission samples provide pairwise ranking supervision for a selector network. The trained selector predicts priorities in a single forward pass. CIFAR-10 simulations demonstrate improved classification accuracy over an importance-based feature selection baseline at the same transmitted feature count and average transmit power. The proposed \textit{TOFS} framework shows 84\% accuracy performance under Rayleigh fading and Gaussian noise, compared with the 68\% performance of a SOTA method.
papers.summary: Task-oriented semantic communication sends only the features a receiver needs for inference, but how useful a feature is depends both on which other features are sent and on distortion from the wireless channel. `Task-Oriented Feature Selection` (`TOFS`) scores candidate feature swaps by the receiver's classification loss after transmission and keeps loss differences that hold up across independent channel samples. These comparisons become pairwise ranking labels for a selector network, which then predicts feature priorities in a single forward pass. In `CIFAR-10` simulations under Rayleigh fading and Gaussian noise, **`TOFS` reaches 84% accuracy versus 68% for a state-of-the-art method** at the same feature count and transmit power.

papers.title: SIFR: Stable Signed Flow Reinforcement
papers.abstract: Reward-based fine-tuning of flow models requires effectively promoting high-reward and suppressing low-reward samples, while maintaining training stability over many rounds of iterative updates. Iterative reward fine-tuning provides a simple starting point, but the positive reward weights give no explicit unfitting signal, and repeated reweighting concentrates the distribution and causes collapse. We propose Stable Signed Flow Reinforcement (SIFR), which replaces the reward weights by signed advantages to supply the missing unfitting signal, and constrains the velocity drift from a reference model to stabilize the updates, with a Lagrange multiplier that adapts the regularization strength to a prescribed drift budget. We further show that existing flow RL methods fall within this framework: they implicitly minimize the signed loss, differing in their regularization choices. We validate SIFR on SD3.5 Medium (2.5B) and FLUX.2 Klein (9B) and scale it to Cosmos 3 Super Text2Image (64B): across all 12 backbone--reward pairs with preference and rule-based rewards, it matches or exceeds existing methods, reaches their peak rewards much faster, and keeps improving over long training where they plateau or collapse.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning flow-based generative models with rewards needs to promote high-reward samples and suppress low-reward ones while staying stable across many update rounds; iterative reweighting with positive rewards gives no signal to unlearn bad samples and tends to collapse. `Stable Signed Flow Reinforcement` (`SIFR`) replaces reward weights with signed advantages and limits velocity drift from a reference model, using a Lagrange multiplier that tunes regularization to a set drift budget. The authors show that existing flow RL methods implicitly minimize the same signed loss and differ only in their regularization. Tested on `SD3.5 Medium`, `FLUX.2 Klein`, and up to the 64B-parameter `Cosmos 3 Super Text2Image`, **`SIFR` matches or exceeds existing methods on all 12 backbone-reward pairs**, reaches peak reward faster, and keeps improving where the other methods plateau or collapse.

papers.title: TailDART: Compute-Efficient Foundation Models for Financial Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Although time-series foundation models (TSFMs) achieve strong zero-shot transferability across high-information-density physical systems, applying overparameterized TSFMs to quantitative finance is fundamentally constrained by low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and prohibitive autoregressive decoding latency. To reconcile representation learning with institutional operational constraints, this study presents TailDART, a dense 2.68 million-parameter foundation model engineered for financial time-series forecasting. By integrating grouped-query attention into a lightweight backbone, the architecture drastically reduces Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead, achieving major inference acceleration (up to 48.1%) over prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs to enable low-latency, high-throughput streaming execution.
