Furthermore, multi-asset benchmarks across varying temporal resolutions show that a compact model can remain competitive for market forecasting: TailDART matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines while demonstrating superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.
papers.summary: Large time-series foundation models (TSFMs) transfer well across physical systems but struggle with financial data's low signal-to-noise ratio and non-stationarity, and their autoregressive decoding is too slow for trading workloads. `TailDART` is a dense model with only 2.68 million parameters that uses grouped-query attention to cut key-value cache memory bandwidth. It runs **up to 48.1% faster at inference than prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs**. On multi-asset benchmarks at several time resolutions it matches much larger baselines and handles errors better during high-volatility periods.

papers.title: Analyzing Code Provenance in LLMs for Programming Education
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasing role in programming education, challenging traditional assessment methods as they can generate fully functional code instantly. This disrupts the reliability of student submissions as indicators of learning and effort. To address this issue, code provenance is essential for tracing the origins of code and distinguishing student-authored, AI-generated, and externally sourced components. We extend the Min-K% probability approach by incorporating synthetic non-member code generation and apply it to Python code for membership inference and provenance tracking. Evaluations cover free LLMs such as GPT-2, DistilGPT-2, and DialoGPT, as well as state-of-the-art commercial models including GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Mistral, DeepSeek, and LLaMA 3.3. Before evaluating our approach on higher-education student assignments, we validate its feasibility using Stack Overflow data. The results show that free models enable more sensitive code memorization detection than commercial models. By systematically comparing these LLMs, we assess trade-offs between detection accuracy and privacy protection, taking an initial step toward effective assessment of AI-assisted programming education through combined provenance detection and process visibility.
papers.summary: Because large language models (LLMs) can produce working code instantly, programming courses need code provenance: a way to tell whether code was written by a student, generated by AI, or copied from elsewhere. The authors extend the `Min-K%` probability membership-inference method by generating synthetic non-member code and apply it to Python. They validate it on `Stack Overflow` data before using it on university assignments, comparing free models such as `GPT-2`, `DistilGPT-2`, and `DialoGPT` against commercial ones including `GPT-5`, `Gemini 2.5`, `Mistral`, `DeepSeek`, and `LLaMA 3.3`. **Free models allow more sensitive detection of memorized code than commercial models**, and the study maps out the trade-offs between detection accuracy and privacy.

papers.title: A Taxonomy-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Retrieval Effectiveness and Fairness Evaluation in Hiring
papers.abstract: While machine learning hiring tools are ubiquitous, the need for privacy regulations and commercial sensitivity makes public benchmarking legally complex. We address this challenge by introducing a taxonomy-driven, fully synthetic HR dataset and benchmark to simultaneously evaluate retrieval effectiveness and algorithmic fairness. Grounded in 660K real freelancer profiles, our multilingual corpus features candidate profiles, project briefs, and counterfactual demographic twins. Auditing state-of-the-art embedding models reveals performance divergence from general MTEB scores, alongside fairness disparities in grammatically gendered languages. This demonstrates that general benchmarks are insufficient for HR, requiring tailored evaluations to identify Pareto-optimal models that balance semantic accuracy and fairness.
papers.summary: Privacy rules and commercial sensitivity make it hard to publicly benchmark machine-learning hiring tools. The authors release a fully synthetic, multilingual HR dataset built from a taxonomy and grounded in 660K real freelancer profiles; it contains candidate profiles, project briefs, and counterfactual twins that differ only in demographics, so retrieval quality and fairness can be measured together. Auditing state-of-the-art embedding models shows that **their rankings on this benchmark diverge from their general `MTEB` scores**, and that fairness gaps appear in languages with grammatical gender. The authors conclude that hiring needs dedicated evaluations to find models that balance accuracy and fairness.

papers.title: RoleWalk: training-free structural embeddings for directed graphs that transfer across graphs
papers.abstract: Structural role embeddings describe a node by its position in a graph - hub, bridge, periphery, member of a dense core - rather than by who its neighbours are. Existing methods either learn coordinates specific to one graph (struc2vec, Role2Vec, RESD) or read scales and normalisations from the whole graph (GraphWave, Digraphwave), so the same neighbourhood can receive different coordinates in two graphs; few read edge directions. We present RoleWalk, a training-free embedding that follows a short lazy random walk from each node and records, at each step, two distributions: that of the transition probabilities, through its characteristic function at a fixed grid of frequencies, and that of the walker's distance to its starting node. On directed graphs, walks that go forward then backward add who shares a node's targets or sources. The embedding depends only on a node's neighbourhood within a fixed radius, so its coordinates mean the same thing in every graph. We show that, without curvature, it is the kernel mean embedding of the walk's footprint, that it separates graphs that the Weisfeiler-Leman test cannot, and that pruning small probabilities comes with a per-node error certificate. Empirically, RoleWalk is competitive with the best role embeddings on five classification benchmarks at a fraction of their cost, has the highest scores on real directed roles in Wikipedia adminship, exceeds the published accuracy of Digraphwave at every noise level of its own Enron network-alignment benchmark, transfers centrality predictors to graphs four times larger better than existing inductive embeddings, hand-made features and a trained GIN, and embeds a million nodes in 20 s to 3 min on one CPU core. The code is open source (BSD license): https://github.com/kerighan/rolewalk
papers.summary: Structural role embeddings describe a node by its position in a graph, such as hub, bridge, or periphery, but existing methods either learn coordinates specific to one graph or normalize using whole-graph statistics, so the embeddings don't carry over between graphs, and few of them use edge direction. `RoleWalk` is training-free: it runs a short lazy random walk from each node and records, at each step, the distribution of transition probabilities (through its characteristic function) and the walker's distance from the start, with forward-then-backward walks capturing shared sources and targets in directed graphs. Because it depends only on a fixed-radius neighborhood, its coordinates mean the same thing in every graph, and the authors prove it can tell apart graphs that the Weisfeiler-Leman test cannot. It is competitive on five classification benchmarks at a fraction of the cost, transfers centrality predictors to graphs four times larger better than inductive baselines including a trained `GIN`, and **embeds a million nodes in 20 seconds to 3 minutes on a single CPU core**.

papers.title: Large Language Model Consensus and Corpus-Adaptive Topic Modeling for Classifying and Mapping Patent Innovation
papers.abstract: Patent analytics increasingly relies on transformer representations and large language models (LLMs), yet linking conceptual classification, topic formation and interpretation requires explicit decisions about model roles and the evidence retained at each stage. In this design-oriented study, we propose and demonstrate a patent analytics pipeline that links these tasks and keeps each decision open to audit. Three LLMs separately classify each patent by novelty (radical or incremental) and innovation type (product, process, service). Radical and innovation-type labels each require two supporting votes, with Incremental used as the fallback novelty label. Topics are discovered by clustering PatentSBERTa embeddings, with parameter ranges scaled to corpus size. A patent-specific stopword list is applied only when topics are represented with class-based term frequency--inverse document frequency (c-TF-IDF), and a second embedding model supports inter-topic similarity, hierarchical refinement and visualization. An LLM then labels each topic from its ranked keywords and representative patents. We demonstrate the pipeline on 30,964 public-sector-related patents retrieved from Lens.org. Across five category corpora ranging from 591 to 29,215 patents, the pipeline produced 74 category-specific topic instances with a macro-average document coverage of 98.1% and topic diversity of 0.900--1.000, and fewer than 1% of classification outputs returned UNKNOWN. Because every model vote and the evidence behind each topic label are retained, analysts can audit and revise the outputs. The demonstration establishes the feasibility and traceability of the pipeline; testing its labels against expert coding and benchmarking it against alternative pipelines are identified as the next steps. The pipeline offers a reusable basis for LLM-assisted patent analysis in technology intelligence.
papers.summary: This design study builds an auditable patent-analytics pipeline that connects LLM-based classification, topic discovery, and topic interpretation. Three LLMs vote on each patent's novelty (radical or incremental) and innovation type (product, process, or service), with two votes needed for a label. Topics come from clustering `PatentSBERTa` embeddings with parameters scaled to corpus size, a patent-specific stopword list is applied when topics are represented with class-based TF-IDF, and an LLM names each topic from its keywords and representative patents. On 30,964 public-sector-related patents from `Lens.org`, the pipeline produced 74 topics with **98.1% macro-average document coverage**, and fewer than 1% of classifications came back as UNKNOWN; checking the labels against expert coding is left for future work.

papers.title: Calibrated concept profiles: making the reading of a model's neurons a measurement
papers.abstract:
Interpretability has largely moved from reading a model's neurons directly to reading a second model trained on the first: a probe, a sparse autoencoder, a crosscoder. The move answered real faults -- mixed meanings, thresholds without a unit, readings that did not transfer from one study to the next -- but gave up what a direct reading alone provides: nothing trained in between, the neurons themselves named, and a reading that can be repeated and compared. Here the direct reading is made a measurement.
  A neuron's activation varies with the prompt, so its reading is a distribution over a population of stimuli. We declare that population: every factor around a target construct is drawn at its rate in a reference corpus and logged.
  From the declared distribution we generate a battery of prompts, and draw it twice. From the battery we compute the calibrated concept profile, one number per neuron, stated in units of the neuron's own spread on ordinary input; the two draws give every number a noise unit. Before the profile is read, a fixed set of checks licenses the battery on the model, and the smallest change the profile can resolve across training checkpoints is measured.
  Realised for Python on OpenCoder-1.5B and followed across checkpoints spanning two trillion training tokens, the profile gives what the alternatives do not report: a unit on every number, a chance level for every comparison, and which neurons carry a construct at every checkpoint.
  The battery, the code and the data behind every result are released.
papers.summary: Interpretability research has largely moved from reading a model's neurons directly to training a second model on them, such as a probe or a sparse autoencoder, which gives up readings that are untrained, name the neurons themselves, and can be repeated. The authors make the direct reading a proper measurement: they declare a population of prompts in which every factor around a target concept is sampled at its rate in a reference corpus, then draw the resulting prompt battery twice. From this they compute a **calibrated concept profile that gives each neuron one number, in units of that neuron's normal spread, together with a noise unit**, and they run fixed checks before reading it. Applied to Python on `OpenCoder-1.5B` across checkpoints spanning two trillion training tokens, the profile reports units, chance levels, and which neurons carry a concept at every checkpoint.

papers.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Probabilistic Option Shielding
papers.abstract: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.
papers.summary: Shielding keeps reinforcement-learning agents safe while they learn by blocking unsafe actions, but classical shields need a full environment model, and probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) avoids that need only by looking one or a few steps ahead. `Probabilistic Option Shielding` (`POS`) lifts PLS to options, meaning multi-step temporally extended actions, by training a model-free critic on one-step PLS signals to estimate the probability that a whole option finishes safely. On safe-navigation tasks in the `LogiCity` environment, **`POS` makes training considerably safer** while matching the task performance of step-level PLS and other safe RL baselines.

papers.title: Structure and Lineage Evidence for Vietnamese Statutory Article Retrieval on DRiLL
papers.abstract: We study Vietnamese statutory Article retrieval on DRiLL using features for provision identity and local form, same-law support, and citation and lineage evidence. Across five random seeds, selectors sharing candidates, listwise Qwen evidence, and learner settings improve official $F_2$ from 71.77% to 72.91%, with the largest descriptive gain on two-Article questions. Added features account for 18.20% of the proposed selector's total decision-tree split gain, measured as training-objective reduction, mainly from same-law and citation evidence. Cases reveal base provisions and amendments, companion recovery, distractor removal, and failures. These findings motivate research on other datasets, representations, and learners without establishing individual feature effects or requiring LightGBM, hand-crafted scores, or explicit graphs.
papers.summary: The work targets retrieval of Vietnamese statutory articles on the `DRiLL` dataset, adding features that capture a provision's identity and form, support from other articles in the same law, and citation and amendment-lineage links. Combining selectors over shared candidates, listwise evidence from `Qwen`, and learned rankers **raises the official F2 score from 71.77% to 72.91%** across five random seeds, with the largest gain on questions whose answer spans two articles. The new features account for 18.20% of the selector's decision-tree split gain, mostly from same-law and citation evidence. Case studies show where the method recovers base provisions and their amendments, removes distractors, and fails.

papers.title: Copies Are Not Confirmations: How News Duplication Fools LLM Judges and Continual Learners
papers.abstract: Many news reports of a claim are copies of one source: wire stories, content shared within a media group, syndicated features and press releases. We ask whether LLM judges and continual learners treat such copies as independent confirmations. In 200,000 English CC-News articles, a MinHash detector links 18.9% to a near-copy from another outlet (precision 0.97 once boilerplate is removed); it links 92% of edited reprints to their originals but none of the LLM rewrites by phi4, Llama 3.2 or Gemini 2.5 Flash. Shown three identical reprints of a claim about an unknown person instead of one report, Llama 3.2 3B and phi4 14B raised the share of lies they accepted from 0.06 to 0.71 and from 0.21 to 0.90 and ignored a note that the reports came from one source; Gemini 2.5 Flash already believed a single report, and Gemini 2.5 Pro followed provenance notes and tables. In a simulated continual-learning stream, showing the judge one report per detected chain cut the copied lies it accepted by 0.10-0.24 across four judges, at a mean cost of no more than 4.2 percentage points of accepted truths. Against reworded copies, a test of how many of a report's named entities are absent from an earlier look-alike separates LLM rewrites from 100 labelled independent reports of the same event with AUC 0.98-0.99 and wrongly flags one; entity overlap alone does as well, TF-IDF and a current embedding model come close, and the test catches few natural same-source derivatives. With the miss patterns of generated rewrite networks, it cut the reworded-copy lies accepted from 0.67 to 0.20 (0.40 when the rewriter invents details). Counting reports or chains alone is not a reliable defence, the effect of provenance information depends on the judge, and colluding sources remain the open problem. Code and labels: https://github.com/Metalesaek/copies-experiment
papers.summary: Many news reports of a claim are copies of a single source, such as wire stories or syndicated press releases, and the authors test whether LLM judges and continual learners treat those copies as independent confirmations. A MinHash detector links 18.9% of 200,000 `CC-News` articles to a near-copy from another outlet, but it misses every LLM rewrite. **Shown three identical reprints instead of one report, `Llama 3.2 3B` raised its acceptance of false claims from 0.06 to 0.71 and `phi4` from 0.21 to 0.90**, ignoring notes that the reports shared one source, while `Gemini 2.5 Pro` did use provenance information. Collapsing detected copy chains to a single report, plus an entity-novelty test that catches reworded copies, cuts accepted copied lies substantially at a small cost in accepted truths, although colluding sources remain unsolved.

papers.title: Representational drift in a code model: behaviour settles, which neurons carry it does not
papers.abstract: In neuroscience, representational drift is a change in which neurons carry a representation while behaviour stays the same; we measure its analogue in OpenCoder-1.5B during pretraining, for 169 Python constructs over two trillion tokens at a constant learning rate, with a noise unit on every change, at checkpoints as close as 1,000 training steps. For 16 of the 169, those whose grammar fixes a next token, the loss at those positions reaches its floor within the first 4% of training, while the model's reliance on the neurons carrying them grows to the end: removing them costs 0.06, 0.25 and 0.40 nats more than removing a random set, at 4 billion, 84 billion and 2 trillion tokens. Which neurons carry a construct never settles: for all 169 the carrier set is still changing at the last checkpoint, and an abrupt settling at any date from 84 billion to 1.5 trillion tokens, or a gradual one before 500 billion, would have been detected in 99% of injected cases. The set measured at 84 billion tokens, removed at the end, cannot be separated from a random set, so the function is carried by whichever neurons are current. Up close the change is a persisting pool and a changing sample: a neuron that leaves a construct's set returns at three times the rate of a matched neuron, and no set reassembles. The hypothesis we fixed in advance, that the carriers settle, is refuted; we discuss candidate causes and name the experiment that would separate them.
papers.summary: In neuroscience, representational drift means the neurons carrying a representation change while behavior stays the same. The authors measure an analogue in `OpenCoder-1.5B` over two trillion pretraining tokens for 169 Python constructs, attaching a noise unit to every change. For constructs whose grammar fixes the next token, loss hits its floor within the first 4% of training, yet the model's reliance on the carrying neurons keeps growing. **For all 169 constructs, the set of carrying neurons never settles**: the set measured at 84 billion tokens is indistinguishable from a random set by the end of training, and neurons that leave a set tend to return, which refutes the authors' preregistered hypothesis that the carriers would stabilize.

papers.title: RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now central to training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), but RLM pipelines are difficult to scale and costly to run because each RL step couples multiple large models, heterogeneous stages, cross-step state, and complex asynchronous dependencies. Existing systems typically optimize only parts of this design space. We address this complexity by jointly optimizing the pipeline structure as well as its execution using a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation called RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG). RPEG exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing together with execution optimizations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling, and multi-dimensional model parallelism. It is coupled with a comprehensive analytical performance model for RLM training, jointly capturing compute, communication, memory, and hierarchical rack-, node-, and GPU-level effects. Across systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, our distributed runtime engine implementing RPEG improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL and reduces step latency by up to 2.48x over verl, while increasing hardware utilization by up to 30%. Overall, RPEG provides a graph-driven foundation for next-generation training pipelines for frontier reasoning LLMs.
papers.summary: Reinforcement-learning pipelines for reasoning language models (RLMs) are costly and hard to scale, because each step couples several large models, heterogeneous stages, state carried between steps, and asynchronous dependencies. The authors introduce `RPEG`, a data-centric graph intermediate representation that exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing alongside execution optimizations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling, and multi-dimensional parallelism, all guided by an analytical model of compute, communication, and memory. On up to 256 GH200 GPUs, the runtime is **up to 2x faster than `ReaL` and reduces step latency by up to 2.48x compared with `verl`**, and it raises hardware utilization by up to 30%.

papers.title: On the Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures in LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: Iterative repair returns a failed program's error to a large language model (LLM) and asks it to fix it. After iterative repair, the remaining failures are mostly assertion failures: with four Qwen2.5 models, they make up 79% of residual failures on BigCodeBench, all on HumanEval and 93% on LiveCodeBench. We argue, through an information view of the feedback, that an assertion failure says little about where the fault lies. We propose Breakpoint Debugging (BPD), which returns the failed program annotated inline with its variables' runtime values. We take the tasks that iterative repair failed to fix with five repair attempts and compare two ways of spending five further generations on them: BPD, and resampling. On BigCodeBench, BPD repairs 26.7% of these tasks against 22.4%, and its advantage grows with model size. On HumanEval, BPD outperforms resampling but only slightly, and on LiveCodeBench, fresh sampling repairs more (6.5% against 4.9%). Furthermore, BPD reduces unchanged-code resubmissions from 28% to 8% on BigCodeBench. Using only the first failing test's trace, it outperforms tracing all failing tests while using fewer tokens than both all-trace BPD and plain iterative repair. On LiveCodeBench, BPD gives no gain even on the public tests, so a visible failing input is not enough for a trace to help. These results match the information view: a trace helps only when the test exposes a failing input, and the fault is an implementation slip; otherwise, a repair loop should resample rather than trace.
papers.summary: When an LLM repeatedly repairs its own code from error messages, most of the failures that remain are assertion failures: 79% on `BigCodeBench`, all on `HumanEval`, and 93% on `LiveCodeBench` across four `Qwen2.5` models. The authors argue that an assertion failure reveals little about where the bug is, and they propose `Breakpoint Debugging` (`BPD`), which returns the failed program annotated inline with its variables' runtime values. On tasks that plain repair could not fix, **`BPD` repaired 26.7% of `BigCodeBench` tasks against 22.4% for resampling** and cut unchanged resubmissions from 28% to 8%, while on `LiveCodeBench` fresh sampling did better. The results suggest that traces help only when the test exposes a failing input and the bug is an implementation slip; otherwise, a repair loop should resample.

papers.title: Provable State Estimation with Recurrent Models
papers.abstract: Estimating the state of a dynamical system from observations is a crucial task in robotics and control. Despite their empirical success, recurrent models often lack formal guarantees on convergence and robustness. We bridge this gap by analyzing these architectures from the perspective of nonlinear observer theory. By framing RNNs as a time-discretization of continuous latent dynamical systems (Neural ODEs), we demonstrate that enforcing a contraction condition on the latent flow guarantees the existence of a smooth, injective map of the true physical state into the latent space. We prove that this architecture acts as a tunable observer: by increasing a single scalar gain that scales the latent vector field, the estimation error can be driven to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of zero at an exponentially fast rate. We further establish quantitative bounds on the MLP complexity required to decode this latent state, and extend our formal guarantees to the discrete-time residual RNN implementation. We validate the theory on a real mobile robotic task, where a provably contracting model outperforms a vanilla GRU with substantially more stable training. We also report that unconstrained GRUs converge to contracting dynamics on this task, suggesting that contraction is an emergent property of well-trained sequence models.
papers.summary: Recurrent models are widely used to estimate the state of dynamical systems in robotics, but they rarely come with formal guarantees. Treating RNNs as discretized neural ordinary differential equations (Neural ODEs), the authors show that a contraction condition on the latent dynamics guarantees a smooth, injective map from the true physical state into the latent space. **Increasing a single scalar gain drives the estimation error exponentially fast to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of zero**, and the guarantees carry over to discrete-time residual RNNs, with bounds on the decoder's required MLP size. On a real mobile-robot task, a provably contracting model beats a vanilla `GRU` with more stable training, and unconstrained `GRU`s are observed to converge to contracting dynamics on their own.

papers.title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization
papers.abstract: Automated harness optimization improves agents by learning from trajectories and task feedback. Existing offline methods use reference answers to optimize harnesses for reuse on held-out tasks. However, many real-world tasks are open-ended, while long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address. To study harness optimization in these settings, we introduce PerfRace, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and investigate whether agents can use task-specific experience to recursively improve their harnesses during an ongoing task. To this end, we introduce BOXBOX, which enables agent-triggered harness revision and kernel-managed hot reloading while preserving execution context. We evaluate BOXBOX on PerfRace under matched test-time budgets, comparing it with Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution, and Harness Scaling. BOXBOX achieves higher speedup with more efficient use of task time and model cost, reaching a Speedup@4h of 1.70x, compared with 1.54x for the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Offline harness optimization tunes an agent's scaffolding against reference answers, but open-ended, long-running tasks raise new difficulties that a fixed harness may not handle. The authors introduce `PerfRace`, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and `BOXBOX`, which lets an agent revise its own harness mid-task and hot-reload it without losing execution context. Under matched test-time budgets, **`BOXBOX` reaches a 1.70x speedup after four hours, compared with 1.54x for the strongest baseline**, while using task time and model cost more efficiently than a frozen harness, offline harness evolution, or harness scaling.

papers.title: Khmer PFGen-Bench: Building a Judge-Free Benchmark for Open-Ended Generation in a Low-Resource Language
papers.abstract: Benchmarks for open-ended generation often rely on large language model (LLM) judges, whose reliability in low-resource languages is uncertain. We introduce Khmer PFGen-Bench, to our knowledge the first judge-free benchmark for multi-sentence answers to questions composed directly in Khmer, a low-resource language. Khmer PFGen-Bench adapts the scorer of PFGen-Bench, a benchmark for Japanese that scores responses with keyword rules and n-gram statistics from LLM-generated references. This scoring requires references that are both valid and varied, which LLMs may not produce in Khmer, so we examine how to build such references. We find that post-trained models can give more valid but less varied references than their base variants, and that mixing model families increases variety for the same number of references. Using references from post-trained models in nine families, the benchmark yields model rankings that are stable across reference sets and consistent with a native speaker's ratings. These findings offer guidance for building judge-free benchmarks in other low-resource languages.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for open-ended generation usually rely on LLM judges, which may be unreliable in low-resource languages. `Khmer PFGen-Bench` is the first judge-free benchmark for multi-sentence answers to questions written directly in Khmer; it adapts the scoring of the Japanese `PFGen-Bench`, which uses keyword rules and n-gram statistics computed against LLM-generated reference answers. The authors find that post-trained models produce more valid but less varied references than their base versions, and that mixing model families increases variety. With references from nine post-trained model families, **the benchmark's model rankings are stable across reference sets and agree with a native speaker's ratings**.

papers.title: KLEAR: Knowledge-Matched LLM Evaluation in Korean across Application Requirements via Controlled Benchmark Transformation
papers.abstract: Existing Korean benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) evaluate performance across diverse knowledge domains, but their accuracy scores cannot distinguish whether incorrect responses arise from a lack of required knowledge or a failure to apply that knowledge correctly. Our analysis of existing Korean benchmarks reveals that most questions can be answered through factual recall alone, while those demanding greater application also differ in required knowledge, making it difficult to isolate application ability. To address this, we introduce KLEAR, a framework that constructs knowledge-matched contrasts by varying application demand while preserving the required knowledge. During construction, KLEAR identifies the knowledge underlying each source question as an explicit anchor bundle to guide generation of questions requiring more complex application. Generated candidates then undergo automated and human validation, with iterative revision based on evaluation feedback. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting knowledge-matched sets largely satisfy the intended constraints, enabling controlled evaluation across diverse LLMs. These evaluations reveal that increasing application demand exposes failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided.
papers.summary: Accuracy on existing Korean LLM benchmarks cannot tell whether a wrong answer comes from missing knowledge or from failing to apply knowledge the model has, and most of their questions can be answered by factual recall alone. `KLEAR` builds knowledge-matched contrasts: it extracts the knowledge behind each source question as an explicit anchor bundle, then generates harder variants that require more complex application of that same knowledge, with automated and human validation and iterative revision. Evaluations across diverse LLMs show that **raising application demand exposes failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided**.

papers.title: HMMF-Net: A Lightweight Hierarchical Multi-Frame Multimodal Fusion Network for Accurate Fish Feeding Intensity Assessment
papers.abstract: Automated fish feeding intensity assessment (FFIA) is important for precision aquaculture and feed cost optimization. However, unimodal methods are vulnerable to acoustic noise and visual disturbances, while existing multimodal frameworks often rely on computationally intensive 3D convolutions or Transformers, limiting their use on edge devices. To address these limitations, we propose HMMF-Net, a lightweight multimodal architecture that combines early multi-frame visual encoding and multi-axis acoustic modeling through a hierarchical bidirectional messenger cross-modal fusion (BMCF) mechanism. The visual branch captures temporal variations in feeding behavior by stacking temporally distant frames as a multi-channel input to an adapted 2D EfficientNetB0 backbone. The acoustic branch employs adaptive multi-axis residual units (AMARU) to extract temporal, frequency, and local time-frequency representations from log-mel spectrograms. BMCF progressively exchanges information between the two modalities at intermediate representation levels through compact messenger tokens, reducing the computational overhead of dense cross-modal attention. Evaluated on the AV-FFIA dataset using five-fold cross-validation, HMMF-Net achieves 96.77% accuracy and 96.88% F1-score on the held-out test folds, with 3.987M parameters and 1.002 GFLOPs. Compared with the best-performing visual configuration (95.49% accuracy), HMMF-Net reduces the classification error by 28.38%. Deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano using TensorRT with FP32 precision maintains comparable accuracy, with an inference time of 11.54 ms per 2-second sample and a model size of 18.81 MB. These results demonstrate that HMMF-Net combines effective multimodal representation learning with computational efficiency, enabling accurate and practical FFIA on resource-constrained edge platforms.
papers.summary: Automated fish feeding intensity assessment (FFIA) supports precision aquaculture, but single-modality methods are fragile and existing multimodal models are too heavy for edge devices. `HMMF-Net` stacks temporally distant video frames as input to a 2D `EfficientNetB0` and models log-mel audio spectrograms with adaptive multi-axis residual units. The two branches exchange information through compact messenger tokens in a hierarchical bidirectional cross-modal fusion (`BMCF`) mechanism instead of dense cross-attention. On the `AV-FFIA` dataset it reaches **96.77% accuracy with about 4M parameters and 1 GFLOP**, and runs in 11.54 ms per sample on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano.

papers.title: Fused-Softmax for efficient quantized attention
papers.abstract: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.
papers.summary: On modern GPUs, low-precision matrix throughput is growing much faster than vector arithmetic, so softmax has become the bottleneck that stops attention from using the available GEMM performance. `Fused-Softmax Attention` is a training-free method that reformulates and approximates softmax so its dominant operations fold into the attention matrix multiplications, moving work onto matrix cores, and the extra error it adds stays below the error already introduced by quantizing the operands. On an AMD Instinct MI355X, the MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels deliver **2.1x, 2.8x and 3.2x speedups over BF16 attention**, plus up to 2.05x end-to-end speedup on the `Wan2.2-T2V-A14B` video model. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source `AITER` library and were used in AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 submission.

papers.title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.
papers.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) outputs are often hard for domain experts to use, and LLM-generated explanations can hallucinate and lack traceable sources. The authors propose a clinical decision support system (CDSS) that pairs standard predictive models and XAI techniques with a `Retrieval-Augmented Generation` module that grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge. The module rephrases technical output in natural language and **lets clinicians query the system interactively about model decisions**. Only preliminary experiments are reported.

papers.title: Cross-Layer TopK: Dynamically Allocating Sparsity Across Layers in Transcoders
papers.abstract: Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) decompose the activations of large language models into human-interpretable features and trace how these features interact across layers to form circuits, making them a key tool for mechanistic interpretability. However, training CLTs effectively and efficiently is hard. Beyond the usual trade-off between sparsity and reconstruction quality, a CLT has to model all layers at once, which adds a further challenge. The common JumpReLU recipe controls sparsity only indirectly through a penalty, while the direct extension of TopK selects a fixed number of latents in every layer. Yet reconstruction difficulty differs widely across layers, and intermediate layers are much harder than others, so giving every layer the same budget is suboptimal. We propose Cross-Layer TopK, which sets a single L0 budget for the whole model and dynamically allocates it across layers during training. In a comparison with JumpReLU and other TopK variants on Qwen3-8B-Base, this gives lower FVU while using 20% fewer active latents than JumpReLU. The better reconstruction carries over to circuit tracing, yielding more complete circuits with higher replacement and completeness scores. The fixed per-token budget of Cross-Layer TopK also makes it easy to pair with sparse decoding, which cuts both computation and communication and gives a 2.9x speedup per training step. We further show that Cross-Layer TopK follows scaling laws in both latent size and sparsity. We have open-sourced the weights of our CLT at https://huggingface.co/ByteDance-Seed/Cross-Layer-TopK-CLT.
papers.summary: Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) decompose LLM activations into interpretable features for circuit tracing in mechanistic interpretability, but they are hard to train, and existing recipes either control sparsity indirectly (`JumpReLU`) or give every layer the same fixed number of active latents (`TopK`). `Cross-Layer TopK` sets one sparsity budget for the whole model and allocates it dynamically across layers during training, reflecting that intermediate layers are much harder to reconstruct. On `Qwen3-8B-Base` it achieves **lower reconstruction error than `JumpReLU` with 20% fewer active latents**, yields more complete circuits, and pairs with sparse decoding for a 2.9x per-step training speedup. The method follows scaling laws in latent size and sparsity, and the CLT weights are released.

papers.title: Controllable Molecule Generation via Sparse Representation Editing: An Interpretability-Driven Perspective
papers.abstract: Controllable molecule generation is crucial for diverse scientific applications, such as drug discovery and materials design. While large language models (LLMs) show great promise, their dense and entangled representations impede precise control over the generation of molecules with bespoke substructures or properties. To address this, we propose Sparse Representation Editing (SpaRE), an interpretability-driven framework for fine-grained and precise control in LLM-based molecule generation. The crux of SpaRE is to learn an overcomplete sparse feature space that disentangles LLM representations into a compact set of latent features corresponding to chemically meaningful concepts. Within this space, we can directly manipulate these concept-aligned latent features to achieve (1) local control, by generating target atoms and functional groups at specified positions; and (2) global control, by customizing the overall structural and physicochemical properties within defined ranges. In this way, our framework advances interpretability from post-hoc analysis to actionable generative control. Experiments show that SpaRE can generate chemically desirable molecules under complex constraints in real-world scenarios, while offering mechanistic insights for quantitative structure-property analysis. The code and demo are available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/ICML2026_SpaRE.
papers.summary: LLM-based molecule generation is hard to steer precisely toward specific substructures or properties because the model's internal representations are dense and entangled. `SpaRE` (Sparse Representation Editing) learns an overcomplete sparse feature space in which latent features align with chemically meaningful concepts, and then edits those features directly. This enables both **local control, placing target atoms or functional groups at specified positions, and global control of structural and physicochemical properties within set ranges**. Experiments show it produces chemically valid molecules under complex constraints and offers mechanistic insight for structure-property analysis.

papers.title: DUET: Dual-Sparse Inference for Block Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, yet their inference remains costly due to repeated attention over a growing historical prefix and repeated processing of the entire current generation block. Historical attention becomes increasingly expensive as generation progresses, while all current-block positions are propagated through the Transformer at every denoising step even though only a small fraction are typically resolved at that step. In this paper, we introduce Duet, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework that addresses these challenges through prefix Key-Value (KV) sparsity and early query sparsity, respectively. Specifically, Duet exploits the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention within each generation block to construct a compact historical KV subset that is reused across denoising steps. For query sparsity, Duet predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only the corresponding queries through the suffix Transformer layers, avoiding deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated in the current step. Experiments show that Duet maintains competitive accuracy while achieving 1.34$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end/per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41$\times$/4.72$\times$ on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length.
papers.summary: Block diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel through iterative denoising, but inference is costly because every step attends over a growing prefix and pushes all positions in the current block through the full Transformer. `Duet` is a training-free method with two kinds of sparsity: it reuses a compact subset of historical key-value (KV) entries across denoising steps, exploiting how concentrated and stable prefix attention is, and it predicts from shallow layers which positions will update so that only those queries pass through the deeper layers. At 32K context it keeps accuracy competitive while delivering **2.41x end-to-end and 4.72x per-step speedups on `SDAR-8B-Chat-b32`**, and 1.34x and 2.83x on `LLaDA2.1-mini`.

papers.title: MM-DyGraph: A Dataset, Benchmark, and Model for Multimodal Dynamic Graphs
papers.abstract: Multimodal dynamic graphs are pervasive in real-world applications, where nodes and edges are accompanied by multimodal signals, including text and images. Despite their practical importance, benchmarks and methods that explicitly study multimodal learning in dynamic graphs remain scarce, hindering the full understanding and effective utilization of multimodal information for downstream tasks. To address this gap, we introduce MM-DyGraph, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning, consisting of diverse real-world datasets with fine-grained temporal graph evolution and rich multimodal attributes. MM-DyGraph provides three evaluation tasks to comprehensively assess model performance in dynamic settings. We benchmark representative state-of-the-art dynamic graph methods and reveal that naive feature concatenation yields target-level inconsistencies: multimodal inputs benefit certain prediction targets while harming others. This observation indicates that the modality informativeness depends on the specific prediction target over time. Building on these observations, we propose a Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion (TST-MF) framework, which jointly conditions multimodal fusion on the prediction target and spatial-temporal relations, enabling context-adaptive cross-modal interplay for target-specific representations. Extensive experiments over diverse datasets and tasks show that TST-MF delivers robust and competitive performance, achieving clear gains in multimodal settings.
papers.summary: Dynamic graphs whose nodes and edges carry text and images are common in practice, but there have been no benchmarks for multimodal dynamic graph learning. `MM-DyGraph` provides real-world datasets with fine-grained temporal evolution and three evaluation tasks. Benchmarking existing methods shows that **naively concatenating multimodal features helps some prediction targets while hurting others**. The authors therefore propose `TST-MF`, which conditions multimodal fusion on both the prediction target and spatial-temporal relations and delivers robust gains across datasets.

papers.title: Practical Non-Stationary Graph Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: Gaussian processes on graphs provide a principled framework for prediction and uncertainty estimation, but modelling heterogeneous networks often requires balancing flexibility against parameter complexity. Variability at a node may reflect useful signal that should propagate through the network, unreliable measurements whose influence should be suppressed, or a mixture of both. We introduce Variance-Coupled Gaussian Processes (VCGPs), which use a positive auxiliary signal to modulate graph interactions through a single learned coupling exponent. The exponent controls how strongly high-variability nodes propagate or attenuate information, while a cluster-wise extension accommodates different regimes within the same graph. Under stated structural assumptions, we characterize the unique stationary-rescaling point of the basic family, where correlations match those of a stationary graph kernel while node-dependent variances remain. Experiments on traffic, air-quality and weather datasets show competitive prediction and uncertainty estimation relative to stationary and per-node non-stationary baselines, with the largest gains on networks requiring multiple coupling regimes. Stationary correlations after variance rescaling remain sufficient on some data, and performance depends on the auxiliary signal and model selection.
papers.summary: Gaussian processes on graphs offer prediction with uncertainty estimates, but modeling heterogeneous networks means trading flexibility against parameter count, especially when a node's variability may be signal or unreliable noise. `Variance-Coupled Gaussian Processes` (`VCGPs`) use a positive auxiliary signal to modulate graph interactions through **a single learned coupling exponent** that controls whether high-variability nodes amplify or suppress propagation, with a cluster-wise extension for multiple regimes in one graph. Experiments on traffic, air-quality and weather data show competitive accuracy and uncertainty estimates, with the largest gains on networks that need multiple coupling regimes.

papers.title: Topology as a Design Variable: Joint Architecture-Sizing Optimization for SRAM
papers.abstract: SRAM's power-performance-area-stability trade-off depends on bitcell topology, a discrete architectural choice that interacts non-separably with continuous transistor sizing. However, no open-source SRAM tool treats topology as an optimizable variable. OpenRAM generates SRAM layouts but performs no optimization, while OpenYield supports high-fidelity evaluation but restricts optimization to scalar sizing of a fixed 6T cell. OpenYieldV2 closes this gap through three integrated contributions. First, a fully parameterized compiler generates complete 6T and 10T SRAM macros with peripheral circuits and replica-bitline self-timing, enabling topology comparison under identical simulation conditions. Second, a few-shot TabPFN surrogate learns topology-dependent PPA responses with limited full-macro SPICE samples. Third, a coarse-to-refined multi-objective optimizer combines global exploration of discrete architectural choices with local refinement of continuous transistor sizes. Experiments across varying design conditions reveal a topology decision boundary that shifts with operating constraints rather than following a fixed design rule. Jointly optimizing across this boundary improves hypervolume by up to 17.3\% over the strongest single-topology baseline. OpenYieldV2 is open-source to support reproducible SRAM design research.
papers.summary: SRAM power, performance, area and stability depend on the bitcell topology, a discrete choice that interacts with continuous transistor sizing, yet no open-source tool optimizes over topology. `OpenYieldV2` combines a parameterized compiler for complete 6T and 10T SRAM macros, a few-shot `TabPFN` surrogate trained on a small number of full-macro SPICE simulations, and a coarse-to-fine multi-objective optimizer over both discrete and continuous choices. Experiments show the best topology shifts with operating constraints rather than following a fixed rule, and joint optimization **improves hypervolume by up to 17.3% over the best single-topology baseline**.

papers.title: Rethinking MoE Load Balancing as Feedback Control
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training is often not stationary: the data mixture changes at curriculum boundaries, when a model is continually pretrained into a new domain, or when the corpus is refreshed. Routing is learned against the current mixture, so each such change disrupts the per-expert load the router had converged to, and existing balancing methods have only been evaluated on stationary data. We rethink load balancing as a feedback control problem, in which the deviation of each expert's load from its fair share is the control error and the per-expert routing bias is the control input, and define a family of controllers, the PID-Balancer, from the proportional, integral, and derivative terms of classical PID control. Two widely used methods belong to this family: the auxiliary balancing loss behaves like a proportional controller, and the loss-free bias update is an integral controller acting on the sign of the error. Reading the router as a static map with a one-step delay, we show that the integral term is the only one that both removes persistent imbalance and averages out the step-to-step fluctuation of the measured load, whereas the proportional and derivative terms pass or amplify that fluctuation into the routing bias. We therefore adopt PID (I), the pure-integral member of the family with a single gain. Two settings are evaluated: (i) training an OLMoE backbone from scratch with 16 to 64 experts per layer, through a mid-run mixture switch, and (ii) continual pretraining of the released OLMoE-1B-7B on a new corpus. PID (I) holds balance before the shift and restores it more tightly afterwards than either the auxiliary loss or loss-free balancing, at comparable perplexity.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training data often shifts mid-run at curriculum boundaries, during continual pretraining, or when the corpus is refreshed, which disrupts per-expert load, yet balancing methods have only been evaluated on stationary data. The authors frame load balancing as feedback control and define a `PID-Balancer` family, showing that the auxiliary balancing loss acts like a proportional controller and loss-free bias updates act like a sign-based integral controller. Their analysis shows that **only the integral term both removes persistent imbalance and smooths step-to-step load noise**, so they adopt a pure-integral variant with a single gain. On `OLMoE` trained from scratch through a data-mixture switch, and in continual pretraining of `OLMoE-1B-7B`, it restores balance more tightly than existing methods at comparable perplexity.

papers.title: Zero-Query Transferable Pretend Benign Attacks with Amortized Online Generation for Cooperative Perception
papers.abstract: Cooperative perception enables an ego agent to acquire information from collaborators beyond its own sensors' reach. Yet, the most beneficial messages are often the hardest to verify from local observations. Pretend Benign (PB) exploits this asymmetry by targeting regions with weak local verifiability and applying multi-objective perturbations, making harmful feature changes appear to be benign assistance. However, PB is victim-dependent: selecting regions and optimizing perturbations require the victim model's architecture, parameters, and gradients, limiting transfer to unseen victims. A transferable attack must capture properties shared across cooperative detection models rather than those specific to one network. We address this by building a victim-agnostic attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models and encoding its capabilities in a reusable dictionary to reduce per-message generation cost. Specifically, Transferable Pretend Benign (TrPB) transfers PB's region selection criterion and multi-objective perturbation strategy across heterogeneous surrogates to construct an offline attack. We further propose RT-TrPB, which encodes transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and reusable perturbation dictionary, amortizing per-message attack generation. Experiments on widely used cooperative perception benchmarks show that RT-TrPB bypasses the consensus-based defenses ROBOSAC and FLD with success rates approaching 100% and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms. To counter PB-style attacks masquerading as benign collaboration, we also propose STTrust, which verifies received messages using spatial and temporal consistency and incorporates identity-level trust. STTrust detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception performance to near the attack-free level.
papers.summary: In cooperative perception, an ego vehicle relies on collaborators' messages, and the Pretend Benign (PB) attack exploits regions the ego cannot verify locally, but PB requires white-box access to the victim model. `TrPB` makes the attack victim-agnostic by using a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models, and `RT-TrPB` amortizes it into a region predictor and a reusable perturbation dictionary for real-time generation. `RT-TrPB` **bypasses the consensus-based defenses `ROBOSAC` and `FLD` with near-100% success**, producing each perturbation in under 56 ms. As a countermeasure, the authors propose `STTrust`, which checks spatial and temporal consistency plus identity-level trust, detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores near attack-free performance.

papers.title: Forecasting cumulative intraoperative hypotension burden: patient-disjoint evaluation of quantile boosting and alert policies
papers.abstract:
Background: Binary hypotension forecasts do not describe the depth and duration of future low pressure. Burden forecasts may support graded early warning, but better forecast scores need not yield more useful alerts.
  Objective: To evaluate conditional quantiles of the next 15-minute mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg and distinguish forecasting performance from episode-warning performance.
  Methods: Public VitalDB numeric arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling. Subject-disjoint training, validation and test splits included 70,402, 14,270 and 15,575 labeled windows. We compared climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without additional MAP-history features. Patient-weighted pinball loss and subject-bootstrap intervals evaluated forecasting. Validation selected alert thresholds before a hash-recorded test evaluation.
  Results: In the test split, the prespecified residual-versus-persistence comparison at the 90th percentile yielded losses of 2.256 and 2.900 mmHg-min, respectively (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487). Direct prediction achieved 2.196, and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieved 2.193. Episode-warning results were sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold.
  Conclusions: This retrospective benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance. Findings support further study of direct burden estimation; they do not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.
papers.summary: Binary hypotension alerts do not capture how deep or long future low blood pressure will be, so this study forecasts conditional quantiles of the mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg over the next 15 minutes. Using public `VitalDB` data with patient-disjoint splits, it compares climatology, calibrated persistence, and direct and residual quantile gradient boosting, and evaluates forecasting separately from alert policies. At the 90th percentile, **residual boosting reduced pinball loss from 2.900 to 2.256 mmHg-min versus persistence**, and direct prediction did slightly better still. Episode-warning performance was sensitive to the alert rule and threshold, and the authors stress that patient benefit and generalization beyond the source hospital remain unestablished.

papers.title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery
papers.abstract: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.
papers.summary: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation has regained attention with integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), but hardware impairments in antenna arrays are often ignored and degrade accuracy. The authors build a model-based learning method on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (`SOMP`) algorithm that calibrates gain-phase and antenna-position errors with projected gradient descent, using supervised or unsupervised objectives. It also extends `SOMP` to continuous dictionaries through gradient refinement steps. Simulations show **effective impairment compensation even without labeled data**, outperforming conventional sparse-recovery and subspace-based estimators.

papers.title: Nudging Decision Models: Do Digital Nudges Steer Fast, Generation-Free AI Agents?
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly automate business and consumer tasks but are slow and expensive. Decision models, a new class that chooses among options without generating text, are far faster and less costly. Developers call them "System One models," referencing dual process theory. We ask whether such models can be steered by digital nudges online and whether, as the theory predicts, automatic nudges affect them more than reflective ones. We adapted an online shopping experiment, previously run with humans and LLM agents, to three decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1). Across 600 runs per model, they chose a preselected default in 97.5-99.9% and a product with social influence information in 75-96% of choices, versus 47-49% in the control. All responded more strongly to the automatic nudge, the opposite of what has been reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents. We provide first evidence that non-generative decision models are susceptible to digital nudges in a System 1 pattern, implying agent-type-specific nudge effects.
papers.summary: Decision models are a new class of fast, cheap agent models that choose among options without generating text, often described as System 1 models in the sense of dual process theory. The authors adapted an online shopping experiment previously run with humans and LLM agents to three such models (`Jev`, `Decision-1`, `d1`) to test whether digital nudges steer them. Across 600 runs per model, the models picked a preselected default **97.5-99.9% of the time**, and picked a product with social-influence information 75-96% of the time versus 47-49% in the control. All three responded more strongly to the automatic nudge than to the reflective one, the opposite of what has been reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents.

papers.title: Reconciling European Electricity Data with Diffusion Priors Learned from Observations Alone
papers.abstract: The ENTSO-E Transparency Platform publishes generation, load, and cross-border power flows for European bidding zones. The values carry undocumented errors and violate energy conservation, and data reconciliation consists in correcting them to satisfy that balance. In this work, we formulate data reconciliation as Bayesian inference. Classical methods implicitly take a uniform prior, which we replace with a diffusion model estimated from the observations alone by empirical-Bayes expectation-maximization. The resulting posterior is sampled with a guided process whose projection step makes every sample satisfy the balance exactly. On synthetic systems of six to thirty-five bidding zones, built from ENTSO-E resource-adequacy data, the diffusion prior gives the most accurate reconciliation, increasingly so as the system grows. Its credible intervals are calibrated or conservative, and it remains the most accurate under a misspecified noise covariance. Finally, when the generation of entire zones goes unreported, the classical methods fail while the learned prior recovers it from cross-zone structure.
papers.summary: European electricity data from the `ENTSO-E` Transparency Platform contains undocumented errors and violates energy conservation, so it must be reconciled to satisfy the balance. The authors cast reconciliation as Bayesian inference and replace the implicit uniform prior of classical methods with a diffusion model learned from the noisy observations alone via empirical-Bayes expectation-maximization. Posterior samples come from a guided process with a projection step that enforces the balance exactly. On synthetic systems of 6 to 35 bidding zones the diffusion prior gives the most accurate reconciliation with calibrated or conservative uncertainty, and **it recovers entire unreported zones where classical methods fail**.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison
papers.summary: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand from an explicit specification, with no training. This study tests how far an LLM can do this zero-shot across a ladder of games of increasing difficulty: Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame, with a structurally unrelated replicate game at each rung. Six of the ten networks have complete proofs of correctness, but the chess rung **succeeds 84.1-100% on the one-ply tactics it was built for and collapses to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play**, a gap the authors attribute to an architectural ceiling rather than engineering effort. All networks, oracles and a cold-prompt protocol for cross-model comparison are released.

papers.title: PHISHREV+: An ASP-Based Post-Hoc Defeasible Machine Learning Framework for Phishing Detection
papers.abstract: Phishing website detection remains a critical cybersecurity challenge. Although machine learning classifiers achieve high accuracy on benchmark datasets, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: once trained, their decision boundaries are fixed and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining the model. This work presents \textbf{PHISHREV+}, a hybrid framework that instantiates the notion of \textit{post-hoc defeasible machine learning}. This framework does not replace the classifier. It treats the initial classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them through an Answer Set Programming based non-monotonic reasoning(NMR) layer. The framework operates in two phases. In the machine learning phase, four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on the 87 feature benchmark dataset. In the post-hoc NMR phase, four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis of the training set, and validated through Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, formally revise initial predictions. The proposed framework achieves consistent false positive reduction across all our classifiers SVM (41$\rightarrow$39), KNN (47$\rightarrow$46), DT (62$\rightarrow$61), and RF (52$\rightarrow$51) while maintaining complete false negative parity with zero increase overhead. A comprehensive ablation studies across seven rule configurations confirms that the hierarchical combination of all four defeasible rules is necessary to achieve this optimal balance. Instance level explainability is provided through eXplainable ASP (XASP), which generates formal derivation graphs showing which defeasible rules fired and why the initial belief was retracted, a capability absent from all existing phishing detection approaches.
papers.summary: Trained phishing-website classifiers have fixed decision boundaries and cannot take in new contextual evidence without retraining. `PHISHREV+` treats classifier outputs as defeasible beliefs and revises them with a non-monotonic reasoning layer built in Answer Set Programming (ASP), using four rules derived from exploratory data analysis and checked with statistical tests. Applied to `SVM`, `KNN`, decision tree and random forest classifiers on an 87-feature benchmark, it **reduces false positives by one or two per classifier with no increase in false negatives**. It also produces formal derivation graphs explaining why a prediction was retracted.

papers.title: FondueQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Parametric Compensation in Multi-Hop QA
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show remarkable performance based on parametric knowledge, i.e., their ability to recall facts and associations internalized in a model's weights. However, studying this capability on established multi-hop benchmarks may be complicated by benchmark contamination, as many of these benchmarks have been publicly available long enough to plausibly appear in modern pretraining corpora. As a result, correct answers under missing evidence may reflect either general parametric knowledge or memorization of benchmark-specific instances. To study how models use internal knowledge when retrieval evidence is incomplete, we introduce FondueQA, in which every required multi-hop fact is uniquely localized to a designated evidence document. This enables controlled document-level evidence ablations to study parametric compensation under incomplete retrieval. Our empirical evaluation reveals that parametric compensation strongly depends on both entity popularity and the structural role of missing evidence. Generally, models compensate more successfully for facts involving popular entities. On FondueQA, we show that bridging evidence can be more useful than the answer-bearing document itself. Moreover, models may recall a missing fact in isolation but fail to use it under partial evidence, particularly when the context contains plausible competing entities, which can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points.
papers.summary: Studying how LLMs fall back on internal knowledge when retrieved evidence is missing is complicated by contamination of older multi-hop benchmarks. `FondueQA` localizes every required multi-hop fact to one designated evidence document, which allows controlled document-level ablations of retrieval. Experiments show that how well models compensate depends on entity popularity and on the structural role of the missing evidence, with bridging documents sometimes more useful than the answer-bearing one. Models can recall a missing fact in isolation yet fail to use it under partial evidence, especially when plausible competing entities appear, **reducing Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points**.

papers.title: AudioSphere: Towards Self-Supervised Spatial Audio Representation Models
papers.abstract: Recent audio embedding models learn representations that transfer across clip- and frame-level tasks, yet they operate almost exclusively on single-channel signals and are blind to spatial structure. Spatial audio models capture that structure but rely on clip-level supervision or contrastive objectives, yielding embeddings unsuitable for frame-level tasks like sound event detection and localization (SELD). We argue this dichotomy is not fundamental: patch-level spatial self-supervision can jointly learn acoustic and spatial features at both temporal granularities. We introduce AudioSphere, a multi-channel masked autoencoder trained on Ambisonics recordings that reconstructs both spectral content and directional cues via a joint spatiotemporal masking strategy that masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors. AudioSphere supports frame-level predictions while producing strong clip-level representations via aggregation. Alongside the model, we release RealSELD, a standardized benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real-world multi-channel SELD. AudioSphere enables, for the first time, SELD with a frozen self-supervised backbone, while matching or exceeding prior self-supervised audio embedding models on clip-level classification tasks spanning environmental sound, speech, and music, and on frame-level sound event detection. All code and data are available at https://github.com/labhamlet/AudioSphere and https://huggingface.co/labhamlet.
papers.summary: General-purpose audio embedding models work on single-channel audio and ignore spatial structure, while spatial audio models use clip-level objectives that do not suit frame-level tasks such as sound event detection and localization (SELD). `AudioSphere` is a multi-channel masked autoencoder trained on Ambisonics recordings that masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors, learning spectral and directional features together. The authors also release `RealSELD`, a benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real-world SELD. `AudioSphere` **enables SELD with a frozen self-supervised backbone for the first time**, while matching or beating prior self-supervised audio models on clip-level classification and frame-level event detection.

papers.title: Diversity-Aware Client Selection for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw data, making it attractive for privacy-sensitive and bandwidth-constrained applications. A practical challenge in deploying FL is reducing communication overhead while maintaining model performance under heterogeneous, non-IID data distributions. Selecting which subset of clients participates in each training round offers a principled way to address both challenges simultaneously, yet its impact on data diversity and representativeness remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate three client selection strategies, Power-of-Choice, Fisher information, and Centered Kernel Alignment, evaluating them not only by accuracy and convergence, but through the lens of participation diversity using the Gini coefficient and KL divergence.
