As a result, optimizing CPU throughput or GPU load balance in isolation cannot eliminate pipeline bubbles. We present DataHelix, a metadata-first CPU-GPU co-scheduling data plane for multimodal training. DataHelix jointly reasons about preprocessing demand and GPU execution progress, treating each GPU compute window as the readiness budget for the next batch and coordinating preprocessing across ranks to minimize deadline misses rather than CPU makespan. To avoid expensive data movement, placement is decided while samples remain lightweight descriptors, before decoding and collation amplify them into large tensors. Descriptor-level token-latent-aware batching performs coarse pre-balancing, while cost-gated collective rebalancing corrects residual skew only when its expected benefit exceeds transfer cost. Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, DataHelix reduces mean deadline-miss rate by 67.8% and mean p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, while achieving 2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders and 1.82x over a Ray actor pool under the same CPU budget.
papers.summary: In multimodal model training, both the CPU cost of decoding samples and the GPU compute time vary widely from sample to sample. Under synchronous data-parallel training, a slow input pipeline on any one rank stalls every GPU. `DataHelix` schedules CPU preprocessing and GPU execution together, treating each GPU compute window as the deadline for preparing the next batch. It decides where each sample goes while samples are still lightweight descriptors, before decoding inflates them into large tensors. Token- and latent-aware batching pre-balances the load, and collective rebalancing is applied only when its expected benefit exceeds the transfer cost. Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 `Ascend 910B` accelerators, it cuts mean deadline misses by 67.8% and reaches **2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders** under the same CPU budget.

papers.title: MIRA: Mitigating Pole Geometry Bias in Recurrent Language Models
papers.abstract: We show that the Transformer's recurrent successors --- such as selective state-space models (SSMs), Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV), and Retentive Network (RetNet) --- can be characterized as infinite-impulse-response (IIR) systems. The zero--pole geometries of these IIR systems characterize the temporal modes they can represent. However, to trade parallelism, the algebraic structures of the parameterizations of these recurrent systems often give rise to poles constrained to the real axis, thereby inducing an architectural bias in their recurrent dynamics. To unify these recurrent architectures and eliminate their pole geometry bias, inspired by the lattice--ladder realization of general IIR systems, we present \textsc{Mira} (\textbf{M}odal \textbf{I}IR \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{A}rchitecture), a unified family of linear-time recurrent architectures for building large language models (LLMs) with a highly parallel algebraic structure. Each \textsc{Mira} block realizes a higher-order IIR system that represents temporal modes from token streams through a lattice--ladder structure, followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). This realization enables the model to represent the temporal modes associated with both real and complex-conjugate poles. We pretrain \textsc{Mira-S}, a 12-layer small-scale LLM with 0.14B parameters composed entirely of \textsc{Mira} blocks. Throughout the pretraining, \textsc{Mira-S} achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines, exhibits stronger context-window generalization beyond the training length, and attains higher throughput with a dedicated CUDA kernel.
papers.summary: Recurrent alternatives to the Transformer, such as selective state-space models (SSMs), `RWKV` and `RetNet`, can all be analysed as infinite-impulse-response (IIR) filters. To stay parallelizable, their parameterizations restrict the filters' poles to the real axis, which limits the temporal patterns they can represent. `MIRA` (Modal IIR Recurrent Architecture) is a unified family of linear-time recurrent blocks that implements higher-order IIR systems through a lattice-ladder structure. This lets the model represent both real and complex-conjugate poles while remaining highly parallel. A 0.14B-parameter model built entirely from these blocks, `MIRA-S`, **achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines**, generalizes better beyond its training context length, and runs faster with a dedicated CUDA kernel.

papers.title: SmartBloch-Agent: An Agentic Framework for Automated MRI Sequence Design and Optimization
papers.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences organize radiofrequency excitation, gradient encoding, and signal acquisition, determining magnetization evolution and image formation. Sequence research requires translating imaging objectives into executable protocols meeting physical and acquisition constraints, refined via physical simulation, signal reconstruction, and scientific evaluation. Sequence construction, physical verification, parameter search, and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, limiting automation from objective to verifiable sequence. We develop SmartBloch-Agent, an integrated framework for automated MRI sequence design and optimization. Given objectives and scientific constraints in natural language, an AI agent interprets goals, plans tasks, orchestrates tools, and makes feedback-informed decisions, drawing on a construction module and optimizers for structural design and parameter search. Our GPU-accelerated SmartBloch engine supplies physical computation for both stages, so the framework configures, per sequence and objective, event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction, and scientific evaluation, and closes the loop without external MRI simulators. Results return to the agent to guide sequence revision, parameter optimization, and candidate selection, and the design files carry simulation, reconstruction, and evaluation evidence, forming an output package for a real-scanner workflow. Experiments show the framework automatically designs and optimizes MRI sequences for varied objectives and constraints, refines candidates with physical feedback, and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction. SmartBloch-Agent unifies objectives, design, physical execution, and evaluation into a continuous workflow for end-to-end automation of MRI sequence research.
papers.summary: Designing magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences means turning imaging goals into executable protocols through many tools and manual steps, including construction, physical simulation, reconstruction and evaluation. `SmartBloch-Agent` takes goals and constraints stated in natural language and uses an AI agent to plan the work, call construction and optimization tools, and revise candidates based on feedback. A GPU-accelerated `SmartBloch` engine provides full-Bloch magnetization simulation, signal acquisition, reconstruction and evaluation, so the loop **closes without any external MRI simulator**. Experiments show the agent designs and optimizes sequences for varied objectives and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction.

papers.title: Typed-Centrality Grounding for Agentic GraphRAG: A Symbolic Approach for Agentic Reasoning
papers.abstract:
Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) represent two approaches for knowledge representation and reasoning over heterogeneous data. Recent research has explored their integration through Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) systems, which use KGs to provide structured context to LLMs. However, existing GraphRAG approaches treat KGs as homogeneous graphs and rely on textual similarity between the input prompt and the context, rather than using it as a source of deterministic knowledge.
  This work proposes an agent-based GraphRAG system that introduces a symbolic layer to integrate deterministic reasoning alongside text similarities. This approach is based on the definition of typed centralities for KGs, where centrality measures are computed separately for each specific KG's class. This information is used to construct a symbolic representation that is provided to the LLM as a deterministic source. The proposed system was mathematically validated and evaluated on a real-world POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset, comparing reasoning and information retrieval with and without the symbolic layer. The results indicate that the our approach leads to responses that are more consistent with the context, improving the generated outputs.
papers.summary: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) systems usually treat a knowledge graph as a homogeneous graph and select context by textual similarity, rather than using the graph as a source of deterministic knowledge. The proposed agent-based system adds a symbolic layer built on **typed centralities**, meaning centrality measures computed separately for each class of node in the graph. The result is passed to the LLM as deterministic context alongside the retrieved text. On a real-world `POLE` (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset, adding the symbolic layer made responses more consistent with the underlying context.

papers.title: Future-Informed Actor-Critic
papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods optimize a parametrized policy using a critic to estimate their policy gradient. Recent work has shown that conditioning the critic on features of future states, actions, or rewards can improve sample efficiency and even final return. However, existing methods are restricted to exogenous features (independent of actions), overlooking endogenous features (dependent on actions) that may be crucial for credit assignment. We introduce the future-informed value function, which can be conditioned on both exogenous and endogenous features of future states, actions, and rewards. Then, we express the policy gradient using this value function, yielding the future-informed policy gradient. Building on that, we propose the future-informed actor-critic algorithm. Empirical results show that this algorithm leveraging endogenous features of the future outperforms standard actor-critic algorithms in environments with noisy and sparse rewards.
papers.summary: Earlier work showed that conditioning an actor-critic method's critic on features of the future can improve sample efficiency, but only for exogenous features, which do not depend on the agent's actions. The authors define a future-informed value function that can also condition on endogenous features of future states, actions and rewards, which are often the ones that matter for credit assignment. They derive the matching policy gradient and build a future-informed actor-critic algorithm on it. Empirically, the method **outperforms standard actor-critic algorithms in environments with noisy and sparse rewards**.

papers.title: Agentic AI for Healthcare Claim Denial Analysis: A Policy-Grounded Framework for Privacy Preservation
papers.abstract: In the healthcare sector, claim denials impose significant financial and administrative burdens, emphasizing the need for automated and trustworthy decision-support systems. This paper proposes a modular Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework for healthcare claim denial analysis, integrating specialized agents for denial risk prediction, risk factor identification, diagnosis-procedure-medication code relationship analysis, and counterfactual analysis. The framework integrates predictive analytics, graph-based learning, a Hybrid Contextual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in healthcare policy documents, and a dedicated HIPAA Compliance Agent to support privacy protection. Evaluated on a synthetic healthcare claims dataset, the framework achieved 98% traceability of reported numerical findings, validated 214 of 216 policy citations, and removed all 280 identified sensitive identifiers without modifying the underlying analysis. These findings pave the way for further research into Agentic AI as a framework for explainable, policy-aware, and privacy-preserving healthcare claim denial management.
papers.summary: Healthcare claim denials are costly, which motivates automated decision support that can be traced and audited. The proposed modular agentic system combines agents for denial-risk prediction, risk-factor identification, analysis of diagnosis-procedure-medication code relationships, and counterfactual analysis. It also uses a hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in policy documents and a dedicated agent for compliance with HIPAA, the US health-privacy law. On a synthetic claims dataset, 98% of reported numerical findings were traceable, 214 of 216 policy citations validated, and **all 280 sensitive identifiers were removed** without altering the analysis.

papers.title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as \texttt{BF16} and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama~3.1~8B~Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52$\times$ and 1.48$\times$ over the fastest baseline on an RTX~4060~Ti and an RTX~5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43~bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.
papers.summary: Generating one token at a time for a single user is memory-bound, because every weight must be read from memory for each token, and local or low-latency deployments cannot batch requests to hide this. `MINE` (Memory-efficient INference Engine) applies lossless entropy coding to model weights with `dtANS-LLM`, a GPU decoder that exploits the skewed weight distribution that remains even after quantization. Per-tensor, per-GPU auto-tuning picks the best trade-off between compression ratio and decoding cost, and the system plugs into `vLLM`. On `Llama 3.1 8B Instruct` with a 2.1-bit `EntQuant` checkpoint, it runs **2.52x faster than the fastest baseline on a consumer RTX 4060 Ti** and 1.48x faster on an RTX 5090.

papers.title: DexDICE: Reconciling Safety and Performance via Dual-Expert Offline Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Ensuring high returns while providing strong safety guarantees in offline imitation learning (IL) is a fundamental challenge: existing approaches either rely on explicitly specified cost functions, which are difficult to design for complex real-world safety constraints, or require expert demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, which are often too costly to collect. We introduce dual-expert imitation learning, which leverages two complementary data sources: (i) safety-compliant demonstrations that faithfully follow safety guidelines but may be suboptimal, and (ii) performance-oriented demonstrations that achieve high returns but may violate safety guidelines. To address this problem, we propose DexDICE (Dual-expert offline imitation learning via stationary DIstribution Correction Estimation). Instead of conventional distribution constraints, DexDICE combines DICE-style offline learning with safe support constraints, enabling agents to exploit high-return behaviors while remaining within safety-compliant regions. We prove that the ideal solution satisfying this constraint exactly has zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability. We evaluate DexDICE on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and validate it on a real-world mobile-robot navigation task trained directly from human teleoperation demonstrations, where it substantially outperforms baselines and remains robust to data scarcity and quality degradation.
papers.summary: Safe offline imitation learning usually needs either hand-designed cost functions or demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, and the latter are expensive to collect. Dual-expert imitation learning instead combines safety-compliant but possibly suboptimal demonstrations with high-return demonstrations that may break safety rules. `DexDICE` pairs stationary distribution correction estimation (DICE)-style offline learning with a constraint that keeps the policy within the support of the safe data. The authors prove that an exact solution has **zero visitation of unsafe regions with high probability**. It outperforms baselines on a re-curated `DSRL` benchmark and on a real mobile-robot navigation task learned from human teleoperation.

papers.title: Logit Laundering: Evading Data-Use Auditing in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.
papers.summary: Data-use auditing checks whether a large language model (LLM) was trained on a given dataset, typically by watermarking the data and detecting the watermark in model outputs, but little work has examined how a provider might deliberately evade it. `Logit Laundering` is an inference-time attack that leaves model weights unchanged and reshapes output logits to suppress the statistical signals the watermark leaves behind. A plug-in bias estimator drives the suppression, and a confidence-aware scaling module adjusts its strength based on how certain the next-token prediction is, to limit damage to the model's usefulness. Experiments show it **evades a range of state-of-the-art auditing methods while preserving downstream task performance**.

papers.title: Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Policy entropy is widely used to diagnose exploration and collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), yet its magnitude does not consistently track reasoning performance across optimization objectives. We argue that this ambiguity arises because global token entropy conflates uncertainty in successful and failed trajectories, diversity across correct solution strategies, and variation among realizations of the same strategy. We introduce \textbf{Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation (RCEA)}, a hierarchical diagnostic framework that separates complete-trajectory entropy from average token entropy, conditions uncertainty on verifier outcome and process validity, measures correct-solution-mode retention, and connects these population-level quantities to local covariance-driven updates. In controlled sweeps over six RLVR objectives at two model scales, entropy trajectories do not induce a stable ordering of reasoning accuracy. Token entropy is higher for verifier-failed than successful trajectories under both broad separately aggregated estimates and a common-question paired analysis, whose confidence intervals exclude equality at 10 of 12 displayed endpoints. A local covariance approximation predicts the direction of adjacent-checkpoint entropy change in 95.5\% of nonfailed transitions; a reward-stratified endpoint proxy further shows that positive chosen-token covariance is more tail-concentrated within failed prefixes. Every reportable trained endpoint exhibits some contraction in independently audited correct-solution-mode breadth, whose positive association with large-\(k\) coverage remains exploratory. These results show that entropy collapse should be diagnosed by which uncertainty is removed, rather than by global entropy alone.
papers.summary: Policy entropy is a common diagnostic for exploration and collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), yet its magnitude does not reliably track reasoning performance. `RCEA` (Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation) breaks entropy down by whether a trajectory passed the verifier and whether its reasoning process was valid, tracks how many distinct correct solution strategies the model retains, and links these to local covariance-driven updates. Across six RLVR objectives at two model scales, entropy trajectories do not consistently rank methods by accuracy, and token entropy is higher in failed trajectories than in successful ones. A local covariance approximation **predicts the direction of entropy change in 95.5% of transitions**, and every trained model loses some breadth of correct solution strategies, which suggests collapse should be diagnosed by which uncertainty disappears rather than by global entropy.

papers.title: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
papers.abstract: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.
papers.summary: Agent skill documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (`LoRA`) to save context, which keeps the behaviour but makes the skill hard to read, audit or move to another model. The authors test whether the text can be recovered: reading the weights directly recovers almost nothing, but the `Executing Writer`, a small writer that runs on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of key instructions and restores 85-91% of the original task gain for adapters trained on the document. Adapters trained only on behaviour are much harder to invert. For those, an agent that compares the base and adapted models' outputs writes skills that recover 58-71% of the gain on `ALFWorld` and transfer to models that cannot load the adapter, **lifting `Llama-3.1-8B` from 5% to 55%**.

papers.title: Definitions, Label Names, or Demonstrations? Auditing What Governs LLM Annotation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate social-science texts, but high accuracy does not establish that they apply researcher-supplied category definitions: predictions may instead reflect prior associations with category labels or labeled demonstrations. We introduce a counterfactual audit that reassigns definitions among output labels, distinguishing adherence to supplied definitions from preservation of a dataset's original mapping. Across three political-text datasets, models rarely follow reassigned definitions, and standard fine-tuning strengthens the original mapping without reliably increasing definition adherence. We then study retrieval-augmented annotation. Retrieving the nearest training examples generally outperforms retrieving examples separately within each category despite using fewer demonstrations. On the two tasks with substantial gains, direct \(k\)-nearest-neighbor classification recovers 74--93\% of the improvement, indicating that neighborhood labels provide much of the predictive signal. Relabeling fixed demonstrations redirects predictions, whereas aligning demonstrations with reassigned definitions substantially increases adherence to the new mapping. Thus, accuracy-improving interventions need not increase codebook adherence; definitions, category labels, demonstrations, retrieval, and training data should be aligned and validated jointly.
papers.summary: When large language models (LLMs) annotate social-science text, high accuracy does not show that they are applying the category definitions researchers supply. A counterfactual audit tests this by swapping definitions between labels. Across three political-text datasets, models **rarely follow the reassigned definitions**, and fine-tuning strengthens the original label mapping rather than adherence to the definitions. Retrieving nearest-neighbour examples improves accuracy, but plain `k-nearest-neighbor` classification recovers 74-93% of that gain, which indicates the neighbours' labels carry most of the signal. The authors conclude that definitions, labels, demonstrations, retrieval and training data need to be aligned and validated together.

papers.title: Consensus-Constrained Dual-Federated Optimization with Client-Side Dynamic Weighting for Distributed Android Device Threat Defense
papers.abstract: Smartphones, smart-home hubs, and wearables are increasingly exposed to sophisticated Android malware, while centralized threat-detection pipelines raise privacy and scalability concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without collecting raw client data, but partial participation and variation in local model quality can destabilize global optimization. In this article, we propose DW-FedADMM, a federated optimization framework that combines primal-dual coordination with performance-dependent client-side weighting. The dynamic coefficient modulates each participating client's local state before the augmented-Lagrangian update, while the dual variables regulate disagreement between local and global model states. We evaluate DW-FedADMM on three Android malware benchmarks, namely Drebin, Malgenome, and TUANDROMD, with 5, 10, and 15 clients holding IID data shards, partial client participation, and communication budgets of 5 and 10 rounds. Each configuration is repeated with ten random seeds. DW-FedADMM obtains the highest seed-averaged accuracy on Drebin (97.64% +/- 0.20%) and the best mean accuracy in 9 of the 18 dataset-client-round configurations, including 7 of the 9 configurations with a 10-round budget. Pooled over all configurations, it reaches 95.42% accuracy, 94.62% F1-score, 96.06% precision, and 99.45% AUC, compared with 95.32%, 94.51%, 95.56%, and 99.41% for FedADMM, while also giving the lowest mean false-positive rate and the smallest client update norm among the six compared methods. Both primal-dual methods are well ahead of the averaging- and proximal-based baselines on Malgenome and TUANDROMD, where the latter often remain at the majority-class solution when clients are fragmented. The gain of dynamic weighting over FedADMM is most pronounced on Drebin and with the longer communication budget, where it also reduces the variation across seeds.
papers.summary: Detecting Android malware with federated learning avoids collecting raw user data, but partial client participation and uneven local model quality can destabilize training. `DW-FedADMM` combines primal-dual coordination based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) with dynamic, performance-based weighting of each client before the global update. Across the `Drebin`, `Malgenome` and `TUANDROMD` benchmarks with 5 to 15 clients and ten random seeds, it reaches **97.64% accuracy on `Drebin`** and the best mean accuracy in 9 of 18 configurations. It also gives the lowest false-positive rate, although its pooled gains over plain `FedADMM` are small.

papers.title: ENGRAM: From Agent Experience to Weights through Verified Consolidation
papers.abstract: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.
papers.summary: Language-model agents can use past experience through retrieval or by training it into their weights, but consolidating experience into weights raises two questions: which experiences to train on, and when the stored records can be dropped from retrieval. `ENGRAM` separates these decisions. It admits a skill for training based on the student model's mastery or on enough successful teacher demonstrations, and releases the skill's stored records only after a verification gate. That gate checks that the updated model without retrieval matches the base model with retrieval on held-out probes. Across interactive and reasoning benchmarks, it beats frozen-weight controls, and verified release **substantially shrinks the retrievable memory while staying close to retain-all performance**, with fewer input tokens and model calls.

papers.title: LEMMO: A Large Electromagnetic Model leveraging Pretrained LLMs for Million-Sample Signal Understanding
papers.abstract: Large language models have expanded beyond text to vision, audio, and other modalities, but understanding raw electromagnetic (EM) signals remains challenging. Wideband recordings can contain millions of samples, whereas existing waveform-based EM models are primarily evaluated on short in-phase and quadrature (IQ) segments, leaving long-recording understanding and detailed description insufficiently explored. We introduce LEMMO, a large EM model for instruction-driven recognition and description of long raw IQ recordings. LEMMO combines a linear-attention EM encoder with anti-aliased temporal resampling to process up to eight million complex samples. Its EM-text interaction module conditions learnable queries on instructions before retrieving signal evidence. Compact queries support recognition, while structured queries with auxiliary factual supervision organize scene-level properties, signal attributes, and cross-signal relationships for detailed description. We also construct and release a unified 1.38-TB corpus of real-world and synthetic EM signals, including LEMMO-ShortQA and LEMMO-LongDesc. Compared with MERLIN-LoRA, LEMMO improves mean EM-Bench perception accuracy by 15.77 %, mean strategy-generation ROUGE-L F1 by 4.38 points, and mean LEMMO-ShortQA accuracy by 14.31 %. It also improves categorical and numerical fact F1 on both LEMMO-LongDesc tasks while preserving its language backbone's MMLU performance. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/N1rv4n4/LEMMO and https://huggingface.co/datasets/DaftJun/RFLAS, respectively.
papers.summary: Existing models of raw electromagnetic (EM) signals handle only short in-phase and quadrature (IQ) segments, while wideband recordings can contain millions of samples. `LEMMO` pairs a linear-attention EM encoder with anti-aliased resampling to handle **up to eight million complex samples**, and uses instruction-conditioned queries to pull signal evidence for both recognition and detailed scene description. The authors also release a 1.38-TB corpus of real and synthetic EM signals, including the `LEMMO-ShortQA` and `LEMMO-LongDesc` benchmarks. Compared with `MERLIN-LoRA`, `LEMMO` improves `EM-Bench` perception accuracy by 15.77% and `LEMMO-ShortQA` accuracy by 14.31% while keeping its language backbone's `MMLU` performance.

papers.title: An Effective Spoken Language Understanding Approach Leveraging Query-Adaptive Intent Detection
papers.abstract: Large language models enable fine-tuning-free spoken language understanding (SLU) through in-context learning, but direct query-based retrieval may select semantically similar yet intent irrelevant demonstrations. This paper presents Query-Adaptive Intent Detection via Prototype Extraction (APEX), a two-stage retrieval framework that first selects candidate intents using intent-level prototypes and then retrieves contextual exemplars within the selected intent space. Experiments on the SLURP dataset evaluate joint SLU performance using Exact Match Accuracy (EMA) under full-transcript and perplexity-stratified conditions, with additional retrieval analysis on ASR-generated transcripts. Compared with query-based retrieval, APEX improves EMA by 4.34 and 3.97 percentage points with Qwen3 4B and Gemma-3-4B, respectively, on full transcripts. Under high-perplexity inputs, APEX also yields EMA gains of 7.66 and 2.13 percentage points. Retrieval analysis further indicates that prototype-guided candidate selection achieves higher ground truth intent coverage across multiple input conditions.
papers.summary: Large language models can perform spoken language understanding (SLU) without fine-tuning by using in-context examples, but retrieving examples by query similarity can pick ones that sound alike yet carry the wrong intent. `APEX` uses two-stage retrieval: it first picks candidate intents using intent-level prototypes, then retrieves examples only from within those intents. On the `SLURP` dataset, it **raises exact-match accuracy by 4.34 and 3.97 percentage points** with `Qwen3 4B` and `Gemma-3-4B`, and by up to 7.66 points on high-perplexity inputs. Prototype-guided selection also more often includes the correct intent among its candidates, including on speech-recognition transcripts.

papers.title: FusionCLIP: Multimodal Contrastive Pretraining for Fusion Plasma Diagnostics
papers.abstract: Visible-light videos and multivariate diagnostic signals provide complementary observations of tokamak discharges. However, existing fusion pretraining methods, primarily learn representations by reconstructing or predicting observations, leaving the correspondence between these modalities underexplored. Representation learning is further challenged by the fact that plasma-related regions occupy only part of each video frame and diagnostic variables have substantially different sampling rates. We propose FusionCLIP, a multimodal contrastive pretraining framework. Spatiotemporal Stability Selection retains informative visual tokens, while a Temporal Query Encoder integrates asynchronous diagnostic signals using their observation timestamps. Contrastive learning then aligns the two modality representations. We construct EAST Multimodal Diagnostics (EAST-MMD), comprising 1307 EAST discharges, and evaluate the model on three independently fine-tuned tasks: disruption prediction, edge-localized mode (ELM) classification, and $H_{98}$ regression. FusionCLIP achieves an aggregate score of 89.07\%, exceeding the best general-purpose pretraining configuration and an in-domain contrastive pretraining configuration without Spatiotemporal Stability Selection by 6.27 and 2.12 percentage points, respectively. Ablations and attention visualizations further support the contributions of its key components.
papers.summary: Pretraining for fusion-plasma diagnostics has focused on reconstructing or predicting observations, rather than aligning visible-light video with multivariate diagnostic signals from tokamak experiments. `FusionCLIP` uses contrastive learning to align the two. A stability-based selection step keeps only informative video tokens, and a timestamp-aware query encoder merges diagnostic signals sampled at different rates. On the new `EAST-MMD` dataset of 1,307 discharges from the `EAST` tokamak, it reaches an **aggregate score of 89.07%** across disruption prediction, edge-localized mode (ELM) classification and H98 regression, 6.27 points above the best general-purpose pretraining.

papers.title: Mosaic:montage-agnostic self-distilled graph learning for subject-independent ieeg seizure detection
papers.abstract: Intracranial EEG provides high signal-to-noise ratio and spatial resolution for detecting epileptic activity, but patient-specific electrode placement leads to substantial variation in channel count and montage across subjects. This heterogeneity limits the generalization of existing detectors under subject-independent evaluation. We propose MOSAIC (MOntage-agnostic Self-distilled Adaptive Inter-channel Connectivity learning), a lightweight graph-learning framework for subject-independent iEEG seizure detection. MOSAIC pairs a shared convolutional channel encoder with a patient-agnostic channel-attention module that infers a weighted inter-channel adjacency matrix from the encoded features, requiring no fixed montage graph. An exponential moving average self-distillation objective regularizes each prediction toward a slowly updated per-patient teacher. Across four public iEEG corpora (SWEC-ETHZ long- and short-term, Mayo, FNUSA), MOSAIC outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in F2 and Cohen's $\kappa$ while learning more stable inter-channel adjacencies, demonstrating that self-distilled connectivity learning transfers across unseen implantations.
papers.summary: Seizure detectors for intracranial EEG (iEEG) generalize poorly across patients, because electrode count and placement differ from person to person. `MOSAIC` encodes each channel with a shared convolutional encoder and uses patient-agnostic channel attention to infer the connections between channels, so it needs no fixed electrode layout. An exponential-moving-average self-distillation objective regularizes training. Across four public iEEG datasets (`SWEC-ETHZ` long- and short-term, `Mayo`, `FNUSA`), it **outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on F2 and Cohen's kappa** in subject-independent evaluation and learns more stable inter-channel connectivity.

papers.title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
papers.abstract: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.
papers.summary: Lloyd's `k-means` algorithm remains the standard for clustering in retrieval, quantization and data curation, but it is slow on very large embedding datasets. `e-means` replaces it with mini-batch exponential-moving-average updates and uses empirical scaling laws to set the decay rate and batch size without hyperparameter sweeps. Across many embedding datasets, it beats the loss Lloyd's `k-means` reaches after 25 epochs within 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, a **10-45x GPU wall-clock speedup** over state-of-the-art implementations, and often beats `k-means++`. It clusters `DINO10B`, a set of 10 billion `DINO` embeddings, into 16 million clusters in 2.5 epochs.

papers.title: TimeOmni-Live: Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding with Long-Term Memory
papers.abstract: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
papers.summary: Most time series language models process fixed-length inputs one at a time and keep no state between them, which does not suit streaming applications that need reasoning across windows. The authors define Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (`CL-TSU`) and release `LiveTS-Suite`, which covers 18 tasks with over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, plus an evaluation protocol that scores timeliness, accuracy, and efficiency together. Their 4B-parameter model, `TimeOmni-Live`, combines hybrid time series encoding, a stream-persistent hybrid memory, and an elastic synchronization strategy that reduces processing lag. It scores **90.0 versus 79.3 for `Opus 5`**, achieves 206x lower p95 latency than its backbone, and runs in real time on a `Jetson` edge device.

papers.title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.
papers.summary: Automatic image-captioning metrics usually return a single score with no indication of how reliable it is, which is a problem under ambiguous inputs or domain shift. `BEiTScore++` extends the `BEiTScore` metric with conformalized quantile regression, so a single forward pass produces both an alignment score and a calibrated confidence interval over human judgments. Across several human-rated benchmarks it keeps the ranking correlation of the original metric, and **its interval widths track prediction error more closely than `Monte Carlo dropout`** on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows on degraded images and on out-of-domain artwork.

papers.title: On the Effectiveness and Limitations of Open-Weight LLMs for Low-Resource Offensive Language Detection in Danish
papers.abstract: We study the effectiveness and robustness of open-weight large language models (LLMs) for Danish offensive language detection, an underexplored low-resource task. We evaluate four model families (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen) across eleven prompting strategies spanning five design categories, cross-prompt generalization, Danish orthographic variation, and robustness under balanced and naturally imbalanced class distributions. We compare against three BERT-family baselines with distinct pre-training strategies, evaluated via both masked language model prompting and supervised fine-tuning. Even without task-specific fine-tuning, LLMs can surpass all three fine-tuned BERT baselines, and lightweight finetuning yields substantial further gains. No single model or prompt category dominates, underscoring that prompt design interacts with model pre-training in ways that cannot be predicted a priori. Semantically grounded prompts transfer more robustly, while format-constrained patterns consistently fail to generalize. ASCII transliteration of Danish-specific characters ({\ae}, {\o}, {\aa}) generally degrades performance, indicating these characters encode meaningful signal. At the same time, the gap between a balanced test set (best F1 of 0.84) and the corpus's natural class skew (0.62 trained on skewed data, 0.70 trained on balanced data) -- relative drops of 26.2\% and 16.7\% -- shows that class imbalance remains a critical open challenge. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/PASHAADC/Danish-LLM-HateSpeech.
papers.summary: The study tests open-weight large language models (LLMs) on detecting offensive language in Danish, a low-resource task. It evaluates the `Llama`, `Mistral`, `Gemma`, and `Qwen` families with eleven prompting strategies and compares them with three BERT-family baselines. Without task-specific fine-tuning, the LLMs can beat all three fine-tuned BERT baselines, and lightweight fine-tuning improves them further. No single model or prompt type wins everywhere, semantically grounded prompts transfer better than format-constrained ones, and replacing æ, ø, and å with ASCII generally hurts performance. Class imbalance remains the main open problem: **the best F1 of 0.84 on a balanced test set falls to 0.62–0.70 under the corpus's natural class skew**.

papers.title: V-STORM: A Structure-Aware Grounded Chain of Thought Dataset for Faithful and Fine-Grained Spatio-Temporal Video Reasoning
papers.abstract: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often recognize what happens in a video but struggle with fine-grained reasoning about when and where the supporting evidence appears. `V-STORM` turns videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and builds Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) annotations from validated evidence paths, so each reasoning step can be traced to specific evidence. With it, the authors build a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark. Experiments show that **current MLLMs can often locate the relevant cues but fail to combine them into correct multi-step reasoning**, a gap that answer-only evaluation hides. Fine-tuning on `V-STORM` improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.

papers.title: A Physics-Informed Learning Framework for Linking Microscopic Surface Degradation to Bolted Joint Functional Behavior
papers.abstract: Returned products in circular engineering often have heterogeneous degradation histories, making remaining function difficult to assess. For bolted joints, corrosion alters surface morphology, contact, friction, preload retention, and mechanical response. This paper presents a physics-informed multimodal framework for linking microscopic and camera-based degradation observations to functional indicators of corroded bolted joints. The workflow defines the corrosion failure mode, generates synchronized inspection and functional-response records, preprocesses image, roughness, exposure, and joint descriptors, aligns microscopy and camera observations through similarity learning, and constructs a calibrated corrosion-severity field. Partial differential equation (PDE) discovery is applied to this field to identify candidate effective mesoscale laws rather than complete electrochemical mechanisms. The corrosion-evolution model is coupled to a separate functional model, with friction coefficient as the primary target and preload loss included when clamp-force data are available. The contribution is a reproducible pathway for physically constrained assessment of degraded bolted-joint behavior.
papers.summary: In circular engineering, it is hard to judge how much function remains in returned bolted joints that have uneven corrosion histories. The proposed physics-informed multimodal workflow aligns microscopy and camera observations through similarity learning, builds a calibrated corrosion-severity field, and applies partial differential equation (PDE) discovery to find candidate effective mesoscale laws. This corrosion model is coupled to a functional model whose main target is **the friction coefficient**, with preload loss included when clamp-force data are available. The authors present the work as a reproducible pathway for physically constrained assessment rather than a complete electrochemical model.

papers.title: Benchmarking Speaker Embedders in the Sub-Second Regime for Real-Time Voice AI Agents
papers.abstract: Real-time Voice AI agents must separate the active user from intelligible background speech that survives conventional noise suppression. Background sources include television audio, family members, and colleagues. Production denoisers remove non-stationary environmental noise effectively. Background speech shares the spectral characteristics of the target and passes through, causing false acceptances in downstream speaker verification (SV) and automatic speech recognition (ASR). We benchmark open-source speaker embedders TitaNet-Large, TitaNet-Small, ECAPA-TDNN, CAM++, and SpeakerNet under a strict sub-second latency budget. Evaluation combines a controlled benchmark with a weighted human-annotated production set. Our controlled benchmark is built from real calls in which a second real speaker is injected into silence intervals at modulated amplitude. We report three findings. First, denoising before embedding is generally harmful and raises equal error rate (EER) across architectures. Second, truncating audio below the full voice-activity segment degrades every model. Third, roughly half of the TitaNet embedding is redundant for this task. Trailing dimensions encode population attributes such as language and gender. Such attributes carry little discriminative value in a demographically homogeneous user base. We distill these results into deployment guidance. Verification should run on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks. Thresholds should favor precision over F1. Truncated embeddings reduce the cost of similarity search.
papers.summary: Real-time voice AI agents have to tell the active user apart from background speech, such as a television or nearby people, that passes through noise suppression and causes false acceptances in speaker verification (SV) and automatic speech recognition (ASR). The authors benchmark open-source speaker embedders (`TitaNet-Large`, `TitaNet-Small`, `ECAPA-TDNN`, `CAM++`, `SpeakerNet`) under a sub-second latency budget. They use a controlled benchmark built by injecting a second real speaker into real calls, along with a human-annotated production set. They find that **denoising before embedding generally raises equal error rate (EER)**, that truncating audio below the full voice-activity segment hurts every model, and that about half of the `TitaNet` embedding is redundant for this task. From these results they recommend running verification on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks, choosing precision-favoring thresholds, and using truncated embeddings to make similarity search cheaper.

papers.title: Active Learning of Robust Models
papers.abstract: In many domains from species identification to cancer diagnosis, labelling data to train predictive models remains costly. In these settings, it is advantageous to intelligently select data points to label to achieve the maximum information gain, this is the motivation behind the study of active learning. In addition to the high costs of acquiring data in such domains, there is the added complexity of data distribution shifts that can occur between training and deployment. For example, the features of cancerous skin cells taken in one country may be different in another region of the world. These two challenges - efficient labelling of data, and learning models robust to distribution shifts have been studied separately but not together, even though these challenges often co-occur in real-life settings. We identify failure modes of standard active learning approaches when the distribution of data at deployment is different from the distribution in which the data is sampled for labelling. We propose a new strategy for efficiently learning classifiers that generalise under specific forms of distribution shift, namely subpopulation shift. Drawing on work in learning from heterogeneous data, we aim to train models that perform well across subpopulations of the data, through active learning. To handle this challenging setting, we exploit the fact that many datasets include metadata about data collection that can serve as a noisy proxy for each sample's underlying subpopulation. We demonstrate how to leverage these noisy labels during active learning selection, and demonstrate empirically that our approach improves classifier accuracy across subpopulations.
papers.summary: Active learning reduces labeling costs, and robust learning handles shifts between training and deployment data, but the two have mostly been studied separately even though they often occur together. The authors show how standard active learning fails when the deployment distribution differs from the one used to sample points for labeling. They propose a selection strategy aimed at subpopulation shift that uses data-collection metadata as a noisy stand-in for each sample's subpopulation. Experiments show **improved classifier accuracy across subpopulations** compared with standard active learning.

papers.title: Atik: A Shared-Mesh Transformer Accelerator for RISC-V
papers.abstract: Transformer inference repeatedly invokes dense matrix multiplication and attention, including its data-dependent softmax normalization. We present Atik, an open-source RoCC accelerator for RocketChip that executes matrix multiplication and dense attention through one shared fixed-point MAC mesh. Atik accepts and returns BF16 tensors, uses a streaming online-softmax schedule that never materializes the full score matrix, and is invoked through a small descriptor-based ABI. We evaluate three meshes cycle-by-cycle on FireSim and report standalone Sky130 physical-design area. Across 137 logged FireSim test records, all tests pass their benchmark tolerance with zero reported output mismatches. Relative to the same scalar Rocket BF16 reference, the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul speedup and 225.8x peak attention speedup. Hybrid projections for the single-layer workload-derived C models, using directly measured accelerator-kernel cycles, give aggregate speedups of 44.2x, 77.1x, and 32.3x for ViT, TinyBERT, and GPT-2 prefill, respectively; these are not full-model hardware replays.
papers.summary: `Atik` is an open-source accelerator for the `RocketChip` RISC-V platform that runs both matrix multiplication and dense attention on one shared fixed-point multiply-accumulate (MAC) mesh. It takes BF16 tensors and uses a streaming online-softmax schedule that never builds the full attention score matrix. In cycle-accurate `FireSim` evaluation, all 137 test records pass, and the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul speedup and **225.8x peak attention speedup** over a scalar Rocket BF16 baseline. Hybrid projections give aggregate speedups of 44.2x, 77.1x, and 32.3x for `ViT`, `TinyBERT`, and `GPT-2` prefill, though these are not full-model hardware runs.

papers.title: StockASkill: A Local-First AgentSkill for Intelligent Stock Selection
papers.abstract: Quantitative equity selection and portfolio construction in emerging and cross-border markets frequently suffer from computational bottlenecks, remote API fragility, survivorship bias, and rigid execution constraints such as discrete board lots and investor-mandated drawdown limits. In this paper, we present StockASkill, a local-first, full-data-driven AgentSkill engineered as a specialized Quant Co-Processor for autonomous AI agents and quantitative researchers. Tailored for agile portfolios (10^5 ~ 10^7 RMB) where discrete lot execution and capital protection are mandatory, StockASkill embeds a columnar DuckDB OLAP engine over 42.44 million historical price records and 186,432 financial disclosures spanning 26 years across China A-shares, Hong Kong, US equities, and ETFs. By eliminating ad-hoc network dependencies during analysis, StockASkill reduces cross-sectional screening latency across 5,400+ equities from over 25 seconds to sub-0.5 seconds (a 95%+ reduction). We formalize an end-to-end mathematical pipeline integrating a 7+1 factor alpha model, an SLSQP convex optimizer under smooth CVaR drawdown surrogates with exact path projection, dynamic 100-share board lot integer quantization, and an autonomous thesis lifecycle finite-state machine. Furthermore, we provide a zero-disk, strongly-typed JSON streaming interface designed for high-throughput LLM tool-calling. Open-sourced at https://github.com/axjing/stockaskill, comprehensive empirical benchmarks from 2018 to 2024 demonstrate that the architecture achieves annualized Sharpe ratios exceeding 1.48 and Calmar ratios up to 2.17, while reducing max drawdown by up to 85% relative to benchmark indices.
papers.summary: `StockASkill` is a local-first AgentSkill that gives AI agents a quantitative stock-selection and portfolio tool, aimed at small portfolios that must trade in whole board lots and stay within drawdown limits. It embeds a `DuckDB` analytics engine over 42 million price records and 186K financial disclosures covering 26 years of Chinese, Hong Kong, and US markets, which **cuts cross-sectional screening of 5,400+ equities from over 25 seconds to under 0.5 seconds**. The pipeline combines a 7+1 factor alpha model, an `SLSQP` optimizer with CVaR drawdown surrogates, board-lot integer quantization, and a typed JSON streaming interface for LLM tool calls. Backtests from 2018 to 2024 report annualized Sharpe ratios above 1.48 and up to 85% lower maximum drawdown than benchmark indices.

papers.title: PreForceVision: Physics-Guided Optical Estimation of Bolt Preload from Bolt-Head Deformation
papers.abstract: Bolt preload is a decisive functional quantity in bolted joints because it determines whether external loads are transmitted primarily through frictional clamping or directly through the bolt. Existing preload measurement techniques, including strain-gauge bolts, force washers, ultrasonic methods, and bolt-length measurements, are effective in certain applications but require additional hardware, coupling, calibration, or joint modifications. This limits their scalability for large numbers of standard fasteners and motivates a non-contact optical approach. This paper proposes PreForceVision, a physics-guided optical framework for estimating bolt preload from preload-induced surface deformation of the bolt-head front face. The method treats preload estimation as an inverse deformation-to-force problem, where deformation of the optically accessible bolt-head surface is extracted from reference-loaded image pairs and related to the internal preload state. Preliminary results for an M16 strength class 8.8 bolt show an approximately \SI{12}{\micro\meter} simulated head-face depression at \SI{90}{\kilo\newton}, strain-gauge measurements of comparable magnitude, and an optical 3D measured central depression of approximately \SIrange{10}{20}{\micro\meter}. The contribution is a physics-guided optical methodology combining controlled image-pair acquisition, DIC- or optical-flow-based deformation extraction, multimodal validation, and uncertainty-aware regression for rough preload estimation under controlled conditions.
papers.summary: Existing ways to measure bolt preload, such as strain-gauge bolts, force washers, and ultrasonic methods, need extra hardware or calibration, which makes them hard to scale. `PreForceVision` treats preload estimation as an inverse problem, recovering the clamping force from deformation of the bolt-head face extracted from reference-loaded image pairs with digital image correlation (DIC) or optical flow. Preliminary results for an M16 class 8.8 bolt show **a simulated head-face depression of about 12 micrometers at 90 kN**, consistent with strain-gauge readings and with optical 3D measurements of 10–20 micrometers. The method targets rough, uncertainty-aware preload estimation under controlled conditions.

papers.title: Graph representations of dislocation networks
papers.abstract: The mechanical response of a crystal is governed by the evolving network of dislocations it contains, yet quantitatively linking the `state of that network' to its yield stress remains challenging. Here we represent the dislocation networks obtained from discrete dislocation dynamic simulation as graphs, using five distinct graph representations, characterize each network through a compact set of topological properties, and predict the yield stress from these graph properties and the applied strain rate using a standard random forest model evaluated with strain rate stratified cross-validation. The model predicts the yield stress with $R^2\approx0.86-0.90$ across all box sizes and $R^2\approx0.91-0.94$ for larger box sizes, and this accuracy is consistent across all five representations, indicating that the topology-stress relationship is a robust feature of the graph properties rather than an artefact of any single graph representation. We propose graph topology as a compact and robust route for connecting the microstructural state of a dislocation network to its mechanical response in addition to established variables.
papers.summary: Linking the state of a crystal's dislocation network to its yield stress in quantitative terms remains difficult. The authors convert dislocation networks from discrete dislocation dynamics simulations into graphs using five different representations, summarize each with a small set of topological properties, and predict yield stress with a random forest. **The model reaches R² of about 0.86–0.90 across all box sizes and 0.91–0.94 for larger boxes**, with similar accuracy for every representation. This consistency suggests that the link between topology and stress is robust rather than an artifact of one graph encoding.

papers.title: Multimodal Training with Knowledge Traction for Video Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: The task of weakly supervised video anomaly detection is challenging. Existing approaches mainly model video frame features and determine whether anomalies are present based on their magnitudes. In this work, we propose a novel method that incorporates external knowledge into training to improve model performance, robustness, and generalization. We leverage textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) to establish prior information for the specific task, and employ dictionary learning to normalize and compress this information. Moreover, during experiments, we observed inconsistencies in the textual descriptions extracted from similar video frames by image caption models. To address this, we devise a method that leverages an LLM and auxiliary information to ensure consistency in the textual descriptions of similar frames within a video. Finally, we introduce a feature processing approach that incorporates prior knowledge and cross-modal attention mechanisms. This approach learns the relationships and characteristics among different modalities to construct more accurate and reliable feature representations, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.
papers.summary: Most weakly supervised video anomaly detection methods score frame features by their magnitude. This method adds external knowledge during training: textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) supply task priors, and dictionary learning normalizes and compresses them. Because image captioners describe similar frames inconsistently, an LLM with auxiliary information is used to make those descriptions consistent, and cross-modal attention fuses the prior knowledge with visual features. The authors report that **the method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches**.

papers.title: CID: Measuring Cognitive Work Through Semantic State Change
papers.abstract: Traditional information theory provides powerful tools for analyzing statistical properties of information but offers limited insight into meaning and semantic transformation. It has never been possible to quantify the meaning of an arbitrary piece of information. Large language models represent information as vectors embedded within high-dimensional semantic spaces, enabling meaning to be analyzed geometrically. This paper defines semantic state as the vector representation of information within a model's semantic space and defines cognitive work as the transformation between semantic states, movement through semantic space. To quantify this transformation, we introduce the Contextual Information Differential (CID), a covariance-aware metric based on Mahalanobis distance measuring semantic displacement relative to the structure of the embedding manifold. By treating meaning as a geometric property of semantic space, CID provides a practical method for measuring semantic change, cognitive transformation, and information processing. This framework establishes a foundation for analyzing cognitive processing, learning, reasoning, knowledge generation, synthetic expertise, and human/AI collaboration through implementation-independent measurement of semantic state change in both human and artificial systems.
papers.summary: Classical information theory describes the statistical properties of information but not its meaning or how meaning changes. The author defines semantic state as a vector in a language model's embedding space and cognitive work as movement between such states. To measure that movement, they introduce the **Contextual Information Differential (`CID`), a covariance-aware metric based on Mahalanobis distance** that accounts for the shape of the embedding manifold. The framework is proposed for measuring semantic change in both human and artificial systems.

papers.title: Marginal-Nonuniform Multiclass Learning
papers.abstract: We study the problem of multiclass classification within the framework of marginal-nonuniform learning, where the constants in the learning rate may depend on the unknown marginal distribution generating the unlabeled data, but not on the target concept. This notion naturally lies between classical PAC learning, where the constants are independent of both the marginal distribution and the target concept, and more recent universal learning, where the constants may depend on both. We give a complete characterization of the optimal marginal-nonuniform learning rates, establishing a fundamental trichotomy: exponential, linear, and arbitrarily slow rates. This characterization is witnessed by a new combinatorial dimension, termed the uncentered DS-eluder dimension. A key ingredient in the upper-bound proofs is a set of new distributional exhaustion lemmas that exploit the sequential nature of this dimension and may be of independent interest.
papers.summary: The work studies multiclass classification under marginal-nonuniform learning, a middle ground between PAC learning and universal learning in which rate constants may depend on the unknown marginal distribution but not on the target concept. The authors fully characterize the optimal learning rates and show **a trichotomy of exponential, linear, and arbitrarily slow rates**. A new combinatorial measure, the uncentered DS-eluder dimension, determines which case applies, and the upper-bound proofs rely on new distributional exhaustion lemmas.

papers.title: CoMoFlow: Controllable Protein Conformational Ensemble Generation via Explicit Collective-Mode Modeling
papers.abstract: Protein conformational ensemble generation aims to efficiently characterize the structural variations accessible to a protein beyond a single static structure. Recent flow-based methods efficiently generate conformational ensembles, but they model coordinated structural variation implicitly, which can limit ensemble fidelity and hinder direct control. To address this limitation, we propose CoMoFlow, a controllable framework for generating protein backbone conformational ensembles by explicitly modeling collective variation. CoMoFlow constructs protein-specific collective modes from the equilibrium structure, learns the distribution of their coefficients across the molecular dynamics (MD) ensemble, and uses sampled collective variations to guide SE(3) flow matching through feature conditioning and prior recentering. Experiments on ATLAS and de novo proteins show that CoMoFlow improves reconstruction of MD conformational distributions and coordinated structural variation relative to strong flow-based baselines, while enabling direct control over targeted conformational changes.
papers.summary: Flow-based generators of protein conformational ensembles capture coordinated structural motion only implicitly, which can reduce fidelity and makes the output hard to control. `CoMoFlow` builds protein-specific collective modes from the equilibrium structure, learns how their coefficients are distributed across molecular dynamics (MD) ensembles, and uses sampled variations to guide SE(3) flow matching. On `ATLAS` and de novo proteins, it **reconstructs MD conformational distributions and coordinated variation better than strong flow-based baselines**, and it allows direct control over targeted conformational changes.

papers.title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
papers.abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.
papers.summary: Long-context language models often overlook information in the middle of their input, partly because rotary position embedding (`RoPE`) weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. `QGPM` (Query-Guided Positional Modulation) is a training-free method that uses query relevance from the model's own attention heads to reshape RoPE positions, with broad relevance maps in lower layers and sharp ones in upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, which pulls relevant evidence closer to the query, while slow-rotating planes keep the original layout. On `NoLiMa` and `RULER` it improves over base models and strong baselines across several backbones, with **the largest gains on retrieval tasks**.

papers.title: Optimal Regret for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade
papers.abstract: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.
