papers.summary: In repeated bilateral trade, an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer, earns the difference if both accept, and observes only whether the trade happened. The authors design an algorithm with **regret of Õ(T^{2/3}) against the best fixed pair of prices**, matching the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing up to logarithmic factors. Learning both sides of the market is therefore no harder than learning one, which raises the question of whether this lack of a dimensionality penalty holds in higher dimensions.

papers.title: Solver-Free Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Edge Selection
papers.abstract: Decision-focused learning trains prediction models to improve downstream decisions, but many methods require costly solver calls or optimal-solution labels. We propose a solver-free decision-focused learning framework for NP-hard edge-selection problems with uncertain parameters in the objective, the constraints, or both. A neural optimization layer is first trained without solution labels, using problem objectives and constraint penalties. Graph-informed edge scoring and iterative refinement encourage concentrated and structurally consistent continuous decisions. The layer is then frozen, and a prediction model is trained through its continuous output using a problem-specific loss evaluated under observed parameters. At deployment, the predictor, optimization layer, and a lightweight decoder produce decisions without solving the original NP-hard problem. Experiments on the asymmetric traveling salesperson and endpoint-free orienteering problems show consistently better decision quality than prediction-focused learning and improvements over most evaluated decision-focused baselines. Our framework requires less training time than the evaluated decision-focused baselines, even when optimization-layer pretraining is included. Neural deployment also produces decisions faster than solver-based deployment, offering a better quality-efficiency trade-off. The layer also reduces training cost in existing decision-focused methods when used as an approximate optimization oracle.
papers.summary: Decision-focused learning trains predictors to improve downstream decisions, but most methods need expensive solver calls or optimal-solution labels. This framework first trains a neural optimization layer without labels, using problem objectives and constraint penalties, then freezes it and trains the predictor through the layer's continuous output, so NP-hard edge-selection problems never need to be solved exactly. On asymmetric traveling salesperson and endpoint-free orienteering problems, it **beats prediction-focused learning and most decision-focused baselines while needing less training time**, and it produces decisions faster than solver-based deployment.

papers.title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates
papers.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.
papers.summary: Machine-learning surrogates for computational fluid dynamics lack benchmarks with realistic, time-dependent turbulence. `TurtLES` is a **14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes** produced by high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations, with 400 trajectories of 400 steps each and 3–11 million points per frame, varying geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Benchmarking state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts reveals temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and difficulty learning on large irregular meshes.

papers.title: Alignment by Confident Debate: Preference Learning from Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Post-training language models for reasoning typically rely on gold answers, task-specific verifiers, or learned reward models, limiting scalability when such signals are scarce. Multi-agent debate offers a self-supervised alternative, but converting debate into reliable training supervision remains challenging: majority voting weights agreeing responses equally, lacks a principled tie-breaking rule, and is ill-defined for open-ended tasks without a canonical answer; likelihood-based scoring can conflate fluency with correctness; and homogeneous committees may reinforce correlated errors. We introduce Alignment by Confident Debate (AbCD), which converts debate traces into preference data without gold answer labels. A sampling-diverse committee debates each problem, after which final answers are clustered by task-level semantic equivalence. We use verifiable tasks (mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice quantitative QA, and executable code-generation) as a controlled test bed: their answer keys or executable checkers let us evaluate the quality of debate-derived supervision against ground truth, even though the oracle itself never uses gold labels. Post-training on the resulting preferences outperforms inference-only ensembling and debate, as well as SFT on the same traces, across five model families spanning 1B to 8B parameters and four datasets, improving consensus accuracy, with a maximum gain of $21.5_{pp}$. Ablations show that the approach transfers to a larger model and to code generation, while also revealing limitations of heterogeneous committees and agreement-based weighting. Overall, the results suggest that debate traces can yield useful preference supervision when answer equivalence is combined with confidence-weighted disagreement.
papers.summary: Post-training language models for reasoning usually requires gold answers, verifiers, or reward models, which are scarce for many tasks. Alignment by Confident Debate (`AbCD`) has a committee of sampling-diverse agents debate each problem, groups the final answers by semantic equivalence, and turns confidence-weighted disagreement into preference data without gold labels. On math, quantitative multiple-choice, and code-generation tasks, it beats inference-only ensembling, debate alone, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the same traces across five model families from 1B to 8B parameters, with **a maximum gain of 21.5 percentage points**. Ablations show that the approach transfers to a larger model and to code generation, and they also expose limitations of heterogeneous committees and agreement-based weighting.

papers.title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
papers.abstract: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.
papers.summary: AI weather prediction models are released and run in 32-bit floating point (fp32), even though current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. The authors run five public models (`Aurora`, `Pangu-Weather`, `FourCastNet`, `SFNO` and `FastNet`) on a single 16 GB GPU, keeping the physical state and its normalisation in fp32 while running the network in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against `ERA5`. Running the network in fp16 changes global RMSE by **at most 1.4%** (under about 0.5% for four of the five models), while 10-day forecasts run 1.3 to 3.5 times faster and use 1.4 to 3.7 times less energy. Converting the whole model, state included, causes overflow in fp16 and information loss in bf16; bf16 is less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.

papers.title: Coordinatewise Epsilon for Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
papers.abstract: Adam estimates second moments coordinatewise, but typically adds the same scalar $\varepsilon$ to every denominator. We study how this shared $\varepsilon$ affects convergence when noise and curvature vary across coordinates. Under coordinatewise finite-$p$ noise moments, $p\in(1,2]$, choosing $\varepsilon_i$ from the noise and curvature bounds for each coordinate attains the heavy-tailed $\ell_1$-stationarity benchmark $O(T^{-\frac{p-1}{3p-2}})$, matching the known optimal time exponent for smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization. For $1<p<2$, Adam with a shared $\varepsilon_t$ admits a lower bound of order $\Omega(T^{-\frac{p-1}{2p}})$. This lower bound holds for every predictable scalar choice of $\eta_t$, $\beta_{1,t}$, $\beta_{2,t}$, and $\varepsilon_t$, precluding a dimension-uniform benchmark rate for this class.
papers.summary: `Adam` estimates second moments separately for each coordinate but usually adds the same scalar epsilon to every denominator. The authors analyze how this shared epsilon affects convergence under heavy-tailed gradient noise that varies across coordinates, where noise has only finite p-th moments for p between 1 and 2. Choosing a separate epsilon for each coordinate, based on that coordinate's noise and curvature bounds, attains the known optimal convergence rate for smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization. In contrast, they prove a lower bound showing that **no choice of shared scalar epsilon, step size or momentum schedule can reach a dimension-uniform optimal rate** when p is below 2.

papers.title: RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers
papers.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) extends RL with verifiable rewards to open-ended tasks by scoring each response against query-specific rubrics. Under group-relative optimization, however, a rubric that every sampled response fails (unreachable) or passes (saturated) gives all responses the same outcome and no learning signal; in Qwen3-4B medical training, 60.88% of query-rubric observations are inactive. We find that the two states lack different supervision: stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from 1.13% to 91.25%, whereas responses that all pass a saturated rubric still differ in quality. We therefore propose RuACT (Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers), which assigns each inactive rubric the role that supplies what it lacks. Rubric as Teacher uses unreachable rubrics as privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation, and Rubric as Critic decomposes saturated rubrics into child rubrics that separate current responses while sharing the parent's weight. RuACT outperforms GRPO, rubric reweighting, and rubric-guided exploration on all four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and achieves the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. On initially unreachable rubrics, unguided recovery rises from 35.02% to 42.86%, while child refinement improves reward-quality alignment on independent rollouts from 57.74% to 60.77%. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/RuACT.
papers.summary: In rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) for open-ended tasks, a rubric that every sampled response fails (unreachable) or passes (saturated) gives no learning signal under group-relative optimization; in `Qwen3-4B` medical training, **60.88% of query-rubric observations are inactive**. The authors observe that the two states need different fixes: stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from 1.13% to 91.25%, while responses that all pass a saturated rubric still differ in quality. `RuACT` uses unreachable rubrics as privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation, and splits saturated rubrics into child rubrics that separate current responses. It outperforms `GRPO`, rubric reweighting and rubric-guided exploration on four medical and scientific benchmarks with `Qwen3-4B`, and achieves the best average with `Qwen3-1.7B`.

papers.title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression
papers.abstract: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.
papers.summary: The key-value (KV) cache of a language model grows linearly with context length and quickly outgrows the model on consumer devices: 200,000 entries for `Qwen3-1.7B-Base` take 21 GiB, 6.6 times the weights. `Transformer-FSQ` replaces the key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck, so the cache stores packed integer codes per token with no per-token metadata; converting a pretrained model trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. On long-context retrieval (`RULER`), it is the most accurate of the evaluated methods at **12x to 97.5x compression** for models from 0.6B to 8B parameters, compared against five baseline families. A fused `Triton` kernel decoding directly from the codes matches native attention throughput on uncompressed `Qwen3-8B-Base` at 32x compression and is 1.54 times faster at 97.5x.

papers.title: Coresets for Capacitated Clustering via Dual Concentration
papers.abstract:
We study coresets for clustering problems, focusing on the classical $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. A coreset is a small weighted summary of the input data that approximately preserves the clustering cost for every choice of centers. Such summaries are a central tool for scaling clustering algorithms to large datasets.
  In this work, we consider the capacitated setting, where the clustering is subject not only to choosing centers but also to respecting prescribed cluster-size constraints. This model is a natural generalization of standard clustering and has been widely studied, but its coreset complexity is less well understood. For finite metric spaces, we obtain optimal-size coresets; surprisingly, these match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. We also give improved coreset bounds in Euclidean space, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence in $k$ while being independent of the dimension and input size.
  The main new technical ingredients are concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which allow for both significantly simpler and tighter analyses of the underlying sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.
papers.summary: A coreset is a small weighted summary of a dataset that approximately preserves the clustering cost for any choice of centers. The authors study coresets for capacitated `k-median` and `k-means`, where cluster sizes must also respect prescribed limits. For finite metric spaces they obtain optimal-size coresets that, perhaps surprisingly, **match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering**, and in Euclidean space they give the first coresets with near-linear dependence on k that are independent of dimension and input size. The main technical tool is a set of concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which simplifies and tightens the analysis of the sampling distribution.

papers.title: ReplayAudit: Auditing Outsourced LLM Fine-Tuning via Sealed Records and Selective Replay
papers.abstract: Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.
papers.summary: When LLM fine-tuning is outsourced, the customer needs to check that an untrusted provider actually trained as claimed without re-running the whole job. `ReplayAudit` has the provider seal training records before any challenge, then uses telemetry such as loss changes and parameter-update norms to guide stratified random sampling of intervals, which are independently replayed from sealed checkpoints. A 7B BF16 prototype with `LoRA` training rejects false update-norm reports, false loss reports and skipped updates. Compared with uniform sampling, telemetry-guided budgets **cut median complete-audit time by 49% and 67%** in two learning-rate deviation settings, though the audit costs 38% more when skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum.

papers.title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control
papers.abstract: A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with someone else's and measures the drop in accuracy. But this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch. We examine this problem with a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, using histories from similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without history. Removing history only at evaluation makes this gain appear larger, at 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen during training and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence for an advantage remains inconclusive. A small movie-tagging experiment with one training seed also finds no advantage over other users' histories. These findings show why personalization should be evaluated on unseen users, with histories of similar content and a model trained without history as comparisons. We also find that adding gated cross-attention improves on a prefix-only model under our training setup; whether this holds more broadly remains open.
papers.summary: A common test of LLM personalization swaps a user's history for another user's and measures the accuracy drop, but this also changes the topics in the history. Using a frozen language model on `LaMP-2` news categorization with histories from similar users and synthetic histories, the authors find that category labels alone reproduce 86% of the gap between the user's own history and a random user's. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, **the gap falls to 0.9 percentage points**, and for users not seen in training the advantage over a similar user's history is only 0.65 points and inconclusive. They recommend evaluating personalization on unseen users, comparing against content-matched histories and a model trained without history.

papers.title: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs
papers.abstract: We study kernel-based learning of analytic operators from finite samples, with a focus on how the regularity of the target should determine the choice of the kernel. We establish embeddings of analytic operators into vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and derive finite-sample, high-probability guarantees that quantify the uncertainty due to random sampling: in the noiseless setting, suitable analytic kernels yield rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, while Sobolev-type kernels yield polynomial rates. We apply the theory to the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE, where the training data are themselves finite-element approximations, and obtain bounds that separate the sampling and discretization contributions to the error and prescribe how the mesh size should be coupled to the sample size. The results are illustrated numerically.
papers.summary: The authors study learning analytic operators, such as the solution maps of partial differential equations (PDEs), from finite samples with kernel methods, focusing on how the regularity of the target should guide the choice of kernel. They embed analytic operators in vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and derive high-probability finite-sample guarantees. In the noiseless setting, **suitable analytic kernels give error rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size**, while Sobolev-type kernels give only polynomial rates. Applied to a parametric elliptic PDE trained on finite-element data, the bounds separate sampling error from discretization error and prescribe how mesh size should scale with sample count.

papers.title: Know What You Need: Efficient Activation Checkpointing
papers.abstract: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.
papers.summary: Activation checkpointing saves memory in LLM training by recomputing activations during backpropagation, but this recomputation is expensive, especially for Transformer linear layers. The authors propose an approximate recomputation method that uses information collected in the original forward pass to recompute only the most important layer components, chosen greedily or by randomized sketching, and that can yield unbiased gradient estimates. Ablations show the resulting gradients closely match exact ones. On a `Llama-488M` model, recomputing **only two-thirds of layer components** raises perplexity by 1.7%, 1.2% and 2.5% when applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both.

papers.title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
papers.abstract:
We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds.
  For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt \Sigma)$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{\Sigma_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{\Sigma_B})$, where $\Sigma_S$ and $\Sigma_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations.
  We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.
papers.summary: The authors give one potential-function method for two online problems with one-bit feedback: contextual search, and bilateral trade, where a mechanism sets prices between a buyer and a seller. In a Bayesian setting with a known prior, their algorithms achieve loss bounded by the trace of the square root of the prior covariance, for the target in contextual search and for the seller's and buyer's valuations in bilateral trade. Adapting a dual of this potential to the adversarial setting yields **tight O(sqrt d) regret for both problems**, matching lower bounds up to a constant. This improves on the previous O(d log d) for contextual search and O(d 6^d) for bilateral trade.

papers.title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming
papers.abstract: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.
papers.summary: Neural-network simulators can speed up finite-element (FE) simulation of sheet metal forming, but Transformer-based neural operators tend to smooth out localised responses such as thinning near sharp radii or ribs, which determine formability. `BiLoGo` combines bidirectional node-element `GraphSAGE` message passing on a bipartite graph with a dual-stream Transformer neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact as separate token sets, merged through gated residual fusion. On one cold forming case and two hot stamping cases, it achieves the lowest positional and thinning errors against graph-based and Transformer baselines. Near ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning **rises from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer operators to 0.94**, and it uses 66-69% less training memory than the hierarchical graph network `CAtt-BiUGNN`.

papers.title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
papers.summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) agents still struggle with tasks that need long-term memory and planning. Rather than designing new architectures, Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (`TT-MBRL`) runs gradient descent during each episode to write the episode's observations into the world model's parameters, so the agent effectively learns a separate world model per episode instead of relying only on context. After a proof of concept on a simplified 2D variant of `Memory Maze` across several world model architectures, it **sets a new state of the art on the 3D `Memory Maze` benchmark**. It also keeps strong performance on the non-memory benchmarks `DeepMind Control` and `Atari 100k`.

papers.title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
papers.abstract: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.
papers.summary: Standard post-training produces one language model policy for a fixed weighting of objectives such as helpfulness and harmlessness, even though users' preferred trade-offs vary. `LambdaMix` trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model with group-relative online RL; a preference vector both selects the adapter mixture used to generate responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run then supports changing preferences at inference time. On helpfulness/harmlessness and on math with instruction following, it **achieves higher hypervolume than all conditioned and policy-merging baselines across four models**, while using fewer training completions and adapter parameters than a set of `GRPO` specialist policies.

papers.title: NAVE: A Normalized, Adaptive Conformer for Antarctic Whale Vocalization Detection
papers.abstract: Antarctic whale vocalization detection requires temporally localizing call boundaries in long underwater recordings and classifying them into predefined call types. Training reliable machine learning models for this task is difficult due to the variability and sparsity of whale calls in passive acoustic monitoring datasets. These difficulties are further amplified by time-varying noise that can mask whale calls and by site-specific ambient sound characteristics to which a trained model may not generalize. In this work, we present NAVE, a Conformer-based detector that improves whale-call detection via three components. First, its input representation combines per-bin complex mean subtraction, which suppresses constant site-specific ambient sound characteristics, with an additional per-channel energy normalization (PCEN) channel that adapts to temporal variations in the noise floor. Second, a frequency-dynamic stem processes these noise-aware representations with convolutions that adapt across the characteristic frequency bands of the target call types. Third, we use a Conformer backbone with a convolution kernel matched to the duration of the target calls that adds an inductive bias and improves temporal localization. We evaluate NAVE on BioDCASE 2026 Task 2 using leave-one-site-out cross-validation across the validation sites, which approximates deployment on unseen recording sites. A single NAVE model with a tuned per-class threshold exceeds the stronger WhaleVAD-BPN baseline, using no boundary-proposal network and no search over post-processing parameters. A controlled ablation study shows that the normalized front-end and a duration-matched convolutional kernel each contribute substantially to recovering the D downsweep, the hardest class for previous detectors, with the wide kernel giving the largest aggregate gain.
papers.summary: Detecting Antarctic whale calls in long underwater recordings is hard because calls are sparse and variable, noise changes over time, and models must generalize to new recording sites. `NAVE` is a `Conformer`-based detector whose input combines per-bin complex mean subtraction, which removes constant site-specific ambient sound, with a per-channel energy normalization (`PCEN`) channel that adapts to a shifting noise floor, followed by a frequency-dynamic convolutional stem and a convolution kernel matched to call duration. On `BioDCASE 2026 Task 2` with leave-one-site-out cross-validation, **a single model exceeds the stronger `WhaleVAD-BPN` baseline** without a boundary-proposal network or post-processing search. Ablations show that the normalized front end and the duration-matched kernel each substantially help on the hardest call type.

papers.title: TensorMutation: Learning Weight-Space Mutations of Deep Learning Models on Neural Graphs
papers.abstract: Mutation testing for deep learning (DL) faces a cost-realism trade-off. The pre-training approach produces realistic but computationally expensive mutants, whereas existing post-training operators modify trained models efficiently but produce mutants that less closely resemble real faults. This study asks whether the trade-off is necessary: can the weight-space effect of a fault-informed pre-training mutation operator be predicted from a trained model, without retraining it? We answer this question with TensorMutation, which represents a trained model as a neural graph and uses a mutation-conditioned graph neural network (GNN) to predict parameter changes. The GNN is trained offline and reused across unseen models so that TensorMutation can generate executable mutants without retraining. We construct a corpus of 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers using 11 fault-informed pre-training operators, including 25 newly curated subjects. TensorMutation partially reproduces the behavioral effects of pre-training mutations on nine held-out subjects, and direct weight-space supervision significantly improves weight-space fidelity. On 12 real-fault subjects, TensorMutation achieves the highest median behavioral similarity among the evaluated approaches. The improvement over the post-training tool DeepMutation++ is statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p=0.018), whereas the differences from the pre-training tool DeepCrime and the norm-matched random control are not significant. These results show that fault-informed pre-training mutations leave learnable structure in weight space that transfers to unseen models.
papers.summary: Mutation testing for deep learning must choose between realistic but costly mutants made by retraining with injected faults and cheap but less realistic mutants made by editing trained weights. `TensorMutation` represents a trained model as a neural graph and uses a mutation-conditioned graph neural network (GNN), trained offline, to predict the weight changes a fault-informed pre-training mutation would cause, without retraining. The authors build a corpus of 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 multilayer perceptron classifiers and 11 operators. On 12 real-fault subjects it achieves **the highest median behavioral similarity** among the evaluated approaches, significantly beating `DeepMutation++`, though differences from `DeepCrime` and a norm-matched random control are not significant.

papers.title: Breaking the Privacy Promise: Gradient Inversion Attacks on Federated Low-Rank Adapted Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) of Vision Transformers is popular in federated learning, and its weaker gradient signal is often assumed to limit leakage of client data. The authors find that reconstruction is limited by both the reduced information in LoRA gradients and the lack of spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. They propose a malicious-server attack that prescribes trainable positional embeddings in client fine-tuning, using the resulting gradients as spatial anchors alongside a generative image prior. Adding this anchoring to the `GIAS` attack **improves PSNR by 10.14 dB on `CIFAR-10`** and by 7.83 and 11.74 dB on `CelebA` and `CARS`, with gains holding at larger batch sizes and under `FedAvg`, indicating that LoRA alone does not prevent data leakage.

papers.title: Differentially Private GraphRAG: Protecting Relation Connectivity and Semantics
papers.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) connects information across documents through entity relationships to support relational reasoning. However, black-box access to GraphRAG systems can enable adversaries to reconstruct knowledge graphs and recover both structural connectivity between entities and the semantics of their relationships. Existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees and provide limited protection against such reconstruction attacks. We propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, which provides formal privacy guarantees by mitigating connectivity leakage and protecting relations and their semantic meaning through relation removal. We formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds the distinguishability of mechanism outputs according to the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal. Building on this definition, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitizes source documents before GraphRAG indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing their associated connectivity using the exponential mechanism. Experiments across three GraphRAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks demonstrate that RelGuard provides stronger protection against reconstruction attacks than four existing defense mechanisms while better preserving downstream utility.
papers.summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (`GraphRAG`) links documents through entity relationships, but black-box queries can let attackers reconstruct the underlying knowledge graph, including which entities connect and what the relations mean. `RelGuard` defines relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds how distinguishable outputs are according to the semantic distance between alternative relations, and sanitizes source documents before indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing connections via the exponential mechanism. It is presented as **the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG**. Across three GraphRAG systems and two reconstruction attacks, it protects better than four existing defenses while preserving more downstream utility.

papers.title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
papers.abstract: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.
papers.summary: The authors measure how trimming the conversation history given to an AI agent affects token use and answer quality, using 1,100 questions from the `BEAM` benchmark with fixed retrieval and reader across five passage budgets. Mean scores rose with larger budgets, but **the gain per extra token shrank at the upper budgets**, and abstention scores sometimes improved as budgets shrank. In a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets, retaining user messages helped `Qwen` on direct requirements but not on answers that depended on references to earlier offers, while `Mistral` stayed near the floor. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM's grading unresolved, so the authors stress validating the quality measure alongside choosing the budget.

papers.title: Online Causal Configuration for Networked Systems via Doubly Robust Steady-State Learning
papers.abstract: Measurement exploration reveals how interacting local controllers behave but can alter the steady-state regime a network operator seeks to optimize. Exploratory rewards may therefore fail to identify a configuration's no-exploration value: under full exploration, identical logged distributions can conceal different target values. Identification requires accounting for both action-law mismatch and shifts in the steady-state context distribution. We introduce CAUSAL-UCB, which selects configurations using optimistic bounds on target causal values. Its interference-aware clipped doubly robust evaluator produces predecision certificates separating statistical variation from calibrated identification, transport, and temporal-dependence errors. For any finite horizon and predetermined schedule of measurement-exploration rates $\{\eta_t\}$, we prove lower bounds of $\Omega((1+\sum_t\eta_t)^{-1/2})$ on minimax inference error and $\Omega(\sum_t\eta_t)$ on measurement-induced deployment loss in a stationary, potentially slow-mixing family. We bound regret under valid certificates and selected-information growth, and establish an anytime finite-sample certificate with a shared radius for estimation, selection, and reporting in a restricted known-local-interference model. In a high-mismatch benchmark with 24 paired seeds and 200 rounds, CAUSAL-UCB attains target regret of $1.732$ versus $6.326$ for certified IPS-UCB, with deployment gaps of $30.607$ and $23.217$, respectively. Independent-audit coverage tests and trace-driven semi-synthetic studies further assess certificate coverage and deployment trade-offs.
papers.summary: When tuning configurations of networked systems with interacting local controllers, the measurement exploration used to learn can itself shift the steady state the operator wants to optimize. Logged rewards may therefore misidentify a configuration's value without exploration. `CAUSAL-UCB` selects configurations using optimistic bounds from an interference-aware clipped doubly robust estimator, with certificates that separate statistical noise from identification, transport and temporal-dependence errors, and the authors prove lower bounds on the trade-off between exploration, inference error and deployment loss. In a high-mismatch benchmark it reaches **target regret of 1.732 versus 6.326 for certified `IPS-UCB`**, at the cost of a larger deployment gap (30.6 versus 23.2).

papers.title: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
papers.abstract: Robots increasingly choose actions by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences, in model-predictive control or best-of-$N$ selection; we measure what this does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic labels and blind labels from the two authors, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76%: with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from, while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97. On plate-slide human labels are exploited less than synthetic ones, and on window-open search helps. True return roughly follows how far the planner's weights move from its proposals ($\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}}$) for both weighting rules we test, and best-of-$N$ with a verifier from synthetic labels falls below a single noisy action. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, that no positive gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own, and that an episode's return splits exactly into per-step terms, of which the guarantee covers the selection terms. Calibrated from 100 proposal pairs ranked by true return (an oracle) on start states the evaluation never uses, this rule is the safest fix we test: with each of five independent sets it succeeds in every arm run and keeps on average 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on plate-slide and drawer-open, though it is cautious where search helps. Calibration from a person's comparisons cannot detect a bias the scorer learned from that person; correcting for the pairs people cannot tell apart, or a second person, limits the damage.
papers.summary: Robots increasingly select actions by searching against reward models learned from human preferences, through model-predictive control or best-of-N selection, and the authors measure how this search exploits reward model errors. On `HalfCheetah`, `Hopper` and `Meta-World` tasks, stronger `MPPI` search **cuts true return by up to 76%** even when held-out label accuracy is 0.75-0.97; with human labels, the drawer-open task succeeds in 0 of 20 runs versus 10 of 10 for the cloned starting policy. They prove that chi-squared-regularized MPPI with a temperature set by the scorer's error spread is worst-case optimal, and calibrating this from oracle-ranked proposal pairs keeps 86-94% of the cloned policy's return, though it is cautious where search would help. Calibrating from one person's comparisons cannot detect bias the scorer learned from that same person.

papers.title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.
papers.summary: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs fluid flow from the motion of tracer particles, but the camera position is usually fixed by an operator, which limits how well the flow feature of interest is resolved. The authors treat camera placement as a sequential decision problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to move a camera on a 6-DoF robot arm. The agent sees only the estimated velocity field and its uncertainty, and it is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of a water tunnel, with hydrofoil wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). After **zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel**, the policy reliably finds and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils, resolving them more finely and with lower error than a fixed view, in about half the time of a full scan.

papers.title: The Multiscale Single-Index Model: An MSE Analysis of Online SGD Dynamics
papers.abstract: We consider the Multiscale Single-Index Model (MSIM), first introduced by Oymak and Soltanolkotabi (2021), as a stylized model for hierarchical feature learning with scale separation. Each layer extracts a shared single-index feature at one physical scale and passes it to the next, giving a tractable setting in which to study how deep architectures learn local multiscale representations. Under non-degeneracy and delocalization assumptions on the link function and planted features respectively, for the two hidden-layer case ($K=2$), we analyze joint online spherical SGD under MSE loss, which is a canonical regression objective, in discrete time and show that it achieves weak recovery from random initialization in $O(d\log^2 d)$ samples, followed by strong recovery to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in $O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))$ additional samples. The main technical challenge arises from the non-Gaussian learned features observed by the second layer. We address this challenge through a quantitative Gaussian comparison using delocalization, combined with sharp trajectory-level control of the coupled SGD dynamics. This work is a companion to Bruna (2026, arXiv:2607.03347), which studies recovery under a correlation objective for general $K$.
papers.summary: The Multiscale Single-Index Model (`MSIM`) is a simplified model of hierarchical feature learning in which each layer extracts one shared feature at a single scale and passes it to the next layer. For the two-hidden-layer case, the authors analyze joint online spherical SGD under mean squared error loss and prove that it achieves weak recovery from random initialization in **O(d log² d) samples**, followed by strong recovery to accuracy ε in O(d log(1/ε)) further samples. The main technical difficulty is that the second layer receives non-Gaussian learned features, which the authors handle with a quantitative Gaussian comparison argument and tight control of the coupled SGD trajectories.

papers.title: SURE:Spatiotemporal Uncertainty Representation for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Learning
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, but their effectiveness still depends heavily on large volumes of demonstration data. In manipulation tasks, this dependence is compounded by structured spatiotemporal uncertainty in the action space: multiple nearby actions or trajectories may successfully solve the same task, while semantically equivalent demonstrations often unfold at different speeds. Standard pointwise supervision treats each demonstrated action as an exact target, imposing an unnecessary learning burden under such uncertainty. We present SURE, a data-efficient VLA training framework that explicitly models both spatial and temporal uncertainty. SURE augments a VLA backbone with a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that captures spatial uncertainty through local correlations among neighboring action bins. It further introduces Soft-DTW alignment supervision to accommodate local timing variations between predicted and demonstrated action chunks. Together, these two components reduce sensitivity to demonstrator-specific poses and execution timing, enabling more data-efficient action learning. We evaluate SURE on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks. Even with only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps, SURE achieves manipulation success rates that match or surpass baseline VLAs.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies need large amounts of demonstration data, partly because standard training treats every demonstrated action as an exact target, even though many nearby actions would succeed and demonstrators move at different speeds. `SURE` adds a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that models spatial uncertainty across neighboring action bins, and uses `Soft-DTW` alignment to tolerate local timing differences between predicted and demonstrated action chunks. On `LIBERO`, `RoboTwin 2.0`, and real-world manipulation tasks, `SURE` matches or beats baseline VLAs **using only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps**.

papers.title: Verifier Noise Is a Temperature: Testing Tilt Predictions in Finite-Budget LLM-Guided Search
papers.abstract: LLM-guided search loops propose a modified candidate, score it, and keep it if it scores better. When both candidates are re-scored at every comparison, as in the minibatch acceptance gates of prompt optimizers, keep-if-better is a reversible Markov chain if the score difference is logistic and the mutation operator is reversible, and its stationary law is the mutation equilibrium tilted by exp(beta f). For any continuous symmetric noise difference the same tilt is the stationary law of a small-step diffusion limit, with beta = 4F'(0); for a minibatch gate beta grows with the square root of the minibatch size. Caching the incumbent's score instead inflates the recorded score. We test the tilt as a prediction for LLM-guided program search, committing each prediction from calibration data before the search runs. The level after 150 steps rises with the minibatch size in six of seven settings, but its predicted value fails: on bin packing, search attains 62-88% of the predicted gain when the proposer edits the parent and 109-119% when it writes new heuristics. The attained fraction falls with the parent-child quality correlation of unselected mutation; a registered test on two new settings confirmed the direction, but not the quantitative agreement after a correction. Further registered tests found that runs started from a good program kept losing quality over 300 steps, more so from starts that search had selected, by a margin that passed its registered rule narrowly. Runs from different starts had not reached a common level, so whether the tilt describes the stationary law of LLM editing remains open. A registered test in prompt optimisation on frozen task-model scores failed: search exceeded the tilt, and the bin-packing relation did not transfer.
papers.summary: LLM-guided search loops, such as prompt optimizers and program search, propose a modified candidate and keep it only if it scores better. The authors show that when both candidates are re-scored with noisy evaluations, this keep-if-better loop converges to a predictable stationary distribution in which verifier noise acts like a temperature, with the effective inverse temperature growing with the square root of the minibatch size. They registered quantitative predictions before running LLM-guided program search: the final score level rose with minibatch size in six of seven settings, but the predicted values were often off, ranging from **62–88% of the predicted gain on bin packing when the proposer edited the parent program to 109–119% when it wrote new heuristics**. A registered test on prompt optimization failed outright, so whether the theory describes LLM editing at equilibrium remains open.

papers.title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure
papers.abstract: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.
papers.summary: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context LLM inference by letting each query attend to only part of the context, but existing training-free methods choose how finely to select relevant regions with fixed heuristics. `HASA` (Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention) instead derives each attention head's selection resolution from the head's own query-key operator. It uses that operator's singular spectrum to set a per-head effective rank, and merges neighboring token regions whose responses point in coherent directions. Exact attention is then computed over the selected regions. `HASA` captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and beats the `UNIQUE` baseline by up to 3.47 points on `RULER` and 2.57 on `LongBench-Pro`, with **up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention**.

papers.title: Where Should Learning Live? Regret Analysis for Text, Parameter, and Joint Adaptation
papers.abstract: Language-model systems can select prompts and parameter adapters repeatedly during deployment, using feedback to guide later choices. Earlier choices may change the context or environment inherited by later configurations. We study selection among preconstructed candidates and compare cumulative loss with the best fixed prompt--parameter pair used from the beginning. This excess loss separates into three terms: selection regret within the available family, the gap from restricting that family, and the benefit or harm of the actual deployment history. Selection is evaluated using the history each candidate would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from the effects of switching. When loss functions are fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affect loss for only a bounded number of rounds, and every candidate's own-history loss is revealed, limiting switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family. We also quantify the costs and additional assumptions of independent probing and deployment-only feedback. Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can either lower or raise deployed loss, depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection, yet produces more failures because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.
papers.summary: Deployed language-model systems can repeatedly choose among prompts and parameter adapters based on feedback, and earlier choices can change the context that later choices inherit. The authors split the excess loss relative to the best fixed prompt–adapter pair into three parts: selection regret within the candidate family, the cost of restricting that family, and the effect of the actual deployment history. They prove that limiting how often the selector switches yields sublinear expected regret, under assumptions that include past choices having only bounded-duration effects. Experiments with `Qwen3.5-9B` on `Spider` show that **text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection but produces more failures**, because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.

papers.title: Empirical Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in SSH Infrastructure
papers.abstract: With the anticipated arrival of Q-day, quantum computers threaten current cryptographic schemes for encryption and digital signatures. In response, major content delivery networks and cloud service providers are already adopting Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The current state-of-the-art focuses on benchmarking the operational performance of implementing PQC, but the real-world adoption status remains under-researched. This work utilizes large-scale SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanning tool to analyze PQC adoption across 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 entities. Our study shows that the PQC transition in the SSH protocol is underway but highly polarized: 45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC, while 54.8% remain classical-only. At the entity level, 39.9% have enabled PQC on at least one host, whereas 60.1% have no PQC support. By correlating PQC adoption with industry, geography, and organizational size (digital and financial), this study provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of PQC adoption status in SSH infrastructure.
papers.summary: Studies of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) mostly benchmark its performance, and less is known about how widely it has actually been deployed. Using SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanner covering 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 organizations, the authors measure PQC adoption in SSH and relate it to industry, geography, and organization size. Adoption is underway but polarized: **45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC**, and 39.9% of organizations have enabled it on at least one host.

papers.title: Empirical Assessment of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in TLS
papers.abstract: Anticipating Q-day security concerns, major CDNs and cloud providers are migrating to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While existing literature benchmarks PQC performance, empirical research evaluating real-world adoption data remains scarce. We present an empirical assessment of PQC deployment across seven critical protocols (HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS, and RDP) using 10,000 target IP addresses per protocol. At the origin-server level, PQC algorithm support reaches 9.1% for HTTPS and 7.39% for LDAPS, while falling below 1% for all other evaluated protocols. At the entity level, PQC support is 11% for HTTPS and 5.4% for LDAPS, while the remaining protocols have less than 5% of entities supporting PQC on the hosted servers. We further correlate these adoption trends against organizational digital and financial footprint, and industry sectors, yielding a multi-dimensional empirical assessment of PQC deployment. Finally, at the domain level, we perform a comparative analysis of PQC adoption in Cloudflare-hosted domains against baseline Cloudflare datasets. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into the current state of PQC readiness over Transport Layer Security (TLS).
papers.summary: The authors measure real-world post-quantum cryptography (PQC) deployment over TLS across seven protocols (HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS, and RDP), scanning 10,000 IP addresses per protocol. Server-level PQC support is **9.1% for HTTPS** and 7.39% for LDAPS, and below 1% for every other protocol. They relate adoption to organizations' digital and financial footprint and industry sector, and compare PQC adoption among Cloudflare-hosted domains against baseline Cloudflare datasets.

papers.title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
papers.abstract:
RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped.
  Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B.
  On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.
papers.summary: `RidgeFill` speeds up prefill by running only a model's lower layers exactly on the prompt. From the hidden state at a split layer, per-layer maps predict the inputs of every later layer, and those layers write their key-value caches from the predictions. Unlike `YOCO` or `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`, where this projection is trained into the model, the maps here are ridge regressions fitted in closed form from one pass over calibration text. The final few thousand tokens and every decoding step still run the full model. In a `llama.cpp` fork on an A100, `Qwen3.8-27B` reaches the first token **1.25–1.31x faster** at 16K–120K tokens, with `RULER` and `LongBench v2` drops of about 1–1.4 points whose confidence intervals include zero. On `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` in `vLLM`, prefill is 1.50–1.60x faster. The authors also find that loss averaged over all tokens hides the approximation error, so they rely on needle retrieval, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests to locate where the error comes from.

papers.title: ICare-DT: a digital twin for continuous forecasting of intensive care patients
papers.abstract: Digital twins of intensive care patients should update forecasts from new data and predict treatment responses, but few studies test whether routine records support either. We propose ICare-DT, a Transformer-based twin that updates a latent patient state hourly from new measurements without retraining. We trained it on 140,473 eICU-CRD stays to forecast vital signs crossing their training-set means. On test data, later forecasts beat the twin's own hour-6 forecasts of the same windows in all 12 settings (+0.073 to +0.153 AUROC). On validation data, controls that withheld or swapped the new hours traced the gain to the patient's own measurements. Without refitting, the model kept its gain on a second database (8 of 9 settings, +0.025 to +0.114 AUROC) in a prespecified evaluation of the previously analyzed MIMIC-IV test split. Refitted within MIMIC-IV, a twin state fine-tuned on clinical endpoints gave gradient boosting a significant gain for acute kidney injury (+0.0035 AUROC; hypotension +0.0010, not significant). To test response prediction, we built a benchmark that replaces the treatments in real records with simulated doses and injects responses of known size, visible only at measurement times. Ridge models supervised with injected effects recovered them from real records only through frequently measured variables (heart rate) read at their measurement times. We asked standard learners to predict these effects for a dosing regime no patient had received. No standard learner outperformed predicting zero effect at an out-of-support query. When told how the simulated responses were generated, a separate learner recovered the effects from the same records without seeing their true values (R2 0.30 to 0.40 at one effect size). Routine records support forecasts that improve with each patient's new data, and our benchmark is a testbed for models that learn how responses are generated.
papers.summary: `ICare-DT` is a Transformer-based digital twin of intensive care patients that updates a latent patient state every hour from new measurements without retraining. Trained on 140,473 stays from `eICU-CRD`, its later forecasts of vital signs beat its own hour-6 forecasts of the same windows in all 12 settings (**+0.073 to +0.153 AUROC**), and the gain held without refitting on `MIMIC-IV` in 8 of 9 settings. To test whether the model can predict treatment responses, the authors built a benchmark that injects simulated dose responses of known size into real records. No standard learner beat predicting zero effect for a dosing regime outside the training data, although a learner told how the responses were generated recovered part of the effect.

papers.title: Intent-Aware Caching for Efficient LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Modern LLM serving systems use prefix caching to accelerate multi-turn conversational workloads. They cache the key-value states of previous conversation prefixes and reuse them when subsequent requests share the same prefix, to avoid redundant prefill computation and reduce serving latency. However, achieving a high cache hit rate remains challenging because cache reuse depends on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Our analysis of real workloads shows that user intent is a useful signal for this behavior, as different intents exhibit different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Based on this key insight, we propose Intent-Aware Caching (IAC), an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs and leverages these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy. Extensive evaluation on real workloads (WildChat and ShareChat) shows that IAC reaches a 34.6% cache hit rate. This substantially outperforms both the previous learning-based approach (18.8%) and traditional methods such as least recently used (LRU, 12.2%), while reducing average serving latency by up to 46.1%.
