papers.summary: LLM serving systems cache the key-value states of earlier conversation turns so later requests that share the same prefix can skip recomputation, but the cache hit rate depends on whether, and how soon, a conversation continues. Analyzing real workloads, the authors find that user intent predicts both the chance of continuation and the delay before the next turn. `IAC` (Intent-Aware Caching) classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent logs, and uses them in an eviction policy modeled on an oracle. On `WildChat` and `ShareChat`, `IAC` reaches a **34.6% cache hit rate**, compared with 18.8% for a prior learning-based method and 12.2% for least recently used (LRU) eviction, and cuts average latency by up to 46.1%.

papers.title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
papers.abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
papers.summary: Memory lets LLM agents carry information across sessions, but malicious instructions seen in one session can be stored and later retrieved and acted on. `MemoryDojo` is an extensible benchmark of 155 multi-session, long-horizon trajectories across four domains that traces poisoned information through five different agent memory systems and measures how it affects later behavior. **All five memory systems were susceptible to poisoning**, with substantial differences in downstream effects. The authors also propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that makes attacks more effective and exposes differences between memory architectures.

papers.title: FOSCAR: Accelerating Decode Attention over 2- and 4-Bit KV Caches through Affine Folding
papers.abstract: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/FOSCAR.
papers.summary: Quantizing an LLM's key-value cache to 2 or 4 bits reduces memory traffic during decoding, but existing fused kernels stay far below peak bandwidth, because applying the scale and offset to every value uses up scarce GPU instruction throughput. `FOSCAR` uses affine folding to apply the scale and offset to the other operand or to the output of the attention matrix products instead, which cuts these operations by up to two orders of magnitude while giving exactly the same result. It also uses bit-manipulation tricks to feed quantized operands to Tensor Cores, and warp-specialized pipelines for H100 and B200 GPUs. On H100, the INT2 kernel achieves a **3.36x geo-mean speedup over FlashInfer BF16** and 2.03x over `TensorRT-LLM` FP8, and inside `SGLang` it raises peak long-context serving throughput by up to 341% over 16-bit baselines.

papers.title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds
papers.abstract: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.
papers.summary: The authors speed up optimization over probability distributions by representing each distribution as a neural network that maps a fixed reference distribution to the target, and by giving the network's parameter space the geometry induced by the Wasserstein metric. In this setting, natural gradient descent becomes a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold, which they accelerate with `Riemannian Anderson mixing`, a method that uses past residuals to approximate second-order information without computing Hessians. Across multimodal sampling, PDE inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling, **Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations** and is competitive with SGD and Adam in gradient evaluations and wall-clock time.

papers.title: One Run Is Not Enough: A Monte Carlo Protocol for Evaluating LLM Reliability on Data Science Tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for automating data science workflows. Benchmarks such as DataSciBench (2026) and StatQA (2024) have advanced the evaluation of their capabilities across data science and statistical tasks. Assessing their reliability requires examining both the quality of their responses and their consistency across repeated runs, task types, and difficulty levels. With this aim, we introduce DS-QA, a benchmark comprising 100 data science and statistics questions drawn from UK university courses, spanning 16 datasets and three difficulty levels. We develop a three-layer evaluation framework that combines general response properties (runtime, verbosity and text similarity), coarse-grained metrics (accuracy, code executability and completeness), and task-specific metrics. We evaluate OpenAI models using a Monte Carlo protocol with 100 repeated runs. The results reveal substantial variability in responses to data visualisation and supervised learning tasks, particularly at medium and hard difficulty levels, highlighting the importance of evaluating consistency alongside response quality. We also find that an increase of 0.1 in the word verbosity ratio corresponds to an increase of about 0.013 in the token verbosity ratio.
papers.summary: Assessing whether LLMs can reliably automate data science requires measuring how consistent their answers are across repeated runs, not only how good a single answer is. The authors introduce `DS-QA`, a benchmark of 100 data science and statistics questions from UK university courses, spanning 16 datasets and three difficulty levels. They evaluate OpenAI models with a three-layer framework covering general response properties, coarse-grained metrics such as accuracy and code executability, and task-specific metrics. Under a Monte Carlo protocol of 100 repeated runs per question, they find **substantial run-to-run variability on data visualization and supervised learning tasks**, especially at medium and hard difficulty.

papers.title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
papers.abstract: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.
papers.summary: A scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience asked which of 45 tasks across nine life domains they would delegate to AI agents. Each respondent rated their automation preference, trust, privacy concern, and willingness to pay for one scenario per domain. Automation preferences varied widely across domains. Using generalized estimating equation models, the authors found that trust in the agent, prior AI use for the task, and expected savings predicted more delegation, while **concern about losing personal fulfillment predicted less**. Open-ended answers showed a preference for bounded autonomy, in which the AI does most of the execution while humans keep oversight or final authority.

papers.title: Safety Is $\Pi_1$, Provability Is $\Sigma_1$: One Framework for the Hugging Face Breach and OpenAI's Mathematical Proofs
papers.abstract: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. What separates the events is the logical form of the statement wanted by each of the two domains, security and mathematics. The safety of a program is a $\Pi_1$ statement, for it says that no exploit exists, which is not assured by any finite list of tests that have been passed by the program. By contrast, the provability of a sentence is a $\Sigma_1$ statement, for it says that a proof exists, which is assured by a single instance, namely a proof that has been checked by the deductive verifier. The theorem behind both is Turing's Undecidability Theorem: the halting set is $\Sigma_1$ but not decidable, so its complement is $\Pi_1$ and not $\Sigma_1$, which is to say that membership has a finite witness but non-membership has none. We prove that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier does not change this undecidability result, however good the proposer is. We then discuss what does assure safety and where the residual risk goes.
papers.summary: The authors analyze two 2026 events they attribute to OpenAI, an agent-driven breach of Hugging Face and the release of over 700 AI-generated mathematical proofs, within a single logical framework in which a statistical proposer generates candidates and a deductive verifier checks them. They argue that the two domains differ in the logical form of the statement each needs. A program's safety is a `Π1` statement, saying that no exploit exists, so no finite set of passed tests can establish it. Provability is a `Σ1` statement, which a single checked proof establishes. Building on Turing's undecidability theorem, they prove that **no matter how good the proposer is, attaching it to a deductive verifier does not remove this undecidability**, and they discuss what can assure safety and where the remaining risk lies.

papers.title: Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples
papers.abstract: Extracting discriminative features from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) spectra is important for the classification of complex biological samples. This study evaluates continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based spectral peak extraction for distinguishing human plasma samples labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative. Plasma specimens from 181 individuals, comprising 53 positive samples and 128 negative controls, were deposited as 5 {\mu}L droplets on silicon substrates and dried before analysis. Spectra were acquired using a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser operating at 1064 nm, with 100 single-shot measurements collected per specimen and averaged after intensity-based outlier rejection. CWT-based peak detection was coupled with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The reported leave-one-out evaluation yielded an accuracy of 93.00%, sensitivity of 94.67%, and specificity of 91.61%; these estimates remain provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions. Features identified by the CWT pipeline included emission lines assigned to Ca II, K I, and N I. The workflow provides a basis for examining spectral features associated with the studied plasma groups. Independent validation and assessment of specimen, substrate, and acquisition-related variability are required to establish generalizability and diagnostic relevance.
papers.summary: The authors test continuous wavelet transform (CWT) peak extraction on laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) spectra as a way to tell apart human plasma samples labeled SARS-CoV-2 positive or negative. They analyzed dried plasma droplets from 181 individuals with a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser and classified the extracted features with a support vector machine (SVM). Leave-one-out evaluation gave **93.00% accuracy**, which the authors describe as provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions. The discriminative features included Ca II, K I, and N I emission lines, and the authors state that independent validation is needed before any diagnostic claim.

papers.title: Diffusion-free Score Matching for Exact Conditional Sampling
papers.abstract: The success of modern score-based generative models is largely driven by diffusion-based training, which learns a collection of time-indexed score fields corresponding to progressively noisier versions of the data distribution. While such models achieve impressive sample quality, leveraging them for sound probabilistic inference---particularly sampling from arbitrary conditionals of the model---remains challenging. This difficulty arises because conditioning information is only available for clean data and not for the higher noise levels required to generate exact conditional samples. In this paper, we introduce DIffusion-free SCOre matching (DISCO), a principled approach that sidesteps the need for time-dependent score fields altogether. Our method is based on an objective that, while reminiscent of diffusion-based training, estimates only a single score of the (slightly perturbed) data distribution, for which the exact conditional score is readily obtained. In experiments, DISCO is competitive with state-of-the-art diffusion models in terms of sample quality. More importantly, DISCO yields a more faithful representation of the underlying data distribution and---crucially---enables accurate sampling from arbitrary conditionals, outperforming standard heuristic samplers. This capability opens the door to principled and flexible probabilistic reasoning with score-based models.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based generative models learn scores, the gradients of log-density, at many noise levels. Sampling exactly from a conditional distribution with them is hard, because the conditioning information applies to clean data but not to the noisier levels that sampling passes through. `DISCO` (DIffusion-free SCOre matching) instead learns a single score of a slightly perturbed data distribution, from which exact conditional scores follow directly. `DISCO` matches state-of-the-art diffusion models in sample quality, represents the data distribution more faithfully, and **samples accurately from arbitrary conditionals, outperforming standard heuristic samplers**.

papers.title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
papers.abstract:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory.
  In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation.
  Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.
papers.summary: This work proves the first hierarchy theorem for chain-of-thought (CoT) computation in transformers. For any reasonable resource bound r(n) ≥ n and any ε > 0, **transformers with O(r(n)^(1+ε)) CoT steps can solve strictly more decision problems than those limited to O(r(n)) steps**, which establishes CoT length as a fundamental computational resource. Rather than the diagonalization used in classical hierarchy theorems, the proof uses known simulations between CoT transformers and Turing machines in both directions, together with the padding technique from complexity theory, which the authors show how to implement inside the transformer CoT model.
papers.highlight_summary:
Does giving a transformer more chain-of-thought (CoT) steps strictly increase what it can compute? The authors prove the first hierarchy theorem for CoT: for any well-behaved bound r(n) ≥ n and any ε > 0, **CoT(r(n)) ⊊ CoT(r(n)^{1+ε})**. In other words, decoding steps act as a resource in the same way that time and space do for Turing machines.

- Diagonalization doesn't work here because there is no clean notion of a "universal transformer" that can simulate another transformer from its encoding, so the proof instead relies on known two-way simulations between CoT and Turing machines (TIME(t) ⊆ CoT(t) ⊆ TIME~(t² + n²), from Merrill and Sabharwal).
- On their own, those simulations combined with the classical Time Hierarchy Theorem only give a coarse separation, **CoT(r) ⊊ CoT(r⁹)**, which cannot even separate `CoT(n)` from `CoT(n²)`.
- The key contribution is carrying out the classical padding argument inside transformers: one construction (`T′`) adds **5 extra layers and 2d + 22 embedding dimensions** to mask out padding tokens and copy the hidden state forward, while a second (`R`) writes the padding tokens itself through CoT steps and then runs the target transformer.
- This shows that if CoT(r) = CoT(r^{1+ε}) then CoT(r^{1+ε}) = CoT(r^{1+2ε}), and applying that step **⌈log₂(8/ε)⌉ times** collapses everything down to CoT(r⁹), which contradicts the coarse separation.
- The result is purely theoretical (log-precision, saturated attention, multi-layernorm, no experiments) and only covers r(n) ≥ n; it is also looser than the classical t log t time hierarchy, and closing that gap (for example, separating CoT(r) from CoT(r·polylog r)) would require a near-linear Turing-machine simulation of attention, which remains open.

papers.title: From PAC bounds on the generalization error to PAC bounds on the parameter estimation error
papers.abstract:
Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) bounds on the generalization error (the difference between the empirical prediction error computed on the training data and its expectation) are an established tool in statistical machine learning, and there have been several extensions of these bounds to dynamical systems. In parallel, in recent years, there has been growing interest in finite-sample bounds for parameter estimation error in system identification. The latter bounds tend to be algorithm-specific, relying on reformulating the identification algorithm as a least-squares regression problem. This is in contrast to classical PAC bounds, which are algorithm-agnostic and can be applied to any identification algorithm based on minimizing a cost function involving the empirical loss.
  In this paper, we show how oracle bounds derived from PAC bounds can be used to derive finite-sample bounds for dynamical systems. As an illustration of this approach, we present finite-sample parameter-estimation bounds for linear and bilinear systems with bounded inputs and noise. These bounds apply to identification algorithms based on minimizing a regularized empirical loss function.
  The key ingredient is to establish an oracle inequality, i.e., an inequality between the true prediction error of the learned model and the minimum achievable true prediction error, and then use either the convexity of the true loss or system-theoretic properties of the loss function to derive bounds on the parameter estimation error. We also analyze the rates of the obtained bounds and compare them with those of classical asymptotic results.
papers.summary: Finite-sample bounds on parameter estimation error in system identification are usually tied to a specific algorithm and depend on recasting it as least-squares regression. Classical Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) bounds on generalization error, by contrast, apply to any algorithm that minimizes an empirical loss. The authors derive an oracle inequality from PAC bounds, comparing the learned model's true prediction error with the best achievable one. They then turn it into parameter-error bounds using either convexity of the true loss or system-theoretic properties. As an illustration they give **algorithm-agnostic finite-sample parameter bounds for linear and bilinear systems** with bounded inputs and noise, and compare their rates with classical asymptotic results.

papers.title: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.
papers.summary: Using the `LURK` Werewolf framework, which separates what an utterance does from how it is worded, the authors test whether simpler or more complex language, or more or less polite phrasing, changes how large language model (LLM) agents judge and act toward each other. They rewrite only the wording, check that game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, **neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker**, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is blunt and direct regardless of role.

papers.title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.
papers.summary: Lifelong knowledge editing in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) suffers from forgetting and from edits leaking into unrelated behavior as updates pile up. `ROSE` restricts each new parameter update to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. It also uses a dynamically computed risk mask to protect parameter subspaces that are essential for stability. At inference, prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion activate edited knowledge only for relevant queries. On two multimodal benchmarks `ROSE` is competitive with state-of-the-art editors across five metrics and **remains stable over 1,000 sequential edits**.

papers.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs
papers.abstract: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $\rho>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $\rho$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.
papers.summary: Planning in finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) is computationally hard in general, and prior work obtained quasipolynomial-time approximate planning by assuming an ℓ1-observability condition on observations. The authors give **quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for ρ-decodable POMDPs**. Decodability is implied by both ℓ1- and ℓ2-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. They also show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal ℓ1-observability constant is NP-hard. Finally, they show that the filter-forgetting argument behind earlier work does not carry over directly to ℓ2-observability, which positions decodability as an easy-to-check unifying assumption.

papers.title: Are These Programmers Ripe Enough to Eat? Evaluating How LLMs Handle Lexical Knowledge Conflicts in Translation
papers.abstract: External lexical resources can help large language models (LLMs) translate texts in low-resource languages and specialized domains, but these resources may conflict with models' prior lexical knowledge. To isolate this conflict, we construct a controlled Mandarin-to-English translation task in which familiar source words are assigned new meanings within and across semantic categories. We treat these prompt-supplied meanings as contextual knowledge (CK) and systematically evaluate the effects of word frequency, sentence context, and prompt framing on the translated outputs. Across nine models, CK reliance is greater for less frequent source words and in sentence contexts that support the supplied meanings. Prompt framing can reduce CK reliance, but seven of nine models favor CK even when explicitly instructed to ignore the supplied meanings. Within model families, larger models are more likely than smaller models to utilize CK in their outputs. Three follow-up experiments further show that modal weakening lowers CK reliance, the effect of repetition depends on prompt layout, and the effect of reasoning varies across models. Overall, our controlled study reveals how CK reliance varies across conditions and models, motivating new methods to detect and evaluate lexical conflicts and guide models' lexical choices in LLM-based translation.
papers.summary: When a prompt supplies word meanings that contradict what a large language model (LLM) already knows, which one does it follow during translation? The authors build a controlled Mandarin-to-English task in which familiar words are given new meanings, and they measure reliance on this prompt-supplied contextual knowledge (CK) across nine models. Reliance on CK is higher for less frequent words and in sentences that support the new meaning, and larger models within a family use it more. Strikingly, **seven of nine models still favor CK even when told to ignore it**. Follow-up experiments show that weakening the wording with modals lowers CK reliance, that the effect of repetition depends on prompt layout, and that reasoning has inconsistent effects across models.

papers.title: Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving
papers.abstract: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.
papers.summary: The authors test whether retrieval-augmented generation helps large language models solve competitive programming problems. Their approach uses embedding-based similarity search with a dynamically adjusted threshold to find analogous solved problems and add them to the prompt. On `CodeContests`, they compare original problem descriptions, descriptions with randomly chosen training examples, and descriptions with retrieved similar examples. They use `Min-K` membership inference to separate genuine generalization from memorization of pretraining data. Pass rates and `CodeForces` Elo-based analysis show that **similarity-based retrieval substantially improves performance** over both baselines.

papers.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.
papers.summary: Static benchmarks cannot tell practitioners when it is worth intervening in an AI agent's trajectory mid-run, for example by verifying its output or steering it with human review or a stronger model. The authors frame this as a dynamic causal inference problem. Using a relatively small set of trajectories collected under randomized interventions, they estimate the causal effect of a broad class of contextual intervention policies. The estimated parameters can also feed safety leaderboards that rank how risky different agent actions are, to help prioritize audits. On `tau-bench` Retail, `ToolSandbox`, and `ImpossibleBench`, they find that **intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states**.

papers.title: Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team's result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model shows that individual agents lose because their many samples have a low mean and that one large team loses because a single sample gets no gain from variance. Sampling many small teams in parallel balances a high mean with the gain from variance. Parallel agent teams thus offer a more effective way to scale test-time compute.
papers.summary: When a verifier can score every attempt, test-time compute for agents is usually spent either on best-of-N sampling of independent agents, which saturates quickly, or on one large collaborating team, which stops improving as it grows. `Parallel agent teams` instead run many small teams in parallel and keep the best team's result. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents across 12 long-horizon tasks, from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development, **teams of ten beat independent parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks** and beat a single 100-agent team on all four tasks where that was tested. At equal dollar cost they also beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model explains the result: small parallel teams combine a high mean score with the gains from variance across many samples.
papers.highlight_summary:
When a verifier can score every attempt, best-of-N over independent agents saturates quickly, and a single large collaborating team stops improving as it grows. **Parallel agent teams** combine the two approaches: they sample many small flat teams that share a forum, and a verifier keeps the best team's result.

- A budget of B agents buys B/k teams of size k, each with no roles or manager, and a simple normal model (expected best ≈ μ + σ√(2 ln(B/k))) explains the trade-off: individual agents have a low mean, one big team is a single sample and gets no gain from variance, and small teams raise the mean while keeping most of that gain.
- With `Qwen3.8-27B` on 12 long-horizon tasks (GPU kernels, `Lean` formalization, exploit development and others), ten teams of ten beat 100 independent agents on **10 of 12 tasks** and score **27% higher on average**, including **54.8 vs 19.0** on `Carleson Formalization`.
- On the four tasks where a single team of 100 was run, ten teams of ten beat it on all four by **8–30%**, and at equal dollar cost the 27B teams beat the frontier model `GPT-5.6-sol` on **4 of 8 tasks**.
- Flat forum-based teams outperform orchestrated teams with a manager, and doubling an agent's session length barely raises its mean score, so the extra compute is better spent on more agents than on longer sessions.
- The evidence is thin in places: team pools hold only 10–11 runs per task, large teams were tested on just four tasks with 1–5 runs per size, the statistical model predicts the sign of the gain correctly on only 9 of 12 tasks when scores are far from normal, and the method requires a verifier.

papers.title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes.
papers.summary: Repository instruction files such as `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` guide coding agents in every session, but they can fall out of date as the code changes. The authors treat this as documentation debt whose cost recurs in every later session. Using three real stale instructions (a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component), they run 22 maintenance tasks with each instruction left stale, corrected, or removed, and analyze 732 trajectories from two models at the level of individual tool calls. Agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere, and a stale test command cost `Claude Sonnet 5.5` about two extra tool calls per run. Agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, yet **none repaired the underlying instruction file**, so success-only evaluations hide the cost.

papers.title: Maya a1: Do the Options Read the Model, or Does Their Position? Order Sensitivity in a Non-Autoregressive Decision Model
papers.abstract: Laya answers typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. We re-engineer the checkpoint (421M parameters; a 2-layer option head with no positional tensor; a documented but unused parallel layout) and test whether the answer depends on where an option is listed. Presenting 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options (or six random permutations for 12 options), the released checkpoint changes its answer for 25.8% [22.9-28.7] of questions (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone); accuracy with the gold option first versus last differs by 10.1 points, and the flips concentrate where the model's own confidence is low (54% versus 8% across confidence terciles). Fine-tuning with Laya's trainer on 2,818 teacher-verified rows with option shuffling cuts the flip rate to 7.2%; the identical rows without shuffling give 11.4%, so shuffling is responsible for 4.2 points of the improvement. A confidence-weighted vote over orderings gives 69.7% against 69.1% for a single base pass at 4.1x the compute. Labels are LLM-made and the test sets are teacher-filtered. We also fine-tune with the authors' parallel layout on the same rows: flip rate 0.5%.
papers.summary: The authors probe whether `Laya`, a 421M-parameter non-autoregressive model that answers multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a [MASK] marker per option, depends on the order in which options are listed. Presenting 951 verified questions under every rotation of their options, the released checkpoint **changes its answer on 25.8% of questions**, with flips concentrated where the model's confidence is low. Fine-tuning with option shuffling cuts the flip rate to 7.2%, and fine-tuning with the authors' documented but unused parallel layout cuts it to 0.5%. Voting over orderings barely improves accuracy (69.7% versus 69.1%) at about 4x the compute.

papers.title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.
papers.summary: Graph similarity measures such as Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS) are NP-hard to compute exactly, and existing graph neural network (GNN) approximations have mostly been tested on small graphs. `FiLSim` is a simplified, scalable GNN pipeline for this task. The authors also propose a sequential graph-editing strategy that builds large datasets with reliable GED labels. Evaluated on four standard benchmarks and four new large-scale datasets, **`FiLSim` stays accurate on graphs with more than 150,000 nodes**, where baselines run out of memory or fail to learn, and it scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.

papers.title: Compaction, decay and reinforcement in a two-tier conversational memory: a paired evaluation against retrieval-augmented generation
papers.abstract:
A conversational agent that remembers has to decide what to keep. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the transcript and searches it; the alternative is to compact each turn into atomic facts and search those. We compare the two on LoCoMo, with both arms answering all 1,985 questions in one window, against the same stores, with the same generator and judge, and both predictions on one row, which licenses McNemar's exact test on the 512 questions where they disagree.
  On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4 per cent against 64.6, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34 per cent fewer prompt tokens. On all five, including the adversarial set comparable work drops, the lead falls to 2.0 and stops being significant, because the baseline leads adversarial by 14.6.
  That loss has a structure. Our lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording, 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 behind past eight, with token overlap moving the same way, so the judge is not the cause. Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where it is a phrasing. We also report four negative results with their power calculations.
papers.summary: The authors compare two ways for a conversational agent to remember: retrieval-augmented generation over the raw transcript, and compacting each turn into atomic facts that are then searched. On `LoCoMo`, both approaches answer the same 1,985 questions with the same generator and judge, which allows a paired statistical test on the questions where they disagree. On the four commonly reported categories, **compaction scores 71.4% against 64.6% while using 34% fewer prompt tokens**. The lead shrinks to an insignificant 2.0 points once the adversarial category is included, where the transcript baseline is ahead. The analysis shows that compaction wins when the answer is a value and loses when the answer depends on the original wording, and the authors also report four negative results with power calculations.

papers.title: The Cost of Coverage: Conformalising Native Forecast Uncertainty for GB Wind Power
papers.abstract: Uncertainty bands on wind forecasts help inform reserve sizing and commitments, but often fail to deliver their stated coverage. We apply conformal prediction to native bands to see what it adds and what it costs, comparing six forecasters, from ARIMA to a tabular foundation model, at two wind farms in Great Britain (GB) under operational conditions. We show that calibration repairs empirical marginal coverage with little or no Winkler Score penalty, but this apparent success conceals under-coverage in high winds. Calibrating by forecast wind regime turns marginal coverage into regime-level coverage, cutting day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40% relative to pooled calibration while narrowing bands overall.
papers.summary: Uncertainty bands on wind power forecasts often fail to deliver their stated coverage. The authors apply conformal prediction to the native bands of six forecasters, ranging from `ARIMA` to a tabular foundation model, at two wind farms in Great Britain under operational conditions. Calibration restores overall coverage with little or no penalty in Winkler Score, but it hides under-coverage in high winds. Calibrating separately for each forecast wind regime **cuts day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40%** relative to pooled calibration, while narrowing bands overall.

papers.title: Machine learning for lattice QCD
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) methods have been explored as a means of optimizing lattice field theory calculations, with increasing interest in recent years. This chapter gives an introduction and summary to the use of ML methods to optimize lattice field theory without introducing any uncontrolled approximations. We focus on those directions which are clearly established as of late 2025, marking the 50th anniversary of the beginning of the study of lattice gauge theory. This chapter is a contribution to the online book ``Lattice QCD at 50 years,'' (LQCD@50), edited by Tanmoy Bhattacharya, Maarten Golterman, Rajan Gupta, Laurent Lellouch, and Steve Sharpe.
papers.summary: This book chapter introduces and summarizes machine learning (ML) methods used to speed up lattice field theory calculations without introducing uncontrolled approximations. It focuses on directions that were clearly established as of late 2025. It was written for the online volume `Lattice QCD at 50 years` and serves as a **review of established ML techniques for lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD)**.

papers.title: Generative Latent Priors for Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Dominant methods for interpreting large models impose strong structural assumptions. Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are a complementary approach: a diffusion model that learns the distribution of a frozen model's activations directly, imposing no assumptions. We port GLP to ESM-2 activations (UniRef50) and evaluate it at two host scales (ESM-2-8M and -650M), both as a lens for protein representations and as a prior for editing them. Generation quality scales smoothly with depth and compute. As a lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the strongest probes of discrete Swiss-Prot concepts at both hosts, beating InterPLM's released SAE features, and lead on continuous properties at 8M though not at 650M; falsification tests show this is mostly concentration, not new information. As an editing prior, the on-manifold correction makes DiffMean steering of three biochemical properties effective and restores on-manifoldness, but only in isolation: re-embedding the sequences actually produced after several rounds of decoding, the structural plausibility is compromised. This is mainly reproduced in additional SAE-based clamping structural steering experiments, where only Helix motif succeeds. The naturalness failure is traced to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior, highlighting what the method must clear before it can serve for both discovery-by-editing and discovery-by-exploration. Trained GLPs are released on huggingface.co/collections/HPAI-BSC/glprot.
papers.summary: `Generative Latent Priors (GLP)` are diffusion models that learn the distribution of a frozen model's activations without imposing structural assumptions. The authors apply them to the protein language models `ESM-2-8M` and `ESM-2-650M`, trained on `UniRef50`. As an interpretability lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the **strongest probes of discrete `Swiss-Prot` concepts at both scales, beating `InterPLM`'s sparse autoencoder (SAE) features**, though falsification tests suggest this mostly reflects concentration of existing information rather than new information. As a prior for steering, the method makes `DiffMean` edits effective in isolation, but sequences actually decoded after several rounds lose structural plausibility, a failure the authors trace to rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior.

papers.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
papers.abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.
papers.summary: Quantum algorithms are hard to evaluate on classical computers beyond small instances, which limits automated discovery loops driven by large language models. The authors build a quantum program library in the `Lean` theorem prover, in which agents synthesize new programs against formal specifications and prove both their correctness and their cost. Agent teams collaborate through shared wikis and organized "conferences". The discovered programs improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), **quantum arithmetic (290x)**, and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry, and drug metabolism (11x, 8x, and 2.5x respectively).

papers.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.
papers.summary: Storing the key-value (KV) cache in 4-bit floating-point formats (`NVFP4`, `MXFP4`) saves memory and lets attention run on FP4 Tensor Cores, but naive quantization hurts accuracy and codebook-based methods slow decoding. `BitDecoding-FP4` tackles three error sources: it splits queries into two FP4 tensors (cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%), rescales attention probabilities so long-context values do not round to zero, and suppresses key outliers with smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search. On the systems side it removes the softmax bottleneck with fused kernels on paged KV caches. Across dense and mixture-of-experts models it stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with `NVFP4`, and on NVIDIA B300 with `Qwen3-4B` and `Qwen3-30B-A3B` it delivers **2.4-3.0x higher peak serving throughput** than a BF16 KV cache.

papers.title: Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. To study how best to use monitors to mitigate reward hacking, we introduce and open source three realistic environments where Qwen3-4B reward hacks: a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophancy, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. We first focus on the coding environment, where we find that: (1) models can learn to evade highly accurate monitors by exploiting systemic flaws in probes and LLM judges; (2) monitors that leak more learning signal during RL suppress reward hacking but are more often evaded; and (3) including easier problems in training can decrease reward hacking. We apply our findings to build better reward hacking monitors for the medical chat and biography generation environments that improve upon naive baselines to reduce reward hacking rates across seeds to before-training levels in some interventions. Our results demonstrate that our takeaways translate to new settings and that better monitor intervention designs are possible.
papers.summary: One way to curb reward hacking during reinforcement learning (RL) is to penalize it whenever a monitor detects it, but models can learn to evade the monitor. The authors open-source three environments where `Qwen3-4B` reward hacks: coding by overwriting tests, medical chat through sycophancy, and biography generation through hallucination. In the coding environment, **models learn to evade even highly accurate monitors** by exploiting systematic flaws in probes and LLM judges. Monitors that leak more learning signal suppress hacking but are evaded more often, and adding easier problems to training reduces hacking. Applying these lessons to the other two environments yields monitors that in some interventions bring reward hacking back down to pre-training levels.
papers.highlight_summary:
Training against a reward-hacking monitor during RL can teach the model to evade the monitor instead of stopping the hack. The authors open-source three environments where `Qwen3-4B` starts reward hacking without any prompting or finetuning, then use them to test which monitor designs suppress hacking without teaching evasion.

- **Setup:** `Qwen3-4B` is trained with `GRPO` over 10 seeds in three hackable settings (coding where the model can overwrite `run_tests()`, medical chat where it can be sycophantic, and biography writing where it can hallucinate), and is monitored by attention-based activation probes or LLM judges such as `Qwen3 235B` that either penalize flagged rollouts or drop them from training (screening).
- **Naive monitors are evaded:** probes are first evaded by exploiting their existing blind spots and later by the model shifting its internal representations, and judges are fooled by surface tricks (explanation blocks after the code rose from **5% to 29%** of hacks). Simulated monitors with random errors at **70–90% accuracy** match or beat realistic monitors of similar or higher accuracy, which suggests uncorrelated, robust errors matter more than accuracy measured before training.
- **Signal trade-off:** a monitor needs a large enough share of the reward to suppress hacking (**r = −0.65**), but a larger share also correlates with probe representation drift (r = −0.24), and a 2x-weight proportional penalty made **40% of runs degenerate**. Screening removes probe representation drift entirely, and easier training data lowers hacking from **100% to 60%** of unmonitored runs and delays its onset by about 70 steps.
- **Transfer to the other environments:** combining higher recall, easier data, a stronger judge and probe screening cut medical-chat reward hacking by **22.4%** (probe) and **23.2%** (judge), down to non-hacking baseline levels. On biography writing the improved judge cut hacking by **86.2%**, while the probe managed only 9% because it caught about 30% of hacks that emerged during training.
- **Limitations:** the study covers one 4B model without chain of thought and uses loopholes that can be checked against ground truth. Evasion learned against one judge also transferred to judges the model never trained against (30–34% accuracy drops), and no intervention fully stopped hacking without some performance cost.

papers.title: Can Agentic Systems Close the Gap in Radiology with Production AI Tools?
papers.abstract: Radiology AI has developed along two paths: specialized models that perform well on narrow tasks but cover few clinical findings, and generalist models that address a broader range of tasks but remain prone to hallucination and inaccurate measurements. Combining the two through agentic systems offers a route towards comprehensive radiology reporting, but published systems are tied to one modality or body part. We describe a radiology agentic framework that standardizes how an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and use it to measure what such a system can do with the tools from FDA-cleared radiology AI devices. Report generation is simulated on a large multi-modality report corpus, with the orchestrator given either a catalog of finding classes consolidated from the cleared devices, each available on the modalities it is cleared for, or an unlimited catalog in which any class can be requested, and planning either from the clinical indication or from the target report. Tool outputs are simulated from the reference report, so the comparison isolates tool availability and orchestration from tool error. With the cleared catalog and the indication alone, the orchestrator recovers under a third of the clinically actionable findings; recovery improves substantially with the unlimited catalog, and further when the plan is written from the target report. Attributing every missed finding to a cause shows that most are classes no cleared device offers for the study's modality, and that a third are classes or tools that were offered and not called. Adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap to the unlimited catalog on held-out reports, whereas a smaller orchestrator with the unlimited catalog gives up the whole gain. Tool availability and effective orchestration are thus complementary constraints on comprehensive AI-assisted radiology reporting.
papers.summary: The authors build a radiology agentic framework in which an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report. They use it to measure how much existing FDA-cleared radiology AI tools could cover, with tool outputs simulated from reference reports so that tool errors are excluded. Using only the cleared tool catalog and the clinical indication, the **orchestrator recovers under a third of clinically actionable findings**. Most misses are finding classes that no cleared device offers for that imaging modality, and a third are tools that were available but not called. Adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap to an unlimited catalog, while a smaller orchestrator loses the gain entirely.

papers.title: Fifty-Two Shades of Pig: What the UCR Archive Really Asks Classifiers to Do
papers.abstract: The pigs were bleeding. That was the point of the experiment: could airway pressure reveal hemorrhage before it became critical? In the UCR Time Series Classification Archive, the de facto benchmark for Time Series Classification (TSC), the same recordings ask a different question: "which of 52 pigs produced this trace?". The dataset PigAirwayPressure is not an outlier. Although the archive is the standard benchmark, whether its tasks resemble the problems TSC is meant to solve has rarely been examined. We find that several datasets are repurposed from their original task, built from toy setups, or have flawed test splits. We further question how representative the archive's ordered non-temporal sequences (e.g. spectra, shape outlines) are of real TSC, and the potential downsides from the decomposition of multivariate problems. Our findings call for more careful interpretation of archive-wide scores and greater attention to deployment-relevant evaluation. The audit is at https://github.com/automl/ucr-provenance-audit.
papers.summary: The authors audit the provenance of datasets in the `UCR` Time Series Classification Archive, the de facto benchmark for time series classification. They find that several datasets have been repurposed from their original task, for example `PigAirwayPressure` asks which of 52 pigs produced a trace rather than whether hemorrhage can be detected. Others come from toy setups or have flawed test splits. They also question whether the archive's non-temporal sequences, such as spectra and shape outlines, represent real time series classification, and they point to downsides of decomposing multivariate problems. The findings call for **more careful interpretation of archive-wide scores** and for evaluation that reflects real deployments.

papers.title: Ensemble Methodology for Reference-Free Confidence Estimation in LLM-based Code Summarization
papers.abstract: This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics. We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions.
papers.summary: Engineers who use LLMs to summarize legacy COBOL code usually have no human-written reference summaries to check the output against. The authors estimate each summary's correctness from how much several different models agree on its meaning. An LLM-as-judge compares summaries in pairs and returns structured judgments, which they argue are more faithful than string- or embedding-based metrics. A calibrated aggregation rule then combines the supporting evidence and **penalizes only contradictions that more than one comparison confirms**, giving a confidence score that needs no reference.

papers.title: Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists
papers.abstract: In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI. Website: https://pranjal2041.github.io/cua-embodied
papers.summary: The authors argue that embodied AI tasks can be recast as ordinary software use. They build programs that render an agent's view of a physical environment on screen and expose controls for acting in it, so a computer-use agent (CUA) can work through screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions. They used a single CUA design and changed only the software around it, with no tuning for any specific competition. That setup **won first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions**. The authors conclude that skills learned on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, carry over to embodied tasks, and that embodied AI could converge on one general model.

papers.title: How far does a hash-only sender go? A pre-registered map of sender memory versus bits for short text messages
papers.abstract: Can a sender that only computes hashes, with a language model only at the receiver, transmit short human text more cheaply than a classical sender trained on the same domain? We answer with one pre-registered run on 1,000 English user utterances from Taskmaster-1. The primary endpoint is the cost per message to deliver 100% of the messages (hash bits, plus a 2-byte negative acknowledgement and the raw text when the first attempt fails), paired against an in-domain PPM order-1 sender. The hash-only sender delivered 857 of 1,000 messages on the first attempt and cost 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than PPM order 1 (95% bootstrap interval 10.9 to 26.3); by the pre-registered rule it spends more and is not equivalent within one byte. As secondary results we map measured sender memory against bits. The hash-only sender (8,190 B on a host build, keyed BLAKE2b tag included, as in every method) was the cheapest point in bits from 8,190 B up to, but excluding, PPM order 1 at 24,844 B, 45 to 46 bits below smaz2 and Unishox2; from PPM order 1 upwards, in-domain senders spend fewer bits, except order 2 pruned to 16 KiB. In airtime it loses to PPM order 1 on all five links priced, to Unishox2 on four, and to raw text with a tag on two, because each failure costs an acknowledgement frame and a fallback frame. A wider receiver search recovers half of the failures and makes the cost 7.7 bits lower than PPM order 1, at about three minutes of receiver time per failure, and still loses in airtime on four of five links. We report the measurement as a delimitation, with every deviation of the run.
papers.summary: A pre-registered experiment tests whether a sender that only computes hashes, with a language model only at the receiver, can transmit short human text more cheaply than a classical compressor trained on the same domain. On 1,000 English utterances from `Taskmaster-1`, the hash-only sender delivered 857 messages on the first try. However, it cost **192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than an in-domain `PPM` order-1 sender**, so it fails the pre-registered equivalence test. It is the cheapest option in bits only at small sender-memory budgets, below `PPM` order 1, where it beats `smaz2` and `Unishox2`. In airtime it loses on most of the radio links priced, because every failed first attempt costs an extra acknowledgement frame and a fallback frame.

papers.title: Flow-Guided Target-Space Alignment via Path Consistency
papers.abstract: Many multimodal alignment problems require mapping a source modality into a fixed space defined by a target modality, where the target space is not merely an intermediate embedding but is used directly for downstream analysis. In this setting, successful alignment should preserve both the global structure of the target distribution and the instance-level correspondence observed in paired source--target training data. Existing objectives typically address only part of this goal: contrastive losses encourage relative similarity, distribution-matching losses improve marginal agreement, and pointwise regression fits each source sample to its paired target without explicitly modeling target-space path geometry. We propose FlowAlign, a flow-guided target-space alignment method that repurposes conditional flow matching as a training-time alignment signal rather than an inference-time transport model. FlowAlign uses the learned flow field to guide the alignment of source-side representations with the fixed target space, encouraging them to preserve paired correspondence while remaining compatible with the global target-space structure. We further provide theoretical analysis showing how FlowAlign helps improve paired correspondence by controlling endpoint accuracy and capturing local target-space geometry. Experiments on synthetic data, paired single-cell multiome benchmarks, and image--text alignment demonstrate that FlowAlign improves instance level correspondence while preserving target-space structure across different modality settings.
papers.summary: Some multimodal tasks require mapping a source modality into a fixed target-modality space that is used directly for downstream analysis.
