A good mapping there has to keep both the global structure of the target space and the instance-level pairing from training data. `FlowAlign` repurposes conditional flow matching as a training-time alignment signal rather than as a transport model used at inference. The learned flow field guides source representations toward their paired targets while keeping them consistent with the overall target-space geometry. Theory and experiments on synthetic data, paired single-cell multiome benchmarks, and image-text alignment show that it **improves instance-level correspondence while preserving target-space structure**.

papers.title: Grasp-TAGS: Task-Aware Grasp Selection via Critic Distillation for Prehensile Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: https://rpm-lab-umn.github.io/Grasp-TAGS-web-page/
papers.summary: When a mobile manipulator rearranges large objects, different stable grasps can lead to very different downstream results, yet learning-based methods usually assume a fixed initial grasp. `Grasp-TAGS` trains a single `PPO` reinforcement learning policy across many initial grasp configurations. It then distills the policy's critic into a lightweight network that scores candidate grasps using only the grasp configuration and the goal. The highest-scoring grasp is chosen before the robot makes contact, which raises **average rearrangement success to 89.84% versus 79.87% for the best single-grasp policies** and lowers final orientation errors on every object tested.

papers.title: GRAC: Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning for Surgical Scene Description
papers.abstract:
Purpose: Surgical operative reports support procedural documentation, surgical training, performance assessment, and workflow review. However, extracting meaningful information often requires extensive manual review and clinical expertise. Automated surgical scene descriptions could reduce this burden by leveraging recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge.
  Methods: We propose GRAC (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning), a framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs capturing relationships among instruments, actions, and anatomical structures. Given an input scene graph, GRAC learns to retrieve relevant graph-caption pairs from training data. It compares instrument-tissue interactions between retrieved examples and the input scene, using comparison features to condition retrieved-caption representations during generation.
  Results: On the EndoVis-18 benchmark, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.88, compared with 4.23 for SGT and 3.36 for the strongest conventional Transformer baseline. Exact instrument-action-target triplet-set accuracy reached 52.6%, compared with 32.7% for SGT and 26.2% for the strongest conventional baseline. These results demonstrate improvements in language quality and factual agreement. On TORS, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.06, compared with 3.80 for the strongest baseline.
  Conclusion: GRAC demonstrates that combining structured surgical scene representations with retrieved examples improves surgical scene captioning and produces more contextually meaningful descriptions.
papers.summary: `GRAC` (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning) generates automated descriptions of surgical scenes to reduce manual review of operative recordings. Each scene is represented as a graph of instruments, actions, and anatomical structures. The model retrieves similar graph-caption pairs from training data and conditions generation on how the retrieved instrument-tissue interactions differ from the input scene. On `EndoVis-18` it reaches a `CIDEr-D` of 5.88 versus 4.23 for `SGT`, and **exact instrument-action-target triplet accuracy of 52.6% versus 32.7%**. It also leads on `TORS` with a `CIDEr-D` of 5.06.

papers.title: CodeQuant2: Enhanced Outlier Mitigation and Adaptive Clustering for Low-Precision LRMs
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve task performance by generating longer intermediate reasoning traces, but this substantially increases inference costs and makes low-precision quantization increasingly important. However, aggressively quantized models often perform poorly on reasoning tasks. We observe larger activation fluctuations during the first decoding steps of reasoning. Calibration that omits these early states may miss their activation fluctuations. To address these reasoning-specific quantization challenges, we propose \textbf{CodeQuant2}, a clustering-based LUT quantization framework for low-precision large reasoning models. CodeQuant2 mitigates activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, and adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of each layer. Guided by our observation of reasoning-time activation behavior, CodeQuant2 further improves calibration sample selection to better match actual decoding statistics. Combined with our customized LUT CUDA kernel, CodeQuant2 delivers substantial accuracy improvements on reasoning benchmarks while achieving up to $2.85\times$ speedup over BF16.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) produce long reasoning traces that make inference expensive, but aggressive quantization tends to hurt their reasoning accuracy. The authors find that activations fluctuate more during the first decoding steps, which standard calibration sets miss. `CodeQuant2` is a clustering-based lookup-table (LUT) quantization framework that tames activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, and sizes each layer's codebook to its quantization difficulty. It also picks calibration samples that match real decoding statistics, and with a custom LUT CUDA kernel it improves accuracy on reasoning benchmarks while running **up to 2.85x faster than BF16**.

papers.title: On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose \emph{Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO)}, which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.
papers.summary: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts language models to unlabeled data using majority-vote pseudo-labels whose reliability is poorly understood. The authors split the error of these labels into population-majority bias, which cannot be identified without outside supervision, and variation caused by drawing only a finite number of rollouts per prompt. They target the second with `PC-Dr.DPO` (Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust Direct Preference Optimization), which makes updates more conservative on prompts whose votes are unstable. A cache-based mechanism limits forgetting during online adaptation. Across six math and knowledge-intensive benchmarks and five model backbones, it **matches or beats the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings**.

papers.title: Graded convolutional networks: scale invariance without the scale and robustness to unknown blur
papers.abstract: The Gaussian jet of an image is a graded vector space: a dilation by $\lambda$ multiplies derivatives of order $k$ by $\lambda^{-k}$. Local graded convolutions are exactly homogeneous differential operators, and a local feature is dilation-invariant if and only if it factors through the scale-normalized jet or, without the scale, through the retraction onto the weighted sphere of the grading. Under unknown Gaussian blur the retraction changes only by a change of scale, whereas the scale-normalized jet acquires a grading factor that no radial normalization removes. At the zero jet the retraction separates image families that radial normalizations and continuous classifiers cannot. Networks built on the retraction are universal for invariant features. On MNIST such a network keeps 88.4% accuracy under a two-pixel blur, against 66.2% for the same network on scale-normalized derivatives; in Lindeberg's Gaussian derivative network the retraction raises accuracy at that blur from 91.5% to 95.1%.
papers.summary: The authors treat the Gaussian jet of an image, its stack of derivatives at a point, as a graded vector space. They prove that a local feature is invariant to dilation exactly when it depends only on the scale-normalized jet, or, without needing to know the scale, on a projection onto a weighted sphere defined by the grading. Under unknown Gaussian blur this projection changes only by a change of scale, whereas the scale-normalized jet picks up a distortion that normalization cannot remove. Networks built on the projection can represent any invariant feature. On `MNIST` with a two-pixel blur, such a network **keeps 88.4% accuracy versus 66.2% when using scale-normalized derivatives**, and the projection raises Lindeberg's Gaussian derivative network from 91.5% to 95.1%.

papers.title: FlowMoP: Stochastic Multi-Person Motion Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting the future motion of multiple people is inherently stochastic: the same observed history admits many plausible continuations depending on intent, coordination, and social context. Yet the dominant paradigm in multi-person 3D motion prediction remains deterministic, with existing methods producing a fixed number of outputs per agent. In contrast, we present a conditional flow matching framework that jointly generates diverse future motions for multiple agents, modeling both global trajectories and root-relative poses. A B-spline reparameterization compresses the generative state space while enforcing temporal smoothness, and a dual-stream transformer conditions each agent's predictions on observed neighbor motion for interaction-aware forecasting. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on CMU-Mocap (UMPM) and 3DPW, outperforming deterministic baselines on joint position error, pose error, and final displacement error despite producing a full predictive distribution. We additionally establish the first motion prediction baseline on WorldPose, a large-scale professional soccer dataset, where social conditioning demonstrably concentrates predictive uncertainty along interaction-constrained directions.
papers.summary: Most multi-person 3D motion prediction methods are deterministic, even though the same observed history can lead to many plausible futures. `FlowMoP` uses conditional flow matching to generate diverse future motions for several people jointly, covering both global trajectories and body poses relative to the root joint. A B-spline reparameterization shrinks the generative state space and keeps motion smooth, and a dual-stream transformer conditions each person's prediction on their neighbors' movement. It **achieves state-of-the-art results on `CMU-Mocap (UMPM)` and `3DPW`** while producing a full predictive distribution. It also sets the first baseline on the `WorldPose` professional soccer dataset.

papers.title: On the (non-)closedness of the set of ReLU networks
papers.abstract: We prove that the set $\mathcal{N}_N$ of ReLU networks with one hidden layer and at most $N\in\mathbb N$ neurons is weakly closed in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, for a bounded connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$. Consequently, every coercive, weakly lower semicontinuous energy on this space attains its minimum over $\mathcal{N}_N$. This covers the Deep Ritz method with convex integrands, Sobolev training and Lipschitz learning. Moreover, as the weight decay parameter tends to zero, minimizers of the regularized problem converge, up to subsequences, to minimizers with minimal parameter norm. We also prove that the set of ReLU networks with two hidden layers of bounded widths is not closed in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ or in $C(\overline\Omega)$. This disproves a conjecture of Petersen, Raslan and Voigtlaender.
papers.summary: The authors study whether sets of ReLU networks are closed in Sobolev spaces, which determines whether training objectives over those sets are guaranteed to have a minimizer. They prove that one-hidden-layer ReLU networks with at most N neurons form a weakly closed set in W^{1,p}. As a result, the `Deep Ritz` method with convex integrands, Sobolev training, and Lipschitz learning all attain their minima. Minimizers of the weight-decay-regularized problem also converge to minimum-norm minimizers as the decay parameter goes to zero. In contrast, **networks with two hidden layers of bounded width are not closed**, which disproves a conjecture of Petersen, Raslan and Voigtlaender.

papers.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
papers.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.
papers.summary: Language models re-solve similar problems from scratch every time, mixing up working out a solution with applying it. Agentic reasoning caching turns LLM reasoning traces into agentic reasoning caches (`ARCs`) that run on a CPU and apply a learned solution to new instances of a task with little help from a language model. The authors report that `ARCs` match frontier LLMs on a range of hard math and science tasks. They describe the caches as fully explainable, continually trainable, and robust to input perturbations, and **16 to 291 times cheaper to invoke than the source model**.

papers.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
papers.abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
papers.summary: In agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), a generalist AI model controls a robot arm directly and adjusts its actions as the task unfolds, instead of relying on specialist vision-language-action models (VLAs) or world-action models (WAMs) trained on demonstrations. The reference harness `AMP1` runs unchanged on single-arm, bimanual, and mobile robots, with no built-in grasping, pushing, or placing skills. Without demonstrations or task-specific training it **reaches 85.6% zero-shot success on `RoboLab-120` versus 49.2% and 42.9% for the leading VLA and WAM policies**. It also succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials. The agent devises its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects and using objects as tools, and a persistent memory carried across episodes cuts its failure rate on `RoboDojo` bimanual tasks by 4.6 times.
